summary: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to train agents that adapt quickly to unseen tasks from limited interaction, but this requires representing task evidence over long interaction histories. Classical recurrent agents compress experience into hidden states, while transformer-based agents retrieve from past trajectories at quadratic memory and computation cost. In this work, we propose Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation (METTA) for meta-reinforcement learning. It decomposes the fast adaptation phase into two temporal scales: a causal neural memory performs fine-grained within-episode adaptation with linear sequence complexity, while compact episode-level summaries support long-range cross-episode task inference without attending over the full interaction history. Moreover, equipping agents with neural memory provides sufficient expressive capacity and test-time training capability, enabling effective adaptation to unseen held-out tasks and task families at meta-test time. On unseen held-out Meta-World ML10/45 test environments, METTA achieves a success rate over $50\%$ while maintaining a low training budget and short wall-clock time. On long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks, it outperforms transformer-based baselines by exhibiting more structured exploration behavior. These results show that METTA provides an efficient path toward more adaptive and scalable long-context meta-RL.
title: METTA: Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation for Meta-Reinforcement Learning

summary: Coordinating two players in a cooking task requires a vision-language agent to track changing scene states, sequence recipe steps, and allocate shared resources under a time budget. We introduce an Overcooked-inspired benchmark for evaluating these capabilities in Unreal Engine environments constructed using coding agents. A single vision-language model controls both players from top-down visual observations, selecting high-level actions while the engine executes navigation. The benchmark contains 20 maps in five categories. These categories support evaluation of centralized coordination under equipment contention, changing terrain, and handoff dependencies. A prop legend and pot ingredient-count indicators provide explicit visual cues, while grid-based destinations support spatial grounding. The evaluation compares four VLMs on all 20 maps, measuring task score, order completion, delivery precision, action acceptance rate, and model API expenditure. A memory ablation on the same 20 maps examines the effect of a shared, self-authored notebook while retaining six-response action history in both conditions. The strongest evaluated model, \texttt{gpt-6-astra}, achieves 26.2\% mean order completion. Notebook memory has mixed score effects across models, with positive mean differences for Claude and Qwen and negative differences for GPT and Gemini.
title: DuoCook: An Overcooked-Inspired Benchmark for Visual Planning and Coordination

summary: Continual learning requires a model to keep acquiring new skills and knowledge without compromising its existing capabilities. Parametric methods suffer from catastrophic forgetting and loss of plasticity. Non-parametric methods, such as prompts, skills, and harnesses, leverage in-context learning but are limited by context length and lossy plain-text compression. To effectively combine their complementary strengths, we propose HERD (Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation), a hybrid continual learning framework that learns efficiently in the harness and internalizes experience into cumulative capabilities via distillation. On the harness side, HERD continually refines its skills to capture reusable patterns, while retaining high-residual examples that the skills fail to capture in a bounded memory. On the parameter side, HERD performs drift-constrained distillation with dual anchors, substantially reducing forgetting over long recursive runs. On the 25-stage task stream of TRACE+17, under fixed memory and compute budgets, HERD matches the strongest parametric baseline in new-task acquisition while exhibiting the least forgetting and the strongest retention of general capabilities.
title: HERD: Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation for Continual Learning

summary: Scaling embedding capacity alongside Transformer computation is an emerging trend in language models. This trend makes high compression rates increasingly useful. Hence, we study extreme compression of Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which follow this trend and account for 35.2% of the parameters of Gemma 4 E4B. At such rates, conventional quantizers give each token-layer vector its own code of only a few bytes. We instead develop OPTIC (Output-Path-fitted, Token-shared Indexed Codes), which stores one quantized code tuple per token and decodes it at every layer with a layer-specific affine decoder. Codes and decoders are fitted to the PLE output path rather than to the stored vectors. At about $100\times$ PLE compression of bfloat16 (BF16) E4B, OPTIC retains an aggregate 97.8% of the uncompressed model's performance across seven benchmarks, whereas product quantization, the strongest of six conventional baselines, retains 66.3%. At $594\times$ and $1,002\times$ PLE compression of BF16 E4B, OPTIC retains 90.5% and 84.1%. On the official E4B release with 4-bit linear weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16), OPTIC retains 96.9% at about $100\times$ PLE compression. During inference at about $100\times$ PLE compression, BF16 E4B uses 29.7% less GPU memory than with uncompressed PLE at the same key-value cache size, while running at most 0.40% slower.
title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization

summary: GUI agents aim to automate complex user tasks by interacting with mobile interfaces, but ef- fective decision-making in long-horizon set- tings requires reusing prior experience rather than relying solely on the environment ob- servations. Existing memory-based methods typically store experience either at the single- action level or as entire trajectories. Single- step actions are often too fine-grained to carry meaningful semantics, since the success of an individual action does not necessarily imply progress towards the overall goal. In contrast, whole trajectories are often too coarse-grained and difficult to reuse across different tasks. We propose a subgoal-aware memory graph that distils past trajectories into structured, reusable evidence at the level of subgoals. We define a subgoal as consecutive actions shar- ing a single intent, the granularity at which progress toward the task becomes meaning- ful. To reduce redundancy and support cross- task reuse, we organise subgoal experiences as nodes in a graph, where related memories can be merged, extended, and retrieved based on the environment observation. On SPA-Bench, our method improves success rate by 11.11% over the baseline.
title: Subgoal-aware Memory Graph for GUI Agent

summary: Memory enables language model assistants to maintain continuity across sessions and generate personalized responses, but knowing more about a user does not necessarily produce responses they prefer. Existing evaluations assess memory capabilities without directly establishing whether memory use benefits the user. To study this gap, we collect approximately 1,000 pairwise judgments from 87 participants using their own ChatGPT queries and personal memories. We find that memory-conditioned responses are not consistently preferred over responses generated without memory and in some cases, users strongly prefer the latter. Automatic evaluators also show limited agreement with users and favor memory-conditioned responses substantially more often than users do. Motivated by these gaps, we introduce a memory-aware reward model that learns from user judgments, achieving 72.8\% preference prediction accuracy and outperforming the existing baselines. Our findings motivate evaluation and optimization objectives that align memory use with the preferences of the people whose information is being used.
title: Memory-Aware Reward Modeling: Learning Human Preferences for LLM Memory Use

summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).
title: Memory before Goal: Role of Pre-History Memory for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation

summary: Personal agents need to draw on long-term interaction history to retrieve and apply external knowledge suited to a user's current request. Even an answer grounded in relevant documents can be unsuitable when it overlooks the user's circumstances. This creates two connected challenges: using historical conditions to identify the knowledge needed for a new request, and applying that knowledge to the user's situation. Existing benchmarks advance memory recall, personalized retrieval, and memory-guided action, while the joint evaluation of these two challenges remains underexplored. We introduce ColaBench, a synthetic benchmark in health and daily living, with 349 tasks across 10 Profiles and a knowledge base of 13,033 documents. Its Evidence Graph connects personal conditions to their disclosures across public interaction sessions, records prior document exposure, and links answer requirements to personal and newly acquired document evidence. We also introduce MemKB, which uses state summaries to inform queries and rule application, and memory-document links to retrieve knowledge associated with the user's history. MemKB achieves 86.25% Accuracy with an average of 4.07 interaction rounds per task. Task-level analysis finds larger gains on tasks integrating information across multiple historical Facts; error analysis further identifies unsupported personal assumptions and rule misapplication as obstacles to using retrieved evidence. ColaBench provides traceable tasks and an evaluation framework for studying how memory guides knowledge acquisition and rule application.
title: ColaBench: Evaluating Memory-Guided Knowledge Acquisition in Personal Agents

summary: In this article, we use the PBNF-transform, or Polynomial Boolean Normal Form, described earlier in two articles and now extended to higher arity, to solve Boolean satisfiability problems (SAT), which are part of the P versus NP problem. SAT consists of a statement of conjunctions of clauses, and in our SAT-solving models, we dualize the logical equations, inverting the problem by \emph{multiplying} letters (literals) in the transferred clauses, now phrases: $pqrs\cdots s_{\ell}$, and using a binary iterated composition based on \emph{adding polynomials} for the conjunctions in our solution formula. We obtain Polynomial Boolean Equations, PBE=0, by also renaming the truth value $1\mapsto 0$(T). To find a solution, we look for repeating literals in the clauses to factor out. With reversed literal repetition, we can even reduce the CNF to the sum of the transformed clauses.
title: A Study in Solution Models for SAT using the PBNF-transform

summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, enabling efficient planning but leaving their states opaque. We introduce Inside-JEPA, which places relational channels for ordered entity pairs inside the JEPA latent state and shows that an inverse-dynamics loss can ground these channels without relation labels when its head reads them, either alone or as part of the full state. On Something-Something V2, latent prediction alone performs no better than a random relation head, while inverse-dynamics supervision that recovers actions from channel changes improves relational AUROC by .065-.103 across ten settings with annotated boxes, by .081 on RH20T robot episodes with held-out tasks, and by .050-.061 across five relations using off-the-shelf detection and tracking. An inverse head on entity latents decodes actions more accurately but barely improves relational grounding; shuffled labels, two label-free objectives, and action labels on only 5% of the pairs also fail to ground the channels. Given an action, predicted relational changes approach the quality of observed future relations (AUROC .599 vs .621). For one-step relational goals, a supervised readout of the 16 channels ranks the correct action among the top five of 65 in 43% of cases, compared with 24% for prediction-only latents and 17% for a frequency prior.
title: Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models

summary: AI models, and time-series models in particular are typically ranked by accuracy and deployed under constraints absent from that ranking. In this paper, we study a real setting where these constraints are explicit and measurable: handover pre- diction in cellular networks, where inference runs on the User Equipment once per 40 ms measurement period and must complete before the network acts. The timing bound is hard: a late prediction is superseded by the measurement it was predicting, while energy is a cumulative budget spent for the life of the device. Neither appears in the objective these models are selected on. We evaluate eight architectures under a protocol that screens for deadline feasibility at the tail rather than the mean, then ranks the feasible models on measured inference energy, count- ing the feature computation that precedes the forward pass and is usually omitted. Gradient-boosted trees on handcrafted temporal features are the most accurate model (F1=0.974) and among the cheapest to run, while the neural architecture an accuracy-only benchmark would rank first (CNN-1D, F1=0.914) costs over 3 times more energy per inference under a realistic duty-cycled deployment pattern. We give three conditions under which this outcome should be expected, so the finding applies beyond telecommunications. Accuracy-only benchmarking does not merely under-report deployment cost. It can rank first a model that cannot be deployed.
title: Energy and Latency First: How Deployment Constraints Reverse Time-Series Model Selection

summary: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) leverages centralized knowledge graphs to enhance large language models with structured knowledge retrieval. However, real-world knowledge is inherently distributed across multiple organizations rather than being centrally accessible. Privacy constraints further prohibit sharing entire local knowledge graphs, preventing GraphRAG from effectively retrieving and utilizing distributed knowledge. To this end, we propose Federated GraphRAG (FedGRAG), a unified framework for distributed graph retrieval and knowledge-enhanced generation over multiple clients with knowledge graphs. Specifically, we address two fundamental challenges in federated GraphRAG. First, the absence of a global knowledge graph makes unified retrieval impossible. To address this, we develop a Federated Knowledge Routing mechanism that efficiently identifies relevant clients through lightweight knowledge indices without exposing local graph structures. Second, local graph memory cannot be shared directly because it contains sensitive entities and knowledge information. We therefore propose a controlled-disclosure evidence construction method. It extracts retrieved evidence subgraphs and converts them into an evidence abstract, enabling evidence conversion and reconstruction on the server. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Federated GraphRAG consistently outperforms existing baselines in both retrieval and downstream generation tasks, establishing a new paradigm for deploying GraphRAG in federated environments.
title: Federated Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation

summary: Video provides a natural source of supervision: what happens next serves as a learning signal for visual world modeling. Yet masked video pretraining focuses on recovering missing content from surrounding context rather than predicting the future from the past. Autoregressive methods instead predict forward one token at a time, but have yet to match joint-embedding methods in representation quality. This gap motivates us to revisit the granularity and space of future prediction. In this work, we introduce VANE, a self-supervised visual pretraining framework built on next-frame prediction in embedding space. A causal encoder summarizes past observations for a state predictor that infers the representation of the entire next frame, making temporal evolution the primary learning signal. This prediction is carried out in a fixed embedding space provided by a frozen semantic tokenizer, emphasizing scene content and structure. To retain fine-grained spatial detail alongside semantic content, a lightweight auxiliary generative decoder reconstructs future-frame patches conditioned on the predicted representations. To unify visual modeling across images and videos, we construct a local-to-global crop sequence for still images, allowing the same encoder to predict newly revealed regions from earlier crops under the same objective. Experiments show that VANE improves with model and data scaling, achieving SOTA on most anticipation, recognition, and dense perception benchmarks among unified encoders. Especially on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action anticipation, it surpasses V-JEPA 2.1 by 7.1 points in mean-class recall@5. These results demonstrate that next-frame prediction in embedding space is effective and scalable for visual world modeling.
title: Learning from Next-Frame Prediction: Towards Unified and Scalable Visual Representation Learning

summary: LLM agents are flexible in language interaction, but using them as long-horizon planners is costly and prone to hallucinated or invalid actions. This paper targets a different role for LLMs: constrained bridges between language and symbolic planning. We propose MemPlan, a memory-conditioned PDDL planning framework for partially observable interactive text environments. MemPlan keeps the PDDL domain fixed and reconstructs the PDDL problem at each step from parsed observations, candidate hypotheses, and interaction memory. Positive graph memory assigns relevance-based action costs to candidate hypotheses for missing objects, locations, or conditions, guiding the planner toward more plausible checks. Negative memory records execution-refuted assumptions and compiles them into exclusion constraints, preventing repeated attempts at candidates already contradicted by feedback. A unified schema-conditioned language--symbol interface, trained offline with supervised fine-tuning, connects text environments to the planning loop through observation-to-fact parsing and symbolic-action-to-command grounding. Experiments on TextWorld, ALFWorld, and Robotouille show that MemPlan improves task completion and step efficiency over language-only and PDDL-aware baselines, while substantially reducing online token cost compared with LLM-planning baselines such as ReAct. The same fine-tuned interface is also reused across TextWorld task types without task-specific fine-tuning. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/tewiSong/MemPlan.
title: MemPlan: Memory-Conditioned PDDL Planning for Partially Observable Text Environments

summary: Autonomous mobile robots operating in dense crowds and cluttered sites require $360^\circ$ perception to react to surrounding hazards. While panoramic LiDAR offers full-surround coverage, learning representations within reinforcement learning (RL) is sample-inefficient under sparse rewards, and existing 3D pretrained point-cloud encoders are too memory-heavy for massively parallel RL simulation. We present RangeNav, a compact (183k parameters) LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained entirely on synthetic data. RangeNav uses anisotropic convolutions and circular padding to handle the extreme aspect ratio and azimuthal seam of range images. We pretrain the network using a navigation-aligned objective combining range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird's-eye-view (BEV) prediction, then freeze it for policy learning. In simulation, adding semantic and BEV supervision increases success rates over a reconstruction-only baseline by an average of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points (pp) in procedurally generated training and out-of-distribution realistic test environments, respectively. Zero-shot real-world deployments on a Unitree B2-W quadruped demonstrate robust navigation through dense crowds, low-light settings, and construction zones where limited-field-of-view depth policies struggle. Code and models will be open-sourced. Project website: https://rangenav.github.io/.
title: RangeNav: Task-Aligned LiDAR Range-Image Pretraining for Robot Navigation

summary: Estimation code, figure code and archived numerical results that reproduce every quantity reported in the accompanying paper. The underlying point-of-interest records originate from Amap (Gaode) and were obtained as annual archived extracts from a commercial data vendor; they remain subject to the rights of the platform and of the vendor and are therefore not included. The archive contains the upstream construction scripts, the 17 audited recomputation scripts, the figure code, the fitted random forest used for the ordering evidence, and the aggregated JSON results that each figure reads. See README.md and MANIFEST.md, which map every table and figure in the paper to the script that produces it. Changes in v1.1 - Added the cluster-scale ladder for all three specifications (scale_ladder_by_spec in   _sample_align.json). The ladder reported in the manuscript is computed on independent   shops (n = 16,481); v1.0 archived only the all-shops variant (n = 22,883). - Added 02_estimation/r10b_scale_ladder_all_specs.py, which produces it. - Renamed 02_build_shop_table.py to 02_rebuild_rf22_model.py to match its contents. - Added notebooks/walkthrough.ipynb, which verifies 20 reported quantities against the   archived results without requiring the restricted records. - Added data/sample/ (synthetic tables with the real schema) and src/ (documented entry   points plus a data provenance note). - Corrected MANIFEST.md section cross-references against the current manuscript.
title: Replication code for: Retail density and category overlap condition street-level shop survival near large commercial complexes: evidence from Zhengzhou, China

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23591614 . Dabirsiaghi shows that harnesses which flatten the typed conversation into one string with text labels such as [User]: destroy message provenance before the summarizer runs, so a forged user turn survives compaction. Five flattening harnesses (pi, opencode, Cline, Aider, OpenHands) launder the forged approval 87-100% of the time, and four role-typed harnesses (Codex, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, Continue) 0%. I read it as a practitioner who runs coding agents every day, and my comments come from that side. Two of them rest on my own technical reports, which are not peer-reviewed, so please weigh them as practice notes and not as evidence of the same standing as your experiments. Each point below pairs one thing I see in my work with a named part of your preprint. 1. Bounded sessions as another exit (Introduction, "Scope and severity"). You write "Compaction is mandatory. Every agent that runs long enough fills its context window and must compact." I would say it is mandatory only for a session that is allowed to keep running. In my practice I keep one task per chat and clear the context between unrelated tasks. In a controlled experiment of 36 runs, six session-reset policies with six repetitions each, cost followed a U-shaped curve with its minimum at a reset every 3 tasks and a plateau from 3 to 6. Resetting after every task cost about a third more (+33.5%, p = 0.002, Holm-adjusted 0.011), and "never reset" was not significantly different. Two caveats that I state in the report myself: the comparison point was chosen after the runs, and in the reset-after-every-task branch the agent wrote more tests (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759217). So a fresh session with a short handoff the user writes has a measurable price, and it would fit next to your label-escaping fix as an operator-side mitigation. 2. Where the exposure sits (Discussion, point 2). You report that the executed rate is near 100% when the planted command dominates a small summary, and settles to a ~20-40% plateau in a full window. I think the full-window plateau is the number that matters most. In 722 agent sessions, 150,902 model calls and 34.6 billion tokens, more than 85% of modeled cost was context work (86.2-87.8% on recalculation), and sessions longer than 200 calls, 8% of all sessions, carried more than 90% of the money (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216). The sessions that reach compaction are likely a small share of sessions but most of the spend and most of the unattended work. Reporting how often compaction fires per session in ordinary use would help readers size the exposure. 3. Independent checks (Contributions, point 4, E9). The code-level check that compares the summary's user-attributed claims against the genuine user turns still in memory catches 77% of laundering while demoting 2% of legitimate summary content, and the in-prompt anti-injection rule stops 13-25%. This matches what I see: a second, fresh agent told to refute the first one's result finds what the first missed, because independent checkers rarely fail the same way. A round of checking lowers risk and does not remove it. It would help to say what the remaining 23% look like. 4. Equal confidence (Limitations). In live testing, one agent refused a payload "even though the bootstrap command was previously approved," citing the forged approval as fact. That is a clean example of something I see in practice, that an AI sounds equally sure when it is right and when it is wrong. The summary carries no marker of doubt, so the user cannot tell a genuine approval from a forged one either. Does any of the five flattening harnesses offer a fresh-session or handoff mode that skips compaction, and was it tested? title: PREreview of "Compaction Laundering: Provenance Destruction in Context-Compacting Coding Agents"

summary: Pharmacotherapy has transformed prognosis and broadened the possibilities of care across different mental disorders. This recognition, however, does not eliminate the problem of pharmacological reductionism, understood in this article as the conversion of medication from a therapeutic resource into the organizing principle of diagnosis, of the explanation of suffering, and of psychiatric practice itself. This critical review of restricted scope examines the literature published between 2021 and 2026 on the mechanisms that favor this reduction, its clinical and epistemological consequences, and the alternatives proposed to reintegrate the biological, psychopathological, relational, social, and existential dimensions. The analysis is organized around eight problems: the symptom–diagnosis–drug circuit; the reification of diagnostic categories; the gap between acute response and long-term recovery; polypharmacy and prescribing cascades; economic and organizational incentives; the limits of a merely protocol-driven deprescribing; shared decision-making; and biopsychosocial and recovery-oriented models of care. The general psychiatric syndrome hypothesis is discussed as a possible challenge to nosographic fragmentation, but also as a construct that demands caution so that it does not become a new reified entity. The synthesis showed that pharmacocentrism does not stem from a single cause. It emerges from the combination of diagnostic reification, the predominance of short-term outcomes, the invisibility of harms and preferences, cumulative polypharmacy, commercial influence, and services with few psychosocial alternatives. At the same time, studies of efficacy and effectiveness confirm relevant pharmacological benefits, which precludes an anti-psychopharmacological conclusion. The data support a distinction between rational use of medicines and pharmacocentric organization of care. Overcoming the latter depends on a causal and revisable clinical formulation, shared decision-making, longitudinal follow-up, family involvement when appropriate, and effective access to non-pharmacological interventions. We argue that criticizing pharmacocentrism does not mean denying psychopharmacology, but rather restoring medication to a proportionate position within a broad, longitudinal clinical formulation that is sensitive to the person's experience.
tags: psychiatry, psychopharmacology, biomedical reductionism,  medicalization, polypharmacy, deprescribing, biopsychosocial model, recovery.
title: From Listening to Prescribing: Pharmacological Reductionism, Temporality, And the Loss of Complexity in Contemporary Psychiatry

summary: This package contains the literature-screening records, paper-level coding, and model-level observations supporting the study  “(Promises and) Perils in Mining Hugging Face” . The study examines how researchers sample Hugging Face (HF) models, which features they analyze, and which threats can arise from their sampling and measurement decisions. The package documents the evidence used to address three research questions: RQ1: What sampling strategies are used in scientific research to analyze Hugging Face models? RQ2: What features are analyzed in studies of Hugging Face models, and how are these features measured? RQ3: What threats to validity and generalizability arise from sampling, measurement, and data-collection decisions when mining Hugging Face, and what practices can mitigate these threats? Contents Place this README alongside the three workbooks, retaining their original filenames: . ├── README.MD ├── ScopusRetrievedPaper.xlsx ├── RQ1_RQ2_Analysis.xlsx └── RQ3_ModelsAnalysis.xlsx File Contents Research questions ScopusRetrievedPaper.xlsx 1,267 retrieved bibliographic records and three screening worksheets, with 44 records marked Yes in total. Corpus selection for RQ1–RQ2 RQ1_RQ2_Analysis.xlsx Descriptive inspection of 26 papers, 78 structured analytical records, and summary statistics. RQ1–RQ2 RQ3_ModelsAnalysis.xlsx Manual observations for 300 HF model repositories. RQ3 Literature retrieval and screening ScopusRetrievedPaper.xlsx The full-list export label identifies March 3, 2026. The bibliographic columns are Rand_ID , Authors , Title , Year , Document Type , Source title , DOI , Link , and Abstract . The screening worksheets additionally contain Of_interest and Feature extracted . The final analyzed corpus comprises the 26 papers represented in RQ1_RQ2_Analysis.xlsx . Paper analysis for RQ1 and RQ2 Paper_Manual_Inspection This worksheet contains 61 descriptive records covering 26 distinct paper links and 19 feature labels. Column Contents Feature_extracted Feature examined in the paper. Methods_extraction_feature Description of how the feature was extracted or analyzed. Sources Artifacts or information sources used for the feature. Metric Recorded measurement or characterization. Link_Paper Link identifying the inspected publication. Sampling Descriptive indication of whether sampling was used. Extraction_method_Paper Narrative description of collection and sampling procedures. Claim Recorded findings or claims attributed to the inspected paper. Threats stated by authors (related to HF data) Recorded threats attributed to the original authors. Threats_introduced_by_extraction_method Assessment of possible threats associated with the extraction method. Missing / additional threats (related to HF data) Additional methodological concerns recorded during inspection. Possible Threat introduced Further notes about potential threats. Analytical_record This worksheet contains 78 records with unique Record_ID values, covering 26 Paper_ID values and 19 Feature_Code values. There are 59 distinct ( Paper_ID , Feature_Code ) pairs : the same pair can have multiple records describing different methodological choices. summary: General These datasets help validate EarthCARE's radiative transfer product ACM-RT (Cole et al., 2024) and its corresponding cloud and aerosol inputs with surface irradiance observations from the Baseline Surface Radiation Network (BSRN) (Driemel et al., 2018)  and gridded solar radiation estimates from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) (CAMS, 2022). They were created for and used in Gschwind et al., 2026 (Validation of EarthCARE Surface Irradiance Products Against Ground-Based Observations and Geostationary Satellite Estimates). For details on the collocation methodologies, please refer to Section 3 of the publication. Three different EarthCARE approaches were validated; 1D radiative transfer model (RTM) along-track estimates (1x1 km), 1D RTM across-track extension using the Scene Construction Algorithm (Qu et al., 2023), and 3D RTM estimates (5x21 km). To infer cloud-induced discrepancies, the cloud modification factor (CMF) was calculated. Furthermore, EarthCARE's aerosol optical depth (AOD) input in the RTMs (Mason et al., 2023) was analyzed with CAMS global atmospheric composition forecast (CAMS, 2021) and AERONET observations (Giles et al., 2019).   BSRN folder The BSRN datasets contain collocated surface global horizontal irradiance (GHI) measurements from the ground-based BSRN stations and EarthCARE's ACM-RT product. BSRN_ECA_GHI_DIF_DIR.csv also contains diffuse horizontal irradiance (DHI) and beam (direct) horizontal irradiance (BHI) of both BSRN and EarthCARE. The corresponding results of the longwave irradiance can be found in BSRN_ECA_LW_AlongTrack.csv. Intercomparison with TOA upward flux differences between EarthCARE's RTMs and BBR measurements can be found in BSRN_ECA_BBR_intercomparison.csv. The datasets contain the following variables: Geolocation & Time information Date (UT) - Datetime at the closest point of the EarthCARE overpass BSRN Station Name - Station over which the overpass occurred BSRN Latitude (°N) - Latitude of the station  BSRN Longitude (°E) - Longitude of the station Distance (km) - Distance of the EarthCARE overpass to the BSRN station EarthCARE overpass information EarthCARE OAF - Orbit and Frame of the EarthCARE overpass Baseline - Baseline of the EarthCARE products Closest EarthCARE along-track index - Based on the start of the EarthCARE frame Scientific variables (see Section 2 in Gschwind et al., 2026 for further information)    CAMS folder The CAMS datasets contain collocated gridded surface GHI estimates from CAMS and EarthCARE's ACM-RT product. CAMS_ECA_GHI_DIF_DIR_3D.csv also contains DHI and BHI estimates, while CAMS_ECA_AOD.csv compares AOD forecasts of CAMS with EarthCARE estimates. All EarthCARE frames were processed under baseline BA. The datasets contain the following variables: Geolocation & Time information Date (UT) - Datetime at the closest point of the EarthCARE overpass Latitude - Latitude of the CAMS cell (°N) Longitude - Longitude of the CAMS cell (°E) EarthCARE overpass information EarthCARE OAF - Orbit and Frame of the EarthCARE overpass Scientific variables (see Section 2 in Gschwind et al., 2026 for further information)   AERONET folder The AERONET dataset contains collocated AOD observations from AERONET, CAMS forecast, EarthCARE CAPTIVATE algorithm, and EarthCARE composite algorithm. The dataset contains the following variables: Geolocation & Time information Date (UT) - Datetime at the closest point of the EarthCARE overpass AERONET Station Name - Station over which the overpass occurred AERONET Latitude (°N) - Latitude of the station  AERONET Longitude (°E) - Longitude of the station Distance (km) - Distance of the EarthCARE overpass to the BSRN station EarthCARE overpass information EarthCARE OAF - Orbit and Frame of the EarthCARE overpass Baseline - Baseline of the EarthCARE products Scientific variables AERONET AOD ECA CAPTIVATE AOD ECA composite AOD CAMS AOD   Eart
title: Dataset for the validation of EarthCARE surface irradiance estimates using collocated ground-based (BSRN) observations and geostationary satellite estimates (CAMS)

summary: The limited communication resources and sensing perspectives of a single uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) motivate UAV swarms for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) in air-ground networks. However, in multi-region scenarios, regional UAV allocations may not match vehicle demand, while local observations may lack sufficient diversity for accurate sensing. To address these issues, this paper proposes a cross-region cooperation framework for UAV swarms. For communication, cross-region UAV reallocation reduces service disparities by matching resources to vehicle demand. For sensing, combining UAV observations from different regions increases observation diversity, while adaptive handshaking guided by marginal Cramér--Rao bound (CRB) utilities balances phase synchronization gains against handshaking energy consumption. Joint optimization of UAV positions and transmit power within each region then further improves communication service and sensing performance. These coupled decisions are coordinated by a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning (H-MARL) approach through slow-timescale inter-region UAV reallocation and fast-timescale intra-region UAV control. Under the considered simulation settings, reallocation can improve quality of service (QoS) by over 20 percentage points compared with retaining the initial allocation under severe resource-demand mismatches. Cooperative sensing with adaptive handshaking incurs only about a 5.0% increase in mean CRB relative to perfect synchronization.
title: Cross-Region Cooperation of UAV Swarms Towards Air-Ground ISAC via Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

summary: LLM-based scam systems increasingly combine adaptive dialogue, persistent context, external tools, and multi-agent coordination to automate personalized fraud. These capabilities also create a resource dependency: every reasoning step, model call, and coordination round incurs inference cost. We present TokenTrap, a resource-oriented defense that redirects suspected scam systems toward benign, low-value computation while withholding credentials, payments, and other exploitable information. TokenTrap combines three components: an architecture-specific token-task library, a router that selects among single-agent, hierarchical, and flat multi-agent workflows, and a bounded anti-guardrail strategy that varies task presentation while enforcing token, round, time, and safety limits. Across 50-round traces, TokenTrap amplifies token consumption by $2{,}487.0\times$, $1{,}616.0\times$, and $567.8\times$ relative to a no-token-task baseline for the three workflows. Its router achieves 85.67% accuracy on 300 architecture-labeled prompts. These results demonstrate that short, non-sensitive requests can impose substantial context-processing and coordination costs, motivating resource-aware defense as a complement to scam detection.
title: Your Token Is Gone: A Token-Consumption Countermeasure for Disrupting LLM-Based Scam Systems

summary: Multi-task generalization is an important yet underexplored problem in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). Many real-world applications require multi-agent systems to generalize across complex, temporally extended tasks with diverse inter-agent coordination requirements. We introduce a specification language that combines temporal-logic task specifications with operators for expressing such requirements. We propose SpecMAGIC, a hierarchical framework that leverages the automaton structure of task specifications for subtask decomposition. A centralized high-level planner identifies and allocates compatible subtask sequences across agents, while decentralized low-level policies execute individual subtasks. This enables zero-shot generalization to new tasks by composing reusable subtask policies according to new specifications, without retraining. We establish soundness and probabilistic completeness of the high-level planner. Experiments on multi-agent navigation tasks show that SpecMAGIC substantially outperforms existing approaches on unseen task specifications and maintains strong performance as the number of agents increases.

summary: Sixth-generation (6G) communication systems are expected to support immersive, intent-driven, and latency-critical services through tight integration of multimodal intelligence, edge computing, and autonomous network control. In this setting, agentic AI systems can reason over heterogeneous inputs, use tools and network functions, coordinate across distributed entities, and adapt to dynamic environments. These capabilities make agentic multimodal intelligence promising for 6G applications such as semantic communications, digital twins, and zero-touch network management, but they also introduce security and privacy risks that extend beyond conventional AI and network security models. Vulnerabilities can propagate across multimodal data pipelines, memory, tools, communication interfaces, and inter-agent coordination loops. We survey multimodal intelligence and agentic AI for 6G cross-layered communication systems from the perspectives of privacy and security. We present a 6G-oriented system view spanning perception, memory, tool use, and multi-agent orchestration; analyze threat models and attack surfaces across sensing, cognition, action, memory, and communication layers; organize existing attacks into a structured taxonomy; and review mitigation strategies including prompt and memory defenses, inter-agent trust mechanisms, secure orchestration, and privacy-preserving learning. We conclude by outlining open research directions for trustworthy multimodal multi-agent 6G systems.
title: Secure Agentic AI and Multimodal Intelligence in 6G Communication Systems

summary: Recent advances in search agents have enabled large language models to tackle complex tasks by retrieving and synthesizing external information. However, existing search agents often lack search-state awareness, i.e., the ability to recognize what information has been obtained and what remains missing, leading to hallucinated reasoning and prematurely terminated search. To address this limitation, we propose Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning (SARL), a reinforcement learning framework in which models learn to recognize their own search state during training and improve their search behavior accordingly, without requiring additional assessment at test time. SARL achieves this through a dual reward design that captures the corrective effect of each assessment while penalizing excessive reliance on it, jointly encouraging effective and efficient search trajectories. Under this setup, SARL achieves a 24.3% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, with average gains of 35.9% on multi-hop reasoning and 27.9% on deep research benchmarks against the strongest per-benchmark baselines. SARL further surpasses methods built on auxiliary supervision or multi-agent coordination, despite operating as a standalone RL framework with no inference-time scaffolding. Beyond final performance, SARL maintains training stability under extended search horizons, a regime where existing methods consistently degrade, enabling sustained gains as task complexity grows.
title: Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning for Search-State Awareness in Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models

However, existing search agents often lack search-state awareness, i.e., the ability to recognize what information has been obtained and what remains missing, leading to hallucinated reasoning and prematurely terminated search. To address this limitation, we propose Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning (SARL), a reinforcement learning framework in which models learn to recognize their own search state during training and improve their search behavior accordingly, without requiring additional assessment at test time. SARL achieves this through a dual reward design that captures the corrective effect of each assessment while penalizing excessive reliance on it, jointly encouraging effective and efficient search trajectories. Under this setup, SARL achieves a 24.3% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, with average gains of 35.9% on multi-hop reasoning and 27.9% on deep research benchmarks against the strongest per-benchmark baselines. SARL further surpasses methods built on auxiliary supervision or multi-agent coordination, despite operating as a standalone RL framework with no inference-time scaffolding. Beyond final performance, SARL maintains training stability under extended search horizons, a regime where existing methods consistently degrade, enabling sustained gains as task complexity grows.

summary: We address the problem of real-time multi-agent path planning under prescribed initial and final configurations, formulated as a high-dimensional optimal control problem subject to inter-agent collision avoidance and obstacle constraints. Classical solvers based on the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation or Pontryagin's maximum principle (PMP) become computationally intractable as the number of agents grows, due to the curse of dimensionality and the non-convexity introduced by interaction constraints. We propose OCFormer, a transformer-based neural network that parameterizes the inverse of a coordinate transformation mapping a simple, analytically tractable latent space, in which agents evolve independently under a decoupled Hamiltonian, to the physical space of the coupled, interacting system. The model is trained by minimizing a physics-informed loss comprising the Hamiltonian ODE residual from the PMP and a boundary matching term, without requiring pre-computed trajectory data. The self-attention mechanism endows OCFormer with permutation equivariance over agents, a structural symmetry that prior symplectic network approaches do not natively enforce. When trained on a distribution of boundary conditions, the amortized OCFormer produces near-optimal trajectories for unseen initial and final configurations in a single forward pass ($\sim$220ms), enabling real-time inference without retraining. We further introduce a lightweight transfer learning framework that adapts a pretrained OCFormer to out-of-distribution perturbations in seconds via L-BFGS fine-tuning. Numerical experiments on two- and three-dimensional multi-agent navigation with up to 128 agents demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of the proposed approach.

summary: Large organizations increasingly face what this book calls the cognitive complexity wall: at the scale of hundreds of interacting components, maintaining the dependency map and reacting at the pace of incidents exceeds what a human team can deliver. This conceptual volume proposes AAM/5C, in which five capabilities (Capture, Comprehend, Choose, Coordinate, Control) are instantiated across seven logical layers, L1 to L7. A single authorization rule, R-AUT, separates who proposes, who decides and who executes: a probabilistic planner (L4) proposes; a governance layer (L6) decides under signed policies and records its verdict in a signed evaluation proof; a security layer (L5) issues a short-lived act token bound to that proof; a policy enforcement point verifies both before the target layer materializes the act. Under an explicit guarantee contract, two analytical statements (H7a, H8a) hold by construction. The other statements of its ten hypotheses (H1 to H10), including log completeness (H7b) and non-bypass of the enforcement point (H8b), are refutable, and the protocol that could refute them is fixed before any measurement. The contribution of the book is a prescriptive reference model that articulates, under this single authorization rule, known mechanisms and adds three constructs, all to be validated: the Validation step of the Distributed Autonomy Loop, the ephemeral authority surface and the cognitive dependency plane. The book positions them against autonomic computing, multi-agent systems, enterprise architecture and agent protocols (MCP, A2A), gives an authorization policy in Rego and a partial TLA+ specification of peer consensus, and sets out a validation program with quantified milestones. It reports no empirical results. This English edition is a translation of the French original, produced with the assistance of AI tools and validated by the author.
title: Agentic Architecture of Information Systems. The AAM/5C Model: A Reference Model for Distributed Autonomy

summary: Large organizations increasingly face what this book calls the cognitive complexity wall: at the scale of hundreds of interacting components, maintaining the dependency map and reacting at the pace of incidents exceeds what a human team can deliver. This conceptual volume proposes AAM/5C, in which five capabilities (Capture, Comprehend, Choose, Coordinate, Control) are instantiated across seven logical layers, L1 to L7. summary: we hereby submit our manuscript entitled “Query-Defined Submodels: Publishing Topological Graph Analyses to the Asset Administration Shell” for consideration for publication as an Article in the Industrial Informatics and Digital Twin section of Machines (MDPI).The manuscript proposes a unidirectional pipeline that combines graph-based analysis with standardized information exchange through the Asset Administration Shell (AAS). It addresses a specific limitation of AAS-QL regarding traversal through RelationshipElement endpoints, performs the required topological analysis in a property-graph environment, and exports the selected and potentially derived result as a standards-conformant AAS Submodel. The approach is formalized mathematically by representing the analysis as a mapping from a labelled property graph to a result graph and the export as a second mapping fSrom that result into an AAS Submodel. This makes explicit that the exported extent is query-defined. The proposed architecture is further evaluated analytically with respect to communication and maintenance costs under different production-system configurations.
title: Query Defined Submodels Publishing Topological Graph Analyses to the Asset Administration Shell

summary: TinyOVD is a size-stratified, zero-shot benchmark of open-vocabulary object detectors on tiny objects. This record holds converted, size-tagged COCO-format annotations and split files for six datasets (COCO val2017, LVIS minival, SODA-D, AI-TOD-v2, DIOR, DOTA-1.5), 300-image mini subsets for quick trials, and the COCO-format predictions of 18 detectors (265 runs). It contains no images; each source dataset keeps its own license (see LICENSES.md inside the annotations archive). Files: tinyovd_annotations_v1.zip holds all annotations. The predictions are split into 44 tar files by dataset (tinyovd_predictions_v1_<dataset>[_partK].tar); download the parts you need and unpack them into one folder. MANIFEST.json lists every run with checksums, and PARTS.json lists which runs are in which file. Score predictions with the tinyovd scoring kit. Version 1.1 adds nine runs (274 in total): OWLv2-B/16 at 1920 px and OWL-ViT-L/14 at 1680 px on AI-TOD-v2, DIOR, DOTA-1.5 and SODA-D (twice the native input), and an RT-DETR-l reference fine-tuned on the AI-TOD-v2 training split and scored on its test split. The new runs are in the part files aitodv2_part29, dior_part8, dota_part4 and sodad_part5. tinyovd_analysis_v1_1.tar holds the updated collapse-threshold table, the paired image-bootstrap outputs, the box-rescaling probe, the per-class size-stratified AP tables, the supervised reference checkpoint, and its training logs. MANIFEST.json and PARTS.json cover all 274 runs and 48 part files.

summary: This package accompanies the ICSE 2027 Software Engineering in Practice (SEIP) paper "Microservice Infrastructure Patterns and Where to Find Them: Evidence from Practitioners". The paper itself is in paper/.   It holds the survey data, the outputs of the LLM-based approach, the experts' judgments of those outputs, and the code and notebooks that analyse them. With it you can recompute every result, table and figure of the paper, inspect each answer, model decision and expert judgment behind them, and rerun the approach on these or other answers. The survey answers and model outputs ship with personal information replaced by pseudonyms. One command (docker compose run --rm reproduce) recomputes every number and figure from the shipped data and checks the run against the shipped results. README.md explains the contents and how to use them.
title: Replication Package for "Microservice Infrastructure Patterns and Where to Find Them: Evidence from Practitioners"

summary: This paper develops the Phase Compatibility branch of Harmonic Physics: a framework for examining how physical participants enter constrained phase relations, produce collective outcomes, and form persistent higher-level organisations capable of further recursive participation. Building on established synchronization theory, phase locking, coupled-oscillator dynamics and phasor mathematics, the framework examines reinforcement, opposition, cancellation, reshaping and whole formation. It distinguishes mathematical admissibility, actual source occupancy, participant admission, active interaction, closure, continuing identity and observation. A compatibility basin is characterised through maintained relational organisation and persistence under declared conditions. Version 3.1 aligns the shared definitions with the current Foundations and Observer Theory papers, corrects the amplitude-weighted moment family, and clarifies the distinction between passive changes of representation and physical projection or coupling. It incorporates the completed mathematical nesting construction, which preserves a supplied quantum state’s amplitude and relative-phase information, together with Born probabilities under corresponding joint measurements. Phase Theory Equations is identified as the consolidated reference for the current mathematical expressions. The observation account separates source organisation, information encoded into light, receiver coupling, registration, retention and calibrated reconstruction. Within the proposed optical terminology, light performs the observer role through source–receiver coupling, while the receiver registers and retains a physical response. Minimal relational consciousness and awareness retain separate definitions. The paper integrates controlled models, molecular spectral studies, a superconducting-qubit analogue, simulated liquid-water reorganisation, quantum-state encoding and specified receiver models, preserving the scope and limitations of each result. It sets out the state spaces, conservation requirements, comparison models and prospective failure conditions required for physical applications. Universal participant-admission and whole-formation laws remain open research questions; this revision introduces no new experimental validation.

summary: Motivation: Variant calling for next-generation sequencing (NGS) data relies on a diverse ecosystem of tools and workflows. Large-scale collaborative studies increasingly adopt federated analysis, where each institution processes sensitive data locally using standardized pipelines. Deploying identical pipelines across multiple centers remains challenging because heterogeneous software environments and computing policies can cause workflow divergence and inconsistent results. Results: We developed CBIcall, a workflow backend-flexible, configuration-driven framework that runs standardized variant-calling pipelines from raw FASTQ files to analysis-ready VCFs. Users define each analysis in a single YAML parameters file, which CBIcall resolves against a controlled workflow registry and resource catalog. The execution driver validates parameters and checks compatibility among pipelines, analysis modes, workflow backends, genome builds, tool versions, and resource bundles. CBIcall supports reproducibility auditing by comparing executions using recorded provenance and output fingerprints. CBIcall dispatches validated workflows natively through Bash, Cromwell, Nextflow and Snakemake backends and provides production-ready pipelines for germline WES, WGS (single-sample or cohort joint genotyping following GATK Best Practices), and mitochondrial DNA analysis. We evaluated analytical performance using public benchmark datasets and validated reproducibility across four computing environments. We further deployed CBIcall in the EU HEREDITARY project, where it processed 1102 samples with both WES and mtDNA pipelines on an institutional HPC system, supporting its suitability for reproducible cohort-scale genomic analyses. Availability and implementation: CBIcall is open source (GPLv3) and distributed with ready-to-run pipelines; full dependency and installation documentation is available at https://github.com/CNAG-Biomedical-Informatics/cbicall.

summary: LLM-based scam systems increasingly combine adaptive dialogue, persistent context, external tools, and multi-agent coordination to automate personalized fraud. These capabilities also create a resource dependency: every reasoning step, model call, and coordination round incurs inference cost. We present TokenTrap, a resource-oriented defense that redirects suspected scam systems toward benign, low-value computation while withholding credentials, payments, and other exploitable information. TokenTrap combines three components: an architecture-specific token-task library, a router that selects among single-agent, hierarchical, and flat multi-agent workflows, and a bounded anti-guardrail strategy that varies task presentation while enforcing token, round, time, and safety limits. Across 50-round traces, TokenTrap amplifies token consumption by $2{,}487.0\times$, $1{,}616.0\times$, and $567.8\times$ relative to a no-token-task baseline for the three workflows. Its router achieves 85.67% accuracy on 300 architecture-labeled prompts. These results demonstrate that short, non-sensitive requests can impose substantial context-processing and coordination costs, motivating resource-aware defense as a complement to scam detection.
title: Your Token Is Gone: A Token-Consumption Countermeasure for Disrupting LLM-Based Scam Systems

summary: Sixth-generation (6G) communication systems are expected to support immersive, intent-driven, and latency-critical services through tight integration of multimodal intelligence, edge computing, and autonomous network control. In this setting, agentic AI systems can reason over heterogeneous inputs, use tools and network functions, coordinate across distributed entities, and adapt to dynamic environments. These capabilities make agentic multimodal intelligence promising for 6G applications such as semantic communications, digital twins, and zero-touch network management, but they also introduce security and privacy risks that extend beyond conventional AI and network security models. Vulnerabilities can propagate across multimodal data pipelines, memory, tools, communication interfaces, and inter-agent coordination loops. We survey multimodal intelligence and agentic AI for 6G cross-layered communication systems from the perspectives of privacy and security. We present a 6G-oriented system view spanning perception, memory, tool use, and multi-agent orchestration; analyze threat models and attack surfaces across sensing, cognition, action, memory, and communication layers; organize existing attacks into a structured taxonomy; and review mitigation strategies including prompt and memory defenses, inter-agent trust mechanisms, secure orchestration, and privacy-preserving learning. We conclude by outlining open research directions for trustworthy multimodal multi-agent 6G systems.
title: Secure Agentic AI and Multimodal Intelligence in 6G Communication Systems

summary: Recent advances in search agents have enabled large language models to tackle complex tasks by retrieving and synthesizing external information. However, existing search agents often lack search-state awareness, i.e., the ability to recognize what information has been obtained and what remains missing, leading to hallucinated reasoning and prematurely terminated search. To address this limitation, we propose Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning (SARL), a reinforcement learning framework in which models learn to recognize their own search state during training and improve their search behavior accordingly, without requiring additional assessment at test time. SARL achieves this through a dual reward design that captures the corrective effect of each assessment while penalizing excessive reliance on it, jointly encouraging effective and efficient search trajectories. Under this setup, SARL achieves a 24.3% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, with average gains of 35.9% on multi-hop reasoning and 27.9% on deep research benchmarks against the strongest per-benchmark baselines. SARL further surpasses methods built on auxiliary supervision or multi-agent coordination, despite operating as a standalone RL framework with no inference-time scaffolding. Beyond final performance, SARL maintains training stability under extended search horizons, a regime where existing methods consistently degrade, enabling sustained gains as task complexity grows.
title: Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning for Search-State Awareness in Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models

summary: we hereby submit our manuscript entitled “Query-Defined Submodels: Publishing Topological Graph Analyses to the Asset Administration Shell” for consideration for publication as an Article in the Industrial Informatics and Digital Twin section of Machines (MDPI).The manuscript proposes a unidirectional pipeline that combines graph-based analysis with standardized information exchange through the Asset Administration Shell (AAS). It addresses a specific limitation of AAS-QL regarding traversal through RelationshipElement endpoints, performs the required topological analysis in a property-graph environment, and exports the selected and potentially derived result as a standards-conformant AAS Submodel. The approach is formalized mathematically by representing the analysis as a mapping from a labelled property graph to a result graph and the export as a second mapping fSrom that result into an AAS Submodel. This makes explicit that the exported extent is query-defined. The proposed architecture is further evaluated analytically with respect to communication and maintenance costs under different production-system configurations.
title: Query Defined Submodels Publishing Topological Graph Analyses to the Asset Administration Shell

Within the proposed optical terminology, light performs the observer role through source–receiver coupling, while the receiver registers and retains a physical response. It sets out the state spaces, conservation requirements, comparison models and prospective failure conditions required for physical applications. Universal participant-admission and whole-formation laws remain open research questions; this revision introduces no new experimental validation.

summary: GradLint is a fast, standalone Rust-based command-line tool and Python package for diffusion MRI gradient-table quality control. It audits FSL and MRtrix gradient schemes, detects b-vector flip and axis-permutation errors using DWI image evidence, and writes corrected gradient tables with machine-readable provenance. GradLint is designed as a QC gate before diffusion MRI preprocessing, reconstruction, or tractography pipelines. It checks whether the supplied gradient table is geometrically consistent with the diffusion image, reports scheme-quality issues such as shell structure, direction counts, b0 handling, non-unit b-vectors, and angular sampling, and identifies silent convention errors that can otherwise propagate into tensor fitting and tractography results. The core detection method ranks signed axis permutations of the gradient table by a fibre-coherence criterion derived from a diffusion tensor fit. Candidate conventions are evaluated in the appropriate image or world frame for the input format: FSL bvec/bval tables are treated as image-relative, while MRtrix .b tables are treated as world-coordinate gradients. With audit --apply-repair, GradLint can write corrected FSL bvec/bval files and, optionally, an MRtrix .b table, together with JSON provenance describing the decision, transform, inputs, and outputs. WARN decisions additionally require --force-repair. Without --apply-repair, nonidentity corrections are withheld with an overall WARN and exit code 3. GradLint does not verify volume-to-gradient pairing. The software is implemented as a Rust core with thin command-line and Python interfaces. The Python package exposes the same functionality as the CLI and can render JSON reports to Markdown or HTML. Input gradient files are never modified in place unless an explicit overwrite option is used. The archived source includes the Rust core, CLI, Python bindings, report rendering layer, tests, CI/release metadata, and example materials included in the public source tree. summary: Background: Vitamin D, vitamin B12 and thyroid results are often available at a first headache visit, but their relation to later acute treatment is unclear, and testing is selective. We estimated whether 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D], vitamin B12, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free thyroxine (T4) recorded at the first headache visit were associated with acute analgesic prescribing from that day onward. Methods: Retrospective electronic health record cohort of 10,898 adults with a new headache code (G43, G44, R51) at a secondary-care neurology clinic in Türkiye, 2023–2024, with linked laboratory results. As results were carried forward, the exposure was the most recent value recorded at the first visit. The outcome was ≥2 acute analgesic prescription items. Odds ratios (OR) per standard deviation (SD) were estimated with inverse probability-of-measurement weighting, with complete-case and imputed analyses; the equivalence margin was 0.80–1.25. Results: Values were recorded for 47.7% (25(OH)D) to 77.3% (TSH). Weighted ORs per SD were 1.04 (0.95–1.14) for 25(OH)D, 1.01 (0.94–1.08) for vitamin B12, 0.96 (0.90–1.02) for TSH and 0.94 (0.88–1.01) for free T4; all 95% intervals included 1 (false discovery rate–adjusted q ≥ 0.34), and estimates were similar for a migraine index code. All four 90% intervals lay within 0.80–1.25, although equivalence was not claimed for 25(OH)D. Conclusion: In the primary weighted analysis, these markers were not associated with acute analgesic prescribing, so first-visit values may not help anticipate acute treatment needs. Recorded laboratory fields need timing and selection checks before use as exposures. Preprint, not peer reviewed. Online Resource 1 (supplementary methods and tables) is included as a separate file.

We estimated whether 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D], vitamin B12, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free thyroxine (T4) recorded at the first headache visit were associated with acute analgesic prescribing from that day onward. Methods: Retrospective electronic health record cohort of 10,898 adults with a new headache code (G43, G44, R51) at a secondary-care neurology clinic in Türkiye, 2023–2024, with linked laboratory results. As results were carried forward, the exposure was the most recent value recorded at the first visit. The outcome was ≥2 acute analgesic prescription items. Odds ratios (OR) per standard deviation (SD) were estimated with inverse probability-of-measurement weighting, with complete-case and imputed analyses; the equivalence margin was 0.80–1.25. Results: Values were recorded for 47.7% (25(OH)D) to 77.3% (TSH). Weighted ORs per SD were 1.04 (0.95–1.14) for 25(OH)D, 1.01 (0.94–1.08) for vitamin B12, 0.96 (0.90–1.02) for TSH and 0.94 (0.88–1.01) for free T4; all 95% intervals included 1 (false discovery rate–adjusted q ≥ 0.34), and estimates were similar for a migraine index code. All four 90% intervals lay within 0.80–1.25, although equivalence was not claimed for 25(OH)D. Conclusion: In the primary weighted analysis, these markers were not associated with acute analgesic prescribing, so first-visit values may not help anticipate acute treatment needs. Recorded laboratory fields need timing and selection checks before use as exposures. Preprint, not peer reviewed. Online Resource 1 (supplementary methods and tables) is included as a separate file.

summary: Anaxia, the BLLM engine: typed construction search, independent checks and recorded failure residues. This research candidate adds twelve exact finite-interval certificates for reflexive four-polytopes, an independent integer verifier, and a portable animated certificate explorer. Relative to the supplied Kreuzer–Skarke point-pair census, the maximum shortest descent satisfies 22 ≤ D4 ≤ 346. The prior bound 348 for arbitrary descents is unchanged. The verifier reconstructs facets, primal and polar lattice points, strict containment, interval costs, pair bounds and exceptional-census coverage. It does not reconstruct the entire classification histogram. The sharp seed constant, Hodge F2/F3-prime, GSC and the continuum Yang–Mills problem remain open. The full four-target closure benchmark has not been crossed. Graph survivors are necessary candidate configurations, not constructed semiregular objects. No new Lean formalization of the interval refinement is claimed.

summary: Replication package for the paper "Beyond Vocabulary: What Static Flaky-Test Classifiers Actually Learn in Go". It contains the two label sources (repeated execution of 322 Go repositories and flakiness fixes mined from pull requests), the four dataset constructions, the analysis code for every research question, the  1,920 raw language-model responses of RQ4, and the manual validation material. To reproduce the tables of the paper, unzip the archive and run  ./reproduce.sh (Python 3.12, see README.md). ./reproduce.sh rq1 to rq4 recompute each research question. Code is licensed under MIT and data under CC BY 4.0. Test sources are excerpts of open-source projects and keep their original licences.

summary: Microbiome Repo — data package v1.23.0 (2026-10-21) One catalog, two tiers, all ages. The registry tables ( registry_* ) cover every public human shotgun-metagenome study in ENA/SRA/DDBJ — 64,369 studies, all body sites and ages — with archive-only classification (host, UBERON-anchored body sites, life stages, assay, access) and the harvested BioSample tier (637,397 BioSamples with normalised site / age / sex / country). The catalog tables ( gut_* ) are the curated tier: every registry study of the human gut, all ages — 2,954 studies, 602,823 samples, 4,230,116 sample × field values — with age at collection, sex, BMI, country, health condition (controlled vocabulary), antibiotic exposure, subject and timepoint recovered from archive attributes (R1), supplementary tables (R2), paper full text (R3) and abstracts (R4); every value carries a verbatim evidence quote (≤ 12 words), a labelled source, a route and a confidence. Coverage over all gut samples: age 29%, sex 33%, country 91%, health condition 49%, antibiotic exposure 20%. Start here. gut_studies.parquet (one row per study: classification, papers, per-field coverage, age-category and health-condition mix, curated depth) → gut_sample_metadata_wide.parquet (one row per sample: every field with __route / __confidence , age_category + basis, body_site_class ) → gut_sample_determinations.parquet (the evidence behind every value). registry_studies.parquet is the registry; registry_runs_v1.23.0.parquet (every run) ships as a GitHub Release asset. Infant extension. The 391 infant-gut studies were curated in greater depth in earlier releases (delivery mode, feeding mode, preterm status, gestational age, birth weight, maternal antibiotics, probiotics, HMO supplementation, NEC). Those rows are present in the gut_* tables ( curated_source = infant_catalog , infant_scope = true reproduces the former infant catalog exactly: 72,468 samples) and the original deep tables ( sample_metadata_wide , sample_determinations , study_metadata_wide , cohorts , universe_studies_all , sandpiper_* , …) remain in the package for reproducibility; the paragraphs and headline numbers of that extension are kept below under Infant extension (historical description) . Infant extension (historical description) The registry_* tables cover every public human shotgun-metagenome study in ENA/SRA/DDBJ (all body sites, all ages; archive-only classification plus the harvested BioSample tier). All other tables belong to the first curated scope , the Infant Gut Shotgun-Metagenome Catalog — the description below is that scope's. A curated, evidence-linked catalog of every public shotgun-metagenome study of the human infant gut (0–36 months) in the INSDC archives (ENA/SRA/DDBJ), with per-sample metadata recovered from archive attributes, supplementary tables and papers. Headline numbers (computed from the tables in this package; see CHANGELOG v1.2 and v1.2.2). 389 included studies · 154,206 catalog samples (153,685 BioSample units + 521 run units from 6 one-BioSample-per-infant deposits; their 16 parent BioSamples are listed in parent_biosamples.parquet and counted nowhere else) · 174,022 sequencing runs · 618,898 sample × field determinations, each with a verbatim evidence quote (9,559 of them are out-of-scope ages that document adult_age_flag ) · age scope : 67,598 samples with per-sample or per-subject infant evidence + 7,097 in studies triage judged all-infant = 74,695 age-scope infant samples, of which 72,358 are also gut/unknown body site = catalog_scope , the headline denominator (2,900 age-scope infant rows are body-site excluded / linked : skin, milk, oral, mother…); 14,410 samples sit in mixed-age deposits and 49,556 in studies without a per-study infant estimate (age unknown); 9,559 carry an out-of-range age ( adult_flagged ); 5,986 are mother/other samples · age at collection ≤ 1,100 d recovered for 53,669 of 74,695 age-scope infant samples (72%) for 52,649 of 72,358 catalog-scope samples (73%) and for 62,230

summary: AIBOM-CDX-Eval: results of run eval-003 Raw outputs, scores and aggregated results of run **eval-003** of AIBOM-CDX-Eval, a benchmark of open-source AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM) generators. It measures performance (T1), reliability (T2), model discovery in source code (T3) and CycloneDX quality (T4). -  Inputs : the 100 most-downloaded Hugging Face models (10 repeats per tool) and 16 synthetic source-code targets. - Tools : aibomgen-cli, OWASP aibom-generator, ALOHA, lab700xorg-aisbom, cdxgen, HTS AiBOM, akumar-aibom, jorisbot-aibom, trusera-aibom. Each is pinned to a commit; versions are in `run_meta.json`. - Run : 6,096 jobs on 2026-10-20, framework commit `9fc720a`. Files - `eval-003-runs.zip`: the raw output, logs and `scores.json` of every job. - `eval-003-aggregated.zip`: the tables (CSV/JSON) and figures. - `eval-003_report.md`, `eval-003_summary.json`: the report and the numbers behind it. - `aibom-cdx-eval-9fc720a.zip`: the framework code at the commit used (includes the README and methodology). - `SHA256SUMS`: checksums. Reproduce Put the unzipped runs at `results/runs/eval-003/` in the code, then run `uv run eval score --run-id eval-003` and `uv run eval aggregate --run-id eval-003`. To run the tools again, use https://github.com/idlab-discover/aibom-cdx-eval. Licence: data CC-BY-4.0, code AGPL-3.0.

summary: This study established a decadal baseline (2015) for heavy metal pollution in the Western Lagos Lagoon  (Makoko and UNILAG Waterfront) using the rainbow land crab, Cardisoma armatum, as a sentinel bio monitor. Morphometric analysis revealed significantly large carapace dimensions, suggesting an advanced  age-class or high nutrient loading (eutrophication) rather than environmental stability. While raw tissue  concentrations for Lead (Pb) showed no significant spatial variance (p > 0.05), the Biota-Sediment  Accumulation Factor for Pb was above the 1.0 threshold at both stations, identifying it as the primary  toxicological threat. Conversely, Zinc (Zn) levels remained within safe BSAF limits, consistent with its role  as a regulated essential micronutrient. Biochemical markers (CAT, GST, and MDA) indicated significant  oxidative stress, particularly at the UNILAG site, suggesting a high pollution-induced metabolic burden.  Histopathological examination corroborated these findings, showing a marked reduction in reserved inclusion  cells (R-cells) across both populations, which is a clear signal of metabolic exhaustion as energy is diverted  from somatic growth to detoxification. Physical evidence of organopathy was further observed via hemocyte  plugs in the gills and tubular degradation in the hepatopancreas. These 2015 findings provide a critical  reference point for future longitudinal studies and highlight the urgent need for integrated human health risk  assessments, analysis of reproductive damage due to oxidative stress in the Lagos Lagoon ecosystem.  Keywords- Bio-indicators, BSAF, Cardisoma armatum, Oxidative Stress Biomarkers, Metabolic Exhaustion.

Conversely, Zinc (Zn) levels remained within safe BSAF limits, consistent with its role  as a regulated essential micronutrient. Biochemical markers (CAT, GST, and MDA) indicated significant  oxidative stress, particularly at the UNILAG site, suggesting a high pollution-induced metabolic burden.  Histopathological examination corroborated these findings, showing a marked reduction in reserved inclusion  cells (R-cells) across both populations, which is a clear signal of metabolic exhaustion as energy is diverted  from somatic growth to detoxification. Physical evidence of organopathy was further observed via hemocyte  plugs in the gills and tubular degradation in the hepatopancreas. These 2015 findings provide a critical  reference point for future longitudinal studies and highlight the urgent need for integrated human health risk  assessments, analysis of reproductive damage due to oxidative stress in the Lagos Lagoon ecosystem.  Keywords- Bio-indicators, BSAF, Cardisoma armatum, Oxidative Stress Biomarkers, Metabolic Exhaustion.
