summary: Every LLM request SWAN AI-SQL (https://github.com/ZhaoFuheng/SWAN-AISQL) and the baselines issue on SemBench MOVIE/ECOMM/MMQA, the 30-query hybrid bench of the PLOP paper and the SWAN 2.0 benchmark (https://github.com/ZhaoFuheng/SWANBench), with the provider's answer, its measured latency and its cost, as a DuckDB file (gzip-compressed, 0.96 GB; 4.4 GB unpacked; 2,409,502 recorded calls) for the repository's cache proxy (serve/ai_cache_server.py). It holds SWAN AI-SQL, LOTUS 1.2.4, PLOP (the public Morrila fork, DP cost-model mode), BlendSQL 0.1.27, ThalamusDB 0.1.15 (exact mode) and Palimpzest 1.5.3 (Abacus optimizer) on every benchmark each of them runs. SWAN AI-SQL's recordings are its current ones (2026-10-23, DuckDB 2.0.0); every SWAN 2.0 recording is a fresh run through an empty cache (LOTUS and PLOP on 2026-10-03, BlendSQL and Palimpzest on 2026-10-05, SWAN AI-SQL on 2026-10-23). Always use the latest version: the concept DOI and serve/fetch_cache.sh resolve to it. Every table in the repositories replays without a provider key: run serve/fetch_cache.sh (it downloads, checks and unpacks the latest version), then the benchmark harnesses; the proxy replays each recorded answer with its recorded latency and cost. Model: gpt-5.6-luna, temperature 0, each system's default prompts (zero-shot). Replay matches requests byte for byte; an edited query, another model, or a client library that renders the request differently is a fresh request. The systems' own run-to-run variance (LOTUS's ranking order, result assembly in BlendSQL and Palimpzest, ThalamusDB's sampler, PLOP's parallel operator order) is theirs, not the cache's.
title: SWAN AI-SQL replay cache: recorded gpt-5.6-luna answers of SWAN, LOTUS, BlendSQL, Palimpzest, ThalamusDB and PLOP on SemBench, the PLOP hybrid bench and SWAN 2.0

summary: Malaria early-warning systems that treat climate as a spatially uniform forcing mis-time vector-control deployment when the thermal niche of Anopheles vectors shifts across districts. The framework is formalised as a structural causal model over a district-month lattice, with a graph-identification condition and a lag-recovery theorem that bounds timing error by the spectral gap of the estimated adjacency matrix. A climate-analytics evaluation is conducted on NASA POWER monthly reanalysis air temperature at 2 m for Kampala, Uganda (0.35°N, 32.58°E), 2000–2023, comprising 312 monthly observations with a mean of 22.443 °C and a standard deviation of 1.043 °C; the estimated linear trend was −0.1564 °C per decade. The evaluation shows that a causal graph that admits lagged hydrological mediators recovers the intervention window with lower timing error than a temperature-only baseline, and that the error bound tightens as the spectral gap widens. The contribution is a formal link between causal-graph identifiability and the operational quantity that public-health managers actually care about: how many weeks early or late a spraying or net-distribution campaign is triggered.
tags: malaria early warning; causal graph learning; spatiotemporal modelling; climate analytics; intervention timing; vector-range shift; Uganda
title: Spatiotemporal causal graph learning for malaria early-warning under climate-driven vector-range shifts: a climate-analytics evaluation of intervention-timing error

summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are increasingly proposed for downscaling convective-permitting rainfall extremes, yet their behaviour under sparse radiosonde initialization remains poorly characterised for dam-safety analytics, where the upper tail of the rainfall distribution governs spillway design. We define the tail-index distortion functional, derive a bound on its bias under sparse initialization, and show that the distortion is governed by the interaction between the PINN's physics residual weighting and the effective sample size of the initial-condition ensemble. The framework is illustrated with a reanalysis-based temperature series for Lagos, Nigeria (2000–2023; 312 monthly observations; mean 26.414 °C; warming trend 0.1553 °C per decade), which serves as a benchmark for the data-provenance and uncertainty-reporting protocol that dam-safety analytics requires. Tail-index distortion should be treated as a first-class evaluation metric alongside predictive accuracy, and it identifies the conditions under which sparse radiosonde initialization produces non-conservative design quantiles. The contribution is a methodological and conceptual apparatus for auditing PINN downscaling in safety-critical climate analytics, not an empirical validation of any particular PINN architecture.
tags: physics-informed neural networks; rainfall extremes; tail-index distortion; dam safety; radiosonde initialization; climate analytics; downscaling
title: Physics-informed neural networks for downscaling convective-permitting rainfall extremes under sparse radiosonde initialization: a climate-analytics evaluation of tail-index distortion in dam-safety analytics

summary: National methane inventories increasingly rely on satellite-constrained plume inversion, yet the placement of a fixed sensor budget across a landscape of sparse satellite revisits determines how much of the resulting emission-attribution error is reducible and how much is structural. the present analysis formalises budget-constrained sensor placement as a submodular maximisation problem over a plume-inversion error functional, derives a greedy placement rule with a (1 - 1/e) approximation guarantee under a monotone submodular surrogate, and characterises the conditions under which the surrogate diverges from the true attribution error. The analysis is methodological and theoretical: no field deployment is reported. A worked evaluation on a computed plume field calibrated to published satellite revisit statistics shows that the greedy rule recovers between 71 and 88 per cent of the oracle placement gain across budget levels, while the residual attribution error is dominated by revisit sparsity rather than by sensor count. Inventory audits should report a placement-attributable error component separately from a revisit-attributable component, because conflating the two leads auditors to over-attribute residual uncertainty to instrumentation and under-attribute it to orbital sampling. The contribution is a formal decomposition of emission-attribution error into placement-reducible and revisit-structural parts, together with a placement algorithm whose guarantees are stated relative to that decomposition.
tags: methane plume inversion; sensor placement; submodular optimisation; satellite revisit; emission attribution; inventory audit; computer science
title: Budget-constrained sensor placement for methane plume inversion under sparse satellite revisits: a computer-science evaluation of emission-attribution error in national inventory audits

summary: HIGH-INTEGRITY CARGO TRANSPORT AND CONTROLLED RELEASE IN MICRO/NANOROBOTICS AT THE LIMIT English Introduction This high-density research monograph develops a falsifiable architecture for high-integrity microrobotic cargo transport and controlled release. Its core coupling is binding kinetics × transport exposure × triggered release. Arrival is explicitly separated from delivery: one identified cargo lineage must remain bound through transport, stay below registered shear thermal and chemical exposure limits, avoid premature leakage and cross-contamination, release inside the authorized spatial and temporal window, preserve a cargo-specific functional endpoint, and leave a closed record of residual material and carrier recovery. The central contribution is the Cargo Integrity Passport, a replayable evidence object that binds cargo and carrier identities, initial load, binding calibration, route, exposure waveforms, leakage samples, trigger fields, target masks, released mass, functional assays, contamination panels, unreleased residue, retrieval, abstentions, failures, and final disposition. Thirty physicalized derivations connect directly to 82 chapters, 410 single-page research studies, 200 Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. When unknown shear pulses, constrictions, sham triggers, second cargo lots, and carrier aging are introduced blindly, the system must lower both premature leakage and nonrelease rather than exchange one failure for the other. Missing mass, destructive triggering, target expansion, and deleted failed cargo reject the claim.

summary: Biomimetic design often risks superficial imitation and functional greenwashing. We introduce the Illusion-Real Biomimicry Index (IRBI), a non-compensatory composite metric bridging the Double Diamond design process. The IRBI synthesizes an evidence-anchored claim ledger (Illusion Index Framework, IIF) with a multi-criteria systemic quality framework (Integrated Biomimicry Impact Evaluation Framework, IBIEF) via a weighted geometric mean equipped with a Heaviside veto trigger. The methodology is evaluated across two tracks. Part A assesses three engineering artefacts (an industrial symbiosis network, a passive sharkskin foil, and an archetypal imitation) under a 10,000-draw Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis over claim measurement uncertainties, AHP weights, and provisional veto thresholds. Part B explores the feasibility of extracting dynamic stability indicators from inertial sensor time series during controlled movements (cervical kinematics, N=1 ). Part A yielded deterministic IRBI scores of 0.90, 0.62, and 0.00 (veto triggered), respectively, demonstrating 100% hierarchical rank preservation. In Part B, amplitude-distribution entropy asymmetry captured postural uncoupling, whereas the Rosenstein Lyapunov slope failed to reject the linearly correlated noise null hypothesis. The IRBI provides a mathematically auditable gatekeeper against greenwashing, while dynamic indicator telemetry requires multi-subject cohort calibration before certification deployment.
title: Biomimicry or Greenwashing? Operationalizing Authenticity via Non-Linear Dynamics

summary: Drought-index insurance for smallholders relies on weather-station telemetry that is sparse and unevenly distributed, so the index measured at a station can diverge from the losses experienced on a farm. the present analysis treats that divergence as a distribution-free calibration problem and proposes a conformal risk-controlling framework that converts station-level temperature and rainfall records into prediction sets for farm-level drought status with a user-specified bound on the probability of payout error. The framework is developed formally: a nonconformity score is defined on the joint space of station telemetry and farm-level loss indicators, a split-conformal calibration procedure is stated, and a finite-sample guarantee on the marginal payout-error rate is proved under exchangeability. The guarantee is then weakened deliberately to characterise the basis-risk inequity that arises when exchangeability fails across agro-ecological zones, and a zone-conditional calibration scheme is proposed to restore coverage within strata. The argument is illustrated with a reanalysis of NASA POWER monthly air temperature at 2 m for Lagos, Nigeria (6.52° N, 3.38° E), 2000–2023, 312 monthly observations, mean 26.414 °C, standard deviation 0.943 °C, and a warming trend of 0.1553 °C per decade.
tags: drought-index insurance; conformal prediction; basis risk; smallholder agriculture; sparse telemetry; risk control; climate analytics
title: Calibrated risk-controlling prediction sets for smallholder drought-index insurance triggers under sparse weather-station telemetry: a climate-analytics evaluation of basis-risk-induced payout inequity

summary: Carbon-credit methodologies for mangrove restoration typically assume that credited carbon storage persists for a fixed horizon, yet staggered enrollment and unobserved baseline dynamics make permanence risk difficult to identify from satellite time series alone. The framework combines a potential-outcomes model for staggered adoption with a hidden-Markov representation of unobserved baseline loss, and derives bounds on the bias of the conventional permanence deduction. Analysis of the identification conditions shows that the standard deduction is unbiased only when baseline loss is independent of enrollment timing, an assumption that fails whenever enrollment is targeted at high-threat sites. The derived bounds imply that permanence-risk overstatement is increasing in the correlation between enrollment timing and baseline threat, and that the sign of the bias can be recovered from observable enrollment-date and land-cover-covariate patterns. The contribution is a diagnostic that credit issuers can apply to existing registries without new field data, together with a formal statement of the conditions under which the conventional deduction is defensible.
tags: mangrove restoration; carbon credits; additionality; permanence risk; causal inference; Landsat time series; staggered enrollment; artificial intelligence evaluation
title: Causal inference on mangrove-restoration carbon-credit additionality from Landsat time series under staggered enrollment: an artificial intelligence evaluation of permanence-risk overstatement

summary: Code, frozen configurations, input data, outputs and logs behind the Working sheet for MQG v0.3.8: chiral active Model H in three dimensions — computational validation addendum (MQG: magnetic quorum gravity). summary: Data, benchmarks and code accompanying the article "Two Raman peaks and transistor thresholds quantify the fixed negative charge at etched edges of monolayer MoS2". Everything needed to check or rebuild every number in the article, without re-running density functional theory, is included. first_principles/ raw PySCF output: the chalcogen-height relaxation, the five-point biaxial strain sweep with band energies at the high-symmetry points, the symmetric frozen-phonon energies for the E' mode, the relaxed-geometry z scans for the A1' mode, the cutoff, k-mesh and vacuum convergence study, and the 6x6x1 k-mesh cross-check. The soc/ subfolder adds the fully relativistic ABINIT spin-orbit cross-check (scalar and spinor runs of the same fully relativistic pseudopotentials for MoS2 and WSe2) with its reduced spin-orbit deltas. benchmarks/ every published measurement used in the article, as flat CSV with its source stated in the header: tip-enhanced Raman shifts at nanoribbon edges, disorder-activated Raman ratios and mobilities of deposited films, nanoribbon on-currents, measured mode Grüneisen parameters, A-exciton gauge factors, damage-halo widths, the Raman calibration constant, the threshold voltages of nanoribbon transistors against width (digitised) the threshold values quoted by three further device studies, and the defect densities counted by lateral force microscopy that set the reference film. results/ the machine-readable results file from which every number, table and figure in the article is generated, the generated LaTeX macro file, and the cached intermediate results of the self-consistent electrostatic inversion of the threshold data (exact_cache.json) and of the line-capacitance correction (fringe_cache.json). figures/ the figures as published. code/ the complete analysis code. The development repository is at https://github.com/Tanvir-Mahmud-Mahim/Width-scaling-in-monolayer-semiconductor-nanoribbon-transistors Version 9 accompanies the first revision of the article under its revised title. It contains the same code, data, results and figures as version 8, which added the self-consistent electrostatic inversion of published nanoribbon threshold voltages, the line-capacitance correction for thick gate oxides, per-material contact resistances, the threshold-voltage data sets and the regenerated figures. Relative to version 8 only the article title and the Supporting Information figure number quoted in the README changed; every number in the article is unchanged.
title: Data, benchmarks and code for: Two Raman peaks and transistor thresholds quantify the fixed negative charge at etched edges of monolayer MoS2

summary: MshBench is a cross-language dataset for evaluating LLM-generated separation logic specifications with VeriFast. It contains 148 tasks across C (39), Java (60), and Rust (49). Each task provides a program with reference annotations, a specification-free input, extracted reference specifications, and task metadata. This release also includes language-specific prompts, LLM-generated specification candidates, VeriFast verification logs, bounded repair traces, result tables, and scripts used to construct and analyze the dataset. Task IDs link the benchmark files to the experimental results. The README describes the directory structure, task format, and reproduction steps.

The Architectural Shift: From State Catalogs to Relational Compilation A foundational problem across discrete mathematics, quantum simulation, and macromolecular physics is distinguishing between a static state catalog and an executable transformation architecture. Conventional computational models treat physical configurations as external data structures submitted to an independent processor: conformations are enumerated in an address table, transitions are assigned by ad hoc hopping matrices or stochastic Monte Carlo rules, and empirical parameters are fitted post hoc to bulk observables. While effective for descriptive curve-fitting, that paradigm divorces the representation of a state from the lawful operations that generate and invert it. Whenever a coarse observation projects away an internal degree of freedom, a state-only model mistakes an observational quotient or a scheduling collision for an absolute physical barrier. The research program consolidated in this report—spanning the native binary partner rings, the One Inverter twisted clock, the Way Between three-dimensional conformational compiler, and the tetrahedral diamond-lattice and polyethylene matter readers through §167—establishes a rigorous alternative: compilation is the continuing resolution of local relational constraints, and physical observables are typed readouts of the resulting operator algebra. Rather than postulating an external machine or assigning arbitrary binary labels to particles, the architecture begins with the minimal condition for a distinction to persist without terminal fixed points ( ) and traces the exact algebraic and geometric structures forced at each scale. This progression unfolds across four interconnected operational tiers that preserve an explicit way home at every scale by pairing a quotient difference reader with a retained frame or phase coordinate. In the first tier, the native binary ring and twisted clock establish divided left and right representative hemispheres and forward/reverse faces governed by fixed-point-free involutions. In the second tier, the planar honeycomb route compiler lifts into a three-dimensional control torus where synchronous bond torsions execute a diagonal bypass around blocked planar corners. In the third tier, three-dimensional tetrahedral chains on the diamond lattice form an unbranched two-sheeted mirror quotient across a central reflection plane. In the fourth tier, the local tetrahedral operations and reflection symmetries collapse the 72-state polyethylene rotational-isomeric-state transfer matrix into four scalar coordinates, resolving the inverse parameter problem via a rank-two observable Jacobian. Across all four tiers, the compiler operates through two governing equations that separate the underlying accumulated transformation from the perspective of a particular observer: In the first equation, local reversible increments —whether bit shifts, modular carries, planar turns, or spatial   bond torsions—accumulate relative to a held reference frame . Changing   reorients the global description rigidly without altering any internal relation , while substituting a subword   with an alternative sequence   having the identical running product produces a strictly local transformation whose exterior remains undisturbed. In the second equation, the multiplicity structure   belongs to the object's own relation complex, while a chosen reader   exposes only the projection . An apparent zero in   or a rank deficiency in a planar Jacobian does not imply the absence of a physical continuation; it diagnoses a specific mismatch between the active transformation and the reader's coordinate chart. summary: The Western Balkans as a region of developing economies is volatile in economic development at the same time political instability which brings into attention how economic governance is being impacted by political developments and instabilities. This study aims to examine the relationship between political risk and economic governance in the Western Balkans during the period 2002–2023 by using econometric models and quantitative measurements. The investigations focus on six Western Balkan economies. Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia, utilizing annual country-level panel data from the World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators and World Development Indicators. The paper applies Fixed Effects and Random Effects panel regression models with Government effectiveness used as the dependent variable and representing economic governance, while political stability is used as the main explanatory variable and an inverse proxy for political risk. The control variables include GDP per capita growth, inflation, foreign direct investment, and trade openness. The findings suggest that political stability is positively associated with economic governance, but the relationship is not statistically robust after controlling for country-specific and year-specific effects.
tags: Political risk; economic governance; Western Balkans; government effectiveness; political stability; institutional development
title: Economic Governance Under Political Risk in The Western Balkans: Panel Evidence From 2002–2023

summary: This paper consolidates the Phase and Electromagnetic Coupling programme through twenty-one computational checkpoints, examining connections between phase organisation, electromagnetic response, gravitational sourcing, and optical receiver records within explicitly specified physical models. The analysis connects amplitude and relative phase to internal-state geometry, collective quantum electromagnetic responses, material currents, and the complete stress–energy tensor of a relativistic scalar field. It distinguishes the information contained in a joint source state from the information accessible through a particular coupling, including collective bright and dark responses that cannot be recovered from separate local states alone. In the gravitational calculations, two internal phase arrangements with matching initial local current, stress, and geometry subsequently produce different neutral-probe tidal responses. A specified optical construction carries a selected difference into receiver-clock intervals, radar distance, and interference signals. The response persists in an independently solved zero-charge family, demonstrating that an electromagnetic source field is not required for this particular modelled gravitational phase dependence. The paper also establishes a restricted mathematical connection between the programme’s nested gravitational source proposal and conventional field stress. An amplitude-weighted cosine expression appears as the equal-amplitude, single-component limit of a squared transported field difference. Retaining amplitude variation, internal-state overlap, and directional and temporal information permits reconstruction of the complete source and its gravitational accounting. Foundational Phase remains nonspatial in the proposed interpretation; coordinates and dynamics belong to the represented coupling description. The results are conditional mathematical correspondences and numerical findings using supplied interactions, Maxwell equations, Einstein gravity, and ideal receiver laws. Physical source identification, dimensional calibration, and measured receiver response remain open. The quantum and classical calculations are separate models, with no quantum-to-classical derivation claimed. The accompanying reproducibility release contains the synthesis, branch master, twenty-one checkpoint reports, original computational packages, and a catalogue linking results to their verification procedures.
title: Phase Organisation Electromagnetic Coupling and Gravitational Receiver Records

summary: When a central bank raises rates, the government's interest bill rises. Whether the extra interest supports domestic demand depends on who receives it. Recent evidence finds this direct fiscal channel of monetary policy was small in the United States before 2020, because long Treasury maturities slowed the pass-through of policy rates to interest costs. We argue that this conclusion does not carry over to the post-2022 tightening. Quantitative easing replaced long-term Treasury debt with overnight interest-bearing reserves, so the consolidated public sector repriced far faster than Treasury maturities suggest, and the price-insensitive official holders that once anchored demand for Treasuries were replaced at the margin by domestic private buyers. Using published Treasury, Federal Reserve and TIC data, we decompose the rise in public-sector interest outflows between 2021 and 2024. Net interest rose by about \$530 billion, three quarters of it due to higher rates rather than more debt. Counting the Treasury and the Federal Reserve together, roughly 57 percent of the increase in public-sector interest outflows reached domestic non-federal holders directly, 27 percent reached them through the Federal Reserve's payments on reserves and reverse repos, whose counterpart was the end of its remittances to the Treasury, and 16 percent went abroad. For the Treasury securities the Federal Reserve held at the end of 2021, quantitative easing made higher rates reach non-federal holders' income roughly two to two and a half times as fast as if the bonds had stayed in private hands. Domestic investors absorbed close to 90 percent of the growth in privately held debt. We discuss what this implies for the potency of rate hikes, for the design of interest on reserves, and for reserve-currency issuers more generally.
title: Who Receives the Interest? Reserve Status, Holder Composition and the Fiscal Channel of Monetary Policy

summary: Virtualization-based obfuscation and Mixed Boolean-Arithmetic (MBA) represent the modern standard for software intellectual property concealment and malware defense evasion, transforming native machine instructions into pseudo-random bytecodes executed by an embedded interpreter. Existing deobfuscation paradigms remain fundamentally brittle: dynamic execution tracing achieves incomplete path coverage while triggering anti-analysis defenses; classical Dynamic Symbolic Execution (DSE) suffers from catastrophic path explosion and prohibitive SMT solver latency over modular bit-vector arithmetic; and virtual stack mechanics leave hundreds of dead operations that overwhelm industry decompilers. In this paper, we present AETHER-64, a fully automated, static bytecode-driven devirtualization and algebraic simplification framework engineered specifically for 64-bit protected binaries. AETHER-64 introduces three foundational innovations: (1) Local-Context Handler Symbolic Slicing, which reconstructs complete Control-Flow Graphs (CFGs) through isolated basic block emulation without accumulating global path constraints; (2) a bit-parallel Algebraic Pre-Reduction (APR) filter grounded in Boolean conjunction lattice signatures and fast Moebius inversion over Z/2^64, resolving invariant dispatch conditions in O(1) time; and (3) syntax-directed I/O-guided non-linear MBA synthesis coupled with LLVM Static Single Assignment (SSA) virtual stack elimination. We evaluate AETHER-64 on the Quarkslab Diffing Obfuscation Dataset (104 ground-truth functions across MiniLua, Zlib, and SQLite comprising 56,883 bytecode instructions), 1,000 synthetic Tigress virtual machines, commercial protections (VMProtect 3.4/3.5, Themida 3.1), and 7-layer non-linear MBA expressions. AETHER-64 achieves 100% CFG recovery, resolves 93.91% of branch queries via APR filtering with an empirical 2,072.8x speedup over raw SMT resolution, eliminates 91.8% of instruction bloat, and reconstructs clean, human-verifiable C pseudocode with mathematical bisimulation guarantees.
title: AETHER-64: High-Throughput Binary Devirtualization via Bit-Parallel Algebraic Pre-Reduction and SSA Bytecode Promotion

summary: Analysis code for the manuscript submitted to Kidney International Reports (KIR-S-26-00587). The study uses target trial emulation with clone-censor-weighting (CCW) to estimate the effect of early (<=24 h) vs no/late insulin initiation on AKI progression among sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI) patients, stratified by a glucose-trajectory phenotype (P2 = high-sustained). Includes primary CCW analyses, a negative control outcome (NCO) sensitivity analysis, eICU-CRD 2.0 external validation (phenotypic portability), and an exploratory MIMIC-III CareVue replication. Data sources (PhysioNet credentialed): MIMIC-IV (discovery), eICU-CRD 2.0, MIMIC-III CareVue. Reported under STROBE + RECORD + TARGET.
title: BD2: Insulin timing and glucose-trajectory phenotypes in sepsis-associated acute kidney injury - analysis code

summary: Code and results for the paper “Learning Interpretable Dispatch Rules for Aircraft Disassembly under Disruption” (H. Saleh, submitted). The package contains: an event-driven simulator of aircraft teardown with licensed crews, zone capacity and mass balance; two disruption models, one with announced absences and one with pause-and-resume absences, both with hidden work; an independent schedule checker and the hindsight lower bound; genetic programming for priority rules; the competitors: classic priority rules, a look-ahead (rollout), and CP-SAT re-planning at every event; the result files of every experiment in the paper (15,734 schedules, all valid), with scripts that rebuild the tables and figures from them. The learned rule is priority = LST − 0.5·CERT: the latest start time minus a head start for licensed seats. Benchmark data are not included. The aircraft disassembly benchmark of Thomas and Schaus and the MSLIB instances are downloaded from their sources; the README gives the commands and pinned versions. Code: MIT license. Results and figures: CC BY 4.0.
title: Learned dispatch rules for aircraft disassembly under disruption: code and results

summary: DIGITAL EVIDENCE AND QUALIFICATION ENGINEERING FOR MICROROBOTIC MISSION RELIABILITY AT THE LIMIT English Introduction This high-density research monograph develops a falsifiable qualification architecture for microrobotic mission reliability. Its central coupling is mission evidence x metrological traceability x release contract. summary: The work builds a foundation of physics from a single assumption: everything is a process, and a process is an ideal sine; its centre, the balance, is the observer. Only the square — intensity without phase — passes between levels; from this arise dimensions, the arrow of time, the quantum and the standard. On this basis stable particles are built as standing waves together with their galactic analogues, the initial rules of quantum mechanics and relativity are derived, and the constants are linked to a single number — the speed of light. Agreement with experiment is at the level of a few percent; the model attributes the discrepancies to the imperfection of the standard. Main results The four stable particles (neutrino, electron, neutron, proton) are the four stable states of a standing wave; masses from the speed of light alone: electron +0.7 %, nucleons about −3 % [result given hypotheses]. The Born rule, the randomness of a single outcome, the 2√2 limit in the Bell test, spin ½ and g = 2 [result]. The Lorentz transformation from the “speed budget” c² = v² + v_int², the Klein — Gordon and Schrödinger equations, Schwarzschild gravitational time dilation and the light deflection of 1.75″ [result]. Similarity of the small and the large with the step c⁴: the image of the neutron is the stellar mass of the Milky Way (5.5·10¹⁰ versus (6.1 ± 1.1)·10¹⁰ solar masses) [hypothesis, numerical agreement]. The large end is built by the same logic as the microworld: the construction yields the Hubble constant H₀ = 1/(5c²) ≈ 68.7 km/s/Mpc and the smallest acceleration of galaxies a₀ = 1/(10πc) [result given hypotheses]. The gravitational constant G ≈ c^(−6/5) (0.8 %); the mass of the Universe and the scale of dark energy are expressed through c [hypothesis]. The fine-structure constant has been found as the number 1/α ≈ 4·(c/2π)^(1/5) (0.22 %); its meaning is open [observation]. Limitations: the accuracy is percent-level, not parts per million; the standard and several constants remain open questions. The status of each statement is given in the text. Revision dated 2026-10-24:   The black hole. A black hole is understood as the construction of mass from the large end: particles build mass from the small end, the black hole from the large one. Perception has a limit of tempo: a process whose tempo is below our smallest does not change for us, so the centre is inaccessible, and for us it is space possessing mass and rotation. The horizon is the transition from space into mass; it grows with mass and is not related to the core. The black hole processes volumetric particles into a plane, and the tension of space, when the sizes of galaxies change, again gives birth to particle–antiparticle pairs: the cycle is closed. Only black holes that are analogues of elementary particles are considered. G and α. Both constants have received a geometric reading. Gravity is the work of space in a cross-section, charge is the same work over a closed surface; the surface of a sphere is four times its cross-section, hence the four. Charge is the work of one unpaired half-wave, that is, of one step of the microworld k: 1/α = 4k. G is gravity from the large end: the whole linear path up to the transition and the step linking it with the small end, G = 1/(c·c^(1/5)), without the four. The link of the two constants is G = 4α/((2π)^(1/5)·c). In neutral particles the same transition from flat to volume goes through rotation (support: the magnetic moment of the neutron). The residuals of 0.22 % in α and 0.8 % in G are not yet explained.       Работа строит основу физики из одного допущения: всё — процесс, а процесс — идеальный синус; его центр, баланс, — наблюдатель. Между уровнями проходит только квадрат — интенсивност
title: The Birth of Dimensions: A Formal Skeleton

summary: The onset of ferromagnetic order in one dimension reflects a competition between domain energy and entropy. For Ising chains with arbitrary translation-invariant, nonnegative, summable pair interactions, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for an ordered phase at positive temperature: the energy required to reverse an interval of N spins must be bounded below by a positive multiple of ln N for all sufficiently large N. When this energy is also bounded above by a finite multiple of ln N, we prove a quantitative magnetization gap, implying a nonzero spontaneous magnetization at the critical temperature and a discontinuous onset of order. No monotonicity, regular decay, or nearest-neighbor coupling is required. The results include sparse and irregular interactions for which r^2 J(r) is unbounded. Our results extend the magnetization jump beyond pointwise inverse-square bounds to every chain whose domain energy has logarithmic upper and lower bounds.
title: Onset of Ferromagnetic Order in Ising Chains

summary: This study presents a comprehensive analysis integrating archaeological evidence with modelled radiocarbon dating, isotopic data, and organic residue analysis, offering new insights into prehistoric funerary practices in south-eastern Europe, as exemplified by burial mound number 3 at Mogila, Bulgaria. The mound contained twelve graves, including eleven inhumations and one cremation. The primary chronological classification of the inhumations was based on burial rites and body positions, assigning them to the Early Bronze Age and Middle/Late Bronze Age. Together with a shallowly deposited cremation dated to the Iron Age, three main phases of mound use were identified. Radiocarbon dating enabled the refinement of these phases allowing a detailed reconstruction of the mound’s chronological development and the identification of successive sequences of burial deposition within each period. It also allowed for the chronological attribution of two disarticulated burials. Stable carbon (δ¹³C) and nitrogen (δ¹⁵N) isotope values of the buried individuals revealed similarities within sub-phases of the Early Bronze Age and Middle/Late Bronze Age, as well as dietary differences between individuals from the two periods. In addition, a clay vessel from Middle/Late Bronze Age grave number 10 complemented the isotopic results, indicating the presence of animal lipids, most likely dairy fats.
title: The Long Life of a Burial Mound at Mogila, Bulgaria: From the Bronze Age to the Iron Age

summary: DIGITAL EVIDENCE AND QUALIFICATION ENGINEERING FOR MICROROBOTIC MISSION RELIABILITY AT THE LIMIT English Introduction This high-density research monograph develops a falsifiable qualification architecture for microrobotic mission reliability. Its central coupling is mission evidence x metrological traceability x release contract. A successful demonstration is not treated as an engineering release: every decisive quantity must retain raw ancestry, calibration, uncertainty, protocol version, software identity, failure context, and independent adjudication. The central artifact is the Mission Qualification Capsule. It binds the reference mission, operating domain, hardware and lot genealogy, immutable raw event streams, digital calibration objects, covariance, provenance graph, software and configuration manifests, failure ontology, missingness, terminal functional evidence, threshold history, change control, negative results, and release ruling. A second laboratory should be able to reproduce the metric, failure classification, and final action without private communication from the original authors.

summary: For a finite connected graph $G$, let $e(G)$ be the exponent of its Jacobian and $\Delta(G)$ its maximum degree. For each integer $b\ge1$, the simple biconnected graphs with $e(G)\le b$ form finitely many isomorphism classes if and only if $b\le7$; exactly eleven occur with $e(G)\le7$. The simple biconnected graphs with $e(G)-\Delta(G)\le3$ are $K_n$ ($n\ge3$), $C_4$, $C_5$ and $K_{2,3}$. At exponent eight, the number of vertices is unbounded among simple planar bipartite biconnected graphs of maximum degree four. For every integer $r\ge1$, there is a simple planar biconnected graph whose Jacobian is isomorphic to $(\mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z)^r$, with explicit divisor generators and an orthogonal decomposition of its monodromy pairing. Every simple $3$-connected planar graph satisfies $2|V(G)|-4\le(e(G)-\Delta(G)+1)^2$ and $2|V(G)|-5\le3e(G)^2/5$. Every simple graph with a cellular torus embedding whose full inverse image in the universal cover of the torus is $3$-connected satisfies $|V(G)|\le e(G)^2$. MSC 2020: 05C25, 05C50, 05C10, 05C40, 20K01.
title: Finiteness thresholds and surface bounds for graph Jacobians

summary: Coordinating molecular, cellular, and macroscopic explanations is a core requirement of secondary biology and chemistry, yet classroom assessments still infer a student's developmental level from written answers collected after an inquiry task ends. Digital process telemetry—the timestamped record of a student's clicks, slider sweeps, pauses, and revisions inside a simulation—captures how learners navigate across scales in real time, but raw interaction counts lack a shared unit of measurement with curriculum learning progressions. This study addresses that measurement gap through a two-part validation. First, a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis of 86 studies (312 effect sizes; 48,920 learners) synthesized cross-scale inquiry interventions and yielded a pooled Hedges' g of 0.642, demonstrating that adaptive next-step scaffolding, paste-guarded response entry, and explicit cross-scale representations each significantly amplify learning gains. Second, using a fixed-parameter reconstruction of that empirical benchmark alongside a simulated bilingual cohort of 1,240 secondary learners and 1,000 Monte Carlo replications, we calibrated six non-intrusive behavioural trace indicators against a 12-item ordered multiple-choice progression bank on a unified Rasch partial credit logit scale. Common-scale linking error was 0.118 logits (10.9% of the critical Level 2–3 transition interval). Trace-based classifications reproduced item-based progression levels with 81.45% accuracy and Gwet's first-order agreement coefficient of .768, exhibited strict measurement invariance across language tracks, gender, and prior achievement, and confirmed that genuine self-regulatory behaviours rather than interface guardrails drive diagnostic classification. Behavioural traces can thus provide calibrated, equitable coordinates for real-time formative support in secondary science classrooms.
title: From Clicks to Constructs: Event-Stream Process Mining, TreeSHAP Attribution, and Rasch Partial Credit Calibration of Behavioural Trace Indicators for Cross-Scale Science Reasoning

summary: This Zenodo record accompanies the paper “Scalable Measurement-Based Quantum Simulation Patterns for Benchmarking” arXiv.2605.12502   and provides QPatLib v1.0 measurement-pattern datasets in human-readable JSONL together with a ZIP archive of OpenQASM 3.0 circuits used for validation and reproducibility.  The patterns and circuits implement Pauli string unitaries  for benchmark cases.  Cases include all possible string combinations for less than 6 qubits and strings used in Hamiltonians for certain diatomic molecules for 6 or more qubits.     Format:  Each  pattern_*.jsonl file is containins measurement patterns for all subsets for a given model/instance and subset strategy: it begins with a preamble containing model metadata, subset definitions, provenance, and (when feasible) full-pattern test results, followed by one pattern entry per subset. Each subset entry includes a required  pattern_ascii field storing the measurement pattern in the measurement-calculus/Graphix standard with signal shifting, written left-to-right in the canonical order nodes → edges → measurements (with signal dependencies) → byproduct corrections (X/Z). The circuits are included as circuit_files.zip.   Patterns in this record were validated against the corresponding circuits and checked for causal flow.   Codes for generating these patterns can be found at QPatLib repository on Github

summary: Two datasets recording immigration detention oversight in the inspecting bodies' and ICE's own published language. The inspections dataset (207 rows) gives the most recent published inspection per facility from ICE Office of Detention Oversight reports in the ICE FOIA Library 2025–2026 listing window (179 facilities) plus the 28 facility-specific DHS Office of Inspector General detention inspection reports of fiscal years 2021–2026, with each report's published Facility Rating and deficient-standards count reproduced verbatim, never re-graded. The deaths dataset (84 rows) lists the deaths in ICE custody in ICE's Detainee Death Reporting tables for fiscal years 2021–2026, each with the ICE death report ICE itself published (name, age, country of citizenship, facility, date of death, and cause of death where the report states one). Sources: ICE FOIA Library, DHS Office of Inspector General, and ICE Detainee Death Reporting, retrieved October 23, 2026. Tool: https://inspections-ledger.straitresearch.org/. Direction and final calls by Athena Anthea; research judgment and technical execution shared with an AI assistant. Version 1.1 (October 24, 2026) adds: a published facility-name crosswalk (200 canonical facilities) with single-facility dossiers joining ODO, OIG, and deaths records per facility; an extraction naming the deficient standards behind the published counts for 52 of the 179 ODO inspection rows (validated by hand-checking 10 reports; coverage and per-row failure reasons stated, never guessed); and deaths tables showing cause stated (12) vs not stated (72) by fiscal year and facility.
title: Inspections & Deaths Ledger: detention facility inspection results and deaths in ICE custody from the official record — a Strait Research dataset

summary: pt selection with a position-by-position wild-type amino-acid check; 4. a gene-level inflation test and a silent-mutation (synonymous) control that    distinguishes elevated local background mutation rate from positive selection. The archive contains 16 scripts in two groups. Group 1 (6 scripts) reproduces the filtering cascade, the neutral gene-set control, the TCGA MC3 replication and the reference-panel benchmark. Group 2 (10 scripts, numbered 20-29) implements the silent-mutation control reported in Table 8: donor-level observed/expected ratios, exact Poisson upper-tail P values, the non-silent-to-silent fold with a delta-method 95% confidence interval, and the coding-length-matched percentile. All machine-specific paths have been replaced by environment-overridable defaults (ARG_ROOT, ARG_ANALYSIS, ARG_SILENT); see 00_README.md. Inputs are entirely public (ICGC open-tier simple_somatic_mutation files; 1000 Genomes Phase 3; gnomAD v2.1.1; the TCGA MC3 public MAF). No credentials and no controlled-access data are required.
title: ARG-QC: quality-control pipeline for pharmacogene somatic-mutation analyses of open-access cancer genomics data

summary: Overview This repository contains the replication data, source code, execution logs, and complete analytical outputs for the study: “Detectability of controlled leaks in an Andean water transmission main: a field evaluation of changepoint methods on flow and pressure signals.” The study evaluates the detectability of short-duration controlled leaks using five changepoint and anomaly-detection approaches applied to 30-second flow and pressure measurements collected during two field campaigns in an operational water transmission main in Loja, Ecuador. The evaluated methods are: Pruned Exact Linear Time using the Bayesian Information Criterion (PELT-BIC), Pruned Exact Linear Time using the Akaike Information Criterion (PELT-AIC), Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection (BOCD), Cumulative Sum control charts (CUSUM), Moving-average ±3σ control-chart baseline. The repository contains the complete workflow used to: verify field records and ground-truth leak timings; perform campaign-specific spectral analyses using multitaper estimation; evaluate changepoint-detection performance; quantify event-level leak detectability; compare observed performance against chance-level expectations; assess BOCD sensitivity to hazard-rate and threshold settings; generate precision-recall curves and average-precision statistics; perform cross-campaign validation analyses; estimate theoretical detection-delay bounds for flow-based detection. This version supersedes earlier releases by correcting changepoint-index alignment, revising false-alarm-rate calculations using exposure time outside detection windows, replacing pooled spectral analyses with campaign-specific multitaper analyses, and incorporating event-level detectability, chance-level benchmarking, precision-recall evaluation, cross-campaign validation, and theoretical detection-delay analyses. Dataset Description The repository is organized into raw data files and compressed archives containing the complete computational environment and analytical outputs. 1. Primary Data (Raw) Q_P_80_Leak1.xlsx 30-second flow (Q) and pressure (P) measurements collected during the first controlled-leak field campaign. Q_P_46_Leak2.xlsx 30-second flow (Q) and pressure (P) measurements collected during the second controlled-leak field campaign. 2. Source Code and Execution Logs This archive contains: CHANGEPOINT_Rcode.R Complete R workflow for: data verification and screening; descriptive statistical analysis; event-level leak detectability assessment; multitaper spectral analysis; PELT-BIC and PELT-AIC changepoint detection; Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection (BOCD); CUSUM detection; moving-average ±3σ detection; chance-level benchmarking; hazard-rate × threshold sensitivity analysis; cross-campaign BOCD validation; precision-recall and average-precision analysis; theoretical detection-delay modelling. CHANGEPOINT_Console.txt Complete console log documenting: descriptive statistics; event-level detectability results; spectral-analysis outputs; changepoint locations; detector performance metrics; chance-level comparisons; precision-recall analyses; BOCD validation results; theoretical delay-bound calculations. 3. Model Outputs (analisis_output.zip) changepoint/ ground_truth_trials.csv detector_performance_by_trial.csv detector_performance_extended.csv detector_performance_pooled.csv hazard_threshold_sweep.csv bocd_cross_campaign.csv average_precision.csv pr_operating_points.csv mcnemar_signal.csv mcnemar_methods.csv spectral_summary.csv cusum_delay_bound.csv cusum_delay_curve.csv cusum_delay_mc_check.csv BOCD_Leak1_flow.csv BOCD_Leak1_pressure.csv BOCD_Leak2_flow.csv BOCD_Leak2_pressure.csv changepoint_objects.rds figures/ High-resolution TIFF figures (600 dpi): Fig7.tif: campaign-specific multitaper spectral analyses; Fig8.tif: flow and pressure time series with leak intervals and detected changepoints; Fig9.tif: BOCD posterior probabilities; Fig10.tif: detection lat

The repository contains the complete workflow used to: verify field records and ground-truth leak timings; perform campaign-specific spectral analyses using multitaper estimation; evaluate changepoint-detection performance; quantify event-level leak detectability; compare observed performance against chance-level expectations; assess BOCD sensitivity to hazard-rate and threshold settings; generate precision-recall curves and average-precision statistics; perform cross-campaign validation analyses; estimate theoretical detection-delay bounds for flow-based detection. This version supersedes earlier releases by correcting changepoint-index alignment, revising false-alarm-rate calculations using exposure time outside detection windows, replacing pooled spectral analyses with campaign-specific multitaper analyses, and incorporating event-level detectability, chance-level benchmarking, precision-recall evaluation, cross-campaign validation, and theoretical detection-delay analyses. Dataset Description The repository is organized into raw data files and compressed archives containing the complete computational environment and analytical outputs. 1. Primary Data (Raw) Q_P_80_Leak1.xlsx 30-second flow (Q) and pressure (P) measurements collected during the first controlled-leak field campaign. Q_P_46_Leak2.xlsx 30-second flow (Q) and pressure (P) measurements collected during the second controlled-leak field campaign. 2. Source Code and Execution Logs This archive contains: CHANGEPOINT_Rcode.R Complete R workflow for: data verification and screening; descriptive statistical analysis; event-level leak detectability assessment; multitaper spectral analysis; PELT-BIC and PELT-AIC changepoint detection; Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection (BOCD); CUSUM detection; moving-average ±3σ detection; chance-level benchmarking; hazard-rate × threshold sensitivity analysis; cross-campaign BOCD validation; precision-recall and average-precision analysis; theoretical detection-delay modelling. CHANGEPOINT_Console.txt Complete console log documenting: descriptive statistics; event-level detectability results; spectral-analysis outputs; changepoint locations; detector performance metrics; chance-level comparisons; precision-recall analyses; BOCD validation results; theoretical delay-bound calculations. 3. summary: After more than a decade of development, high-resolution spectroscopy plays a central role in the atmospheric characterization of exoplanets, offering insights into planetary chemical composition, thermal structure, and atmospheric dynamics. Among the most intriguing targets for atmospheric characterization are Ultra-Hot Jupiters (UHJs), which, due to their extreme temperatures and intense stellar irradiation, serve as unique laboratories for studying planetary atmospheres under extreme conditions. In this talk, I will discuss what we can learn and what challenges we must confront when interpreting high-resolution observations of UHJs, using KELT-9b (equilibrium temperature ~4000 K) as a benchmark case. Based on transmission and emission observations obtained with the near-infrared spectrograph GIANO-B at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo (TNG), I explore how different modeling assumptions impact the detectability and interpretation of atmospheric signals. In particular, the extreme irradiation conditions of these planets may give rise to departures from local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE), making non-LTE effects potentially non-negligible. At the same time, the strong day–night temperature contrasts and asymmetric terminator regions expected in UHJs challenge the applicability of 1D atmospheric models, which may lead to biased or incomplete interpretations of the observed signals.   These effects can have important consequences for the inferred atmospheric abundances and bias the interpretation of key quantities such as the C/O and R/H ratios, which are used to constrain planetary formation and evolutionary scenarios. Addressing these challenges is therefore crucial to robustly link high-resolution observations of UHJs to their origins.
title: INTERPRETING EXTREME ATMOSPHERES: Lessons from High-Resolution spectroscopy of an Ultra-Hot Jupiter

At the same time, the strong day–night temperature contrasts and asymmetric terminator regions expected in UHJs challenge the applicability of 1D atmospheric models, which may lead to biased or incomplete interpretations of the observed signals.   These effects can have important consequences for the inferred atmospheric abundances and bias the interpretation of key quantities such as the C/O and R/H ratios, which are used to constrain planetary formation and evolutionary scenarios. Addressing these challenges is therefore crucial to robustly link high-resolution observations of UHJs to their origins.
title: INTERPRETING EXTREME ATMOSPHERES: Lessons from High-Resolution spectroscopy of an Ultra-Hot Jupiter

summary: The spectroscopic analysis of cool dwarfs (T_eff < 4700 K) is challenging due to their low effective temperatures, which produce complex spectra dominated by dense molecular absorption bands. These challenges have limited the availability of accurate and homogeneous chemical abundance measurements for these stars. To address these difficulties, we developed AutoSpecFit (ASF) , an automated, line-by-line synthetic spectral fitting code, together with AutoSpecNorm (ASN) , a complementary code designed to perform local pseudo-continuum normalization of observed and synthetic spectra. The combined ASF+ASN framework enables detailed chemical abundance analysis of cool dwarfs using high-resolution optical and near-infrared spectra. ASF employs multiple χ² minimization procedures and iterative optimization to account for the complex correlations among elemental abundances. ASN independently normalizes each synthetic spectrum, ensuring consistent comparisons with observations and reducing uncertainties associated with continuum placement in molecularly crowded spectral regions. Version 2.0 extends the original abundance-fitting framework by introducing an iterative procedure that alternates between the determination of stellar atmospheric parameters and elemental abundances. This approach accounts for the interdependencies between atmospheric parameters and chemical abundances, while employing selected diagnostic spectral lines and iterative optimization to mitigate parameter degeneracies and achieve a self-consistent solution. The updated methodology has been applied to benchmark M dwarfs with independently determined stellar properties, providing an opportunity to evaluate the reliability and consistency of the derived atmospheric parameters and elemental abundances. The ASF+ASN framework has been developed to measure the abundances of up to 15 key elements in cool dwarfs, including major planet-building elements such as C, O, Mg, Si, and Fe. These measurements provide essential constraints on the chemical compositions of exoplanetary systems and their formation and evolution. Furthermore, the application of this framework to metal-poor cool dwarfs offers opportunities to investigate the chemical enrichment history, structure, and evolution of the Milky Way.
title: Detailed Abundance Measurements of Cool Dwarfs: Prospects for Exploring the Galaxy from Stellar Populations to Star-Planet Chemical Connections

summary: One record for each of 18 major U.S. immigration cases of the current period, verified October 23-24, 2026 against primary or near-primary sources (Supreme Court dockets and slip opinions, CourtListener/RECAP dockets and order PDFs - including docket entries read through the CourtListener API - court opinions, and named litigation trackers). Each record gives the caption, court, docket number, category, filing date, the action challenged, a claims summary, a status from a fixed eight-value vocabulary, the latest significant order with source, a docket link, key primary documents, a per-record verification date, and a status-tension field recording disagreements between sources. Version 1.1 adds, per case: the next dated event with its source (plus a forward calendar export; only fully dated events are calendared), structured practical-effect fields (population affected, geographic scope, relief currently in effect with its basis) transcribed from the complaint or operative order named in each record, and an append-only status-change log seeded with the v1.0 baseline. It also resolves the Massachusetts v. Oz summary-judgment hearing date from the docket itself (held October 22, 2026; CourtListener docket 73546826, entry 143). Coverage: birthright citizenship (4), TPS terminations (3), third-country removals (2), asylum access (2), enforcement practices (2), Alien Enemies Act cases (2), Medicaid work requirements (1), parole (1), detention (1). Tool: https://litigation-map.straitresearch.org/. Direction and final calls by Athena Anthea; research judgment and technical execution shared with an AI assistant.

summary: This record contains the replication data and R code for the study “How much does the publication universe matter? Source discontinuities and panel selection in OpenAlex” by Vladislav Bína and Jiří Přibil. The package includes OpenAlex source-by-year counts for 2010–2025 retrieved on 10–11 October 2026, supplementary OpenAlex and Crossref aggregate counts retrieved on 23 October 2026, a provenance-limited earlier archive of annual totals, and twelve annotated illustrative record checks. It also provides eight R scripts, expected numerical results, numerical inputs to the figures, and English documentation. The default workflow reproduces the saved-data analyses offline using base R. It covers publication growth, continuity panels, source turnover, panel-selection timing, population layers, and sensitivity to comparison horizons and endpoints. Version 2.2 was tested with R 4.5.2 on Windows. Data provenance, variable definitions, limitations and reproduction instructions are documented in README.md. summary: HBB2OBB converts horizontal (axis-aligned) bounding boxes (HBBs) into oriented (rotated) bounding boxes (OBBs) by using existing HBB annotations as prompts for segmentation models from the SAM (Segment Anything Model) family. It targets object detection tasks where objects appear at arbitrary orientations, such as aerial imagery, satellite data, and traffic monitoring, producing oriented boxes that tightly encapsulate non-upright objects without any re-annotation. Beyond conversion, it provides horizontal box detection, evaluation, hyperparameter optimization, an interactive annotation viewer, and annotation format-conversion tools, exposed through both a command-line interface and a Python API. 📖 Documentation: rfonod.github.io/hbb2obb , with a quick start on the bundled sample data, a guide per command, pages on how the conversion works, the confidence score, the metrics and provenance, and a CLI and API reference generated from the code. Why HBB2OBB 🎯 Accurate OBBs from HBBs : prompts SAM-family segmentation models with existing horizontal boxes to fit tight oriented boxes around non-upright objects, with no re-annotation required. 🚗 No HBBs? Detect them : the hbb2obb-detect command runs an Ultralytics detector over the images and writes the horizontal boxes the conversion consumes, confidence column included. 🧩 Model ensemble : combines masks from multiple SAM variants through majority voting for more robust, accurate results. 🛡️ Spatially constrained and safe : region-specific masking and contour refinement keep segmentation inside the object, a mask split by an occluder is fitted back together, and a fallback retains the original HBB when no valid mask is found, counted and reported rather than left to be discovered afterwards. 🔎 Confidence-scored output : every OBB receives a heuristic quality score in [0, 1] that flags silent fallbacks and low-confidence conversions, so you know which boxes to trust; the scores go in the label files or in a side-car directory that keeps them strictly standard, and the detector's own confidence can be carried through instead of, or on top of, that score. 📐 Flexible scaling : positive or negative scale factors, optionally different for the short and long sides, recover cropped object parts or tighten overly conservative annotations. 📊 Evaluate and optimize : evaluation against ground truth on IoU, orientation error, and the share of boxes above a high IoU bar, plus the hbb2obb-optimize command, a hyperparameter search over SAM inference resolution, scale factors, and morphological opening kernel, driven by a configuration file so that a whole benchmark of model ensembles is a single reproducible command. 🔬 Where the score comes from : the hbb2obb-analyze command breaks one evaluation down by the ground truth's orientation, size, frame edge, difficulty and class, and scores the conversion against emitting the horizontal prompt unchanged. 🔄 Five annotation formats : read and write YOLO, DOTA, Pascal VOC, COCO, and LabelMe, for horizontal and oriented boxes alike, with a check that proves every format encodes the same boxes. 🔍 Interactive viewer : the hbb2obb-view command pans and zooms over the annotations, in any format, coloring boxes by confidence and overlaying predictions against ground truth. Where a set ships the same boxes several ways, it names the format on screen and switches between them on a keypress. Features HBB to OBB conversion of YOLO-format annotations using SAM-based segmentation, written in absolute pixels or, with --normalize , relative to [0, 1], the convention Ultralytics reads. HBB detection : produce the horizontal boxes in the first place with any Ultralytics detector, a local file, a link, the Ultralytics catalogue, or Hugging Face, passing any other predictor argument straight through. Multiple model support : SAM, SAM2, SAM2.1, SAM3, Mobile SAM, and FastSAM families. Model ensemble via majority voting for enhanced accuracy. Confidence scoring : a per-OBB quali

summary: Pytest Receptor 1.2.2 fixes external-helper rerun targets and runtime evidence cleanup while preserving pytest outcomes, counts, public profiles and pytest-receptor.events@1 compatibility. Pathless external tests retain their collected test path independently of a helper's crash location; generated reruns select the original tests (#39). Stats, JSONL and terminal streams retain ownership through failures, expose cleanup errors nonfatally and preserve original interrupts/caller evidence (#43). Benchmark tools protect other callers' scratch and reap interrupted direct children (#40/#41); documentation cleanup preserves neighboring work for spaced/leading-dash build paths (#44). Dependency/source publication gates and operational resource ownership are reviewed and retained (#38/#42). README/documentation benchmark references are refreshed using an installed measurement wheel, Python 3.14.7 and saved runtime/harness identities. The optional test_path evidence field is additive; older v1 artifacts/readers remain supported. Release source/tag: 531bafde5d48ddd8974e29ac91ae53ecae0fd787 / 1.2.2 . Python range remains >=3.11,<3.15 , runtime dependency pytest>=8 . Ordinary source CI , full compatibility and documentation pass at that exact source. Native required job/step verification is retained separately from compact reports. Qualified Conda file: pytest-receptor-1.2.2-py_0.tar.bz2 ; SHA-256 c0b075286f45e8fce5ab5852947611bfba82b7d509115fc5dadf1a9572b9dd74 . Staging produced and uploaded those bytes once. Installed qualification passes the complete declared test selection in all eight Linux/macOS arm64 × Python 3.11–3.14 cells outside source imports. Native run/attempt/job/step checks, source/file binding, dependency closures and final provenance rechecks are verified for the same staged file. Producer and qualification source are both the release commit above. Public PyPI delivery and Conda main promotion will be recorded after independent registry and fresh-install verification. Release evidence: pytest-receptor #45 ; version-specific coordination: MolSysSuite #133 .

summary: HIMS-CDI Synthetic Data Archive Companion to: "HIMS-CDI: A Governance Specification and Assurance Architecture for CTI-Driven Cybersecurity Risk Assessment in Healthcare" This archive contains the production synthetic-data pipeline, the prespecified correlation matrix, and the labelled 240-environment dataset used in the Phase I specification-validation study reported in Section 4 of the manuscript. The synthetic corpus comprises 240 healthcare cybersecurity environments, each characterised by 20 indicators across five groups (CTI Modality, Semantic Enrichment, Fusion Strategy, Regulatory Traceability, Explainability). The pipeline applies empirical marginal transformations (beta, categorical), generates labels via the three non-compensatory governance gates (CDI ≥ 0.70, CCR ≥ 0.80, latency < 200 ms, memory < 100 MB), injects Gaussian noise (σ = 0.13), and performs a stratified 60/20/20 split (seed 123). The test split yields exactly 48 environments (32 NOT_DEPLOY_SYNTH, 16 DEPLOY_SYNTH), matching the manuscript's specification. Random seeds: 42 = corpus generation; 123 = stratified split; 10-seed sweep = model-training runs. Provenance: The correlation matrix is a prespecified design parameter, not an empirical estimate. MITRE ATT&CK v14.1 technique frequencies and dwell-time parameters (mean 62 days, SD 28 days) are prespecified simulation assumptions, not observed healthcare incident statistics. Epistemic boundary: This archive supports Phase I specification testing only. It does not contain real healthcare incident data, and the synthetic evaluation does not establish clinical safety, operational effectiveness, real-world predictive validity, or operational deployment readiness. Phase II validation against real healthcare incident outcomes is planned (see manuscript Section 6.2–6.3).

summary: BIODEGRADABLE NANOROBOT MANUFACTURING AND LIFECYCLE ENGINEERING AT THE LIMIT Biodegradable Materials x Functional Manufacturing x Degradation Kinetics This high-density English research monograph develops a falsification-oriented architecture for manufacturing biodegradable biomedical nano- and microrobots whose functional lifetime and terminal fate can be jointly qualified. Its central problem is a dual-clock constraint: the device must preserve propulsion, structure and interface function throughout a declared mission, then degrade or be retrieved within a separate terminal window without leaving unidentified or high-risk residues. The volume refuses to treat in-vitro weight loss as biological clearance. Hydrolysis, molecular-weight reduction, erosion, dissolution, fragmentation, adsorption, retrieval, magnetic-core persistence, biological transformation and safe elimination are defined as distinct measurable states. A five-compartment ledger preserves solid mass, soluble products, fragments, recovered material and unexplained residual; the last category is never presumed safe. The monograph contains 30 distinct mathematical research plates, 82 chapters, 410 independently paginated section studies, 200 detailed Research Gates and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Formula plates state variables, units, assumptions, identifiability, specific blind falsification tests and chapter interfaces. summary: Resolution Geometry: A Kernel–Stabilizer Geometry of Observability Abstract Resolution Geometry (RG) is a protocol-explicit framework for characterizing what a declared observation system can distinguish, preserve, and consistently infer. Its starting point is a family of observation laws together with admissible outcome relabelings, rather than a covariance decomposition, metric, or dynamical model. Equality of the joint observation law defines a kernel groupoid and an observational quotient, canonically identified with the law image. An experiment-internal quantity is identifiable precisely when it is constant on observational fibres. The quotient alone determines neither a metric nor a connection, causal structure, clock, physical scale, or law of motion. The framework separates exact observational equivalence from statistical distinguishability, admissibility, symmetry, and physical realization. The stabilizer of the observation law induces a faithful effective action on the quotient. Liftable symmetry is distinguished from symmetry of the law image: the former can depend on the latent presentation, whereas the observable layer is presentation-invariant once its law-space structures and declarations are fixed. On regular strata, natural modules defined by pullback from law space descend uniquely to the observational quotient. This gives representative independence and projectability for law-defined structures, without asserting that naturality selects those structures. In regular classical experiments, the Fisher tensor supplies infinitesimal distinguishability under the stated Markov-monotonicity assumptions; its radical agrees with the observational vertical space under the corresponding regularity conditions. Quantum protocols require a declared operational task to select within the family of monotone metrics. A central organizing result concerns task-preserving conversion . For a representation map and a declared family of downstream tasks, RG characterizes the exact set of compatible task outcomes on each representation fibre. Unique inference is possible exactly when this residual is a singleton. Otherwise the appropriate output is a correspondence or a typed abstention, not an arbitrary hidden representative. Pairing a representation with its tasks gives a terminal sufficient refinement. For declared operations, observational closure is expressed by the greatest operation-stable congruence contained in the observation kernel. These constructions distinguish local differential rank, global orbit separation, observational completeness, and reconstruction, and make preservation requirements explicit under composition. Second-order realizations provide concrete classification and computational tools. Under a declared block-orthogonal gauge, a covariance datum is encoded by a symmetric matrix tuple whose ordered word traces form a complete pointwise invariant, including repeated eigenvalues, vanishing couplings, and rank-deficient sectors. On simple-spectrum strata, mixed moments recover coupling magnitudes, while independent cycle holonomies complete the residual sign classification. This distinguishes hidden values omitted by a descriptor from distinctions that are genuinely observationally null . Under the different contract of covariance-preserving block-linear transformations, canonical correlations with multiplicity classify pointwise data; constant-type families additionally carry bundle and gluing information. Pointwise classification therefore does not replace the transport, relative alignment, or global data required by field-level tasks. Across rank, symmetry, and protocol changes, RG uses specialization maps when kernel inclusion permits them and correspondences otherwise. Smooth geometry is confined to its regular domain; proper-groupoid and tame settings support stratified descriptions with slices, tangent cones, and orbit-type changes. Finite-resolution statements are separated from exact model state

Equality of the joint observation law defines a kernel groupoid and an observational quotient, canonically identified with the law image. An experiment-internal quantity is identifiable precisely when it is constant on observational fibres. The quotient alone determines neither a metric nor a connection, causal structure, clock, physical scale, or law of motion. The framework separates exact observational equivalence from statistical distinguishability, admissibility, symmetry, and physical realization. The stabilizer of the observation law induces a faithful effective action on the quotient. Liftable symmetry is distinguished from symmetry of the law image: the former can depend on the latent presentation, whereas the observable layer is presentation-invariant once its law-space structures and declarations are fixed. On regular strata, natural modules defined by pullback from law space descend uniquely to the observational quotient. This gives representative independence and projectability for law-defined structures, without asserting that naturality selects those structures. In regular classical experiments, the Fisher tensor supplies infinitesimal distinguishability under the stated Markov-monotonicity assumptions; its radical agrees with the observational vertical space under the corresponding regularity conditions. Quantum protocols require a declared operational task to select within the family of monotone metrics. A central organizing result concerns task-preserving conversion . For a representation map and a declared family of downstream tasks, RG characterizes the exact set of compatible task outcomes on each representation fibre. Unique inference is possible exactly when this residual is a singleton. Otherwise the appropriate output is a correspondence or a typed abstention, not an arbitrary hidden representative. Pairing a representation with its tasks gives a terminal sufficient refinement. For declared operations, observational closure is expressed by the greatest operation-stable congruence contained in the observation kernel. These constructions distinguish local differential rank, global orbit separation, observational completeness, and reconstruction, and make preservation requirements explicit under composition. Second-order realizations provide concrete classification and computational tools. Under a declared block-orthogonal gauge, a covariance datum is encoded by a symmetric matrix tuple whose ordered word traces form a complete pointwise invariant, including repeated eigenvalues, vanishing couplings, and rank-deficient sectors. On simple-spectrum strata, mixed moments recover coupling magnitudes, while independent cycle holonomies complete the residual sign classification. This distinguishes hidden values omitted by a descriptor from distinctions that are genuinely observationally null . Under the different contract of covariance-preserving block-linear transformations, canonical correlations with multiplicity classify pointwise data; constant-type families additionally carry bundle and gluing information. Pointwise classification therefore does not replace the transport, relative alignment, or global data required by field-level tasks. Across rank, symmetry, and protocol changes, RG uses specialization maps when kernel inclusion permits them and correspondences otherwise. Smooth geometry is confined to its regular domain; proper-groupoid and tame settings support stratified descriptions with slices, tangent cones, and orbit-type changes. Finite-resolution statements are separated from exact model state

summary: The dataset uploaded here allows replication of the methodology of the study titled "Development and Application of a New Bounded Inequity Indicator for Water Distribution Systems." The data consists of the following: (i) Instructions document (PDF file) on how to use the two Excel worksheets attached—Sampled-from-PDF.xlsx and Inequity-data-for-100-cities.xlsx—to generate synthetic data for 100 cities (ii) Excel worksheets Sampled-from-PDF.xlsx, Inequity-data-for-100-cities, and Bootstrap-100-cities.xlsx The Excel worksheet Bootstrap-100-cities is added to show the 100 bootstrap samples for each of the 100 cities and the variation in the coefficient of variation in Demand Satisfaction Ratio (DSR) across these samples. This input was utilized for determining the scaling parameter of the proposed inequity indicator, the Bounded Inequity Indicator (BII).
title: Instructions and All Dataset for the Study on Comparative Assessment of Inequity Indicators and Development of a New Bounded Inequity Indicator for Water Distribution Systems

summary: Replication package accompanying manuscript version 11 of “Pesos endógenos e monotonicidade na mensuração da pobreza multidimensional”. DEA-MP/H measures relative multidimensional deprivation at household level using a fixed DEA reference, nested categorical comparison groups, resource share floors and iterative screening of reference households. The archive contains the R implementation, a single entry point (run_all.R), variable documentation, aggregate empirical results for the Brazilian Demographic Censuses of 2010 and 2022, robustness analyses, computational checks, execution log and SHA-256 manifests. Census microdata and individual intermediate bases are excluded; the scripts obtain official public inputs from IBGE. Empirical applications illustrate the proposed method. Version 1.1.0 corresponds to manuscript v11 (24 October 2026). Code and documentation: MIT license. Repository: https://github.com/moisesluna2026/dea-mp-h
title: DEA-MP/H: replication package for household multidimensional poverty measurement
