summary: This candidate extends the LWS research bench with three computational modules. The sequential-context module preserves the protocol and reference outcomes of the five-intersection experiment. The functional-alignment module compares equal feature budgets on already inspected outcomes. The branching module is a development pilot with short movement-specific lanes and a strong lane-aware scalar baseline. Development analyses are not presented as new confirmatory experiments. The package includes fixed protocols, generators, feature inputs, readable model parameters, reference predictions, complete comparison tables and tests. The original public v7 ZIP is included unchanged. New entry points separate integrity checks, cached model refits, engineering simulations and full raw regeneration. Runtime paths are resolved within the extracted package or an explicitly selected work directory. Python dependencies and SUMO must be installed separately at the recorded versions. The candidate was tested from a fresh extraction on Windows with the existing pinned scientific environment. All 17 tests passed. Refitting 54 fixed model variants reproduced all 51,642 saved probabilities with a maximum numerical difference of zero. Ten engineering simulations were regenerated and matched the reference canonical observations and feature rows. Reads from the original study directories were blocked during the checks. These checks establish reproducibility within the tested environment, not new scientific confirmation. Full regeneration of all 494 historical simulations was not performed in this candidate validation. It is available as a separate explicit command. Installation of dependencies on a clean machine and execution on other operating systems have not been tested. The 30 m sequential outcome and the 15 m branching outcome remain separate. No general predictive superiority of functional token boundaries is claimed. Own code is licensed under MIT. Own synthetic results and documentation are licensed under CC BY 4.0. The package excludes manuscripts, expert assessments, consents, signatures, third-party raw trajectories, videos and simulator binaries. The original v7 archive retains its own metadata and licenses. Developed in institutional competitive project STN-AI, no. 210318, funded by the European Union, NextGenerationEU. Data source: pNEUMA – open-traffic.epfl.ch.
title: LWS research bench for LRS referenced traffic measures with sequential context and development comparisons

summary: This report consolidates three mathematical investigations connecting a supplied chiral free-boson sector of string theory with the Phase nesting representation developed within Harmonic Physics: Virasoro algebra, vertex-operator composition, and complete quantum-state nesting. The central result is an explicit nesting isometry that carries a known quantum state into a larger correlated representation while preserving its complete amplitude-and-phase information, norms, and complex inner products. An analytic proof covers every oscillator level in the declared integer-charge Hilbert space. The construction has an inverse on its image and supports consistent repeated nesting under the specified additive phase rule. Transporting operators alongside the state preserves their algebraic products and observable expectations on the encoded image. Vertex operators supply the input coefficients, including charge changes, complex scalar factors, and oscillator excitations. Exact finite calculations, numerical comparisons with error bounds, diagnostic controls, and quantified truncation tails check the implementations. Joint observables retain access to phase information that is absent from an individual register’s reduced state. In the proposed Harmonic Physics interpretation, foundational Phase remains nonspatial relational organisation. Spatial geometry belongs to the represented string and observer-coupling description; oscillator occupations and encoding registers do not introduce intrinsic position or direction into Phase. The result is a bounded mathematical correspondence for supplied states and operators. State formation and the identification of the encoding with a physical string interaction remain separate research questions. The accompanying reproducibility package preserves the three original checkpoints, source code, results, derivations, controls, and a unified replay procedure.

summary: RTL repair benchmarks should measure whether a model can fix broken RTL given a specification. To this end, we construct and hash-bind RTLRepairDataset, 5,784 (broken, fixed) training pairs; RTLRepairBench, 459 held-out cases with 374 syntactic and 85 behavioral mutations; and an evaluation harness supporting simulation and formal equivalence. We then use this infrastructure to identify two measurement confounds. First, simulation and formal scoring give opposite signs for the apparent effect of providing a specification in one evaluated cohort; reset-aware rescoring attributes almost all of the simulation-formal disagreement to reset and first-cycle comparison semantics. Second, on 274 mined model failures, the specification-only minus specification-conditioned recovery point estimate ranges from -8.5 to +18.3 percentage points across six models. Thus, a conventional repair score need not isolate whether the model used the faulty RTL. We translate these findings into evaluation controls: report initialization, reset, first-cycle, and unknown-value semantics; disclose oracle coverage and undecided cases; and include a specification-only baseline. Together, the resources and audit provide both a benchmark for behavioral repair and a protocol for diagnosing what contributes to its measured score. We release the benchmark, the training set, construction code, sanitized aggregate evidence, and reproduction materials at https://github.com/Evaaaz/RTLRepairBench.
title: What Do RTL Repair Benchmarks Actually Measure?

summary: Long-term assistants must follow unfinished tasks across days as information and circumstances change. Finding information or starting an action, however, does not ensure that the task gets completed. We introduce OptionWorld, a benchmark that traces information acquisition, judgments, actions, and outcomes in simulated daily-life tasks to identify where current LLMs fall short as long-term personal assistants. In runs with archived decision inputs, the key facts remain in the model's last input before the deadline in 35.5% of failed instances. Failure analysis identifies the three most frequent problems: needed information is not obtained or combined, available opportunities to act go unused, and agents impose restrictions that the task does not require. Three follow-up experiments show that supplying missing facts restores task success in some cases; action reminders can restart work while subsequent steps still miss the deadline; and correcting a supplied note that wrongly forbids contact restores permitted inquiry. These findings locate shortcomings in maintaining task state: connecting facts to unfinished work, following through before deadlines, and separating actual restrictions from the agent's assumptions.
title: OptionWorld: A Benchmark for Diagnosing Failures of LLMs as Long-Term Personal Assistants

summary: Streaming video understanding requires a model to decide not only what to answer but also when to answer. Evidence arrives progressively, and recent benchmarks identify premature responses, issued before the queried event has concluded, as a recurring failure mode. Existing approaches often learn response timing through additional training, while training-free alternatives typically rely on scalar gating signals that do not explicitly represent when an answer becomes final. We organize chunk-wise streaming errors into three patterns: sampling variation can make an answer unstable, a stable answer may lack support in the observed video, or an answer may be supported by the current evidence while the event remains unfinished. We propose PACE (Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit), a training-free framework designed around these three failure modes. Given a question, PACE drafts a plan specifying what to observe and what will signal completion. As the stream unfolds, it invokes an off-the-shelf video LLM at informative moments, evaluates each draft for stability, grounding in its cited frames, and completion, and records verified observations in an event ledger. Experiments on ProactiveVideoQA and OVO-Bench Forward show that PACE improves over the official protocols by up to 5.9 average PAUC points and 6.2 average accuracy points across proprietary and open-source backbones, yielding state-of-the-art performance.

summary: Autonomous LLM agents act through tools under per-action authorization: a local guard screens each tool call in isolation. summary: The existing theory of stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control problems focuses on open-loop and closed-loop solvability. For finite horizon problems, it is widely accepted that those two types of solvability are not equivalent in general, as demonstrated by explicit counterexamples. In contrast, they coincide in standard infinite-horizon formulations with constant coefficients under suitable stabilizability and integrability assumptions. This paper aims at challenging this well-established paradigm by developing a novel framework of closed-loop solvability, namely generalized closed-loop solvability, which removes the $L^2$-integrability constraint on the feedback strategies from the existing formulation. It will be proven that open-loop and generalized closed-loop solvability are equivalent and the classical closed-loop solvablity is a particular case only when the admissible feedback strategy is $L^2$-integrable over the time horizon. In other words, the previously established non-equivalence between open-loop and closed-loop solvability stems solely from the limitations of the classical formulation which requires the $L^2$-integrability of the admissible feedback strategies over the time-horizon. Therefore, this paper unifies the theory of the solvabilitiy for stochastic LQ control problems. Moreover, our results offer a novel insight to stochastic LQ control problems: open-loop/generalized closed-loop solvability is essentially equivalent to piecewisely local closed-loop solvability in the classical sense. The current paper is focused on homogeneous cases only and non-homogeneous cases will be studied in a subsequent paper.

summary: In variational damage models, Lipschitz regularization can be introduced by imposing a pointwise bound on the gradient of the damage field, thereby controlling its spatial regularity without adding a gradient-dependent contribution to the energy. After spatial discretization, this condition gives rise to local inequality constraints and associated Lagrange multipliers, whose number increases with mesh refinement. This work introduces the Aggregated Lipschitz (A-Lip) formulation, in which these local constraints are replaced by a single differentiable global constraint and a single Lagrange multiplier, independently of the discretization size. Despite this reduction of the dual problem, the local constraint structure is retained through the gradient of the aggregation operator, which defines effective local multipliers. Under suitable structural properties, these multipliers concentrate on the locally active constraints as the aggregation approaches the exact maximum, asymptotically recovering the local Karush--Kuhn--Tucker structure of the original problem. A consistent primal--dual Newton solver is developed for the aggregated damage problem. The resulting bordered system admits a scalar Schur complement reduction. For the class of aggregation operators considered here, the consistent Hessian further decomposes into a sparse local contribution and a rank-one correction. Exploiting this structure through the Sherman--Morrison formula reduces the exact Newton correction to sparse subproblems involving only local contributions, together with low-cost global scalar and vector operations. The sparse computational structure of the underlying local problem can therefore be exploited despite the global nature of the aggregated constraint. One- and two-dimensional numerical assessments confirm the predicted aggregation accuracy, the recovery of the pointwise Lipschitz-constrained response, and the applicability of the formulation under mesh refinement. The results also provide a first assessment of the computational performance of the proposed formulation.
title: Aggregated Lipschitz (A-Lip) regularization of damage and fracture: a single-constraint, single-multiplier formulation retaining local computational structure

Beyond their primary glucose-lowering actions, both drug classes exert profound organ-protective effects. Objective:  This systematic review synthesizes current evidence on the molecular, cellular, and physiological mechanisms driving the cardio- and nephroprotective outcomes of SGLT2i and GLP-1RAs. Methods:  A systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science databases following PRISMA guidelines for studies published between 2018 and 2026. We mapped land suitability in montane northern Vietnam on a 30 m grid from twelve climatic, topographic and soil criteria, weighted by a literature-based fuzzy analytic hierarchy process and screened by a non-compensatory ecological exclusion overriding high scores elsewhere. Climatically suitable land covers 55,182 km²; the exclusion removed 26.6% of the domain. On the ensemble mean it contracts by 19.9–24.4%, and by 16.7–19.8% where at least three of five models agree; the highly suitable class loses 64–69%, and the median elevation of suitable land rises 127–161 m. Intersected with the baseline and a non-agricultural mask, that area yields long-term cultivable land of 44,094 km² (SSP3-7.0) and 41,862 km² (SSP5-8.5). MOTION consists of user agents, location agents, and a global manager agent. MOTION first detects coherent communities from historical mobility using the Leiden algorithm and extracts community-conditioned interaction priors to guide the generation process. summary: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services. Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment. By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).

summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are increasingly used as sources of knowledge for large language models (LLMs), hybrid AI systems, autonomous agents, and machine reasoning. However, conventional knowledge representation does not, by itself, establish whether a KG fact is ethically appropriate for a particular use, legitimately accessible to a particular agent, or endorsed by a relevant epistemic constituency. This paper proposes an EPB-passport framework that associates knowledge claims with explicit qualifications concerning Ethics, Privacy, and Bias (EPB). At the level of an RDF triple, the passport records whether a claim is appropriate for a specified agent or context, whether the agent is legitimately authorized to access or use it, and whether it is endorsed by a relevant epistemic constituency. These dimensions are distinguished from truth, provenance, and technical accessibility: endorsement does not establish truth, and technical retrievability does not establish legitimate access. The framework follows a conservative principle: a qualification must not be assumed merely because a claim exists or can be derived. Missing qualification information is treated as undetermined rather than as an implicit positive or negative judgment. The same principle applies to derived knowledge: an inferred claim cannot automatically inherit the EPB qualifications of its source facts but requires dimension-specific propagation and reassessment. The passport concept is also extended beyond RDF triples to semantic claims produced and manipulated by LLM-based systems, distinguishing computational units such as tokens and semantic spans from epistemic units such as claims and reasoning episodes. The paper develops and analyzes this conceptual and architectural framework, examining its implications for KGs, LLMs, LLM–KG hybrid architectures, and autonomous agents. Rather than reporting an implementation or empirical evaluation, it establishes a basis for explicit, context-sensitive governance of knowledge claims and identifies requirements for their formalization, propagation, and practical assessment.
title: Facts Need Passports: Governing Ethics, Privacy, and Bias in Knowledge Graphs

summary: Anaxia, the BLLM engine, with the source, the Lean development and the checks of the paper BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI by D. Bhattacharjee and U. Bhattacharya. The engine is the Python package eBLLM (command anaxia ), a Lean 4 library and the container image ghcr.io/creelie/bllm-engine, which carries no model weights. The paper proves, in a model with independent runs, that certifying self-modifications costs an entropy (the entropy law), that a sound infinite self-improvement of finite cost exists exactly when one series converges, that a proposer needs a number of proposals set by a Rényi entropy of order one half, and that n verified layers sharing one budget cost at least n log(n/θ). Sixty-five of its theorems are proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib, each depending only on the three standard axioms. The engine combines known constructions in a typed crossing network with a program check and a refuter for every candidate, a shared memory and five target agents, and builds new objects in construction mode. Version 3.1.0 passes its mathematical-physics benchmark: every reflexive descent of each of the 473,800,776 reflexive 4-polytopes of the Kreuzer–Skarke list reaches a seed within 348 steps, so the Calabi–Yau seed conjecture holds; the sharp constants are 5 in dimension two and 11 in dimension three, and in dimension four the sharp constant lies between 22 and 348. The engine also learns from its failures: every failed attempt writes a record with its diagnosis and the one rule of the engine it changed, the loop is proved in Lean to stop, and a skill memory credits each change by the whole run it belonged to. The log holds 10 runs, 73 attempts and 57 rule changes, from the engine's own runs and from the attacks on simple zeros of the zeta function, the Erdős–Straus equation, union-closed families, lonely runners, the Dwork quintic, lattice Yang–Mills and points in convex position. On the Hodge conjecture, every convolution with at most seven line bundles on E 0 6 fails the polarised criterion at every discriminant, and so does every object supported on the 32 Weil threefolds. Version 3.2.0 adds the attack package for the four targets (barrier atlas, bypass search, superstring chain, the audit of a quantum-gravity manuscript, triage and the figure critic), the bridge index of 243 thirteen-crossing knots by transvection representations, and the constructions of the proof that gravity with the form factor of a scale-invariant brane gas has no ultraviolet divergence at any order of perturbation theory for n ≥ 4 (the brane response and its resonant refuter, the power counting, the one-loop tuning, the vacuum energy and the reflection-positivity refuter), each recorded as a CANDIDATE control until refereed. Version 3.3.0 adds the attempts of 21 October 2026 on the Hodge inputs (F2) and (F3') (three results and five construction rounds, all stopped on named walls), the proof that the mirror-fixed clause of the Geometric Selection Conjecture is empty, so that the conjecture is equivalent to a viable vacuum on a component carrying no standard embedding (control gsc-mirror-clause, CANDIDATE), two exact constructions from the TheoPhysEval benchmark, the final passes on Lehmer's totient problem and the brane gas, and a third pass on the knot tables that settles the nonorientable four-genus of 2,093 of the 3,525 open knots with 11 to 13 crossings (control crosscap4d-13, CANDIDATE). summary: Agentic systems have demonstrated strong capabilities on complex tasks by enabling multiple interacting large language model (LLM)-based agents to collaborate and execute subtasks in parallel. However, this collaborative structure introduces new challenges for reliably evaluating and diagnosing system failures, particularly failure attribution: tracing a system's execution to identify the agent step responsible for an incorrect final outcome. These approaches assume that a sufficiently capable model can infer the failing step directly from an interaction transcript. In practice, however, direct prompting often performs poorly, which motivates follow-up work that explores various ways to improve AFA performance, including alternative prompting strategies and inference-time interventions. In this paper, we examine a more fundamental question: whether this weak behavioral performance reflects a genuine capability limitation. Building on this finding, we propose \emph{grafting}, a simple manual intervention that exploits knowledge already encoded in the model to improve AFA performance without requiring ground-truth labels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmark settings demonstrate that grafting consistently outperforms direct-prompting approaches, underscoring the potential of leveraging latent model knowledge for more reliable failure attribution. title: A Mechanistic Study of Automated Failure Attribution in LLM-based Agentic Systems

summary: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. summary: World models let agents compare imagined outcomes before acting, but an agent must still decide which alternatives to explore and when a proposed plan should replace its learned policy. summary: Conservatism in distributed stability certification is often treated as a limitation of the certificate itself, motivating richer Lyapunov functions, tighter relaxations, or stronger optimization. But a more fundamental limitation may arise from the reporting interface: once information is compressed, physically different systems can become indistinguishable. We model information as an information structure that partitions admissible systems into information fibers. The strongest sound certificate for a fiber is determined by its smallest stability margin, yielding a method-independent benchmark. This separates total conservatism into information-induced and method-induced parts and characterizes information order, task sufficiency, and the stability value of additional information. Three network-node studies show that network-spectrum, scalar/eigenvalue-only passivity, and independent-local reports respectively lose network--node alignment, local directional alignment, and cross-node relation. They show that critical missing information is often relational rather than dimensional. We then move from diagnosis to information design. An information-conservatism frontier gives the smallest irreducible conservatism achievable under a prescribed budget, while its inverse gives the minimum information required for a target conservatism. A witness-pair characterization turns this into a weighted covering problem. Besides, a local sensitivity law provides a computable approximation and identifies valuable unresolved quantities. title: Information-Induced Conservatism Frontier of Distributed Stability Certificates

summary: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.
title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty

summary: Experimental outputs for manuscript "Beyond Viewpoint Affinity: Measuring Political Bias in LLMs as a Failure of Epistemic Consistency" Political bias in large language models is often measured by treating responses to political questionnaires as evidence of ideological preference. This approach can conflate bias with differences in evidential support: asymmetric viewpoint preferences are not necessarily biased if one side is better supported by the available evidence. We operationalize this definition in two sets of experimental tasks. In person-attribution tasks, models evaluate nonpolitical items—such as mathematical proofs, logical arguments, or artistic artifacts---while only the political identity of the person associated with the item changes. Debiasing interventions---such as increasing reasoning effort, system prompts that emphasize epistemic rigor, and explicit instructions to ignore specific political cues—mitigate bias, but only partially. These results suggest that current LLMs show little bias based on an individual’s political identity when evaluating nonpolitical or politically orthogonal items. However, on politicized-context tasks, LLMs are persistently biased by task-irrelevant political cues, even when the relevant evidence is objectively assessable or held constant across political variants. This research monograph investigates the scientific and engineering boundaries of quantum-enabled thermometry and microrobotic observation in confined, nonclinical cellular microenvironment models. Topics range from NV resonance cross-sensitivity, microwave and laser heating, photon statistics, soft-matter interfaces, hydrodynamic motion, and anisotropic thermal conduction to causal controls, inverse problems, spatial covariance, interlaboratory comparison, and qualified instrument retirement. Each research chapter connects a physical mechanism to a falsifiable claim, a nonclinical experimental comparator, a measurement endpoint, and an explicit condition for withholding or retiring the conclusion. The Research Gates preserve actionable questions for future investigators. The Phoenix Answer Embryos offer provisional designs that can be separated, reconfigured, or abandoned when evidence contradicts them. DOI-linked scholarly literature supplies foundations for metrology, quantum sensing, microhandling, and thermal-field measurement without being mistaken for validation of the proposed integrated platform. Scientific Scope and Limitations This is a hypothesis-forming research blueprint, not a report of completed laboratory experiments or independently peer-reviewed findings. It does not establish autonomous nanoscale robotic systems, clinical diagnostic performance, therapeutic efficacy, or universal quantum advantage. Its minimum experimental setting uses confined hydrogels, artificial microenvironments, and properly authorized reference materials. A temperature or magnetic-field reading alone cannot establish cell health, metabolism, viability, or treatment outcomes. STARLI Research Philosophy A scientifically responsible observation includes the possibility that observing changed the result. By making such failures measurable, preserving negative evidence, and leaving research questions open to revision, this monograph invites future human and AI researchers to challenge, extend, and reconstruct its proposed methods.

summary: Threading a flux through a ring often shifts its energy levels. In the N-site spin-one Motzkin ring, a boundary flux leaves the entire zero-magnetization spectrum unchanged, yet increases the ground-state entanglement by giving each spin path a phase set by its lowest height. For equal halves and fixed nontrivial flux, the excess von Neumann entropy tends to approximately 1.581 nats, while the excess logarithmic negativity grows as 2 log log N + O(1). The limiting Schmidt weights come in pairs, allowing local operations that conserve each half's magnetization to extract a logical Bell pair with fidelity approaching one. The manuscript also examines controlled deformations and contrasts this response with suppression in a uniformly gapped neutral sector and with the energy response induced by an additional reverse pair-conversion process.

summary: hPartition is a partitioning framework implemented natively inside IQ-TREE 2, which builds a partitioning scheme from site rates rather than from predefined gene or codon boundaries, and does so at a fraction of the time and memory that wrapper-based methods need. ✨ Key Features Native IQ-TREE 2 Integration: Implemented directly in C++ within the IQ-TREE 2 engine. Model fitting, site-wise likelihood evaluation and reassignment share one process and one in-memory alignment, and the framework inherits the engine's alignment and state-space handling rather than reimplementing it. Hybrid Partitioning Strategy: Model-free evolutionary rate estimation via a generalized fastTIGER , then seed binning, candidate-model selection, likelihood-based site reassignment, and a cleanup pass over undersized subsets. Data Types: Benchmarked on nucleotide and amino-acid alignments, and verified to run unchanged on binary data. Codon and morphological data are untested. Invariant Site Handling: Invariant sites are carried through the pipeline at rate zero and settled by likelihood-proportional sampling, so they disperse across the scheme instead of collecting in one zero-variance cluster. Small entirely invariant subsets still occur — in five of the eight DNA schemes examined — but no subset holds more than 11.8% of an alignment's invariant sites. hPartition-PF: An extended variant ( -hPartition-pf ) that passes the scheme to IQ-TREE's relaxed-clustering merge search. It produces markedly smaller schemes on every DNA dataset tested, at three to fourteen times the runtime, and improves BIC on 11 of 17. 📊 Benchmark Results Model fit: Lowest BIC of the methods compared on 16 of 17 empirical DNA alignments, 10 of 12 protein alignments, and three of four multi-locus alignments containing ribosomal or transfer RNA. Topological accuracy: On 100 simulated alignments per dataset, hPartition recovers a closer tree than gPartition on 56 and than PsiPartition on 66 (SimDNA1), and on 70 and 85 respectively (SimDNA2); all four comparisons are significant under a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The advantage is consistent rather than concentrated, but it is not universal. Speed: Against the fastest competitor on each alignment, 1.0–6.4× lower wall-clock time on DNA and 2.4–25.7× on protein. Scalability: Completes alignments on which the alternatives exceed a 10 GB memory allocation. 🧪 Benchmark Scripts & Reproducibility The scripts that produced every experiment in the manuscript are in hPartition_scripts/ , with revision/ holding those added during review (the RNA benchmark, the matched-model-set comparison, the Stage-2 ablation and the binary-data check). hPartition_scripts/README.md documents the two clusters the work ran on, how to point the scripts at your own binaries, and what each one produces. 🚀 Usage To partition an alignment with standard hPartition : iqtree2 -s ALIGNMENT_FILE -mset JC69,F81,HKY,GTR -hPartition # DNA iqtree2 -s ALIGNMENT_FILE -hPartition # protein For the merging extension hPartition-PF , append -pf : iqtree2 -s ALIGNMENT_FILE -mset JC69,F81,HKY,GTR -hPartition-pf # DNA The criterion defaults to BIC; --AIC and --AICc select the others. The scheme depends on the random seed and on the thread count, so hold both fixed within an analysis: every result reported in the manuscript was obtained at -seed 0 and one thread. 🛠️ Compilation from Source Pre-compiled binaries for Linux, macOS, and Windows are in the assets below. To compile from source: ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Do not use the "Source code (zip)" or "Source code (tar.gz)" links GitHub generates at the bottom of this page — they omit the required Git submodules. Download the iqtree-...-source-with-submodules archive from the assets instead. Requirements (Linux): A C++ compiler (GCC >= 4.8, Clang, or Intel C++) CMake >= 2.8.10 Boost, Eigen3 and OpenMP (e.g. sudo apt-get install libboost-dev libeigen3-dev ) # 1. Extract the source archive and enter the directory

summary: Context: Software systems operating in regulated domains must often be adapted as legal and regulatory requirements evolve. While identifying regulatory changes is an important first step, determining which parts of a software repository are affected remains largely manual and knowledge-intensive. Objectives: This paper investigates how regulatory changes can be systematically mapped to affected parts of software repositories, and how this analysis can be supported through an evidence-grounded tool. Method: Following a Design Science Research approach, we conducted a multi-stage empirical investigation in collaboration with an industrial partner. We first developed a category-driven impact model linking regulatory change categories to potentially affected repository artifact types and engineering consequences. The model was then validated and refined with practitioners. Based on these findings, we designed and implemented ReguLens, which was subsequently examined through a formative expert evaluation and refined accordingly. The resulting version was evaluated using a controlled benchmark of 25 historical cases from three regulation-dependent open-source repositories. Results:  Practitioner validation showed that regulatory change categories provide useful structure for reasoning about likely software consequences, but should be treated as contextual guidance rather than deterministic mappings. The formative expert evaluation indicated that ReguLens can support exploration of potentially affected artifacts while still requiring expert interpretation. This observation was reinforced by the benchmark evaluation: ReguLens achieved 99.3% F1-score and 96.0% balanced accuracy for repository-level impact detection, whereas artifact localization was more challenging. For directly affected artifacts, macro F1 reached 64.1% at file level and 60.6% at container level, but decreased to 21.1% at symbol level. Conclusion:  Practitioners can benefit from ReguLens by using it to narrow the search space, identify plausible implementation entry points, and inspect supporting repository evidence. However, incomplete localization shows that human review remains necessary to interpret the evidence and confirm the required software changes. The findings therefore highlight both the potential and the current limitations of AI- assisted support for regulatory impact analysis.
title: Regulatory Impact Analysis in Software Repositories: From Category-Driven Modeling to Evidence-Grounded Tool Support

summary: Forming an accurate theory-of-mind (ToM) is key to successful multi-agent collaboration and requires reasoning under uncertainty to capture multiple possible partner states. This is hard to do in the text representation space native to large language model (LLM) agents, which more easily describe a single partner state. To address this challenge, we introduce ToM2Vec, which learns to form abstract theories-of-mind in a rich latent space via a fixed budget of continuous reasoning tokens. During training, supervision for these tokens comes from the partner's actual thoughts, which the ToM tokens are trained to abstract and match. At test-time, ToM tokens are generated by each agent and act as conditioners for that agent's thoughts and actions. Across several environments covering collaborative, competitive, and mixed-motive settings (Overcooked-AI, multiparty negotiation, Decrypto, Hanabi, and Collab Escape/Capture), we evaluate ToM2Vec's ability to support multi-agent interactions and collaboration, finding consistent improvements over the base model and a variety of competitive trained and prompted baselines. We show that latent reasoning is critical, with performance dropping when reasoning is expressed in text. Moreover, we show that ToM2Vec training generalizes to partner model families not seen at train-time, including a proprietary model (GPT-5.4). In our analysis, we provide evidence that the latent tokens encode a ToM, rather than task-specific information: ToM2Vec's tokens improve the agent's ability to directly answer questions about partner beliefs, desires, and next actions.
title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination

summary: Abstract Modern websites frequently depend on multi-layer dynamic software stacks comprising application runtimes, content-management systems, databases, frameworks, authentication services, third-party APIs, and cloud infrastructure. This architecture provides substantial functionality under normal conditions but can produce an undesirable failure mode: essential public information may become inaccessible even when networking, HTTPS, web servers, and the ability to serve static files remain operational. This paper introduces Web Lifeboat, an experimental architecture and protocol for cryptographically verifiable static fallback publishing. The design seeks to preserve a small, explicitly selected set of essential web information independently of the normal dynamic application stack. Emergency content is represented as static HTML accompanied by a signed manifest describing its identity, integrity, validity period, sequence, and associated trust information. Verification is designed to require neither the site’s database nor its application runtime and to remain meaningful when content is transferred through different transports. Web Lifeboat applies principles of graceful degradation and cyber resilience to web publishing: failure of high-complexity functionality should not necessarily imply failure of low-complexity, mission-essential information delivery. The current protocol draft, version 1.5.2, defines deterministic validation semantics, resource limits, rollback protections, cryptographic verification, key-state handling, clock-uncertainty behaviour, and transition rules. An internal conformance suite contains 42 package and trust-transition cases. The suite currently passes both its own validation process and a separate Go implementation from the same development lineage; genuinely independent implementation testing remains pending. In addition to the protocol design, this work introduces a measurable availability criterion, the Essential Information Preservation Ratio (EIPR), and reports a controlled local PHP-runtime failure experiment. After deliberate termination of the PHP backend while nginx and static serving remained operational, 30/30 fallback requests succeeded and all 20/20 predesignated essential information items remained available, producing EIPR = 1.00 under the tested conditions. This result supports the narrow fallback-availability claim in the experimental configuration; it does not establish Internet-scale survivability, protocol security, or independent interoperability. A reproducibility archive containing raw results, configuration, logs and experiment artifacts accompanies this result. Separately, Web Lifeboat v1.5.2 is being evaluated through a blind external implementation challenge intended to test whether independent implementers can reproduce its precommitted verification outcomes from the written specification alone. Those independent interoperability results remain pending. Conceptually, Web Lifeboat serves a role analogous to an emergency generator in electrical infrastructure: it is not intended to reproduce the full capacity of the normal system, but to preserve a deliberately selected set of essential functions when the primary, higher-complexity path becomes unavailable. The work remains experimental and is not presented as production-ready infrastructure, a completed security protocol, or evidence of Internet-scale survivability. The current results support a narrower proposition: under an explicitly defined failure condition, essential static information can remain available after loss of a dynamic PHP backend when an independent static-serving path has been prepared in advance. The addendum introduces Residual Strategic Optionality as an extension of Stakeholder Coherence Theory, examining the incentives of actors capable of disrupting negotiated settlements. It also compares the Bridge Settlement with Jeffrey Sachs's October 2026 peace framework for Ukraine, identifying areas of conceptual convergence and distinguishing the Bridge Settlement's emphasis on reciprocal economic interests, institutional participation, and self-reinforcing peace mechanisms. This study develops a comparative Bayesian framework for evaluating natural zoonotic and research-associated hypotheses for the proximal origin of SARS-CoV-2 under incomplete evidence. summary: This archive provides the computational methods, structural coordinate files, source data, model outputs, and reproducibility documentation supporting an exploratory investigation of geometric persistence and prediction uncertainty at HIV-1 envelope (Env) glycan sites. The research examines whether local sequence divergence and sparse structural-context observations can improve the identification of unreliable glycan-site geometric predictions. The approach combines sequence-informed error estimation with residual information obtained from six observed glycan-site probes. Held-out evaluations included five BG505-derived Env structures and two JR-FL structures. In the original experiments, the six-probe method improved pooled dangerous-error discrimination relative to sequence-only prediction, with ROC AUC increasing from 0.704 to 0.945 in BG505 and from 0.522 to 0.761 in JR-FL. These results are exploratory. The original evaluations contained only two dangerous underestimates in BG505 and three in JR-FL. Within-structure discrimination did not consistently improve, and training-test construct overlap was identified. Additional construct-family exclusion analyses document the sensitivity of the findings to training composition and failure prevalence. The principal computational outputs were regenerated exactly from archived structural coordinates using the supplied scripts. The archive includes frozen protocols, structural data, prediction tables, provenance audits, family-exclusion analyses, and a companion manuscript draft. The study supports further investigation of sparse structural context for uncertainty assessment but does not establish reliable cross-strain site-level failure detection, glycan occupancy prediction, or protein synthesis prediction. This deposit is intended to support transparency, independent reproduction, methodological evaluation, and future extension of HIV-1 Env structural bioinformatics research. This research extends the author's previously deposited HIV-1 Env glycan-shield investigations by examining the predictive and uncertainty-assessment implications of geometric persistence, local structural constraints, and glycan-site organization.
title: Ensemble Geometric Persistence: HIV-1 Env Glycan-Site Geometry and Sparse Structural-Context Uncertainty Assessment (Reproducibility Archive)

summary: Geometric Observability and Optimal Design for Vehicle Localization by a Three-Dimensional Beacon Array     https://orcid.org/0009-0007-5661-7332 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23575194 Abstract This paper develops a geometric analysis of vehicle-position observability when line-of-sight measurements are obtained from a surrounding beacon array. The vehicle is represented by an unknown Cartesian position, while each beacon contributes a unit line-of-sight vector. The associated Jacobian yields the Fisher information matrix, whose inverse supplies the Cramér–Rao bound on position covariance. In the horizontal plane, beacon directions determine the conditioning of the position estimate through their angular spread; in elevation, nonzero vertical separation supplies sensitivity to depth and suppresses the vertical dilution that occurs in a coplanar arrangement. Design implications are stated in terms of angular diversity, range, symmetry, and beacon elevation, and are formalized through the classical D- and E-optimality criteria. The treatment is first-order and analytical: no field calibration, stochastic measurement data, or performance claim beyond the stated linearized model is made. Index Terms —Beacon localization, Observability, Line-of-sight geometry, Fisher information, Cramér–Rao bound, Optimal experimental design, Position covariance, Vehicle navigation.
title: Geometric Observability and Optimal Design for Vehicle Localization by a Three-Dimensional Beacon Array

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A random walk is robust if an adversary who may change every transition probability by a small relative amount cannot make it much slower to reach its targets. Zuckerman (Markov chain robustness, ITCS 2026, LIPIcs 362, 118) conjectured that the largest safe relative change is at least a constant divided by the graph's diameter (Conjecture 1.16). This package shows the conjecture is false. A graph can have short routes that the walk almost never uses; a small fixed bias away from a target accumulates between rare visits to them and depletes the target's stationary mass, and Kac's formula turns this into a long hitting time. For explicit cubic graphs J_b on N vertices with diameter O(log N), every effective resistance is at most 684 (proof), and a fixed perturbation of size 1/b, with error times diameter tending to zero, multiplies the worst-case hitting time by a factor of order b; the robustness is O(N^(-1/3)). For explicit 3m-regular graphs of diameter exactly three, the mixing time is at most 50(m+1), so with Zuckerman's mixing-time theorem the robustness lies between constant multiples of N^(-1/2) and N^(-1/4) (proof; not matching). An exact computation shows a 5.80-fold slowdown on a 5,995-vertex member with error times diameter 0.74. A diameter-two example, a reversible-perturbation bound and a comparison with Kemeny's constant are included. The archive contains the manuscript (PDF and LaTeX), seven verification scripts with a driver that reproduces the reference JSON results byte for byte under python -B -O, semantic negative controls, figures and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: written proofs; exact checks; producer-side replay including a clean replay in a separate copy; internal AI-assisted review, AI-assisted adversarial reviews (OpenAI gpt-5.6-sol; Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5; OpenAI gpt-6-astra) and a verification re-review. This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Prose, manuscript and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Small diameter does not control hitting-time robustness

summary: We extend the Deep Hough Transform (DHT), which detects semantic lines by aggregating learned features along candidate lines into a two-dimensional parameter space, to higher-dimensional parametric curve families. The extension is hard because the accumulator for a family with d parameters has O(B^d) cells for B bins per axis. We propose a factorized deep Hough transform, a differentiable feature-space voting cascade that splits the parameter vector into a spatial anchor and a shape. A coarse two-dimensional accumulator votes for anchors, and a dense shape accumulator is built only around the top-k anchors, so memory falls from O(B^d) to O(B^d1 + k B^d2). Lines are the degenerate case with no second stage. We also define a curve agreement score that extends the EA line similarity to parametric curves, and a synthetic benchmark of parabolas, circles and ellipses with noise, occlusion and distractors. We evaluate with thresholds selected on a validation split and the test split scored once, and we give the geometric baselines the same treatment. Under this protocol the choice of Stage-1 pooling over probe shapes matters a great deal: max pooling raises parabola F from 0.51 to 0.70 over log-sum-exp (3 seeds). With it, the cascade ties a tuned RANSAC fit on parabolas (0.706 vs. 0.702) and circles (0.743 vs. 0.742) and is slightly behind it on ellipses (0.382 vs. 0.410), while direct regression and query-based heads reach 0.15 and 0.13 on parabolas. So the cascade is competitive with classical fitting rather than better than it, and its practical advantage is memory: at B=32 a dense d=5 accumulator would need about 4 GB (computed, not instantiated) against a measured 236 KB for the cascade. We locate the remaining error in Stage 1. Running Stage 2 at the ground-truth anchors gives F = 0.938 against 0.706, and curves whose anchors lie within about 8 pixels of each other lose about 0.2 F because their Stage-1 peaks merge. We also report a TuSimple lane-detection stress test, which we treat as a feasibility check rather than a competitive result. Code and the benchmark generator are released.

summary: Gratitude can concern a benefit received, a harm that did not occur, or the conditions that make one's own assumptions examinable. We develop the proposal that appreciating these conditions can orient practice toward realizing emptiness: examining how distinctions arise, relinquishing their assumed intrinsic necessity, and retaining their conditional usefulness. The argument distinguishes an observed absence, a missing observation, counterfactual valuation and non-reification, and places their differences in dialogue with explicitly situated philosophical and scriptural sources. We reconstruct Fisher, Sandved Smith and Hohwy's gratitude and gaze notebooks, then separate faithful reconstruction from corrected experiments and new mechanisms. GNN-declared paired recall experiments use 5120 independent agent-world units, matched environmental exposure and replay dose, normalized likelihoods, and independent predictive assessment. Pinned Realizing Emptiness interfaces supply structural admission and finite mathematical comparators. An enacted inquiry model separates appreciation, costly activity, access to alternatives and evidence-responsive retention or revision; explicit learning-to-gaze and joint scene/encoding experiments examine transfer and identifiability. Exact count enumeration, mathematical nulls, paired controls and joint bootstrap inference make the resulting software claims independently checkable. Selective positive recall reduces the declared optimism summary, while its predictive consequences depend on the world mixture and the specified transfer bridge. Counterfactual absence valuation preserves inference by construction. Accessible inquiry can revise a contradicted restriction and retain a useful one; activity without access instead incurs costs while preserving rigid forecasts. Exact analysis exposes rare adverse selections absent from seeded realizations. The original gaze code reproduces the pre-intervention occupancy but contains no implemented after intervention. Our active-scene extension finds a context-dependent access advantage without an additional inquiry-specific predictive advantage. Joint scene/encoding inquiry distinguishes learning an encoding from combining it with scene evidence: observationally equivalent labels remain unidentifiable, and excluded hypotheses cannot be recovered. Known-answer fixtures also retain skew-related undercoverage and unavailable rare-event estimates rather than treating replication size as a remedy for every inferential failure. The contribution is a reproducible account of enabling operations and their limits, together with a falsifiable human research program that separates inquiry value from patience, anticipated good news and instrumental information demand. Synthetic model results establish neither human gratitude nor contemplative realization or clinical benefit. Code, declared models and reproducibility materials are available at github.com/docxology/thanks_for_nothing .
title: Thanks for Nothing: Gratitude, Model Revisability, and the Practice of Realizing Emptiness

summary: Biological-Digital-Twin-Driven Microrobotic Sampling Decisions at the Limit STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 10 What if the next scientific sample could be selected not merely to collect more data, but to distinguish between competing explanations of biological behavior? Biological-Digital-Twin-Driven Microrobotic Sampling Decisions at the Limit explores a prospective research architecture combining versioned biological digital twins, active learning, microrobotic sampling, uncertainty quantification, and mechanistic model discrimination. The central question is whether a computational twin can identify safe, informative sampling actions that distinguish competing biological mechanisms more effectively than conventional experimental schedules, while retaining the ability to recognize model inadequacy and abstain from unsupported decisions. The proposed framework treats biological digital twins as revisable scientific models rather than exact replicas of living systems. Its reference environment is a controlled, nonclinical microfluidic platform containing two declared dynamical mechanisms and a third withheld mechanism reserved for evaluating open-world uncertainty and model failure. The research architecture is organized around five interconnected layers: versioned biological modeling, explicit prior assumptions and knowledge gaps, physically constrained predictive interrogation, comparative adaptive experimentation, and independent requalification. The manuscript develops thirty candidate mathematical research plates covering Bayesian mechanism inference, conditional information gain, experimental identifiability, observation uncertainty, transport dynamics, calibration, model discrepancy, and decision safety. These mathematical structures are connected to eighty-two research chapters, five independently paginated investigation sections per chapter, two hundred detailed Research Gates, and thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Research Gate is intended as a transferable research question that future investigators may test, challenge, refine, or reject. The proposed evaluation compares twin-guided sampling against optimized fixed schedules, established experimental-design approaches, and alternative active-learning policies under matched physical constraints and experimental budgets. Particular attention is given to blinded mechanism identification, probabilistic calibration, out-of-distribution rejection, specimen integrity, model-version accountability, and explicit stopping conditions. The volume includes DOI-linked methodological literature and a staged nonclinical verification pathway. Scientific status and limitations: This manuscript presents a conceptual methodological research program, not completed experimental validation. Its integrated hypotheses, mathematical proposals, and experimental architectures remain subject to independent technical review and empirical testing. The manuscript does not establish clinical efficacy, diagnostic reliability, therapeutic benefit, or proven superiority of microrobotic digital-twin systems. The work also acknowledges remaining editorial limitations, including recurring methodological language that requires further substantive review before the manuscript can be regarded as a fully refined scientific monograph. The broader purpose of this research is to develop scientific systems that can remain useful even when their initial models are incomplete. Rather than demanding certainty from a digital twin, the proposed framework asks whether future autonomous research tools can become more transparent, corrigible, experimentally accountable, and capable of recognizing the boundaries of their own knowledge. Within the STARLI research continuum, this volume is intended as an evolving research inheritance for future human and artificial-intelligence investigators. title: Biological-Digital-Twin-Driven Microrobotic Sampling Decisions at the Limit STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 10 What if the next scientific sample could be selected not merely to collect more data, but to distinguish between competing explanations of biological behavior? Biological-Digital-Twin-Driven Microrobotic Sampling Decisions at the Limit explores a prospective research architecture combining versioned biological digital twins, active learning, microrobotic sampling, uncertainty quantification, and mechanistic model discrimination. The central question is whether a computational twin can identify safe, informative sampling actions that distinguish competing biological mechanisms more effectively than conventional experimental schedules, while retaining the ability to recognize model inadequacy and abstain from unsupported decisions. The proposed framework treats biological digital twins as revisable scientific models rather than exact replicas of living systems. Its reference environment is a controlled, nonclinical microfluidic platform containing two declared dynamical mechanisms and a third withheld mechanism reserved for evaluating open-world uncertainty and model failure. The research architecture is organized around five interconnected layers: versioned biological modeling, explicit prior assumptions and knowledge gaps, physically constrained predictive interrogation, comparative adaptive experimentation, and independent requalification. The manuscript develops thirty candidate mathematical research plates covering Bayesian mechanism inference, conditional information gain, experimental identifiability, observation uncertainty, transport dynamics, calibration, model discrepancy, and decision safety. These mathematical structures are connected to eighty-two research chapters, five independently paginated investigation sections per chapter, two hundred detailed Research Gates, and thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Research Gate is intended as a transferable research question that future investigators may test, challenge, refine, or reject. The proposed evaluation compares twin-guided sampling against optimized fixed schedules, established experimental-design approaches, and alternative active-learning policies under matched physical constraints and experimental budgets. Particular attention is given to blinded mechanism identification, probabilistic calibration, out-of-distribution rejection, specimen integrity, model-version accountability, and explicit stopping conditions. The volume includes DOI-linked methodological literature and a staged nonclinical verification pathway. Scientific status and limitations: This manuscript presents a conceptual methodological research program, not completed experimental validation. Its integrated hypotheses, mathematical proposals, and experimental architectures remain subject to independent technical review and empirical testing. The manuscript does not establish clinical efficacy, diagnostic reliability, therapeutic benefit, or proven superiority of microrobotic digital-twin systems. The work also acknowledges remaining editorial limitations, including recurring methodological language that requires further substantive review before the manuscript can be regarded as a fully refined scientific monograph. The broader purpose of this research is to develop scientific systems that can remain useful even when their initial models are incomplete. Rather than demanding certainty from a digital twin, the proposed framework asks whether future autonomous research tools can become more transparent, corrigible, experimentally accountable, and capable of recognizing the boundaries of their own knowledge. Within the STARLI research continuum, this volume is intended as an evolving research inheritance for future human and artificial-intelligence investigators. summary: Amun Code is an open-source parallel simulation code for astrophysical fluids and plasmas. It solves the equations of hydrodynamics and magnetohydrodynamics in two and three dimensions on uniform or adaptively refined Cartesian meshes. Supported formulations include Newtonian flows with isothermal or adiabatic equations of state, and special relativistic hydrodynamics and magnetohydrodynamics. The code uses Godunov-type shock-capturing methods with selectable approximate Riemann solvers, high-order weighted essentially non-oscillatory and monotonicity-preserving reconstruction, and Runge–Kutta time integration. Embedded integrators provide error-based time-step control. Magnetic-divergence errors are controlled through generalized Lagrange multiplier cleaning. Optional viscosity, magnetic resistivity, and stochastic turbulence driving support studies of turbulence, shocks, and magnetic reconnection. Driving options include the Alvelius method and an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. Amun Code is written primarily in modern Fortran and supports hybrid MPI/OpenMP parallelization. Simulation settings are supplied through parameter files, and outputs use native XML/binary or HDF5 formats. AmunPy provides a separate Python interface for reading simulation data. The code is developed by Grzegorz Kowal and distributed under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later.

summary: Makes canu failures fatal when canu itself could not run. Previously any canu failure during read correction was reported as "This probably means there is low depth, don't be too concerned" and plassembler carried on with uncorrected reads - including when one of canu 's own jobs could not run at all. In the Biocontainers image, canu 's generated job scripts call expr -- ... , which the image's BusyBox expr rejects, so k-mer counting failed every time; continuing with uncorrected reads left Unicycler assembling 110 spurious contigs that the depth filter then had to discard. Thanks @ SieurRicort for the detailed report and diagnosis ( #92 ) plassembler now reads canu 's log to tell its stops apart. A job that failed ( ... jobs failed, tried 2 times, giving up. ) or an internal canu crash stops the run, reports the failing stage alongside canu 's own output, and keeps the canu directory, which holds each job's log. Low read coverage - the expected outcome for a sample with no plasmids - still carries on as before, now with a message saying so. Any other stop also carries on, but shows canu 's reason rather than reassurance. The same applies to canu assembly with --canu_flag
title: gbouras13/plassembler: v1.8.6

summary: Diffusion models have become strong priors for solving inverse problems. However, nonlinear inverse problems such as phase retrieval remain challenging when multiple measurement-consistent solutions are distinguishable only by the prior; we call such measurements ambiguous. Existing diffusion-based samplers rely on local approximations during reconstruction. For an ambiguous measurement, these approximations can allow measurement guidance to favor a measurement-consistent mode that is close to a prior-supported mode but is itself not supported by the prior. Evaluation often masks this type of failure by reporting the best-of-$k$ runs, where the best is selected by comparison to the ground truth. We introduce Prior-Consistent DAPS (PC-DAPS), a variant of Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling (DAPS) designed to address this failure case by maintaining multiple candidate solutions within a single sampling run. As annealing noise decreases, PC-DAPS prunes and replaces weaker candidates according to their prior consistency, without any ground-truth access. PC-DAPS reduces the incidence of prior-inconsistent samples and improves sample quality on nonlinear inverse problems while preserving sample quality and diversity on linear inverse problems.

summary: Overview This software package accompanies the study Resolvability of Ionospheric Currents From Multi-LEO Magnetometry . It provides computational tools for investigating how multi-altitude satellite magnetic observations constrain three-dimensional ionospheric currents. The package implements a divergence-free spherical Mie magnetic-field representation and a Bayesian inversion framework for evaluating magnetic-field and current reconstruction, degrees of freedom for signal (DFS), physical-current information, and posterior uncertainty. Main Features Spherical-harmonic Mie forward modeling and three-component current reconstruction. Bayesian inversion with full posterior covariance propagation. Resolution and recoverability diagnostics for different satellite configurations and observation altitudes. Physical-current information analysis and regularization-sensitivity experiments. Sample Swarm-A/B orbital positions for geometry tests and a self-contained synthetic inversion example. What's New in This Version 3 This release provides a corrected scientific implementation and updated reproducibility tools. The principal corrections include: Correcting the colatitude derivative of the associated Legendre functions used in the spherical-harmonic operator. Restoring the radial magnetic-field contribution of the quadratic poloidal Mie term, ensuring consistency with the continuous divergence-free representation. Updating the corresponding current-reconstruction and recoverability calculations. Clarifying the scaled coefficient parameterization, Bayesian prior, and interpretation of coefficient-space resolution diagnostics. Improving numerical verification, reproducibility workflows, and documentation. The updated calculations continue to support the importance of satellite altitude separation for constraining specified ionospheric current structures, while distinguishing formal information gain from recovery of the complete physical current distribution. Data and Reproducibility The package includes source code, documentation, numerical tests, small reference summaries, sample orbit positions, and a self-contained synthetic example. The synthetic demonstrations can be executed without downloading mission magnetic-field observations. Reproducing the study's observation-based analyses requires the corresponding processed Swarm and Macau Science Satellite-1 data and additional external inputs described in the documentation. summary: USGS Groundwater-Depth Dataset Processing Workflow v1.0.0 is the archived software release of the public processing workflow developed to construct the Version 1.0 quality-controlled daily groundwater-depth dataset derived from the U.S. Geological Survey National Water Information System (USGS NWIS). The workflow processes USGS parameter 72019 (depth to water below land surface), daily mean statistic 00003, Approved source values, and wells classified with USGS code U (Unconfined single aquifer). It implements normalization and quality control, temporal continuity assessment, segmentation of fragmented monitoring histories, development and reserved-validation masking, PCHIP reconstruction of short internal gaps, and final dataset export with explicit source/interpolation provenance. The frozen workflow uses a minimum retained span of 10 years, a maximum internal missing-gap threshold of 30 days, PCHIP interpolation without extrapolation, exactly 50 development masks and 20 reserved-validation masks per required gap length where applicable, and a pooled RMSE acceptance threshold of 0.20 m at every required masking length. Segment selection is fixed before reserved validation, and no alternative segment is substituted after a reserved-validation failure. The software supported construction of a final dataset containing 331 monitoring wells and 2,374,112 daily values, including 2,357,801 retained USGS source values and 16,311 PCHIP-reconstructed values. The associated scientific dataset is archived separately on Zenodo and is not distributed as part of this software record. This repository is a public adaptation of the research workflow with portable paths and reproducibility documentation. The scientific processing criteria and numerical methods of the frozen Version 1.0 workflow are preserved. summary: Prediction intervals from probabilistic time-series forecasters are commonly assessed by marginal coverage, the long-run proportion of observations falling inside the intervals. However, forecast errors in time series are often serially dependent and heteroskedastic, so prediction intervals can attain near-nominal marginal coverage while miscovering systematically during periods of larger local error variance. We identify and address this failure mode, which we call \emph{local scale miscalibration}. We first document the phenomenon using time-series foundation models (TSFMs): across several real-world series, their native intervals often attain near-nominal marginal coverage while exhibiting substantial temporal variation in local coverage, alternating between overcoverage and undercoverage over shorter windows. We then propose Volatility-Corrected Prediction Intervals (VCPI), a post-hoc calibration procedure that uses the base forecaster's predictive scale as a baseline, models the volatility of standardized forecast residuals with a Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) model, and applies a multiplicative correction to produce locally adaptive prediction intervals. We justify VCPI both theoretically and empirically, comparing it against model-agnostic conformal counterparts. We provide a theoretical analysis of interval adaptation of the proposed method following abrupt changes in volatility. Empirically, we evaluate VCPI on Chronos, Moirai, and TimesFM across four real-world datasets and find that it produces more stable local coverage than conformal baselines while maintaining near-nominal marginal coverage and comparable interval width.
title: Volatility-Corrected Prediction Intervals: Locally Adaptive Uncertainty Quantification for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting

summary: Computer-use agents increasingly handle private information and act on users' behalf across desktop and web applications, including email. summary: Detailed image captioning is usually framed as an amount problem: a model should mention more visual facts while avoiding hallucination. summary: In standard acoustic anomaly detection (ASD), models are usually trained separately for each machine or domain using explicit metadata. However, in realistic deployments, machine identifiers are incomplete, unreliable, or simply unavailable. On a single CPU, its hierarchical retrieval achieves a 7.8x speedup over exhaustive search with only a 0.20 percentage-point AUC drop. These results suggest that incorporating explicit geometric partitioning can improve both detection accuracy and retrieval efficiency for ASD. summary: Background : The rapid digitisation of allied health education has led to an alarming rise in Digital Eye Strain (DES), also termed Computer Vision Syndrome (CVS), among undergraduate Bachelor of Physiotherapy (BPT) students. summary: Settlement hierarchy is commonly associated with population size, yet demographic scale does not necessarily correspond to the spatial centrality of settlements within regional systems. This study examines the demographic and proximity-based hierarchy of settlements in the Karabakh Economic Region of Azerbaijan and evaluates the extent to which its spatial organization corresponds to the principles of Central Place Theory (CPT). The analysis integrates official administrative and demographic statistics with OpenStreetMap-derived geospatial data in a GIS-based framework. The official settlement system comprises 669 settlements, including 11 cities, 37 towns, and 621 villages, with a total population of 751.1 thousand people as of 1 January 2026. For settlement-level spatial analysis, 752 OSM-defined village and hamlet points were assigned to their geographically nearest potential central places using Euclidean distance. Population-based classification, nearest-centre allocation, mean, median and maximum distance measures, Voronoi (Thiessen) hinterland delineation, and Pearson and Spearman correlation analyses were applied. The results reveal a pronounced divergence between demographic hierarchy and proximity-based spatial centrality. Barda recorded the largest number of allocated rural settlements ( N i =95), followed by Aghdara (88), Khojaly (74), Fuzuli (71), and Khojavand (59). However, hinterland configurations differed substantially: Barda combined the highest N i with a mean settlement distance of 8.75 km, whereas Aghdara exhibited a considerably more dispersed pattern with a mean distance of 16.83 km and a maximum of 41.62 km. Central-place population was not significantly associated with either the number of allocated rural settlements (Pearson r =0.232, p =0.355; Spearman ρ =0.255, p =0.308) or their mean distance ( r =0.183, p =0.468; ρ =0.285, p =0.252). In contrast, the number of allocated settlements and mean distance were significantly positively related ( r =0.707, p =0.001; ρ =0.618, p =0.006). These findings demonstrate that demographic size and proximity-based centrality constitute distinct dimensions of the Karabakh settlement system. The results provide partial support for CPT by identifying differentiated central places and theoretical hinterlands, while showing that their hierarchy cannot be explained by population size alone. The study provides a spatial baseline for subsequent integration of transport-network accessibility and service-function indicators into a multidimensional assessment of settlement centrality.

summary: The rise of Agentic AI systems has changed the landscape of artificial intelligence by enabling strong reasoning capabilities through specialized multi-agent interaction with structured self-reflection. However, in target-driven reasoning tasks, single- and multi-agent systems are often on par in terms of performance gains. A major challenge is that failures often arise from an ineffective exchange of critical information during inter-agent interaction and coordination. Different from existing multi-agent debate paradigms that rely on synchronous turn-taking and sharing information across different agents, we propose an inter-agent protocol based on shared Memory bUFFer INference - referred to as MUFFIN - in an asynchronous agentic framework. In the first step, an orchestrator routes queries based on their reasoning demands and delegates demanding ones to a multi-agent setting, where a shared memory buffer provides asynchronous exchange of intermediate findings while an agent's private reasoning remains local. Our experiments show that our framework Muffin outperforms established competitors, achieving the best accuracy in 17 out of 20 of our benchmark settings, and provides a better quality-cost trade-off than multi-agent debate: Muffin improves accuracy by 19.2 accuracy points while using 77.4% fewer tokens, without requiring full-trace sharing.
title: Muffin - A Shared Memory Buffer for Asynchronous AI Agents

summary: Large language models can repeat an instruction while failing to keep obeying it. We study this recall-compliance dissociation in long-horizon dialogue and define State Integrity Collapse: a model preserves a stated constraint in memory but stops applying it to later turns. We introduce StateTrack-Bench, a controlled suite of conversations covering numerical, format, role/persona, factual-memory, and logical-rule constraints. Across seven provider-pinned model snapshots and five dialogue-depth probes, strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% to 100.0%, with degradation concentrated in symbolic constraints and in one especially brittle model. A forked recall audit shows that 88.6% of observed failures are behavioral-drift failures rather than ordinary forgetting; excluding the brittle outlier preserves this diagnosis (84.4% of failures). Extended evaluations at depths up to 50 turns confirm that the dissociation persists beyond the core benchmark, while Structured State Anchoring recovers up to 24.4 points on immutable constraints. The results show that reliability cannot be inferred from single-turn instruction following alone; evaluation must track whether remembered constraints remain operational as dialogue state grows. Code and artifacts are available at: https://github.com/xzzvsxd/StateTrack.
title: When LLMs Forget What They Believe: Characterizing State Integrity Collapse in Long-Horizon Dialogues
