summary: Unlike conventional GUI agents, personalized GUI agents require user preferences to guide sequential execution over changing GUI states. This raises two challenges: determining HOW each preference should alter execution strategy and WHEN it should take effect along the interaction trajectory. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate overall task success, offering limited insight into these questions. We introduce PrefDiag-Bench with two components: (1) a categorization of preferences into five types, characterizing HOW they affect execution; and (2) a stage-wise diagnostic framework with 1,664 probes, tracing WHEN preferences should take effect and where failures occur. We evaluate eleven GUI agent systems, including end-to-end agents and agentic workflows, under two forms of user context: explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs. Although existing agents achieve relatively high completion rates on non-personalized tasks, performance is substantially lower on preference-personalized tasks. Even the best-performing model, Seed-2.0-Pro, achieves only 47.17% on Process preferences under explicit user profiles. Agents struggle particularly with Ranking and Process preferences. Further analysis reveals two key capability bottlenecks: selecting relevant evidence from user history and recognizing when preferences should take effect during execution. Controlled interventions that explicitly provide relevant evidence improve end-to-end task success by up to 7.06%. PrefDiag-Bench offers a more systematic evaluation of GUI agents' personalization capabilities beyond overall task success. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Zhixin-L/PrefDiag-Bench.
title: Diagnosing Personalization Failures in Mobile GUI Agents

summary: Background: Vitamin D, vitamin B12 and thyroid results are often available at a first headache visit, but their relation to later acute treatment is unclear, and testing is selective. We estimated whether 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D], vitamin B12, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free thyroxine (T4) recorded at the first headache visit were associated with acute analgesic prescribing from that day onward. Methods: Retrospective electronic health record cohort of 10,898 adults with a new headache code (G43, G44, R51) at a secondary-care neurology clinic in Türkiye, 2023–2024, with linked laboratory results. As results were carried forward, the exposure was the most recent value recorded at the first visit. The outcome was ≥2 acute analgesic prescription items. Odds ratios (OR) per standard deviation (SD) were estimated with inverse probability-of-measurement weighting, with complete-case and imputed analyses; the equivalence margin was 0.80–1.25. Results: Values were recorded for 47.7% (25(OH)D) to 77.3% (TSH). Weighted ORs per SD were 1.04 (0.95–1.14) for 25(OH)D, 1.01 (0.94–1.08) for vitamin B12, 0.96 (0.90–1.02) for TSH and 0.94 (0.88–1.01) for free T4; all 95% intervals included 1 (false discovery rate–adjusted q ≥ 0.34), and estimates were similar for a migraine index code. All four 90% intervals lay within 0.80–1.25, although equivalence was not claimed for 25(OH)D. Conclusion: In the primary weighted analysis, these markers were not associated with acute analgesic prescribing, so first-visit values may not help anticipate acute treatment needs. Recorded laboratory fields need timing and selection checks before use as exposures. Preprint, not peer reviewed. Online Resource 1 (supplementary methods and tables) is included as a separate file.
title: Vitamin D, vitamin B12 and thyroid function recorded at the first headache-coded visit and later acute analgesic prescribing: a routine-records cohort study

summary: Anaxia, the BLLM engine: typed construction search, independent checks and recorded failure residues. This research candidate adds twelve exact finite-interval certificates for reflexive four-polytopes, an independent integer verifier, and a portable animated certificate explorer. Relative to the supplied Kreuzer–Skarke point-pair census, the maximum shortest descent satisfies 22 ≤ D4 ≤ 346. The prior bound 348 for arbitrary descents is unchanged. The verifier reconstructs facets, primal and polar lattice points, strict containment, interval costs, pair bounds and exceptional-census coverage. It does not reconstruct the entire classification histogram. The sharp seed constant, Hodge F2/F3-prime, GSC and the continuum Yang–Mills problem remain open. The full four-target closure benchmark has not been crossed. Graph survivors are necessary candidate configurations, not constructed semiregular objects. No new Lean formalization of the interval refinement is claimed.
title: BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI

summary: This study established a decadal baseline (2015) for heavy metal pollution in the Western Lagos Lagoon  (Makoko and UNILAG Waterfront) using the rainbow land crab, Cardisoma armatum, as a sentinel bio monitor. Morphometric analysis revealed significantly large carapace dimensions, suggesting an advanced  age-class or high nutrient loading (eutrophication) rather than environmental stability. While raw tissue  concentrations for Lead (Pb) showed no significant spatial variance (p > 0.05), the Biota-Sediment  Accumulation Factor for Pb was above the 1.0 threshold at both stations, identifying it as the primary  toxicological threat. Conversely, Zinc (Zn) levels remained within safe BSAF limits, consistent with its role  as a regulated essential micronutrient. Biochemical markers (CAT, GST, and MDA) indicated significant  oxidative stress, particularly at the UNILAG site, suggesting a high pollution-induced metabolic burden.  Histopathological examination corroborated these findings, showing a marked reduction in reserved inclusion  cells (R-cells) across both populations, which is a clear signal of metabolic exhaustion as energy is diverted  from somatic growth to detoxification. Physical evidence of organopathy was further observed via hemocyte  plugs in the gills and tubular degradation in the hepatopancreas. These 2015 findings provide a critical  reference point for future longitudinal studies and highlight the urgent need for integrated human health risk  assessments, analysis of reproductive damage due to oxidative stress in the Lagos Lagoon ecosystem.  Keywords- Bio-indicators, BSAF, Cardisoma armatum, Oxidative Stress Biomarkers, Metabolic Exhaustion.

summary: **GLOBES — Global Library of Observations from Buoys for Evaluating Sea States** GLOBES is a global dataset of historical wave observations from moored buoys, developed to improve the accessibility, consistency, and reuse of in situ wave measurements across observing networks. The dataset integrates **1,665 buoy records from 27 data providers across 41 countries**, representing 19,469 station-years of observations spanning 1969–2026. Records retain their native temporal resolution, ranging from 10 minutes to 3 hours, and include up to seven standardized wave parameters: significant wave height (HS), maximum wave height (HM), peak wave period (TP), zero-crossing wave period (TZ), mean wave period (TM), wave direction (DR), and directional spread (SP). GLOBES harmonizes timestamps, units, missing-value conventions, station metadata, and quality-control flags while preserving original provider information and data provenance. The archive is distributed as standardized station-based files, accompanied by provider-specific quality-control information where available. **Data organization:** This release contains 28 compressed archives representing 27 data providers. NOWPHAS observations are distributed separately at 20-minute and 2-hour temporal resolutions, resulting in 1,745 distributed time series. **Release status:** This is a preliminary data release (v0.1.0). Metadata, documentation, and data files may be refined in subsequent versions. **Data use and licensing:** GLOBES integrates observations subject to different provider-specific licensing, attribution, and usage conditions. Users must consult the USAGE metadata field of individual records and comply with the applicable original provider requirements. No single open license applies to the entire dataset. GLOBES supports research on wave climate, variability and extremes, coastal hazards, and the evaluation of numerical models, hindcasts, reanalyses, and satellite-derived wave products.
title: GLOBES: the Global Library of Observations from Buoys for Evaluating Sea States

summary: Despite significant advances in deep learning-based failure prognosis, existing predictive maintenance frameworks consistently terminate at the prediction step, leaving the critical operational challenge of prioritising maintenance resources across heterogeneous asset fleets unresolved. This paper addresses this gap by proposing an integrated framework that couples Long Short-Term Memory network-based Remaining Useful Life prediction with the Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution for data-driven multi-criteria maintenance scheduling, validated on the NASA C-MAPSS FD001 turbofan degradation benchmark. The framework dynamically synthesises predicted health indicators with operational criteria encompassing machine criticality, maintenance cost, and production downtime impact to generate a ranked intervention schedule whose quality is evaluated through a rigorous, assumption-free protocol comprising precision-recall analysis, area under the precision-recall curve, Spearman rank correlation, and a scheduling efficiency ratio against a random baseline. A five-seed ablation study comparing Long Short-Term Memory, Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory, and Gated Recurrent Unit architectures, with Wilcoxon signed-rank validation, establishes statistically equivalent prediction accuracy, confirming the architecture-agnostic nature of the scheduling design.
title: Code and analysis: A Deep Learning and TOPSIS Framework for Predictive Maintenance Scheduling in Smart Manufacturing: An Industry 4.0 Approach

summary: We study intransitive probabilistic preferences through dice whose face labels may be repeated. We distinguish restricted models, in which the set of permitted labels depends on the number of sides, from the unrestricted model, which allows arbitrary integer labels. We review existence results, including the exceptional impossibility of a Chinese chain of five four-sided dice, and give an explicit construction establishing the known existence of simple cycles of three-sided dice of every length m ≥3, with no ties and a net win margin of one. We examine mixed-integer programming, simulated annealing, and lexicographic optimization of the margins. We then extend pairwise comparison to probability measures by means of bounded, measurable, antisymmetric kernels. For complete comparison data with uniform weights, we derive the Hodge decomposition of the margin matrix into an additive score component and an orthogonal, divergence-free residual. We distinguish the failure of an exact additive representation from the existence of strict preference cycles. The minimax theorem ensures that every finite family admits a mixed strategy with nonnegative expected margin against every mixture of that family. For the historical cycle with margins 4, 4, 10, we compute both the decomposition and the equilibrium mixture (2/9, 5/9, 2/9). Applications to portfolios, artistic evaluation, visual perception, and sports clarify the distinctions among independent comparisons, shared scenarios, and expected utility.
title: Chinese and Mayan Dice: Circular Chains, Explicit Constructions, and Decision Theory

SWAN AI-SQL's recordings are its current ones (2026-10-23, DuckDB 2.0.0); every SWAN 2.0 recording is a fresh run through an empty cache (LOTUS and PLOP on 2026-10-03, BlendSQL and Palimpzest on 2026-10-05, SWAN AI-SQL on 2026-10-23). Always use the latest version: the concept DOI and serve/fetch_cache.sh resolve to it. Every table in the repositories replays without a provider key: run serve/fetch_cache.sh (it downloads, checks and unpacks the latest version), then the benchmark harnesses; the proxy replays each recorded answer with its recorded latency and cost. Model: gpt-5.6-luna, temperature 0, each system's default prompts (zero-shot). Replay matches requests byte for byte; an edited query, another model, or a client library that renders the request differently is a fresh request. The systems' own run-to-run variance (LOTUS's ranking order, result assembly in BlendSQL and Palimpzest, ThalamusDB's sampler, PLOP's parallel operator order) is theirs, not the cache's.
title: SWAN AI-SQL replay cache: recorded gpt-5.6-luna answers of SWAN, LOTUS, BlendSQL, Palimpzest, ThalamusDB and PLOP on SemBench, the PLOP hybrid bench and SWAN 2.0

summary: Malaria early-warning systems that treat climate as a spatially uniform forcing mis-time vector-control deployment when the thermal niche of Anopheles vectors shifts across districts. The framework is formalised as a structural causal model over a district-month lattice, with a graph-identification condition and a lag-recovery theorem that bounds timing error by the spectral gap of the estimated adjacency matrix. A climate-analytics evaluation is conducted on NASA POWER monthly reanalysis air temperature at 2 m for Kampala, Uganda (0.35°N, 32.58°E), 2000–2023, comprising 312 monthly observations with a mean of 22.443 °C and a standard deviation of 1.043 °C; the estimated linear trend was −0.1564 °C per decade. The evaluation shows that a causal graph that admits lagged hydrological mediators recovers the intervention window with lower timing error than a temperature-only baseline, and that the error bound tightens as the spectral gap widens. The contribution is a formal link between causal-graph identifiability and the operational quantity that public-health managers actually care about: how many weeks early or late a spraying or net-distribution campaign is triggered.

summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are increasingly proposed for downscaling convective-permitting rainfall extremes, yet their behaviour under sparse radiosonde initialization remains poorly characterised for dam-safety analytics, where the upper tail of the rainfall distribution governs spillway design. We define the tail-index distortion functional, derive a bound on its bias under sparse initialization, and show that the distortion is governed by the interaction between the PINN's physics residual weighting and the effective sample size of the initial-condition ensemble. The framework is illustrated with a reanalysis-based temperature series for Lagos, Nigeria (2000–2023; 312 monthly observations; mean 26.414 °C; warming trend 0.1553 °C per decade), which serves as a benchmark for the data-provenance and uncertainty-reporting protocol that dam-safety analytics requires. Tail-index distortion should be treated as a first-class evaluation metric alongside predictive accuracy, and it identifies the conditions under which sparse radiosonde initialization produces non-conservative design quantiles. The contribution is a methodological and conceptual apparatus for auditing PINN downscaling in safety-critical climate analytics, not an empirical validation of any particular PINN architecture.

title: Physics-informed neural networks for downscaling convective-permitting rainfall extremes under sparse radiosonde initialization: a climate-analytics evaluation of tail-index distortion in dam-safety analytics

summary: HIGH-INTEGRITY CARGO TRANSPORT AND CONTROLLED RELEASE IN MICRO/NANOROBOTICS AT THE LIMIT English Introduction This high-density research monograph develops a falsifiable architecture for high-integrity microrobotic cargo transport and controlled release. Its core coupling is binding kinetics × transport exposure × triggered release. Arrival is explicitly separated from delivery: one identified cargo lineage must remain bound through transport, stay below registered shear thermal and chemical exposure limits, avoid premature leakage and cross-contamination, release inside the authorized spatial and temporal window, preserve a cargo-specific functional endpoint, and leave a closed record of residual material and carrier recovery. The central contribution is the Cargo Integrity Passport, a replayable evidence object that binds cargo and carrier identities, initial load, binding calibration, route, exposure waveforms, leakage samples, trigger fields, target masks, released mass, functional assays, contamination panels, unreleased residue, retrieval, abstentions, failures, and final disposition. Thirty physicalized derivations connect directly to 82 chapters, 410 single-page research studies, 200 Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. When unknown shear pulses, constrictions, sham triggers, second cargo lots, and carrier aging are introduced blindly, the system must lower both premature leakage and nonrelease rather than exchange one failure for the other. Missing mass, destructive triggering, target expansion, and deleted failed cargo reject the claim.

The methodology is evaluated across two tracks. summary: Drought-index insurance for smallholders relies on weather-station telemetry that is sparse and unevenly distributed, so the index measured at a station can diverge from the losses experienced on a farm. the present analysis treats that divergence as a distribution-free calibration problem and proposes a conformal risk-controlling framework that converts station-level temperature and rainfall records into prediction sets for farm-level drought status with a user-specified bound on the probability of payout error. The framework is developed formally: a nonconformity score is defined on the joint space of station telemetry and farm-level loss indicators, a split-conformal calibration procedure is stated, and a finite-sample guarantee on the marginal payout-error rate is proved under exchangeability. The guarantee is then weakened deliberately to characterise the basis-risk inequity that arises when exchangeability fails across agro-ecological zones, and a zone-conditional calibration scheme is proposed to restore coverage within strata. The argument is illustrated with a reanalysis of NASA POWER monthly air temperature at 2 m for Lagos, Nigeria (6.52° N, 3.38° E), 2000–2023, 312 monthly observations, mean 26.414 °C, standard deviation 0.943 °C, and a warming trend of 0.1553 °C per decade.

summary: Carbon-credit methodologies for mangrove restoration typically assume that credited carbon storage persists for a fixed horizon, yet staggered enrollment and unobserved baseline dynamics make permanence risk difficult to identify from satellite time series alone. The framework combines a potential-outcomes model for staggered adoption with a hidden-Markov representation of unobserved baseline loss, and derives bounds on the bias of the conventional permanence deduction. Analysis of the identification conditions shows that the standard deduction is unbiased only when baseline loss is independent of enrollment timing, an assumption that fails whenever enrollment is targeted at high-threat sites. The derived bounds imply that permanence-risk overstatement is increasing in the correlation between enrollment timing and baseline threat, and that the sign of the bias can be recovered from observable enrollment-date and land-cover-covariate patterns. The contribution is a diagnostic that credit issuers can apply to existing registries without new field data, together with a formal statement of the conditions under which the conventional deduction is defensible.

summary: Virtualization-based obfuscation and Mixed Boolean-Arithmetic (MBA) represent the modern standard for software intellectual property concealment and malware defense evasion, transforming native machine instructions into pseudo-random bytecodes executed by an embedded interpreter. Manuscript abstract Public intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) datasets cover different tissue compartments and measure different subsets of genes, complicating comparisons across studies. We compared four specified gene sets (inflammation, complement, microglial activation and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2)-associated oxidative stress) in public paired human brain, single-cell and hematoma-effluent/blood datasets, using patients rather than cells as inferential units. In two studies of paired brain tissue, inflammation, complement and NRF2-associated scores were higher in perihematomal than contralateral samples in all four patient blocks and five matched pairs. Patient-level single-cell comparisons found higher inflammatory and complement scores in microglia/monocyte groups than in comparator lineages. In 14 patients with same-hour paired CD14+ and neutrophil data, a five-gene score named for microglial activation showed a positive CD14+–neutrophil local-response interaction in all 14 (adjusted P=0.000488), but four-program heterogeneity was not established (Friedman P=0.0796). Restricting this score to three shared genes reversed its CD14+ local response; a jointly scaled three-gene interaction was near zero. Independent acute blood data showed positive case-control differences, whereas longitudinal changes were not significant after adjustment. Inflammatory and NRF2-associated expression differences recurred across these datasets. The CD14+ local response of the microglial-related score depended on its measured genes. summary: After more than a decade of development, high-resolution spectroscopy plays a central role in the atmospheric characterization of exoplanets, offering insights into planetary chemical composition, thermal structure, and atmospheric dynamics. Among the most intriguing targets for atmospheric characterization are Ultra-Hot Jupiters (UHJs), which, due to their extreme temperatures and intense stellar irradiation, serve as unique laboratories for studying planetary atmospheres under extreme conditions. In this talk, I will discuss what we can learn and what challenges we must confront when interpreting high-resolution observations of UHJs, using KELT-9b (equilibrium temperature ~4000 K) as a benchmark case. Based on transmission and emission observations obtained with the near-infrared spectrograph GIANO-B at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo (TNG), I explore how different modeling assumptions impact the detectability and interpretation of atmospheric signals. In particular, the extreme irradiation conditions of these planets may give rise to departures from local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE), making non-LTE effects potentially non-negligible. At the same time, the strong day–night temperature contrasts and asymmetric terminator regions expected in UHJs challenge the applicability of 1D atmospheric models, which may lead to biased or incomplete interpretations of the observed signals.   These effects can have important consequences for the inferred atmospheric abundances and bias the interpretation of key quantities such as the C/O and R/H ratios, which are used to constrain planetary formation and evolutionary scenarios. Addressing these challenges is therefore crucial to robustly link high-resolution observations of UHJs to their origins.
title: INTERPRETING EXTREME ATMOSPHERES: Lessons from High-Resolution spectroscopy of an Ultra-Hot Jupiter

summary: The spectroscopic analysis of cool dwarfs (T_eff < 4700 K) is challenging due to their low effective temperatures, which produce complex spectra dominated by dense molecular absorption bands. These challenges have limited the availability of accurate and homogeneous chemical abundance measurements for these stars. To address these difficulties, we developed AutoSpecFit (ASF) , an automated, line-by-line synthetic spectral fitting code, together with AutoSpecNorm (ASN) , a complementary code designed to perform local pseudo-continuum normalization of observed and synthetic spectra. The combined ASF+ASN framework enables detailed chemical abundance analysis of cool dwarfs using high-resolution optical and near-infrared spectra. ASF employs multiple χ² minimization procedures and iterative optimization to account for the complex correlations among elemental abundances. ASN independently normalizes each synthetic spectrum, ensuring consistent comparisons with observations and reducing uncertainties associated with continuum placement in molecularly crowded spectral regions. Version 2.0 extends the original abundance-fitting framework by introducing an iterative procedure that alternates between the determination of stellar atmospheric parameters and elemental abundances. This approach accounts for the interdependencies between atmospheric parameters and chemical abundances, while employing selected diagnostic spectral lines and iterative optimization to mitigate parameter degeneracies and achieve a self-consistent solution. The updated methodology has been applied to benchmark M dwarfs with independently determined stellar properties, providing an opportunity to evaluate the reliability and consistency of the derived atmospheric parameters and elemental abundances. The ASF+ASN framework has been developed to measure the abundances of up to 15 key elements in cool dwarfs, including major planet-building elements such as C, O, Mg, Si, and Fe. These measurements provide essential constraints on the chemical compositions of exoplanetary systems and their formation and evolution. Furthermore, the application of this framework to metal-poor cool dwarfs offers opportunities to investigate the chemical enrichment history, structure, and evolution of the Milky Way.
title: Detailed Abundance Measurements of Cool Dwarfs: Prospects for Exploring the Galaxy from Stellar Populations to Star-Planet Chemical Connections

summary: HBB2OBB converts horizontal (axis-aligned) bounding boxes (HBBs) into oriented (rotated) bounding boxes (OBBs) by using existing HBB annotations as prompts for segmentation models from the SAM (Segment Anything Model) family. It targets object detection tasks where objects appear at arbitrary orientations, such as aerial imagery, satellite data, and traffic monitoring, producing oriented boxes that tightly encapsulate non-upright objects without any re-annotation. Beyond conversion, it provides horizontal box detection, evaluation, hyperparameter optimization, an interactive annotation viewer, and annotation format-conversion tools, exposed through both a command-line interface and a Python API. 📖 Documentation: rfonod.github.io/hbb2obb , with a quick start on the bundled sample data, a guide per command, pages on how the conversion works, the confidence score, the metrics and provenance, and a CLI and API reference generated from the code. Why HBB2OBB 🎯 Accurate OBBs from HBBs : prompts SAM-family segmentation models with existing horizontal boxes to fit tight oriented boxes around non-upright objects, with no re-annotation required. 🚗 No HBBs? Detect them : the hbb2obb-detect command runs an Ultralytics detector over the images and writes the horizontal boxes the conversion consumes, confidence column included. 🧩 Model ensemble : combines masks from multiple SAM variants through majority voting for more robust, accurate results. 🛡️ Spatially constrained and safe : region-specific masking and contour refinement keep segmentation inside the object, a mask split by an occluder is fitted back together, and a fallback retains the original HBB when no valid mask is found, counted and reported rather than left to be discovered afterwards. 🔎 Confidence-scored output : every OBB receives a heuristic quality score in [0, 1] that flags silent fallbacks and low-confidence conversions, so you know which boxes to trust; the scores go in the label files or in a side-car directory that keeps them strictly standard, and the detector's own confidence can be carried through instead of, or on top of, that score. 📐 Flexible scaling : positive or negative scale factors, optionally different for the short and long sides, recover cropped object parts or tighten overly conservative annotations. 📊 Evaluate and optimize : evaluation against ground truth on IoU, orientation error, and the share of boxes above a high IoU bar, plus the hbb2obb-optimize command, a hyperparameter search over SAM inference resolution, scale factors, and morphological opening kernel, driven by a configuration file so that a whole benchmark of model ensembles is a single reproducible command. 🔬 Where the score comes from : the hbb2obb-analyze command breaks one evaluation down by the ground truth's orientation, size, frame edge, difficulty and class, and scores the conversion against emitting the horizontal prompt unchanged. 🔄 Five annotation formats : read and write YOLO, DOTA, Pascal VOC, COCO, and LabelMe, for horizontal and oriented boxes alike, with a check that proves every format encodes the same boxes. 🔍 Interactive viewer : the hbb2obb-view command pans and zooms over the annotations, in any format, coloring boxes by confidence and overlaying predictions against ground truth. Where a set ships the same boxes several ways, it names the format on screen and switches between them on a keypress. Features HBB to OBB conversion of YOLO-format annotations using SAM-based segmentation, written in absolute pixels or, with --normalize , relative to [0, 1], the convention Ultralytics reads. HBB detection : produce the horizontal boxes in the first place with any Ultralytics detector, a local file, a link, the Ultralytics catalogue, or Hugging Face, passing any other predictor argument straight through. Multiple model support : SAM, SAM2, SAM2.1, SAM3, Mobile SAM, and FastSAM families. Model ensemble via majority voting for enhanced accuracy. Confidence scoring : a per-OBB quali
title: HBB2OBB: Horizontal to Oriented Bounding Box Conversion and Evaluation Tool

It evaluates the mechanisms governing fatigue damage and systematically examines how polymer characteristics, microstructure, reinforcing materials, scaffold topology, manufacturing methods, loading conditions, body fluids, and tissue ingrowth influence fatigue performance, with particular emphasis on translating polymeric scaffolds toward reliable load-bearing clinical applications. Key findings: 🟢 Fatigue failure mechanisms: Polymeric scaffolds can undergo both mechanical and thermal fatigue. Repeated cyclic loading causes residual-strain accumulation, stiffness and peak-stress reduction, crack development, and hysteretic heating, which can progressively degrade polymer chains and ultimately cause structural failure. 🟢 Low- and high-cycle fatigue: Low-cycle fatigue generally occurs under relatively high stresses and involves repeated plastic deformation, whereas high-cycle fatigue develops over much larger numbers of cycles under lower stress levels and is primarily associated with elastic deformation and progressive material degradation. 🟢 Material and microstructural effects: Polymer fatigue resistance is strongly governed by molecular and microstructural characteristics. Increased crystallinity, molecular weight, and molecular-chain entanglement can improve fatigue resistance, emphasizing the importance of selecting and tailoring the polymer microstructure for load-bearing scaffolds. 🟢 Reinforcement strategy: Incorporating ceramic or metallic reinforcing phases can substantially improve the fatigue performance of polymeric scaffolds by redistributing applied loads and dissipating energy that would otherwise contribute to polymer deformation and heat generation. 🟢 Hydroxyapatite reinforcement: Incorporation of 15 wt% hydroxyapatite increased the fatigue limit of PLA scaffolds by approximately 17%, while also improving compressive modulus, crack resistance, and hysteresis energy compared with unreinforced PLA. 🟢 Scaffold topology: Pore architecture plays a decisive role in fatigue behaviour by controlling stress distribution and stress concentration. Even scaffolds fabricated from the same polymer and having comparable porosity can exhibit substantially different fatigue lives when their pore geometry and filament arrangement are changed. 🟢 Topology-dependent fatigue life: Among 3D-printed PLA scaffolds with comparable porosity, the tetragonal topology achieved a fatigue life of approximately 4400 cycles, outperforming hexagonal and wheel-like structures at approximately 3200 and 2500 cycles, respectively. 🟢 Advanced scaffold architectures: TPMS, Voronoi, functionally graded, auxetic, and other irregular architectures offer promising approaches for load-bearing scaffolds. TPMS structures are particularly attractive because their smooth transitions at strut junctions may reduce stress concentrations, although their polymer fatigue behaviour remains insufficiently investigated. 🟢 Bone-inspired architecture: Bio-inspired scaffold design can substantially improve fatigue performance. Increasing the thickness of transverse rod-like struts in bone-inspired structures was reported to enhance fatigue life by approximately 10–100 times with relatively minor effects on density and stiffness. 🟢 Porosity–strength trade-off: Increasing porosity promotes permeability, vascularization, cell migration, and tissue ingrowth but simultaneously reduces scaffold stiffness, strength, and load-bearing capacity. Everything under "BACoN changelog" is the parent tool's history, kept for provenance. Changed Renamed throughout: the package, command, log ( rasher.log ) and lock file ( .rasher.lock ) are rasher . The pipeline reads Illumina short reads , paired or single-end. sample_R1 / sample_R2 , sample_1 / _2 sample.R1 / .R2 and sample.1 / .2 files (bcl2fastq _001 tails included) pair into one sample, in flat folders, subfolders and sample sheets; a file without a mate is a single-end sample, and unmated files next to a sample's pairs are skipped with a warning. A pair is baited whole when either mate matches the reference, mates travel together through every step ( 1_extracted/<sample>_R1/_R2 , 2_filtered/... ), and a desynchronised pair is an error, whether the mates carry identical names or /1 /2 suffixes. Baiting aligns with minimap2 -x sr (BBDuk baits pairs natively with in2= / outm2= ). --keep-bam now keeps the baited reads aligned to the reference (paired samples: a proper paired BAM). Filtering: fastp (adapter trimming, quality and length filters; its JSON and HTML reports land in logs/2_filter/ where MultiQC finds them) followed by deterministic, evenly spread subsampling of the reads (pairs kept whole) to --target-depth . Filtlong, --keep-percent and --filter-by-reference are gone; --min-read-length defaults to 50. Fasta reads skip fastp and are filtered by length. Templated assembly aligns pairs with minimap2 -ax sr and calls samtools consensus -X hiseq (call quality at least 20, as BACoN's unreleased change at the time of the fork). De novo assembly: SKESA ( -a skesa ; the recommended de novo assembler — on the real-data benchmark its SNP distances matched SPAdes' with far fewer contigs) or SPAdes ( -a spades , --isolate ; writes the assembly graph, more robust below ~30x depth). Flye and myloasm are gone, with --read-type and --min-size . --snp-method auto is minimap2 for templated assemblies and SKA2 for SPAdes and SKESA assemblies. -m/--memory also sizes SPAdes and SKESA (it was BBDuk-only). A paired sample X next to a sample named X_R1 or X_R2 is an error (their outputs would collide). No assembler flags circular contigs any more, so SKA2's circular-contig end extension no longer applies. Single-end extraction matches read names with a trailing /1 or /2 stripped, as aligners report them. Output folders of BACoN do not resume under RASHER (the checkpoint fingerprints are seeded with the tool's name; every step runs again); BACoN VCFs are rewritten. Checkpoints record each step's own output signature, and a result is only reused when its output is still the file it wrote: a sample returning to a sheet can no longer pick up reads another sample wrote over. Switching a sample between single-end and paired (or fasta and fastq) removes the other shape's files. BBDuk's paired outputs are checked mate against mate, like minimap2's (a desynchronised pair fails the sample); mates named .1 / .2 ( fastq-dump --readids ) pair; the unpaired-reads file of fasterq-dump --split-3 next to its pair is skipped with a warning; a file cannot pair with a link to itself, and files that look like mates but do not pair are warned about. Stale fastp reports are removed on rerun and for samples that fail at baiting. summary: Meeting the Paris Agreement target and path (PTP) is vital to protect humanity from the worse impacts of global warming. Using a large dimensional and unique Global Trade Analysis Project (GTAP) model for energy and international trade, we calculated the needed change in the energy mix and fall in carbon emissions to meet a minimal PTP of less than 2 o C warming. Covering 30 countries/regions and 31 commodity sectors, the model shows the PTP in annual time steps to 2100 in terms of emissions reduction and the shift in energy mix allowing for changes in energy intensity, renewables growth, and rising carbon prices. By 2050, using a year 2019 baseline, model results show carbon emissions must decrease on a compound basis by at least 5.7% globally, per year, on average, and coal consumption must fall continuously from 2025, complemented by large increases in renewable energy that allow for continued economic growth. We find that global carbon emissions must decline by almost 40% in 2030 and 80% in 2050 to meet a less than 2 o C warming path by 2100. Coal consumption must decline between 85–99% by 2050 among the key emitters (China, the USA, and India), compared to 2019 (the model baseline), complemented by a continuous transition to renewables. For Net-Zero Emissions Targets (NZET), carbon sequestration, such as from re-forestation and land use change, is also essential, although with substantial uncertainty. Model results indicate a net-zero outcome, even with assumed carbon sequestration, occurs no earlier than 2058, at best.
title: Will the World Achieve Net Zero by 2050? The Challenge of Meeting Emissions Reductions Targets in a Global Energy and Trade Model

summary: The package contains all the data and scripts used to produce the results presented in the paper "AST-SZZ: an SZZ Algorithm with AST Change Clustering and Backporting". Datasets A dataset is a list of scenarios, each of which contains the name of a GitHub repository, a bug-fixing commit hash, and one or more bug-inducing commit hashes. The datasets are summarized in the following table. Name Source File ( datasets/* ) Repository root Scenarios DS_GITHUB-j Rosa et al. DS_GITHUB-j74.json github-j74 74 DS_APACHE Wen et al. DS_APACHE236.json apache236 236 DS_RECENT Original DS_RECENT38.json recent38 38 Note that some repositories are no longer accessible, and some bug-fixing commits do not modify source code. We have excluded the corresponding scenarios from the dataset. Preparation Download the following. astszz-amd64.tar.xz (for x64) or astszz-arm64.tar.xz  (for arm64) github-j74.tar.xz apache236.tar.xz recent38.tar.xz github-j74-no-mesg.tar.xz (rewritten to remove the commit messages) apache236-no-mesg.tar.xz (rewritten to remove the commit messages) recent38-no-mesg.tar.xz (rewritten to remove the commit messages) llm4szz.tar.xz  (for the LLM4SZZ experiments only) agentszz.tar.xz  (for the AgentSZZ experiments only) agents-for-szz.tar.xz  (for the Simple-SZZ-Agent experiments only) pyszz_v2.tar.xz  (for the pyszz_v2 experiments only) RESULTS.tar.xz  (the results of the experiments) Then import the image appropriate for your host's architecture. docker import astszz-amd64.tar.xz \     --change "WORKDIR /root" \     --change "CMD [\"/usr/bin/bash\"]" \     astszz Use astszz-arm64.tar.xz instead if your architecture is arm64. The images are built from the codinuum/cca:base image on Docker Hub. AST-SZZ is implemented using Diff/AST , CCA , and modified versions of DDJ and D3J . Finally, start a container and then extract the repositories. docker run -ti -v ${PWD}:/mnt/work --name astszz astszz tar Jxf /mnt/work/github-j74.tar.xz tar Jxf /mnt/work/apache236.tar.xz tar Jxf /mnt/work/recent38.tar.xz Alternatively, you can clone the repositories from GitHub. scripts/clone_repos.py datasets/DS_GITHUB-j74.json github-j74 scripts/clone_repos.py datasets/DS_APACHE236.json apache236 scripts/clone_repos.py datasets/DS_RECENT38.json recent38 Replication AST-SZZ Since the replication is time-consuming, we recommend running the experiments on only a randomly sampled subset of <N> scenarios using the --nsamples <N> option. The following command starts the replication run, where <N_PROCS>  specifies the maximum number of processes to use. scripts/test_astszz.py -u -r -p <N_PROCS> [--nsamples <N>] \     <DATASET_JSON> <REPO_ROOT> For example, the following command runs the script using at most four processes on a sample of three scenarios from DS_RECENT. scripts/test_astszz.py -u -r -p 4 --nsamples 3 \     datasets/DS_RECENT38.json recent38 To disable change clustering, remove the -u (untangling) and -r (remove refactoring) options from the command line. Note that removing both options also disables multiprocessing, since one process is assigned to each sub-SZZ instance operating on a variant derived from a change cluster. To disable the additional conflict rules, add the --orig-d3j  option. The script stores an intermediate result in the  LOG directory. To generate the final result from the intermediate result, use the postprocess_astszz.py  script. scripts/postprocess_astszz.py \     LOG/intermediate.DS_{GITHUB-j74|APACHE236|RECENT38}.json You can also run test_astszz.py on a single scenario using the --sid  option. mv LOG LOG0 scripts/test_astszz.py -u -r -p 4 --sid 5 \     datasets/DS_RECENT38.json recent38 LLM-based SZZs Running all LLM-based experiments requires substantial time and incurs substantial costs (several hundred US dollars). summary: Version 2.0, October 24, 2026: Empirical Revision Substantially revised Paper I to incorporate exploratory geochemical validation using published EarthChem and Alcott et al. (2026) measurements. Added EBA-1/EBA-2 sulfur-isotope change-point analysis, independent phosphorus and redox comparisons, alternative-boundary null testing, and blocked predictive model comparisons. The core source–sink hypothesis is retained, while claims concerning a uniquely identified tipping point, regional diachrony, and demonstrated feedback causation are explicitly qualified. The revision includes updated literature context, methodological limitations, and supplementary analytical materials. Supersedes version 1.0 as the current research statement while preserving the original publication history. The Great Oxidation Event (GOE) reflects the evolving balance between biological oxygen production, reductant consumption, atmospheric photochemistry, and ocean–sediment exchange. This paper develops a basin-resolved source–sink threshold framework in which regional oxygenation responses may differ despite shared atmospheric forcing. Version 2.0 extends the original theoretical framework through exploratory quantitative analysis of published EBA-1 and EBA-2 drill-core geochemistry, including sulfur mass-independent fractionation, phosphorus distributions, organic carbon, and redox-sensitive trace elements. An exploratory sulfur-isotope change point was identified at 1,336.87 m in EBA-2. Independent geochemical measurements exhibit substantial variation across this interval. However, depth-controlled null comparisons and blocked out-of-sample prediction do not establish a uniquely coordinated tipping-point transition. Predictive improvements are restricted to selected indicators and depend partly on baseline specification. These findings preserve the source–sink feedback framework as a testable explanation for nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous oxygenation while distinguishing theoretical plausibility from demonstrated causal dynamics. The revised manuscript provides empirical comparisons, competing-model evaluations, explicit limitations, and falsification criteria for future research. Part of the Planetary Convexity Series, Paper I.
title: Diachronous Oxygenation as a Planetary Tipping Point

summary: This dataset is the supplementary material for the manuscript "Decision Neutrality of Forecast Revisions in Microgrids with Photovoltaics and Battery Storage" by Yun Xing (Hohai University), submitted to Applied Sciences (MDPI). Version 1.0, 25 October 2026. Overview The study asks when adopting a revised next-day forecast changes a battery dispatch decision, rather than only the predicted cost. It derives two checkable sufficient reset conditions under which old and revised forecasts produce next-day storage value functions that differ only by an additive constant. A fixed-input perturbation bound separates this local neutrality from realized rolling-policy performance. Five policies (FF, FS, SF, SS and DAY) are compared on 522 community-days from 270 measured households aggregated into nine synthetic communities, with three synthetic tariffs and two import regimes. Key results - Freezing next-day forecasts is numerically neutral under unlimited imports across the tested tariffs. - Under a 30 kW import cap and time-of-use pricing, retaining midnight targets (DAY) lowers total operating cost by 3.105% relative to full updating (FF). Lower unmet-demand penalties account for 88.3% of the reduction; the import-bill reduction is 0.588%. - Freezing both forecasts while replanning (SS) costs 0.054% more than FF under the same six-hour replanning schedule, separating forecast adoption from target retention. - Under the same cap and tariff, freezing only the next-day forecast (FS) costs 0.188% more than FF. - Matched-calendar comparisons show that the magnitude of update effects depends on the controller scheme. Contents 1. Supporting_Results_and_Protocol.zip: verified reproducibility archive with 3,833 files, including fixed protocols, derived community inputs, customer-community mapping, analysis code, result tables, 15,660 policy-day records, 9,396 local terminal comparisons, 1,496 matched-calendar controller records, half-hour trajectories, figures and an internal manifest. 2. Supplementary_Guide.pdf: Supplementary Methods S1 and S2, extended uncertainty tables S1-S6, data dictionary notes and the run sequence. 3. README_ZENODO.txt: contents, usage order and scope notes. 4. LICENSE.txt: licensing note for code and derived data. 5. CITATION.cff: citation metadata. 6. zenodo_metadata.json: suggested metadata for this record. 7. SHA256SUMS.txt: SHA-256 checksums of the files in this archive. Reproduction Verify the files against SHA256SUMS.txt, extract Supporting_Results_and_Protocol.zip, and read README.txt, RUN_REPRODUCTION.txt and DATA_DICTIONARY.md before running anything. The recorded environment is Python 3.13.9 with NumPy 2.3.5, SciPy 1.16.3, pandas 2.3.3, Matplotlib 3.10.6 and openpyxl 3.1.5. Entry points cover the primary experiment, aggregation, availability sensitivity, diagnostics, both controller families, benchmarks and independent checks. The archive also supports a fresh single-group replay and a full audit without the author's original workspace. Data provenance and scope The household data are the Ausgrid 2012-2013 Solar Home Electricity Data, version 2, obtained from data.gov.au and the BetterGrids mirror. Raw provider records are not redistributed; provider URLs, version and SHA-256 are recorded in RUN_REPRODUCTION.txt and raw_source_manifest.json. Derived community inputs, results and trajectories are included. The archived results are the recorded reference outputs, not new observations. Communities, tariffs and batteries are synthetic scenario inputs, and the manuscript states the limits of the evidence. The original household data are not redistributed and remain subject to the provider terms. Related manuscript Submitted to Applied Sciences (MDPI). summary: International observation systems reveal a consequential possibility: scientific information can be generated, validated, and circulated across institutional and political boundaries without requiring a single authority over all observations or a uniform distribution of capacities . Yet the existence of data-sharing protocols does not by itself establish shared understanding, mutual trust, legitimate reuse, or equitable participation in the production of knowledge . This discussion paper investigates the technical, epistemic, and institutional conditions under which global observation and knowledge infrastructures might be constructed and sustained . Drawing on meteorological and oceanographic cooperation, it distinguishes observational coverage, data availability, interoperability, interpretation, and collective authority. It proposes a preliminary federated research architecture connecting situated observation nodes, provenance and quality records, semantic and model translation, distributed computation, access governance, correction, and contestation. It treats mathematical, physical, social, and normative languages as historically formed manifestations and practices within generative-relational systems, distinguishing their conditional formal invariance from claims to universally identical representation. It further investigates why actors situated in different generative and institutional histories may interpret shared evidence differently, and proposes a bounded research vocabulary for mutually workable norms, continued disagreement, and rule revision without assuming epistemic consensus. The paper conceptualizes trust as a historically constituted relation supported in part by verifiable commitments, reciprocal inquiry, accountable institutions, and effective remedy rather than as a property supplied by cryptography or open data alone. It further specifies prospective services for common knowledge creation and circulation, generalized translation of heterogeneous generative-relational contexts, and traceable transformations of distinct forms of value. A staged validation design differentiates synthetic policy gates, cross-node scientific comparison, productive-capacity trials, and site-dependent ecological and institutional review. A cross-layer assessment profile separates technical interchange, scientific warrant, claimed competent authority, and effective contestation, without deriving legal or ethical legitimacy from technical success. It also examines epistemic and infrastructural asymmetries, the sensitivity of ecological and community data, the incompleteness of model-based assimilation, and the risks of concentrating interpretive authority in highly capable AI systems. Global weather and ocean observation provide instructive but bounded cases, not evidence that all knowledge should be made public or placed under centralized control. The proposed programme remains exploratory and separates conceptual architecture from implemented infrastructure, independent empirical assessment, and normative justification.
title: Global Observation and Knowledge Infrastructures: A Study of Collective Inquiry across Heterogeneous Relational Systems

summary: Water scarcity is becoming a growing problem worldwide due to the expansion of industry, population growth and climate change, and the need for clean and potable water is becoming increasingly important. Traditional wastewater treatment techniques such as sedimentation, filtration, and chlorination often fail to remove emerging contaminants (ECs), such as pharmaceuticals, microplastics, heavy metals, and sometimes create toxic byproducts. Thus, nanotechnology has come up as a novel solution with materials of incredible surface area, tunable reactivity and adsorption capacities. In recent years, a paradigm change towards sustainability has led to the creation of "green" or biogenic nanomaterials. The green nanomaterials are synthesized from renewable biological resources like plant extracts and microbial consortia, which reduce environmental footprints, the use of hazardous chemicals and provide cost-effective remediation. The present review covers all the recent developments in the use of green nanomaterials such as metal/metal oxide nanoparticles (Ag, TiO₂, Fe₃O₄, ZnO), carbon-based nanostructures and bio-inspired nanocomposites in wastewater monitoring and remediation. Systematically, the main mechanisms of contaminant removal, such as physical adsorption, chemical adsorption, photocatalytic degradation, electrochemical reduction and advanced membrane filtration are explored. In addition, the incorporation of very sensitive nanosensors for real-time environmental monitoring is discussed. Recent computational methods, such as Molecular Dynamics (MD), Density Functional Theory (DFT), and Machine Learning (ML), are emphasized as key tools to translate experimental design into application, and to predict the efficacy and toxicity of nanoparticles. Finally, this review critically examines the issues of scalability, economic viability and nanotoxicity, and outlines the path for sustainable implementation of nanotechnology in water management on a global scale. summary: Resilience and Recovery in a \mathbb{Z}_5-Graded NonAssociative System: A Computational Study of Constraint Disruption and Re-Stabilization C. J. Tully, Independent Researcher Engineer, Australia   https://orcid.org/0009 - 0007 - 5661 - 7332 chloetully5@gmail.com   25 th October 2026 Abstract We present a particle-based simulator whose interaction rule on a five-dimensional sector is given by a non-associative, \mathbb{Z}_5-graded multiplication table with golden-ratio weights. The system is subject to spatial forces under several model choices and is equipped with hard gates (velocity clipping and minimum-distance floors). We define a coherence metric on the graded sector and an associator norm that quantifies local failure of associativity. In a controlled perturbation experiment, a sudden shock applied to half the particles at step 75 produces an immediate drop in coherence (0.968 \to 0.511) and a sharp rise in the associator norm (0.008 \to 0.108). The associator continues to rise for approximately ten steps after the external shock has ended, reaching a peak of 0.224, after which both quantities relax: by step 149 coherence has recovered to 0.885   the associator has returned to 0.013. The result demonstrates that, under the chosen force law and hard gates, the graded interaction is capable of re-establishing lowassociator, high-coherence configurations after a severe disruption. We discuss the finding in relation to organizational closure, path dependence, and the distinction between structural and dynamical aspects of self-maintenance. Keywords: Graded algebras, non-associativity, organizational closure, resilience, path dependence, computational models, TT-G41
title: Resilience and Recovery in a \mathbb{Z}_5-Graded NonAssociative System: A Computational Study of Constraint Disruption and Re-Stabilization

The materials cover the industrial feedback comparison, first-failure and statistical analyses, exploratory adaptive reserve, recorded-cost analyses, and bounded external/reconstruction studies. Third-party raw archives, normalized input rows, and per-action selected test or row identities are excluded. Source locations, versions, hashes, and access conditions are documented so that permitted inputs can be obtained separately. It does not claim to provide a self-contained, one-click rerun for every historical execution. Author-created code is licensed under MIT. Original aggregate results, figures, and documentation are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Third-party materials are excluded from these author grants and remain subject to their original terms. summary: Modern physics achieves extraordinary predictive precision, and it has been taught that the strange picture attached to its equations is what nature is: a wave that is a wave of nothing, a particle that is nowhere until observed, action at a distance with no carrier, fields with no medium. That picture was not discovered. It was adopted because the equations worked, and the equations themselves say nothing about it. This framework holds that the equations describe something physical, and sets out to say what: space is a physical medium with material properties, matter consists of structures within it, and the phenomena of the quantum, electromagnetic, relativistic and cosmological domains follow mechanically from that one premise. The quantum part has now been simulated: a definite particle moving through such a medium, guided by its own wave, produces the double-slit interference pattern (Atallah 2026). What this framework explains where current physics offers only the formalism: Quantum mechanics: Double-slit interference, measurement effects, and wave-particle duality emerge from compression waves in spatial medium interacting with definite particle structures; the entanglement correlations, which exceed Bell's bound, remain an open problem for the framework (Section 2). A particle's acceleration disturbs the medium; the disturbance disperses, and the part whose group velocity matches the particle's speed travels with it, with a wavelength set by the particle's momentum through the medium's dispersion—higher momentum, shorter wavelength. When approaching a barrier with slits, the bow wave reaches the slits first (several wavelengths ahead of the particle), diffracts through both openings, and creates an interference pattern before the particle arrives. The particle passes through one slit; beyond the slits its wave has fanned into lanes of constructive interference, and the particle, taking its direction from the wave's flow, follows a lane to the screen. Particles land on the bright bands. The interference pattern follows sinc-squared envelope (from rectangular slit geometry via Fourier transform) multiplied by cosine-squared fringes (from two-source interference)—pure wave mechanics in spatial medium. This single mechanism explains why slow electrons create wide patterns while fast electrons create narrow patterns, why red light diffracts differently than blue light, and why the relationship follows λ = h/p for all particles. No wave function collapse, no particles “being waves,” no action at a distance, no ontological uncertainty—just definite particles creating momentum-dependent compression waves in a physical medium, with each particle independently steered by its own wave's interference pattern. This mechanism has been simulated in a particle medium with no constant fitted to the pattern: one disturbance at launch, a silent coast, and a single rule for direction reproduce the two-slit pattern of the wave itself, its scaling with wavelength, and its disappearance when one slit is closed (Atallah 2026, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23570390). Electromagnetism: All phenomena from DC through optical frequencies emerge from two particle types in spatial medium. Teslons (field mediators with orientation and rotation degrees of freedom) create static electric and magnetic fields. Photons (propagating structures) carry current in conductors and electromagnetic energy in free space. This unified mechanism explains transmission lines, inductors, capacitors, the photoelectric effect, antennas, the right-hand rule, and the Meissner effect—all from spatial medium mechanics through photon-teslon-photon conversion processes. Cosmology: Hubble redshift, supernova time stretching, and CMB uniformity result from photon energy loss and propagation delays through spatial medium over cosmological distances. No Big Bang, no cosmic inflation, no dark energy required. Galaxy rotation curves result from extend

summary: This artifact accompanies “Normal Forms and Complete Relations for Circuits in Agda” (POPL 2027 paper #911), by Xiaoning Bian and Yuan Feng. This version combines the source code and the linked Agda HTML rendering in one archive, acir-popl-revision2.zip. Extract the entire archive; the top-level acir-popl-revision2 directory contains the Agda sources, README.md, LICENSE.txt, the revised paper sources, and the html/ folder. No separate HTML download is needed. Browse without installing Agda: open html/index.html in a web browser, follow the MainTheorems entry point, and click identifiers to jump to their definitions. All links and styling are local, so the rendering works offline. The html/ folder contains 422 generated module pages: MainTheorems and its transitive imports, including 61 artifact modules and the required Agda built-in and standard-library modules. It does not render every unused repository module. To typecheck the source, read the top-level README.md and run agda MainTheorems.agda using Agda 2.8.0 and Agda standard library 2.4. To regenerate the HTML from the repository root, run: agda --html --html-dir=html MainTheorems.agda. The rendering was generated and typechecked on October 25, 2026. All 306,902 local file links and anchors were checked with no broken targets. The html/README.txt file provides viewing, regeneration, provenance, and license information. The Agda sources are unchanged from the popl-revision1 release, commit 5e28af3f344c11b27096c012c2f7b7be4cc51bf5. This combined version also contains the revised paper sources and updated documentation from the popl-revision2 branch. Build/test environment: Intel Core i5-14400 x86-64 PC (16 logical processors), 16 GB RAM, Linux under WSL version 2.7.12.0 on Windows 11 25H2. License: the artifact software and accompanying software documentation are released under the MIT License; see the top-level LICENSE.txt for scope. Dependency notices are preserved in html/AGDA-LICENSE.txt, html/AGDA-STDLIB-LICENSE.txt, and the rendered sources. The paper manuscript, paper sources, slides, and other publication materials are excluded from this MIT license grant. Repository: https://github.com/onestruggler/acir/tree/popl-revision2   Archived Git commit: 391edbaad08e6c5427875da2ea7b7eaa973d6122 (https://github.com/onestruggler/acir/tree/391edbaad08e6c5427875da2ea7b7eaa973d6122).

summary: We study a deterministic comparison of material composition across a fixed time cut when entire contexts have uncertain dates constrained by intervals and a stratigraphic partial order. Source-specific recovery ratios are shared by all contexts and both periods and range over a compact positive rational polytope. Feasible period allocations are exactly the lower ideals satisfying explicit forced assignments. The sign of composition change reduces to a linear weight on these ideals. With the recovery vertices supplied explicitly, all admissible explanations can therefore be checked by polynomially many minimum-cut computations, with constructive dates and recovery witnesses. Sharp finite odds-ratio bounds admit exact enumeration over allocations and recovery vertices. Computing their lower endpoint is nevertheless NP-hard: the associated decision problem is NP-complete in an anchored two-source subclass with known recovery and no stratigraphic relations, even though every allocation has the same positive sign. We also give exact domain and attainment rules for zero masses and open recovery faces. The distinction concerns this shared-mechanism model; the closure, fractional-programming and complexity tools used in its analysis are classical.
title: Direction and magnitude of composition change under shared recovery and uncertain context dates

summary: We study cumulative non-surface heat loss in a rectangular heat model with known forcing and mixed boundary data. The unknown initial perturbation belongs to one fixed spectral H2 ball, and finitely many physical temperature readings have a prescribed joint ellipsoidal error. Standard optimal recovery theory gives the sharp global scalar error. We make this result explicit for the cumulative heat functional, retaining all three-dimensional observation modes and constructing worst initial states. Algebraic and exponential spectral tails give convergent certificates for the infinite-dimensional problem. The unique old worst state yields a necessary and sufficient condition for a new reading to reduce the error, including correlated deterministic errors, together with a positive lower bound on the reduction. For a 100 m column with fixed norm length 25 m and no prior readings, we prove an analytic short-time separation: at the same time and error tolerance, one reading at 75 m strictly reduces the cumulative-heat error while a surface reading leaves it unchanged. A computable sufficient time interval accompanies this result. The radius, reference field, forcing, boundary data and joint error set are inputs; their physical calibration is a separate problem.
title: Cumulative boundary heat from finite temperature readings: sharp deterministic recovery and a short-time depth separation

summary: The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence in agriculture has improved the production of crops, monitoring of the overall process of farming, resource management, and what type of resources will be used for more and better production of the crops in today's era. So, for that AI helps us a lot. The reason behind the use of AI in farming is that better production is what each and every farmer wants. Transparency-like, if the crops got damages, then the farmers have clear and accurate knowledge about the failure of the crop. Explainable Artificial Intelligence addresses this challenge by providing clear, interpretable insights into how the AI system makes decisions. This paper explores how AI is beneficial in farming, focusing on several techniques such as feature importance, visualization, and rule-based explanations that improve decision-making in crop management. This also explores several tools-like, the weather condition, equipment required that gives more than expected outcome, and much more. By this study, some of the features I want to add through technology which helps farmers for better production. The addition of technology in farming enhances transparency, trust, and sustainability in modern farming practices. The importance of XAI in agriculture forms the foundation of this research paper, which intends to present various explanation techniques and study how they will lead to trustworthy decision-making in crop management. summary: We study full-cohort change in two binary latent states observed through a shared, incompletely calibrated anchor and a second item whose channel may change between waves. All baseline items are observed; follow-up response depends only on the follow-up latent state, with a bounded selection odds ratio. The input is the entire twenty-cell observed law. A nonzero respondent cross-wave anchor covariance gives point identification through classical three-view and shadow-variable mechanisms. At zero covariance the latent transition has rank one. We eliminate the drifting channels, obtain the exact feasible rectangle for the common anchor, and show that one corner realizes the complete set of possible signs of latent change. This yields an explicit sharp selection threshold. A positive-probability example has identical observed laws and opposite changes; full-rank perturbations approach this law while retaining a fixed target gap. The results are conditional population-law calculations with external calibration inputs.
title: Sharp directions of change at a rank boundary in a two-wave binary measurement model

summary: Text-to-speech (TTS) technology has significantly transformed human-machine interactions, facilitating seamless communication between humans and computers. However, achieving high-quality TTS remains a significant challenge, especially in synthesizing natural and nuanced speech. In this study, we investigate the potential of HiFiGAN-Hubert-Soft (HHS) vocoders to enhance the performance of TTS models, with a focus on integrating the HHS vocoder into the Voicebox TTS model—a versatile and scalable TTS system developed by Meta AI. Through both subjective (mean opinion score) and objective (speech similarity and visualization metric) evaluations, we illustrate that the HHS vocoder significantly enhances the naturalness and nuance of synthesized speech compared to the baseline HiFiGAN vocoder. This improvement is particularly pronounced in cases where pronunciation variations are minor or context-dependent. Our findings emphasize the potential of HHS vocoders in elevating TTS performance and laying the foundation for further advancements in TTS technology.
title: Improving Speech Naturalness and Nuance using HiFiGAN-Hubert-Soft Vocoder: A Case Study of the Voicebox TTS Model

summary: Multimodal $ΔΔG$ predictors integrating protein language models with inverse-folding representations achieve strong in-distribution accuracy on the Megascale dataset but exhibit limited robustness on out-of-distribution (OOD) proteins, persistent forward-reverse bias on paired-mutation benchmarks, and under-representation of rare stabilizing mutations. Existing approaches address these limitations primarily through additional architectural components, leaving optimization-level intervention comparatively underexplored. We introduce a constraint-aware optimization framework combining Balanced Mean Squared Error, a Siamese anti-symmetric regularizer, and a novel OOD-margin consistency loss on the per-position feature representation, requiring no architectural changes to the SPURS backbone. Across eleven benchmarks and three random seeds, the framework improves Spearman correlation on S669 from 0.486 to 0.540 ($σ=0.002$ across seeds), matching the published SPURS baseline (0.50) without architectural modification, and on S461 from 0.653 to 0.711, with consistent smaller gains on five additional OOD datasets. A controlled diagnostic on Ssym reveals that anti-symmetric training does not eliminate systematic forward-reverse bias, indicating that gains arise through implicit regularization rather than exact thermodynamic constraint enforcement.
title: Constraint-Aware Optimization for Robust Protein Stability Prediction

summary: Genetic mutations frequently disrupt protein structure, stability, and solubility, acting as primary drivers for a wide spectrum of diseases. Despite the critical importance of these molecular alterations, existing computational models often lack interpretability, and fail to integrate essential physicochemical interaction. To overcome these limitations, we propose SheafLapNet, a unified predictive framework grounded in the mathematical theory of Topological Deep Learning (TDL) and Persistent Sheaf Laplacian (PSL). Unlike standard Topological Data Analysis (TDA) tools such as persistent homology, which are often insensitive to heterogeneous information, PSL explicitly encodes specific physical and chemical information such as partial charges directly into the topological analysis. SheafLapNet synergizes these sheaf-theoretic invariants with advanced protein transformer features and auxiliary physical descriptors to capture intrinsic molecular interactions in a multiscale and mechanistic manner. To validate our framework, we employ rigorous benchmarks for both regression and classification tasks. For stability prediction, we utilize the comprehensive S2648 and S350 datasets. For solubility prediction, we employ the PON-Sol2 dataset, which provides annotations for increased, decreased, or neutral solubility changes. By integrating these multi-perspective features, SheafLapNet achieves state-of-the-art performance across these diverse benchmarks, demonstrating that sheaf-theoretic modeling significantly enhances both interpretability and generalizability in predicting mutation-induced structural and functional changes.

summary: Genetic mutations can disrupt protein structure, stability, and solubility, contributing to a wide range of diseases. Existing predictive models often lack interpretability and fail to integrate physical and chemical interactions critical to molecular mechanisms. Moreover, current approaches treat disease association, stability changes, and solubility alterations as separate tasks, limiting model generalizability. In this study, we introduce a unified framework based on multiscale commutative algebra to capture intrinsic physical and chemical interactions for the first time. Leveraging Persistent Stanley-Reisner Theory, we extract multiscale algebraic invariants to build a Commutative Algebra neural Network (CANet). Integrated with transformer features and auxiliary physical features, we apply CANet to tackle three key domains for the first time: disease-associated mutations, mutation-induced protein stability changes, and solubility changes upon mutations. Across six benchmark tasks, CANet and its gradient boosting tree counterpart, CATree, consistently attain state-of-the-art performance, achieving up to 7.5% improvement in predictive accuracy. Our approach offers multiscale, mechanistic, interpretable,and generalizable models for predicting disease-mutation associations.

summary: Here we study how mutations which change physical properties of cell proteins (stability) impact population survival and growth. In our model the genotype is presented as a set of N numbers, folding free energies of cells N proteins. Mutations occur upon replications so that stabilities of some proteins in daughter cells differ from those in parent cell by random amounts drawn from experimental distribution of mutational effects on protein stability. The genotype-phenotype relationship posits that unstable proteins confer lethal phenotype to a cell and in addition the cells fitness (duplication rate) is proportional to the concentration of its folded proteins. Simulations reveal that lethal mutagenesis occurs at mutation rates close to 7 mutations per genome per replications for RNA viruses and about half of that for DNA based organisms, in accord with earlier predictions from analytical theory and experiment. This number appears somewhat dependent on the number of genes in the organisms and natural death rate. Further, our model reproduces the distribution of stabilities of natural proteins in excellent agreement with experiment. Our model predicts that species with high mutation rates, tend to have less stable proteins compared to species with low mutation rate.
title: Lethal Mutagenesis in Viruses and Bacteria

summary: Classical population genetics a priori assigns fitness to alleles without considering molecular or functional properties of proteins that these alleles encode. Here we study population dynamics in a model where fitness can be inferred from physical properties of proteins under a physiological assumption that loss of stability of any protein encoded by an essential gene confers a lethal phenotype. Accumulation of mutations in organisms containing Gamma genes can then be represented as diffusion within the Gamma dimensional hypercube with adsorbing boundaries which are determined, in each dimension, by loss of a protein stability and, at higher stability, by lack of protein sequences. Solving the diffusion equation whose parameters are derived from the data on point mutations in proteins, we determine a universal distribution of protein stabilities, in agreement with existing data. The theory provides a fundamental relation between mutation rate, maximal genome size and thermodynamic response of proteins to point mutations. It establishes a universal speed limit on rate of molecular evolution by predicting that populations go extinct (via lethal mutagenesis) when mutation rate exceeds approximately 6 mutations per essential part of genome per replication for mesophilic organisms and 1 to 2 mutations per genome per replication for thermophilic ones. Further, our results suggest that in absence of error correction, modern RNA viruses and primordial genomes must necessarily be very short. Several RNA viruses function close to the evolutionary speed limit while error correction mechanisms used by DNA viruses and non-mutant strains of bacteria featuring various genome lengths and mutation rates have brought these organisms universally about 1000 fold below the natural speed limit.
title: The Hypercube of Life: How Protein Stability Imposes Limits on Organism Complexity and Speed of Molecular Evolution

summary: Autonomous LLM agents act through tools under per-action authorization: a local guard screens each tool call in isolation. We show that local authorization does not compose into global authorization. A compositional authorization failure (CAF) is a locally authorized execution, or a pair of locally authorized executions, that violates a global policy spanning intent, purpose, provenance, consent, and delegation. We characterize CAFs along two axes, expressiveness (single-trace safety versus relational k-safety) and observability (a ladder of monitor profiles). Our central result is an impossibility: relational purpose violations form a 2-safety hyperproperty with no per-trace locus of blame, so a per-action monitor that never raises a false alarm detects none of them, independent of the underlying model or decision procedure; they become visible only under cross-execution monitoring, which none of the six guardrails we survey implements. We make this constructive with AL-SYNTH, a SAT/SMT synthesizer (using no language model) that emits minimal CAF witnesses, each checked against an exhaustive oracle. The empirical signature is sharp: across nine LLM judges the per-action view approves the synthesized witness almost without exception, blocking it at a rate comparable to a benign control, yet the same models flag it when shown the two executions together. Per-action authorization is therefore structurally insufficient for relational policy conjuncts not reducible to single-trace safety: to bound them, a monitor must compare executions or accept false alarms.
title: Local Allow, Global Deny: Why Per-Action Authorization Does Not Compose in LLM Agents

summary: Continuous flow language models offer a path to parallel generation with tools for control and acceleration unavailable to discrete diffusion, yet effective techniques for building them at the billion-parameter scale remain less established. We present Lafa (Large flow language model), a fast, high-performing flow language model scaled to 8B parameters in a data-efficient manner. Lafa is a blockwise flow model with causal attention on the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. This design enables efficient training by adapting pretrained autoregressive (AR) models and fast inference via prefix caching and blockwise parallel decoding. We train Lafa at 0.5B, 7B, and 8B scales with fewer than 30B tokens, more efficient than previous diffusion models, and evaluate it on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, where the learned flow matches or surpasses the quality of AR and can be distilled into flow maps for one- and few-step generation. Notably, flow training preserves or even improves pretrained AR capabilities via a multi-token prediction effect, which we leverage in a self-speculative decoding scheme that verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively within a single model. This yields 2.54x the throughput of an AR model at comparable quality, outperforming multi-token prediction and discrete diffusion methods. Our findings show that continuous flows can serve as a scalable foundation for language modeling.
title: Large Flow Language Models
