summary: Real-time video generation, interactive world models, and on-device image synthesis are almost a reality. Diffusion Transformers (DiT) achieve excellent sample quality, shifting the bottleneck to the throughput of the models themselves. Natural images are inherently sparse, as large portions of an image are often background, contribute little to the scene content, and are easy to denoise. DiTs fail to exploit this sparsity, as they process image tokens statically and uniformly. We propose MoDDiT, a simple architecture modification that learns to route tokens through both MLP and self-attention operations. By routing tokens through both blocks independently, MoDDiT allows for dynamic compute allocation in MLPs that varies across tokens, images, and denoising timesteps. Using MoDDiT to train image generation models from scratch significantly reduces computational costs of training and inference, processing as few as 12.5% of the tokens. By increasing sparsity and model depth, MoDDiT reduces costs and improves generation performance over unrouted baselines. The learned allocation is interpretable, revealing how computation varies with visual content and noise level. We also use MoDDiT to train video generation models, where allocation correlates with motion, and to distill a dense bidirectional video model into a sparse autoregressive student.
title: MoDDiT: Simple Token Routing in Diffusion Transformers

summary: Online Continual Learning (OCL) requires models to learn from non-stationary data streams under a strict single-pass constraint, making them highly susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. While existing studies have explored various strategies from data, architecture, and optimization perspectives, the optimizer often directly uses generic approaches such as SGD and AdamW. In this work, we reveal a new link between optimization dynamics and OCL needs by recasting Polyak-Ruppert averaging as the engine of "plasticity" and Primal averaging as the anchor of "stability". This inspires our novel optimizer, SPIN (Stability-Plasticity INterpolation), which explicitly decouples plasticity and stability by interpolating between a fast-moving "plasticity" sequence and an adaptive "stability" sequence. We theoretically demonstrate that SPIN implicitly employs an inverse Hessian approximation, providing crucial Tikhonov regularization to damp noisy, single-sample Hessian estimates and mitigate forgetting. More importantly, SPIN can be seamlessly integrated into existing OCL methods by taking resulted gradients as input and replacing standard optimizers. Extensive experiments show that using SPIN instead of standard optimizers yields consistent and significant performance gains across multiple OCL approaches, including the challenging rehearsal-free setting and under strict memory constraints.
title: From Generic to Dedicated: A Novel Optimizer for Online Continual Learning

summary: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision-making. In response, prototype-based models in explainable AI have attracted growing attention for their ability to retrieve visually similar examples as faithful explanations. Although these models achieve competitive classification accuracy, they often exhibit degraded explanation quality across datasets with varying characteristics, limiting their practical applicability. We draw on insights from cognitive neuroscience, particularly the human memory system, which encodes input-relevant information into representations that support recognition. We propose an Engram Memory Network (EMN), a model that emulates the ventral visual stream and inferior temporal cortex in the human brain. Central to this model is a Hopfield-inspired memory module that iteratively retrieves representative prototypes. These memory-refined latents are used for both reconstruction and classification, encouraging the selected prototypes to capture input-relevant information across diverse datasets. To address the lack of standardized evaluation for prototype explanations, we assess three complementary aspects: perceptual similarity (LPIPS and DISTS) for perceived resemblance, subclass alignment, measuring whether prototypes match the input's fine-grained category beyond supervised labels, and information preservation (NMI), measuring how much input information is captured by selected prototypes. Experiments show that EMN improves visual similarity by 17.06%, subclass alignment by 104.57%, and NMI by 42.42% on average across CIFAR-10/100, MNIST, HAM10000, and CUB-200, while achieving the highest average classification accuracy (87.62%) among all methods. These findings underscore the effectiveness of neuroscience-inspired explanation mechanisms in advancing the interpretability and reliability of prototype-based models.
title: Engram Memory Network: Brain-Inspired Prototype Explanations

summary: When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one audited HighwayEnv testbed (1Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We treat the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools) and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port (RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory, a retrieval-free consolidated rulebook, and a flat K-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p=0.011), and even the rulebook's apparent pool-immunity collapsed on five fresh draws. (2) No retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a single 15-token caution instruction, and metrics that price caution erase the rulebook's lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool comparison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We release the testbed, audited ports, seeds, and caches.
title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines

summary: Memory-based temporal graph neural networks (TGN) rely on recurrent node memories to capture evolving interaction histories. However, temporal mini-batching introduces a trade-off between computational efficiency and temporal fidelity: when a node appears multiple times within the same batch, later interactions are evaluated using stale pre-batch memory because the intermediate memory updates have not yet been committed. This problem becomes more severe as temporal batch size increases. To overcome this challenge, we propose AnchorRM, an anchor-based residual memory mechanism that reconstructs event-specific intra-batch node states without executing sequential recurrent updates. AnchorRM treats the last committed node memory at the beginning of each batch as a pre-batch fixed anchor and uses causally preceding same-batch interactions to infer the missing state evolution relative to that anchor. The learned residual then calibrates the anchor to reconstruct an event-specific node memory for each interaction. Because each event-specific residual is predicted directly from the fixed anchor and its causal history, reconstructed states do not depend on previously reconstructed states and can therefore be computed in parallel within the batch while preserving temporal causality. Experiments across four temporal graph datasets and three memory-based backbones demonstrate that AnchorRM achieves an average 6.16x training speedup (up to 10.05x) and 28.67x batch scaling (up to 40x). These results demonstrate that AnchorRM substantially improves the scalability and training efficiency of memory-based temporal graph learning while maintaining competitive predictive performance.
title: AnchorRM: Parallel Intra-Batch State Reconstruction with Anchor-Based Residual Memory for Temporal Graph Neural Networks

summary: A published laboratory number can be verified only when its raw file and extraction method are known. This paper presents the value-level provenance architecture of APS ELN, an electronic laboratory notebook used by both researchers and language-model agents. The architecture was motivated by a production audit in a materials laboratory covering projects performed over almost 5 years. Tracing eight baseline studies from sample to stored value showed that the initial ELN structure preserved the link from sample to raw file. Still, the link from raw file to stored value was lost, mainly due to human factors: manual entries carried no file reference or extractor version. To close this gap, the database design and workflow were reworked so that every stored value records its source file, the data file reader/viewer (DFR) plugin and version, any interactive analysis selection, or the server-side formula for derived quantities. An automated drift check re-runs each DFR on the stored files. In two end-to-end validation studies recorded by agents in X-ray reflectivity and tribology, all stored values retained verifiable provenance with zero drift. A comparison with five other platforms shows that none binds individual stored numbers to both their source files and extractor versions.
title: Value-level data provenance in an electronic laboratory notebook used by humans and language-model agents: An experience report

summary: This is a study commissioned by the Panel for the Future of Science and Technology, European Parliament: Generative Artificial Intelligence could strengthen open science by improving accessibility, findability, and usability. Still, under less favourable conditions, it could also weaken scientific exchange by obscuring provenance, deepening dependency on opaque infrastructures, and reinforcing inequalities and increasing synthetic overload, in which large volumes of AI-generated scientific content overwhelm the capacity of researchers and systems to verify, interpret, and trust information. This study describes how Generative AI is reshaping scientific exchange within the broader framework of open science. It shows that the main policy challenge is not whether Generative AI will be used in scientific exchange, but under what institutional, infrastructural, and normative conditions it can support reliable research, and knowledge valorisation. The European Union should treat scientific exchange as public-interest infrastructure and enact policies to support skills, strengthened provenance, transparency, reproducibility, inclusion, and strategic capacity in an AI-mediated research environment. This report provides specific policy options tackling the risks that can be associated with the use of AI in scientific exchange. This study is prepared for, and addressed to, the Members and staff of the European Parliament as background material to assist them in their parliamentary work. summary: ExM Explorer is a search engine for expansion microscopy (ExM) experiments compiled from the literature. For each study, it records the organisms expanded, the protocol used (fixation, anchoring, gel composition, homogenization, expansion factor), and the antibodies, dyes and stains applied, with their outcome and a link to the source publication. Version 1.0 covers 381 studies, 301 species, 1,483 primary antibodies and 608 dyes and stains. The database was built from 579 full texts identified by searches of PubMed and Europe PMC (including bioRxiv and medRxiv). Each paper was read individually by a large language model (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Anthropic), followed by deterministic curation and eight quality controls. This archive contains the portal (a single HTML file that runs offline), the database with its column dictionary, the provenance of every PDF and the curation log, the EukProt v3 species list used to place coverage on the eukaryotic tree, the code that generates and validates the portal, the extraction and curation scripts with their logs, and the quality-control outputs. Full methods and limitations are described in METHODS.md. Code is released under the MIT License and data under CC BY 4.0.
title: ExM Explorer

summary: In variational damage models, Lipschitz regularization can be introduced by imposing a pointwise bound on the gradient of the damage field, thereby controlling its spatial regularity without adding a gradient-dependent contribution to the energy. After spatial discretization, this condition gives rise to local inequality constraints and associated Lagrange multipliers, whose number increases with mesh refinement. This work introduces the Aggregated Lipschitz (A-Lip) formulation, in which these local constraints are replaced by a single differentiable global constraint and a single Lagrange multiplier, independently of the discretization size. Despite this reduction of the dual problem, the local constraint structure is retained through the gradient of the aggregation operator, which defines effective local multipliers. Under suitable structural properties, these multipliers concentrate on the locally active constraints as the aggregation approaches the exact maximum, asymptotically recovering the local Karush--Kuhn--Tucker structure of the original problem. A consistent primal--dual Newton solver is developed for the aggregated damage problem. The resulting bordered system admits a scalar Schur complement reduction. For the class of aggregation operators considered here, the consistent Hessian further decomposes into a sparse local contribution and a rank-one correction. Exploiting this structure through the Sherman--Morrison formula reduces the exact Newton correction to sparse subproblems involving only local contributions, together with low-cost global scalar and vector operations. The sparse computational structure of the underlying local problem can therefore be exploited despite the global nature of the aggregated constraint. One- and two-dimensional numerical assessments confirm the predicted aggregation accuracy, the recovery of the pointwise Lipschitz-constrained response, and the applicability of the formulation under mesh refinement. The results also provide a first assessment of the computational performance of the proposed formulation.
title: Aggregated Lipschitz (A-Lip) regularization of damage and fracture: a single-constraint, single-multiplier formulation retaining local computational structure

summary: Abstract (it)   Leonardo's Spatial Grammar è l’app che raccoglie le tre ricerche dedicate rispettivamente all’Annunciazione, all’Adorazione dei Magi e al Cenacolo: Leonardo's Rulers , Leonardo's CAD e Leonardo's Score . Non aggiunge una quarta indagine, ma riunisce i tre studi in una lettura unitaria, già depositata nel corpus accademico omonimo. Il corpus mette in discussione l’idea di un’applicazione standardizzata della prospettiva albertiana a base quadrata nell’opera di Leonardo da Vinci e propone, in alternativa, un paradigma metrico-modulare fondato su evidenze geometriche oggettive e falsificabili. Dall’Annunciazione all’Adorazione dei Magi, fino al Cenacolo, emerge una grammatica spaziale in evoluzione: la rigida scacchiera lascia il posto a un sistema di righelli inseriti; la misura, inizialmente monodirezionale, diventa un’architettura ritmica e stereometrica. Il metodo è la retroingegneria CAD, applicata secondo il « banale aristotelico »: partire da ciò che l’opera mostra e che si può misurare. Bugne, mattonelle, arcate, arazzi e cassettoni non sono quinte, ma strumenti lasciati in vista, da cui le proporzioni — la progressione 1:2:3, il modulo 4:3 e i ritmi 1:4:1, 2:1:2 e 1:6:1 — si ricavano dalle stesse opere. Gli spazi restituiti sono misurabili, architettonicamente rimontabili e strutturati sulle misure umane. Le interpretazioni esoteriche e le simbologie non falsificabili restano fuori dal perimetro. L’app come strumento di lettura Leonardo’s Spatial Grammar riunisce le app dedicate alle singole ricerche e ne offre un accesso coordinato. Queste applicazioni sono strumenti di supporto alla lettura: facilitano l’esplorazione delle ricostruzioni, dei moduli e dei confronti geometrici, integrando la ricerca accademica senza sostituirla. App e studi costituiscono un sistema speculare in continuo aggiornamento: le revisioni della ricerca alimentano gli strumenti digitali e, reciprocamente, il loro impiego rende più immediata la verifica dei risultati. Spatial Grammar applica a Leonardo il principio che Leonardo stesso indica come fondamento del conoscere: prima l’esperienza, poi la ragione. La sequenza operativa è precisa: Pura Visibilità, esperienza, ragione, verifica. La Pura Visibilità consiste nel lasciare che l’opera si mostri prima di essere spiegata: nell’osservarne i segni sensibili senza imporre loro un significato. Segue l’esperienza, cioè la raccolta dei dati visibili — conci, cassettoni, gradini, allineamenti, proporzioni. Solo allora interviene la ragione, che riconosce moduli e ritmi; ma ogni ipotesi deve tornare all’immagine per essere verificata. Non si impone una griglia a Leonardo: si legge la griglia che l’opera stessa rende percepibile. Il Rasoio di Occam fa da cardine tra questa priorità del visibile e il metodo induttivo: non si porta la griglia all’opera, si ricava la regola da ciò che l’opera mostra. I segni sono visibili, i numeri e le proporzioni elementari. «Il Re è nudo!» diventa « Res patet ». Gli spazi sono ricostruibili, alla portata del CAD o di qualsiasi riga e squadra. Pura Visibilità: vedere prima di misurare, misurare prima di interpretare. summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are increasingly used as sources of knowledge for large language models (LLMs), hybrid AI systems, autonomous agents, and machine reasoning. However, conventional knowledge representation does not, by itself, establish whether a KG fact is ethically appropriate for a particular use, legitimately accessible to a particular agent, or endorsed by a relevant epistemic constituency. This paper proposes an EPB-passport framework that associates knowledge claims with explicit qualifications concerning Ethics, Privacy, and Bias (EPB). At the level of an RDF triple, the passport records whether a claim is appropriate for a specified agent or context, whether the agent is legitimately authorized to access or use it, and whether it is endorsed by a relevant epistemic constituency. These dimensions are distinguished from truth, provenance, and technical accessibility: endorsement does not establish truth, and technical retrievability does not establish legitimate access. The framework follows a conservative principle: a qualification must not be assumed merely because a claim exists or can be derived. Missing qualification information is treated as undetermined rather than as an implicit positive or negative judgment. The same principle applies to derived knowledge: an inferred claim cannot automatically inherit the EPB qualifications of its source facts but requires dimension-specific propagation and reassessment. The passport concept is also extended beyond RDF triples to semantic claims produced and manipulated by LLM-based systems, distinguishing computational units such as tokens and semantic spans from epistemic units such as claims and reasoning episodes. The paper develops and analyzes this conceptual and architectural framework, examining its implications for KGs, LLMs, LLM–KG hybrid architectures, and autonomous agents. Rather than reporting an implementation or empirical evaluation, it establishes a basis for explicit, context-sensitive governance of knowledge claims and identifies requirements for their formalization, propagation, and practical assessment.
title: Facts Need Passports: Governing Ethics, Privacy, and Bias in Knowledge Graphs

summary: Act No. 328/2025 Coll., on Research, Development, Innovation and Knowledge Transfer, represents the most significant recodification of the Czech RDI system in more than two decades. It replaces Act No. 130/2002 Coll., whose repeated amendments gradually reduced the clarity of the original framework and weakened its ability to respond to the changing needs of the research and innovation system. The Act constitutes a comprehensive reconstruction of the legal framework, complemented by Amending Act No. 329/2025 Coll. and implementing regulations. This article interprets the Act as a framework for a more investment-oriented governance of public support for RDI: in other words, as a basis for deciding how the state supports the creation, development and use of knowledge and innovation. Its key principle is the connection between excellence and impact. Excellent research is no longer treated as a value in itself, but as a precondition whose contribution must be demonstrable in terms of the country’s prosperity, security and international credibility. The Act therefore not only strengthens the capacity of research organisations to translate results into practice, but also opens space for instruments that may increase demand for knowledge, technologies and innovation. The text is not a legal commentary on the new legislation. Rather, it offers a sociological, historical and economic analysis that places the new legal framework within the broader context of the Czech RDI system. It is structured as a coherent arc: context – changes – implementation conditions – discussion – recommendations – conclusion.
title: Act No. 328/2025 Coll., on Research, Development, Innovation, and Knowledge Transfer: Recodification of the R&D&I legal framework in the Czech Republic

summary: Third-party pretrained checkpoints are now the default starting point for computer-vision disease detectors in digital agriculture, yet the poisoning rate at which a backdoor trigger survives fine-tuning on clean crop imagery has not been characterised as a design quantity. the present analysis treats the backdoor trigger as a property of the checkpoint supply chain rather than of the attacker, and asks what poisoning rate a defender must assume when the provenance of the pretrained weights is unknown. A formal model of trigger persistence is developed in which the backdoor is represented as a parameter-space displacement whose survival under gradient fine-tuning depends on the ratio of trigger-aligned to task-aligned curvature. From this model a persistence bound is derived, and the bound is then embedded in a before-after-control-impact design that treats the poisoned checkpoint as the intervention and the clean checkpoint as the control. Operating characteristics were evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD of 6.0, residual SD of 4.5 and intraclass correlation of 0.64. The design required 54 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point difference at 80% power.
tags: backdoor triggers; poisoning rate; pretrained checkpoints; crop disease detection; before-after-control-impact; intraclass correlation; AI supply chain
title: Backdoor-Trigger Evaluation for Computer Agriculture Disease-Detection Models Under Third-Party Pretrained Checkpoints: An Artificial Intelligence Poisoning-Rate Audit

summary: The Decolonial Intelligence Algorithmic (DIA) Framework™: Twenty-First Edition Christian ZacaTechO Ortiz DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23547322 15 September 2026 | Revised 21 October 2026 Abstract Bias in artificial intelligence is not a technical accident. The Decolonial Intelligence Algorithmic (DIA) Framework™ is an operational decolonial architecture for identifying, interrupting, and replacing the epistemological and governance conditions through which Racial Empire Logic is reproduced in artificial intelligence. Rather than treating bias as a defect that can be corrected solely through post hoc fairness metrics, the Framework moves the site of intervention upstream into data formation, classification, model development, evaluation, deployment, and governance. Xam-Xam bu Gore: The Framework of Liberated Knowledge is the epistemological root of the DIA Framework. Authored by Christian ZacaTechO Ortiz and rooted in Wolof, Afro-Indigenous, and decolonial lineage, Xam-Xam bu Gore establishes that knowledge must exist in a state of liberation from colonial capture, epistemicide, institutional gatekeeping, extraction, and imposed hierarchies of intelligence. Its commitments to epistemological sovereignty, relational knowledge production, living knowledge, and liberation as the governing standard shape the Framework’s treatment of artificial intelligence as a knowledge system rather than a neutral technical instrument. The DIA Framework operationalizes these commitments through Four Pillars: Decolonizing Data Collection, Algorithmic Transparency and Accountability, Intersectional Impact Assessment, and Decolonial AI Governance and Accountability Mechanisms. Together, these pillars locate technical decisions inside their political, historical, cultural, and material conditions. The Framework requires attention to intersecting structures of race, gender, sexuality, disability, neurotype, class, caste, citizenship, language, migration, and colonial status, while rejecting the assumption that Western institutional categories constitute the universal baseline against which all other epistemologies must be measured. This Twenty-First Edition extends the Framework from governance-at-inference toward governance-at-formation through Decolonizing Large-Scale Self-Supervised Pretraining on Heterogeneous Corpora . The protocol identifies corpus construction, provenance, language representation, weighting, training objectives, and corpus revision as sites of epistemic governance. It advances accountable reclamation rather than archival purity, recognizing that knowledge survives through occupation, displacement, translation, institutional capture, resistance, and recovery. Its pluriversal approach seeks meaningful engagement across knowledge systems without requiring those systems to surrender their distinct epistemological structures to a dominant Western frame. Global participation is therefore positioned as decision-making authority over how knowledge enters, shapes, evaluates, and may be revised within an AI system. summary: This reproducible code and data documents substantial errors in the Science paper " The air pollution benefits of low-severity fire " (Higuera-Mendieta & Burke 2026), that, when corrected, reverse the core conclusions of the paper. You can find their code here: https://zenodo.org/records/20944436   Their paper uses low-severity wildfire as a proxy for prescribed fire to estimate the tradeoff between the smoke generated by treatment (the costs) and the smoke it avoids in future wildfires (the benefit). However, the analysis contains errors that 1) substantially overestimate benefits and 2) underestimate costs. Correcting these issues reverse the paper's reported air pollution benefits.  The analysis relies on two contradictory definitions of low-severity treatment that artificially inflate the benefit-cost tradeoff. The paper argues that low-severity wildfire (dNBR 100-270) is a valid proxy for prescribed fire when estimating treatment benefits, but then assumes that prescribed fire emits only ~15% as much smoke when estimating treatment costs (it assumes a much lower prescribed fire severity range of dNBR 10-40). Actual empirical ranges of MBTS-mapped prescribed fire in their focal landscapes have a mean fire severity of 133 dNBR. Correcting this issue (either using empirical MTBS dNBR ranges, or more appropriately, using an equivalent 100-270 dNBR low-severity fire range) reverses the findings of net air pollution benefits (their Figure 4 and Figure 5c).  The analysis of the benefit-cost ratio (their Figure 4) also demonstrably overestimates benefits by counting emissions reductions that are not physically possible. For example, their analysis often counts modeled reductions in dNBR that exceed the the observed dNBR in the grid cell (e.g., counting a reduction of 169 dNBR units of emissions when there are only 79 dNBR units of observed wildfire), and counts reductions in dNBR when there was no observable wildfire in the first place (e.g., observed dNBR < 0). Together, this error artificially inflates actual emissions reduction benefits of treatments.
title: Code and data to document substantial errors in "The air pollution benefits of low-severity fire" by Higuera-Mendieta & Burke (2026)

summary: This repository contains the anonymised aggregated data, Python analysis code, and supporting documentation for the Bayesian hierarchical analysis of time to antibiotic administration in the PALOH-UK study. PALOH-UK was a prospective, multicentre implementation study evaluating the introduction of rapid point-of-care MT-RNR1 genotyping into routine neonatal care across 14 neonatal units in England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland between March 2025 and June 2026. The study assessed whether incorporating pharmacogenetic testing into neonatal admission pathways affected the timely administration of antibiotics. The repository provides the data and code used to estimate changes in time to antibiotic administration following implementation, accounting for differences between neonatal units, uncertainty in baseline measurements, and repeated post-implementation audits. The primary analysis included 863 admissions with antibiotic administration times greater than zero and up to 120 minutes. Sensitivity analyses extended the upper threshold to 180 minutes (948 admissions) and removed the upper threshold entirely (990 admissions). The repository includes the analysis scripts, input datasets, model specifications, reproducibility instructions, and outputs from the primary and sensitivity analyses, including convergence diagnostics. Associated manuscript: McDermott JH et al. National implementation of point-of-care MT-RNR1 testing to prevent aminoglycoside-induced ototoxicity in newborn infants: a prospective multicentre study.   Study registration: ISRCTN10216938. summary: In this article, we propose ContactFlowFilter, a novel approach for contact estimation that determines the number of active contacts, their locations, and the associated force vectors. We consider a robot manipulator equipped with joint torque sensors and a base force/torque sensor; such a proprioceptive-only setup presents a challenging inverse problem characterized by (i) multi-modality from non-unique solutions, (ii) temporal dependencies in state evolution, and (iii) discrete contact events involving contact addition/removal. Existing approaches, such as particle filters (PFs) and learning-based methods, often struggle to address these challenges simultaneously. To overcome this, ContactFlowFilter integrates a generative model into the PF framework. The recursive structure of the PF captures temporal dependencies, while the flow matching model serves as an auxiliary proposal distribution to track multi-modal beliefs and detect contact events. Extensive validation in both simulation and real-world experiments confirms the effectiveness of the proposed method. In real-world settings, ContactFlowFilter achieves the lowest dissimilarity from the target distribution, with errors of only 0.36 cm and 0.88 cm for single- and dual-contact scenarios, respectively, while operating at 0.69 ms and 2.69 ms.
title: Mixture of Flow Matching and Particle Filter for Proprioception-Based Online Contact Estimation

summary: Malicious actors frequently obfuscate their code to hinder investigative reverse engineering efforts. Among the most formidable techniques is virtual machine (VM) obfuscation: programs are translated into bytecode for a custom VM, often with a randomized virtual instruction set and distributed alongside a corresponding interpreter. Manual analysis and deobfuscation scale poorly due to the complexity of VM obfuscation and the diversification techniques that render each VM and interpreter unique. Existing methods primarily focus on simplifying execution traces and identifying virtual execution boundaries. However, comparatively little attention has been given to recovering higher-level program semantics from VM-obfuscated code. To address this gap, we propose VMSpec, a novel decompiler-based approach that automates the construction of VM processor specifications, enabling existing, well-known decompilers to analyze the VM-obfuscated code. We evaluate our prototype of VMSpec on 147 programs from an established obfuscation benchmark, comprising hash functions, standard algorithms, and randomized functions, obfuscated with different configurations of the Tigress and Code Virtualizer obfuscators. To demonstrate real-world applicability, we additionally include six domain generation algorithms stemming from real-world malware. VMSpec completely strips VM-obfuscation from nearly all obfuscated samples, producing output comparable to Ghidra's decompilation of the original code. Furthermore, it is the first method capable of reconstructing the complete program behavior of VM-obfuscated programs with infinite, input-dependent paths and recursive calls.
title: VMSpec: A Decompiler-based Approach against Virtual Machine Obfuscation

summary: Despite the success of foundation models in image synthesis, achieving fine-grained spatial control remains a significant challenge, typically requiring auxiliary structural adapters or complex inference-time steering. While modern vision-language (VLM) text encoders possess the latent capacity to represent spatial coordinates, generative models often fail to leverage this information. We demonstrate that the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) distribution is a critical determinant of spatial grounding in flow-matching models. Using a novel synthetic benchmark of geometric primitives, we isolate structural mechanics from textural complexity inherent in natural imagery and introduce a rigorous color-aware layout metric to quantify spatial fidelity. We show that training on a centered SNR distribution results in poor layout adherence (25.9%). Instead, we identify high-noise regimes as a "critical learning phase" for spatial grounding. Shifting the training focus toward these stages increases layout adherence to 80.8%, effectively reaching the 83.6% reconstruction ceiling of the underlying variational autoencoder. We find that the necessity for this shift scales with resolution and aspect ratio variance, and that the conservative noise schedules employed by models like FLUX.1 are insufficient for precise layout adherence. Finally, we show that these findings translate to real-world imagery via the COCO dataset (1.0 vs. 57.3 Average Precision), where state-of-the-art layout adherence is unlocked through distribution tuning alone, without architectural modifications.

summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) based on PPO-style clipping has become an effective approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, standard token-level clipping measures policy change only through the conditional probability of the current token, while the prefix conditioning context is itself generated by the policy. This mismatch becomes especially consequential in long-response and off-policy training. We reformulate autoregressive generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and derive its performance-difference identity under behavior-policy sampling. The resulting change of measure identifies the cumulative likelihood ratio of the generated prefix as the exact importance weight for each stepwise policy-improvement term. Starting from the monotonic-improvement principle of trust-region policy optimization, we then construct a prefix-level trust region using the exact reverse-KL coordinate $r-1-\log r$, whose behavior-policy expectation equals the corresponding prefix-distribution KL divergence. This yields EPIC, a PPO-style sequence-clipping method that directly regulates prefix-level policy drift without relying on a local quadratic approximation or expert-routing replay. Experiments on off-policy reinforcement learning with a sparse mixture-of-experts language model show that EPIC consistently outperforms standard and sequence-level clipping baselines across mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, while remaining competitive with routing-replay-based alternatives. Code is available at https://github.com/LiChengxi666/EPIC.
title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping

summary: We study joint moments of characteristic polynomials and their second derivatives for Haar-distributed matrices from the unitary symplectic and orthogonal groups. We establish their large-$N$ asymptotics throughout the full admissible range of the moment parameters and identify the limiting coefficients probabilistically in terms of the first inverse power sum of the Bessel point process. This extends the corresponding results of Assiotis, Gunes, Keating, and Wei [Proc. Lond. Math. Soc., 132 (2026), e70136] to the full admissible parameter range. Throughout this full range, we also express these limits in terms of a distinguished solution of the $σ$-Painlevé III' equation. Our approach reduces the problem to singular inverse-power statistics of the Jacobi unitary ensemble and combines their finite-$N$ $σ$-Painlevé V representation with a refined Riemann-Hilbert analysis yielding precise small-$x$ asymptotics and uniform derivative estimates for the finite-$N$ correction term. A key ingredient in the probabilistic identification is a kernel-based proof that the rescaled first inverse power sum of the Jacobi ensemble converges in distribution to its Bessel point process counterpart.
title: Painlevé representations for joint moments of characteristic polynomials from the orthogonal and unitary symplectic groups

summary: The iron-based ferromagnetic materials have emerged as a promising system for spintronics due to their high Curie temperatures and significant anomalous Hall effect (AHE) driven by Berry curvature. While there have been investigations into the epitaxial growth of non-layered iron-based ferromagnetic materials, the realization of high-quality single crystal thin films continues to be a formidable obstacle. Meanwhile, the issues such as grain boundary scattering further hinder their characterization and application. Here, we report the first chemical vapor deposition (CVD) synthesis of single-crystalline cubic D0$_3$-Fe$_3$Ge nanoplates. This compound represents a substantial departure from the conventional hexagonal phases typically observed in the Fe-Ge system. Structural characterizations confirm the cubic lattice and stoichiometric purity of the crystals. Structural analysis identifies a strong epitaxial effect, resulting in a giant compressive strain of ~4.16% at the interface that relaxes gradually toward the surface. The second-harmonic generation (SHG) signals might further reveal that such interfacial strain disrupted the inherent centro-symmetry of the cubic phase. SQUID magnetometry shows robust room-temperature ferromagnetism and clear magnetic anisotropy. Magneto-transport measurements reveal a robust AHE that remains stable at temperatures far exceeding room temperature. The scaling observed between the anomalous Hall resistance and longitudinal resistance strongly suggests that this effect is dominated by the intrinsic Berry curvature mechanism. Furthermore, density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the huge epitaxial strain induces band reconstructions and creates dense spin-orbit coupling gaps near the Fermi level, effectively doubling the anomalous Hall conductivity to match our experimental observations.
title: Robust Anomalous Hall Effect in Epitaxial Cubic D0$_3$-Fe$_3$Ge Nanoplates Grown by Chemical Vapor Deposition

summary: Driven by recent advancements in hearing assistive devices, target speaker extraction (TSE) in multi-talker environments has drawn significant attention. To address this, hearing technologies identify attention using neural signals recorded via electroencephalography (EEG) to guide TSE, enabling neuro-steered auditory attention decoding. However, most existing techniques rely on time-frequency masking, which suffers from low fidelity in spectro-temporally overlapping regions and is often restricted to narrowband audio. In contrast, we introduce NeuroCodec, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first generative EEG-guided TSE framework operating in the latent space of a neural audio codec. Specifically, NeuroCodec models spatial EEG dependencies via graph convolutions and fuses cross-modal EEG and speech representations through attention mechanisms and Mamba-based temporal modeling. We further introduce a six-phase training curriculum that progressively incorporates latent reconstruction, multi-scale spectral, and adversarial objectives to ensure stable, high-fidelity speech generation. Experiments on the public Cocktail Party and KUL datasets show NeuroCodec outperforms baselines, across several perceptual metrics. A listening experiment with 20 participants validated that NeuroCodec offers greater perceptual accuracy, achieving a mean score of 82.24 compared with 49.63 for M3ANet. Additionally, the proposed method is seen to enable 44.1 kHz reconstruction with spectral content extending up to 20 kHz, further supporting the perceptual results. Finally, we extend NeuroCodec with a causal streaming formulation suited for real-time processing, providing a basis for hearing assistive devices.
title: NeuroCodec: EEG-Guided Latent-Domain Generative Model for High-Fidelity Target Speaker Extraction

summary: We explore the inverse problem of determining the reaction coefficient $q(x',t)$ in the time-fractional diffusion equation ${}^CD_t u-Lu+q(x',t)u=f$ in $\mathbb{R}^n\times(0,T]$, $x=(x',x_n)$, $0<α<1$, from the trace of the solution on the hyperplane $\{x_n=0\}$. Here ${}^CD_t$ is the Gerasimov--Caputo derivative and $L$ is a uniformly elliptic second-order operator with variable, $x_n$-independent coefficients and without zero-order term. For $L=Δ$ this problem was studied in dimensions $n=1,2,3$ by methods based on pointwise bounds of the kernels, which are not available for $n\ge4$. Our approach relies on the Eidelman--Kochubei fundamental solution: although its singularity on the diagonal depends on the dimension, we show that it satisfies integral bounds of the same form for all $n\ge1$. Using these bounds, we prove existence, uniqueness and stability of regular solutions of the direct problem with a Hölder continuous reaction coefficient. Without assuming additional smoothness of the solution, we show that the inverse problem is equivalent to a closed system of integral equations for $q$ and the derivatives $\partial_{x_n}u$, $\partial^2_{x_n}u$. For the inverse problem we establish a conditional Lipschitz stability estimate on the whole time interval and global uniqueness in every dimension, and prove local existence of a solution. In the case $a_{in}\equiv0$, $b_n\equiv0$ we obtain a stability estimate with explicit constants, which reduces to the known estimates for the Laplacian. An explicit two-dimensional example with a mixed coefficient and a normal drift shows that the hypotheses of the main theorems are compatible and that the corresponding terms in the trace condition cannot be omitted.
title: Recovering the reaction coefficient in a time-fractional diffusion equation with variable coefficients in any spatial dimension

summary: Conservatism in distributed stability certification is often treated as a limitation of the certificate itself, motivating richer Lyapunov functions, tighter relaxations, or stronger optimization. But a more fundamental limitation may arise from the reporting interface: once information is compressed, physically different systems can become indistinguishable. If stable and unstable systems produce the same report, no sound method can separate them. This paper asks where this information limit lies and how much additional information is needed to move it. We model information as an information structure that partitions admissible systems into information fibers. The strongest sound certificate for a fiber is determined by its smallest stability margin, yielding a method-independent benchmark. This separates total conservatism into information-induced and method-induced parts and characterizes information order, task sufficiency, and the stability value of additional information. Three network-node studies show that network-spectrum, scalar/eigenvalue-only passivity, and independent-local reports respectively lose network--node alignment, local directional alignment, and cross-node relation. They show that critical missing information is often relational rather than dimensional. We then move from diagnosis to information design. An information-conservatism frontier gives the smallest irreducible conservatism achievable under a prescribed budget, while its inverse gives the minimum information required for a target conservatism. A witness-pair characterization turns this into a weighted covering problem. Besides, a local sensitivity law provides a computable approximation and identifies valuable unresolved quantities. The framework indicates whether conservatism should be reduced by improving the certificate or enriching the information.
title: Information-Induced Conservatism Frontier of Distributed Stability Certificates

summary: We present \textit{ab initio} no-core shell-model calculations of the electric dipole ($E1$) polarizabilities and photoabsorption cross sections of the $A=3$ mirror nuclei $^3$H and $^3$He using the Daejeon16 nucleon-nucleon interaction. The polarizabilities are obtained by direct summation over discretized continuum states in the harmonic-oscillator basis, while the same spectral information is used to reconstruct the cross sections. This work provides the first extension of the approach from the spin-zero $^4$He to nonzero-spin nuclei by calculating the $1/2^-$ and $3/2^-$ final-state contributions separately and demonstrating their model-space convergence. In both nuclei, the $3/2^-$ contribution is approximately twice the $1/2^-$ contribution. After quantifying finite-basis and excitation-energy-truncation uncertainties, we identify a clear difference between the mirror polarizabilities, induced entirely by the Coulomb interaction because the Daejeon16 interaction is isospin symmetric. The reconstructed cross sections remain stable under variations of the inversion parameters of the Lorentz integral transform and exhibit the same angular-momentum hierarchy. These results extend the discretized-continuum approach to integrated and energy-resolved $E1$ observables in nonzero-spin nuclei with multiple final-state angular momenta.

summary: The Vertex Silicon Plane (VSP), installed close to the target in BM@N Run 9, can extend the tracking acceptance of the central tracking system toward larger polar angles. Using Monte Carlo simulations of Xe+Sn collisions at 3 AGeV, we reconstruct short tracklets from the primary vertex, one VSP hit, and hits in the first two Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) stations. These tracklets extend the reconstructed primary-proton coverage toward midrapidity and higher transverse momenta. For the 10-30% centrality interval of the independent validation dataset, the conditional reconstruction efficiency for reconstructible high-$p_T$ primary protons after BDT selection is 67.0%, while the tracklet purity reaches 86.5%. For $p_T>1.2$ GeV/c, the VSP-assisted tracklets increase the number of reconstructed primary protons by 17.5% relative to standard BM@N tracking. Of these additional protons, 84.6% lie within $|y|<0.3$, where the relative reconstruction gain reaches 45.5%. The added acceptance is concentrated in the high-$p_T$, near-midrapidity region relevant for identified-proton observables. Its use in data requires particle identification in the same region.
title: Monte Carlo study of extending the BM@N tracking acceptance toward midrapidity with the Vertex Silicon Plane

summary: We consider uplink multiuser channel estimation for a generalized flexible intelligent metasurface at the base station, under narrowband far-field propagation and a twin-time-scale mechanical protocol: on the slow time-scale the panel translates rigidly over a planar grid, while on the fast time-scale the surface morphs along its normal direction. Both share a minimum description length front-end for automatic tensor-rank detection. We derive Kruskal identifiability conditions that relate the numbers of elements, morphing states and grid positions to the maximum number of recoverable multipath components, and show that the tensor model reconstructs the channel at panel configurations beyond the training grid. This prediction capability drives a configuration-selective multiuser transmit precoder that searches the entire motion grid without additional pilot overhead. Numerical results confirm the identifiability limits and show that, once the model order is resolved, the configuration search makes the same choice from estimated as from perfect channel state information. The reconfiguration gain over a fixed panel of identical aperture and training budget grows with the user load, and fast morphing proves valuable for conditioning the tensor factorization rather than as a source of beamforming gain.

summary: Diffusion language models generate by iteratively denoising a masked sequence under bidirectional attention, without the strict left-to-right commitment of autoregressive decoding. Whether this difference affects how reliably they remain grounded in structured inputs is largely unexplored. We study this question in table-to-text generation using ToTTo, where highlighted source cells make factual grounding directly testable. We compare the masked diffusion models MDLM and LLaDA with GPT-2 and GPT-Neo under an identical retrieval-based few-shot protocol, together with a QLoRA-adapted LLaDA, and we score reference similarity and source grounding as separate axes. The two pull apart. Within LLaDA, additional demonstrations raise BLEU from 11.3 to 22.0 while NLI entailment against the source table falls from 0.78 to 0.52; QLoRA reaches the best BLEU of the study, 24.15, and grounds no better for it. Manual annotation shows the failure modes differ in kind: the autoregressive baselines tend to wander off the table, while LLaDA-based models more often stay on topic and swap out individual entities. Reference-based metrics alone are insufficient to assess faithfulness in table-to-text generation.
title: A Diagnostic Study of Faithfulness in Diffusion Language Models for Table-to-Text Generation

summary: Long-term memory for multimodal agents remains challenging, as it must preserve fine-grained visual evidence while tracking entity evolution across sessions. Existing abstraction-based memories compress images into text, often discarding visually discriminative details, whereas pixel-preserving memories retain raw observations but struggle to reliably associate diverse observations with persistent entity identities and track their evolving states. To address these limitations, we propose MHG-Mem, a multimodal hypergraph memory that jointly organizes entity identity, state evolution, and provenance to visual evidence. Specifically, MHG-Mem represents distinct entity mentions and their observed facts as individual nodes, grouping identity-consistent mentions and facts through occurrence hyperedges. It then synthesizes aspect-specific evolution states from these grouped observations and links them to supporting entities, facts, and source evidence through evolutionary and evidential hyperedges. To navigate this structured memory, we introduce hypergraph-based agentic search, which adaptively selects an entry layer, traverses typed hyperedges across memory levels, and inspects source observations when fine-grained verification is required. These designs support both detailed visual verification and reasoning over cross-session state changes. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of MHG-Mem, improving performance by 8.20-9.98% over the strongest baseline.
title: Remembering Through Change: Provenance-Preserving Hypergraph Memory for Multimodal Agents

summary: Autonomous mobile robots operating in dense crowds and cluttered sites require $360^\circ$ perception to react to surrounding hazards. While panoramic LiDAR offers full-surround coverage, learning representations within reinforcement learning (RL) is sample-inefficient under sparse rewards, and existing 3D pretrained point-cloud encoders are too memory-heavy for massively parallel RL simulation. We present RangeNav, a compact (183k parameters) LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained entirely on synthetic data. RangeNav uses anisotropic convolutions and circular padding to handle the extreme aspect ratio and azimuthal seam of range images. We pretrain the network using a navigation-aligned objective combining range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird's-eye-view (BEV) prediction, then freeze it for policy learning. In simulation, adding semantic and BEV supervision increases success rates over a reconstruction-only baseline by an average of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points (pp) in procedurally generated training and out-of-distribution realistic test environments, respectively. Zero-shot real-world deployments on a Unitree B2-W quadruped demonstrate robust navigation through dense crowds, low-light settings, and construction zones where limited-field-of-view depth policies struggle. Code and models will be open-sourced.
title: RangeNav: Task-Aligned LiDAR Range-Image Pretraining for Robot Navigation

summary: This archive contains the replication code and data for the paper "Artificial Intelligence Diffuses at Historical Rates despite Unprecedented Cost Declines" (Wagenvoort). It reproduces every figure, table and number in the main text and supplementary materials of both submitted versions, from data snapshots and stored MCMC posterior draws. run_all.sh rebuilds everything and compiles both papers in about 15 minutes and compares every output with the version the papers were built from. Regenerating the posteriors themselves is an optional step, run_mcmc.sh , about 18 minutes. The archive is organised into code (the pipeline and figure scripts), data (public source snapshots, with the URL, licence and access date of every source), engine (the diffusion model this paper's forecasts are built on), posteriors (the stored MCMC draws) and paper (both submitted versions). The top-level README.md describes the environment ( environment.yml ) and gives the full file-by-file provenance of every source. 150 third-party files whose licence does not clearly permit redistribution are not included. data/restricted/fetch_restricted.sh downloads the ones with a stable URL and verifies each against a recorded checksum; the rest need the manual steps documented alongside it. Without them, run_all.sh still runs and skips only the six steps that need them. The diffusion model, its sampler and the 120-technology data are those of the method paper above, archived at Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.20977583) and Dryad (doi:10.5061/dryad.0cfxpnwhf), and included here with the consent of its co-authors.
title: Artificial Intelligence Diffuses at Historical Rates despite Unprecedented Cost Declines

summary: QUANTUM SENSING AND MICROROBOTIC PERTURBATION ANALYSIS OF CELLULAR MICROENVIRONMENTS AT THE LIMIT Microenvironment Gradients × Quantum Readout × Measurement-Induced Perturbation Separation STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 13 What happens when an instrument changes the very microenvironment it is supposed to measure? This research monograph investigates the scientific and engineering boundaries of quantum-enabled thermometry and microrobotic observation in confined, nonclinical cellular microenvironment models. Its central question is whether a localized temperature or magnetic-field gradient can be separated from disturbances introduced by the sensing and manipulation apparatus itself. The proposed research architecture combines hydrogel phantoms, controlled heat sources, nitrogen-vacancy (NV) diamond sensors, independent classical fluorescent thermometry, spatial reference points, blinded sham-actuation experiments, and uncertainty-aware thermal-field reconstruction. Rather than treating a sharp image or improved instrument sensitivity as proof of biological discovery, the study asks how to establish the physical origin, spatial validity, and reproducibility of each reported field. The 770-page volume contains 82 research chapters, five independently paginated research sections per chapter, 30 interconnected mathematical derivation plates, 200 Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Topics range from NV resonance cross-sensitivity, microwave and laser heating, photon statistics, soft-matter interfaces, hydrodynamic motion, and anisotropic thermal conduction to causal controls, inverse problems, spatial covariance, interlaboratory comparison, and qualified instrument retirement. Each research chapter connects a physical mechanism to a falsifiable claim, a nonclinical experimental comparator, a measurement endpoint, and an explicit condition for withholding or retiring the conclusion. The Research Gates preserve actionable questions for future investigators. The Phoenix Answer Embryos offer provisional designs that can be separated, reconfigured, or abandoned when evidence contradicts them. DOI-linked scholarly literature supplies foundations for metrology, quantum sensing, microhandling, and thermal-field measurement without being mistaken for validation of the proposed integrated platform. Scientific Scope and Limitations This is a hypothesis-forming research blueprint, not a report of completed laboratory experiments or independently peer-reviewed findings. It does not establish autonomous nanoscale robotic systems, clinical diagnostic performance, therapeutic efficacy, or universal quantum advantage. Its minimum experimental setting uses confined hydrogels, artificial microenvironments, and properly authorized reference materials. A temperature or magnetic-field reading alone cannot establish cell health, metabolism, viability, or treatment outcomes. STARLI Research Philosophy A scientifically responsible observation includes the possibility that observing changed the result. By making such failures measurable, preserving negative evidence, and leaving research questions open to revision, this monograph invites future human and AI researchers to challenge, extend, and reconstruct its proposed methods.

summary: GOcean-CH4 is a compilation of methane observations from marine sediments, seawater, and the marine atmosphere. This dataset supports the manuscript “Global Ocean Methane Database Construction and Interface Flux Reconstruction” by Xin Ni. The workbook compiles information from public scientific repositories, published articles and supplementary materials, and existing specialist databases. It contains methane measurements and associated metadata, including geographical coordinates, observation times, measurement definitions, original values and units, depth information, source identifiers, and quality-control notes where available. Methane concentration, partial pressure, gas-phase mole fraction, and flux are represented in separate fields. Sediment burial depth, seafloor water depth, and seawater sampling depth are also distinguished. Users should consult the original measurement definitions, source references, conversion notes, and quality-control information before selecting records for analysis. The file GOcean_CH4.xlsx contains a main worksheet named “甲烷数据” and an auxiliary worksheet named “子表2_未知来源”. The auxiliary worksheet retains records labelled as having unresolved provenance or classification, including records identified as outside the marine scope. These records should not automatically be treated as verified marine observations. The observations originate from different sampling periods. The 1991–2020 period discussed in the associated manuscript refers to climatological environmental forcing used for flux reconstruction, rather than a common observation period for all records in this workbook. This deposit provides the observational compilation. Any reconstruction code, gridded flux products, or additional model outputs should be documented separately if included in this or a related deposit. Please acknowledge the original data sources when reusing individual observations.

summary: Threading a flux through a ring often shifts its energy levels. In the N-site spin-one Motzkin ring, a boundary flux leaves the entire zero-magnetization spectrum unchanged, yet increases the ground-state entanglement by giving each spin path a phase set by its lowest height. For equal halves and fixed nontrivial flux, the excess von Neumann entropy tends to approximately 1.581 nats, while the excess logarithmic negativity grows as 2 log log N + O(1). The limiting Schmidt weights come in pairs, allowing local operations that conserve each half's magnetization to extract a logical Bell pair with fidelity approaching one. The manuscript also examines controlled deformations and contrasts this response with suppression in a uniformly gapped neutral sector and with the energy response induced by an additional reverse pair-conversion process.
title: Flux-Enhanced Entanglement with an Unchanged Zero-Magnetization Spectrum in a Motzkin Ring

summary: Ensuring the provenance and authenticity of raw herbal materials in B2B supply chains requires integrating rapid species verification with immutable record-keeping. Existing centralized systems suffer from single-point trust vulnerability, while public blockchain architectures incur high gas fees and execution delays. This paper presents AyurAuth, a unified framework combining lightweight Edge-AI species classification using fine-tuned MobileNetV2 with a permissioned Hyperledger Fabric v2.x blockchain ledger. Deployed via a Node.js REST API and Flask microservice, AyurAuth achieves an empirical top-1 leaf classification accuracy of 85.00% (88.6 ms inference latency) across five key Ayurvedic herb species. Benchmark testing via Hyperledger Caliper demonstrates a peak write throughput of 408.47 TPS with a commit latency of 145.8 ms at 100 TPS, and a read throughput of 485.44 TPS at 41.5 ms latency with 100% success rate. End-to-end batch onboarding completes in 394.4 ms, while buyer QR verification queries execute in 28.5 ms without exposing internal ledger credentials.
title: AyurAuth: A Decentralized Edge-AI and Permissioned Blockchain Framework for Herbal Supply Chain Authenticity

summary: Abstract Modern websites frequently depend on multi-layer dynamic software stacks comprising application runtimes, content-management systems, databases, frameworks, authentication services, third-party APIs, and cloud infrastructure. This architecture provides substantial functionality under normal conditions but can produce an undesirable failure mode: essential public information may become inaccessible even when networking, HTTPS, web servers, and the ability to serve static files remain operational. This paper introduces Web Lifeboat, an experimental architecture and protocol for cryptographically verifiable static fallback publishing. The design seeks to preserve a small, explicitly selected set of essential web information independently of the normal dynamic application stack. Emergency content is represented as static HTML accompanied by a signed manifest describing its identity, integrity, validity period, sequence, and associated trust information. Verification is designed to require neither the site’s database nor its application runtime and to remain meaningful when content is transferred through different transports. Web Lifeboat applies principles of graceful degradation and cyber resilience to web publishing: failure of high-complexity functionality should not necessarily imply failure of low-complexity, mission-essential information delivery. The current protocol draft, version 1.5.2, defines deterministic validation semantics, resource limits, rollback protections, cryptographic verification, key-state handling, clock-uncertainty behaviour, and transition rules. An internal conformance suite contains 42 package and trust-transition cases. The suite currently passes both its own validation process and a separate Go implementation from the same development lineage; genuinely independent implementation testing remains pending. In addition to the protocol design, this work introduces a measurable availability criterion, the Essential Information Preservation Ratio (EIPR), and reports a controlled local PHP-runtime failure experiment. After deliberate termination of the PHP backend while nginx and static serving remained operational, 30/30 fallback requests succeeded and all 20/20 predesignated essential information items remained available, producing EIPR = 1.00 under the tested conditions. This result supports the narrow fallback-availability claim in the experimental configuration; it does not establish Internet-scale survivability, protocol security, or independent interoperability. A reproducibility archive containing raw results, configuration, logs and experiment artifacts accompanies this result. Separately, Web Lifeboat v1.5.2 is being evaluated through a blind external implementation challenge intended to test whether independent implementers can reproduce its precommitted verification outcomes from the written specification alone. Those independent interoperability results remain pending. Conceptually, Web Lifeboat serves a role analogous to an emergency generator in electrical infrastructure: it is not intended to reproduce the full capacity of the normal system, but to preserve a deliberately selected set of essential functions when the primary, higher-complexity path becomes unavailable. The work remains experimental and is not presented as production-ready infrastructure, a completed security protocol, or evidence of Internet-scale survivability. The current results support a narrower proposition: under an explicitly defined failure condition, essential static information can remain available after loss of a dynamic PHP backend when an independent static-serving path has been prepared in advance. Likewise, the ultimate purpose of the work is to uphold a simple, yet highly important resilience principle: when a complex web application cannot safely operate, a website should retain the ability to publish a small amount of authenticated, human-readable information through a substantially simpler p
title: Introducing Web Lifeboat: Toward Preserving as Much of the Web as Possible During a Large-Scale PHP Outage

summary: SlideRule is an open source server-side framework for on-demand processing of science data in the cloud. The SlideRule project offers a new paradigm for NASA archival data management – rapid delivery of customizable on-demand data products, rather than hosting large volumes of standard derivative products, which will inevitably be insufficient for some science applications. The scalable server-side components of SlideRule run in the AWS cloud with optimized functions to read HDF5 data hosted by NASA in S3 cloud object storage. While SlideRule can be accessed by any HTTP client (e.g., curl) through GET and POST requests, the sliderule-python client provides a user-friendly API for synchronous interaction with the SlideRule service. The client library returns standard Python data containers (i.e., Pandas DataFrame) and facilitates serialization with provenance metadata for reproducible science. SlideRule uses a plugin framework to support different NASA missions and data products. The ICESat-2 SlideRule plugin offers customizable algorithms to process the archive of low-level data products from the NASA Ice Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) laser altimetry mission. The user defines a geographic area of interest and key processing parameters via an interactive web interface or the API, and SlideRule returns high-level surface elevation point cloud products in seconds to minutes, enabling rapid algorithm development, visualization and scientific interpretation.

summary: TRUSTWORTHY AUTONOMOUS BIOLABORATORIES THROUGH MICROROBOTICS AND QUANTUM SENSING AT THE LIMIT Replayable Experiments x Permission Governance x External Metrology STARLI Research Institute XXIX - Flagship Research Monograph 20 Can an autonomous biolaboratory become scientifically useful without acquiring the authority to redefine its own permissions, validate its own evidence, or release untraceable measurements? This nonclinical research monograph investigates a bounded laboratory architecture connecting microrobotic sample handling, quantum-enabled and classical sensing, independent metrological reference chains, experiment replay, physical safe stopping, and human authority. Its central proposition is that reliable autonomy is a property of the entire evidence pathway rather than of any single robotic manipulator or AI model. A laboratory result is eligible for release only when sample identity and integrity, authorized execution, traceable references, justified uncertainty limits, and external acceptance are all demonstrated. An apparently successful action is not equivalent to a scientifically accepted sample. Digital replay does not replace physical replication, cryptographic event integrity does not guarantee sensor truth, and a quantum hardware label does not establish a practical sensing advantage. The research design is developed across 82 chapter-level inquiries with five independently paginated investigations per chapter, 30 connected mathematical research plates, 200 distinct Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The chapters address typed authority graphs, specimen provenance, sample exposure, closed-chip physics, covariance-aware sensing, AI planning within finite action spaces, common-cause fault injection, external interlocks, blinded classical benchmarks, evidence DAGs, cross-site replication, data retention, and responsible system retirement. The proposed minimum experimental prototype uses a closed microfluidic chip with interchangeable handling modules, two independently referenced readout channels, simulated or inert-tracer specimens, a separate audit service, and a physically verifiable stop mechanism. Proposed tests include unauthorized-action challenges, hidden calibration drift, interrupted events, sample contamination, unannounced network partitions, and independent laboratory replay or rerun. DOI-linked scientific references establish the relevant literature in automated laboratories, microrobotics, quantum sensing, uncertainty metrology, FAIR data stewardship, and computational reproducibility. They do not independently validate the integrated system proposed here. SCIENTIFIC STATUS AND LIMITATIONS This book is a hypothesis-forming nonclinical research architecture. It reports no completed microrobotic or quantum biosensing experiments, no demonstrated clinical performance, no universal quantum advantage, and no autonomous system capable of authorizing itself. Statistical models, formulas, and decision policies require experimental verification, specialized review, and appropriate boundary conditions. A failed external reference, unavailable provenance chain, or revoked permission requires abstention rather than inference by convenience. STARLI RESEARCH PHILOSOPHY A trustworthy laboratory must remain answerable to evidence outside itself. Autonomy becomes scientifically meaningful when an experiment can be stopped, questioned, reconstructed, and handed to future researchers who retain the right to refuse its original assumptions.

summary: Version 2.0 preserves the original June 2026 Bridge Settlement manuscript and adds a separately dated October 2026 supplement. The addendum introduces Residual Strategic Optionality as an extension of Stakeholder Coherence Theory, examining the incentives of actors capable of disrupting negotiated settlements. It also compares the Bridge Settlement with Jeffrey Sachs's October 2026 peace framework for Ukraine, identifying areas of conceptual convergence and distinguishing the Bridge Settlement's emphasis on reciprocal economic interests, institutional participation, and self-reinforcing peace mechanisms. The original manuscript remains unchanged. This study develops a comparative Bayesian framework for evaluating natural zoonotic and research-associated hypotheses for the proximal origin of SARS-CoV-2 under incomplete evidence. To reduce double counting, correlated observations are consolidated into three causal blocks addressing phenotype and proximal adaptation, the Huanan Seafood Wholesale Market and early epidemic topology, and the Wuhan sarbecovirus research environment. The central calibration yields a likelihood ratio of approximately 1.49 favoring research-associated emergence, while alternative defensible calibrations reverse or strengthen that preference, demonstrating substantial sensitivity to evidentiary weighting. The paper introduces the “Missing Bridge” as the unresolved proximal viral population and transmission history connecting deeper sarbecovirus ancestry to sustained human transmission. It argues that provenance-rich evidence—including authenticated proximal viruses, earliest-human genomic and epidemiological linkage, and upstream ecological or research records—has substantially greater discriminatory value than additional circumstantial observations. The resulting assessment is characterized as  preference without closure .
title: The Missing Bridge

summary: This archive provides the computational methods, structural coordinate files, source data, model outputs, and reproducibility documentation supporting an exploratory investigation of geometric persistence and prediction uncertainty at HIV-1 envelope (Env) glycan sites. The research examines whether local sequence divergence and sparse structural-context observations can improve the identification of unreliable glycan-site geometric predictions. The approach combines sequence-informed error estimation with residual information obtained from six observed glycan-site probes. Held-out evaluations included five BG505-derived Env structures and two JR-FL structures. In the original experiments, the six-probe method improved pooled dangerous-error discrimination relative to sequence-only prediction, with ROC AUC increasing from 0.704 to 0.945 in BG505 and from 0.522 to 0.761 in JR-FL. These results are exploratory. The original evaluations contained only two dangerous underestimates in BG505 and three in JR-FL. Within-structure discrimination did not consistently improve, and training-test construct overlap was identified. Additional construct-family exclusion analyses document the sensitivity of the findings to training composition and failure prevalence. The principal computational outputs were regenerated exactly from archived structural coordinates using the supplied scripts. The archive includes frozen protocols, structural data, prediction tables, provenance audits, family-exclusion analyses, and a companion manuscript draft. The study supports further investigation of sparse structural context for uncertainty assessment but does not establish reliable cross-strain site-level failure detection, glycan occupancy prediction, or protein synthesis prediction. This deposit is intended to support transparency, independent reproduction, methodological evaluation, and future extension of HIV-1 Env structural bioinformatics research. This research extends the author's previously deposited HIV-1 Env glycan-shield investigations by examining the predictive and uncertainty-assessment implications of geometric persistence, local structural constraints, and glycan-site organization.
title: Ensemble Geometric Persistence: HIV-1 Env Glycan-Site Geometry and Sparse Structural-Context Uncertainty Assessment (Reproducibility Archive)

summary: This package contains the code and data needed to reproduce every table, figure, and number in El Akrouchi and Mhada, “When one funder is the field: reporter concentration, voluntary sustainability disclosure, and the measurement of philanthropic development finance” (Frontiers in Sustainability). The study uses OECD Creditor Reporting System (CRS) microdata on philanthropic development finance, 2009 to 2023. It shows that a 2017 discontinuity in policy-marker coverage across nineteen subsystems follows the identity of one dominant reporter rather than reporter concentration. It then reconstructs thematic targeting for the unreported period from project text and examines commitment horizons and crop-system content in agricultural philanthropy. Contents: Notebook 1 ( 1_concentration_all_sectors.ipynb ): extraction of philanthropic grants across all sectors and the concentration test (Tables 1, 2, S1, S3, S16 to S20; Figures 2 and S1). Notebook 2 ( 2_disclosure_horizons_crops.ipynb ): the agricultural analyses, including the text-based reconstruction with bootstrap uncertainty, commitment horizons, and crop-system content (Tables 3, 4, S2, S4 to S15, S21 to S25; Figures 1 and 3 to 7). data/ : the agricultural extraction, the public ODA control series, derived all-sector datasets, the hand-coded audit of the crop dictionary, the crop dictionary, and the reporter list. outputs/ : every table and figure, named after the manuscript item it produces, and the fitted reconstruction model (serialized objects and portable coefficients). Both notebooks run top to bottom with fixed random seeds. The README describes data sources, run order, software versions, and where each result is produced.
