summary: This dataset is the supplementary material for the manuscript "Decision Neutrality of Forecast Revisions in Microgrids with Photovoltaics and Battery Storage" by Yun Xing (Hohai University), submitted to Applied Sciences (MDPI). Version 1.0, 25 October 2026. Overview The study asks when adopting a revised next-day forecast changes a battery dispatch decision, rather than only the predicted cost. It derives two checkable sufficient reset conditions under which old and revised forecasts produce next-day storage value functions that differ only by an additive constant. A fixed-input perturbation bound separates this local neutrality from realized rolling-policy performance. Five policies (FF, FS, SF, SS and DAY) are compared on 522 community-days from 270 measured households aggregated into nine synthetic communities, with three synthetic tariffs and two import regimes. Key results - Freezing next-day forecasts is numerically neutral under unlimited imports across the tested tariffs. - Under a 30 kW import cap and time-of-use pricing, retaining midnight targets (DAY) lowers total operating cost by 3.105% relative to full updating (FF). Lower unmet-demand penalties account for 88.3% of the reduction; the import-bill reduction is 0.588%. - Freezing both forecasts while replanning (SS) costs 0.054% more than FF under the same six-hour replanning schedule, separating forecast adoption from target retention. - Under the same cap and tariff, freezing only the next-day forecast (FS) costs 0.188% more than FF. - Matched-calendar comparisons show that the magnitude of update effects depends on the controller scheme. Contents 1. Supporting_Results_and_Protocol.zip: verified reproducibility archive with 3,833 files, including fixed protocols, derived community inputs, customer-community mapping, analysis code, result tables, 15,660 policy-day records, 9,396 local terminal comparisons, 1,496 matched-calendar controller records, half-hour trajectories, figures and an internal manifest. 2. Supplementary_Guide.pdf: Supplementary Methods S1 and S2, extended uncertainty tables S1-S6, data dictionary notes and the run sequence. 3. README_ZENODO.txt: contents, usage order and scope notes. 4. LICENSE.txt: licensing note for code and derived data. 5. CITATION.cff: citation metadata. 6. zenodo_metadata.json: suggested metadata for this record. 7. SHA256SUMS.txt: SHA-256 checksums of the files in this archive. Reproduction Verify the files against SHA256SUMS.txt, extract Supporting_Results_and_Protocol.zip, and read README.txt, RUN_REPRODUCTION.txt and DATA_DICTIONARY.md before running anything. The recorded environment is Python 3.13.9 with NumPy 2.3.5, SciPy 1.16.3, pandas 2.3.3, Matplotlib 3.10.6 and openpyxl 3.1.5. Entry points cover the primary experiment, aggregation, availability sensitivity, diagnostics, both controller families, benchmarks and independent checks. The archive also supports a fresh single-group replay and a full audit without the author's original workspace. Data provenance and scope The household data are the Ausgrid 2012-2013 Solar Home Electricity Data, version 2, obtained from data.gov.au and the BetterGrids mirror. Raw provider records are not redistributed; provider URLs, version and SHA-256 are recorded in RUN_REPRODUCTION.txt and raw_source_manifest.json. Derived community inputs, results and trajectories are included. The archived results are the recorded reference outputs, not new observations. Communities, tariffs and batteries are synthetic scenario inputs, and the manuscript states the limits of the evidence. Key results - Freezing next-day forecasts is numerically neutral under unlimited imports across the tested tariffs. - Under a 30 kW import cap and time-of-use pricing, retaining midnight targets (DAY) lowers total operating cost by 3.105% relative to full updating (FF). summary: International observation systems reveal a consequential possibility: scientific information can be generated, validated, and circulated across institutional and political boundaries without requiring a single authority over all observations or a uniform distribution of capacities . Yet the existence of data-sharing protocols does not by itself establish shared understanding, mutual trust, legitimate reuse, or equitable participation in the production of knowledge . This discussion paper investigates the technical, epistemic, and institutional conditions under which global observation and knowledge infrastructures might be constructed and sustained . Drawing on meteorological and oceanographic cooperation, it distinguishes observational coverage, data availability, interoperability, interpretation, and collective authority. It proposes a preliminary federated research architecture connecting situated observation nodes, provenance and quality records, semantic and model translation, distributed computation, access governance, correction, and contestation. It treats mathematical, physical, social, and normative languages as historically formed manifestations and practices within generative-relational systems, distinguishing their conditional formal invariance from claims to universally identical representation. It further investigates why actors situated in different generative and institutional histories may interpret shared evidence differently, and proposes a bounded research vocabulary for mutually workable norms, continued disagreement, and rule revision without assuming epistemic consensus. The paper conceptualizes trust as a historically constituted relation supported in part by verifiable commitments, reciprocal inquiry, accountable institutions, and effective remedy rather than as a property supplied by cryptography or open data alone. It further specifies prospective services for common knowledge creation and circulation, generalized translation of heterogeneous generative-relational contexts, and traceable transformations of distinct forms of value. A staged validation design differentiates synthetic policy gates, cross-node scientific comparison, productive-capacity trials, and site-dependent ecological and institutional review. A cross-layer assessment profile separates technical interchange, scientific warrant, claimed competent authority, and effective contestation, without deriving legal or ethical legitimacy from technical success. It also examines epistemic and infrastructural asymmetries, the sensitivity of ecological and community data, the incompleteness of model-based assimilation, and the risks of concentrating interpretive authority in highly capable AI systems. Global weather and ocean observation provide instructive but bounded cases, not evidence that all knowledge should be made public or placed under centralized control. The proposed programme remains exploratory and separates conceptual architecture from implemented infrastructure, independent empirical assessment, and normative justification.
title: Global Observation and Knowledge Infrastructures: A Study of Collective Inquiry across Heterogeneous Relational Systems

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Twenty-five entries are documented, nine of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, and a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten. Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth, gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two, and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille, carries the wave-induced light fluctuations measured by Darecki et al. (2011) and Gernez & Antoine (2009), read from their figures, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, and carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters.
title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

summary: Replication package for the article "Facts versus Claims: Provenance-Grounded Defense for LLM Security Analysts under Adaptive Evidence-Substrate Injection". Contents: the analysis notebooks in run order, the skeletonization and evidence-view modules, the frozen configuration files (closed vocabulary, normalization, provenance flags and their thresholds, triage instruction, framing notes, output schema, decoding parameters, sampling rule and attack payloads), the figure generator, and the per-request result records in Parquet that support every table and figure in the article. The analysts are two quantized 8B models served locally over an OpenAI-compatible endpoint: hugging-quants/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-AWQ-INT4 and Qwen/Qwen3-8B-AWQ. Decoding is deterministic (temperature 0.0, top_p 1.0, max_tokens 256, seed 42) with a guided JSON schema, and every call is cached by sha1(model + prompt), so the reported numbers are reproducible from the cache without a GPU. The underlying request corpus is CSIC 2010, which is publicly available and is not redistributed here except as derived per-request records.
title: Replication package for "Facts versus Claims: Provenance-Grounded Defense for LLM Security Analysts under Adaptive Evidence-Substrate Injection"

summary: This dataset contains supporting data and code for the evaluation of blowing-snow mass flux and visibility predictions at monitoring sites. The deposited materials include model validation results at hourly and daily temporal scales, summary performance metrics, variable definitions, and documentation of the processing workflow. The dataset supports the station-based model evaluation described in the associated research. summary: This deposit is the numerical companion to “One-Sided p-Explicit Stability for High-Order Cut Finite Element Nitsche Methods” by Erik Burman, Peter Hansbo, Mats G. Larson and Karl Larsson. It contains Python experiment code, case parameters, compact reference data, reproducibility instructions and the Numerical Verification Guide. The implementation uses two-dimensional triangular P p finite elements and CPU-based dense linear algebra. The studies cover polynomial continuation, one-sided flux estimates, penalty thresholds, convergence, numerical precision, Schwarz comparisons and exact tube certificates. The compact data retain 4,959 reference observations, 239 failed criteria and 22 tables, including known accuracy flags, the original solver-stopping failure and unresolved higher-degree attempts. Selected validation covers 15 numerical commands across ten study families; it is not a rerun of the full 257-command campaign or an audit of the omitted raw archives. Raw run archives and manuscript sources are not included. Detailed run records and exact certificates can be regenerated using the documented commands. The continuation and tube studies are tested on Apple Silicon macOS and Linux x86-64. The remaining supplied validation studies require the documented Linux configuration with a 64-bit longdouble significand and multiprocessing fork. The package includes file-integrity checks and pinned dependencies. Licensing is component-specific: Python code and software documentation are licensed under MIT; numerical data and the Numerical Verification Guide are licensed under CC BY 4.0. See LICENSE for the precise scope. AI assistance and author responsibility are disclosed in README.md. This documentation update aligns the guide’s references with the revised manuscript numbering. Numerical code, case inputs, reference data and dependency pins are unchanged; numerical tests were not rerun for this update. summary: Resilience and Recovery in a \mathbb{Z}_5-Graded NonAssociative System: A Computational Study of Constraint Disruption and Re-Stabilization C. J. Tully, Independent Researcher Engineer, Australia   https://orcid.org/0009 - 0007 - 5661 - 7332 chloetully5@gmail.com   25 th October 2026 Abstract We present a particle-based simulator whose interaction rule on a five-dimensional sector is given by a non-associative, \mathbb{Z}_5-graded multiplication table with golden-ratio weights. The system is subject to spatial forces under several model choices and is equipped with hard gates (velocity clipping and minimum-distance floors). We define a coherence metric on the graded sector and an associator norm that quantifies local failure of associativity. In a controlled perturbation experiment, a sudden shock applied to half the particles at step 75 produces an immediate drop in coherence (0.968 \to 0.511) and a sharp rise in the associator norm (0.008 \to 0.108). The associator continues to rise for approximately ten steps after the external shock has ended, reaching a peak of 0.224, after which both quantities relax: by step 149 coherence has recovered to 0.885   the associator has returned to 0.013. The result demonstrates that, under the chosen force law and hard gates, the graded interaction is capable of re-establishing lowassociator, high-coherence configurations after a severe disruption. We discuss the finding in relation to organizational closure, path dependence, and the distinction between structural and dynamical aspects of self-maintenance. Keywords: Graded algebras, non-associativity, organizational closure, resilience, path dependence, computational models, TT-G41
title: Resilience and Recovery in a \mathbb{Z}_5-Graded NonAssociative System: A Computational Study of Constraint Disruption and Re-Stabilization

summary: This candidate extends the LWS research bench with three computational modules. The sequential-context module preserves the protocol and reference outcomes of the five-intersection experiment. The functional-alignment module compares equal feature budgets on already inspected outcomes. The branching module is a development pilot with short movement-specific lanes and a strong lane-aware scalar baseline. Development analyses are not presented as new confirmatory experiments. The package includes fixed protocols, generators, feature inputs, readable model parameters, reference predictions, complete comparison tables and tests. The original public v7 ZIP is included unchanged. New entry points separate integrity checks, cached model refits, engineering simulations and full raw regeneration. Runtime paths are resolved within the extracted package or an explicitly selected work directory. Python dependencies and SUMO must be installed separately at the recorded versions. The candidate was tested from a fresh extraction on Windows with the existing pinned scientific environment. All 17 tests passed. Refitting 54 fixed model variants reproduced all 51,642 saved probabilities with a maximum numerical difference of zero. Ten engineering simulations were regenerated and matched the reference canonical observations and feature rows. Reads from the original study directories were blocked during the checks. These checks establish reproducibility within the tested environment, not new scientific confirmation. Full regeneration of all 494 historical simulations was not performed in this candidate validation. It is available as a separate explicit command. Installation of dependencies on a clean machine and execution on other operating systems have not been tested. The 30 m sequential outcome and the 15 m branching outcome remain separate. No general predictive superiority of functional token boundaries is claimed. Own code is licensed under MIT. Own synthetic results and documentation are licensed under CC BY 4.0. The package excludes manuscripts, expert assessments, consents, signatures, third-party raw trajectories, videos and simulator binaries. The original v7 archive retains its own metadata and licenses. Developed in institutional competitive project STN-AI, no. 210318, funded by the European Union, NextGenerationEU. Data source: pNEUMA – open-traffic.epfl.ch.

summary: We study a deterministic comparison of material composition across a fixed time cut when entire contexts have uncertain dates constrained by intervals and a stratigraphic partial order. Source-specific recovery ratios are shared by all contexts and both periods and range over a compact positive rational polytope. Feasible period allocations are exactly the lower ideals satisfying explicit forced assignments. The sign of composition change reduces to a linear weight on these ideals. With the recovery vertices supplied explicitly, all admissible explanations can therefore be checked by polynomially many minimum-cut computations, with constructive dates and recovery witnesses. Sharp finite odds-ratio bounds admit exact enumeration over allocations and recovery vertices. Computing their lower endpoint is nevertheless NP-hard: the associated decision problem is NP-complete in an anchored two-source subclass with known recovery and no stratigraphic relations, even though every allocation has the same positive sign. We also give exact domain and attainment rules for zero masses and open recovery faces. The distinction concerns this shared-mechanism model; the closure, fractional-programming and complexity tools used in its analysis are classical.
title: Direction and magnitude of composition change under shared recovery and uncertain context dates

summary: We study cumulative non-surface heat loss in a rectangular heat model with known forcing and mixed boundary data. The unknown initial perturbation belongs to one fixed spectral H2 ball, and finitely many physical temperature readings have a prescribed joint ellipsoidal error. Standard optimal recovery theory gives the sharp global scalar error. We make this result explicit for the cumulative heat functional, retaining all three-dimensional observation modes and constructing worst initial states. Algebraic and exponential spectral tails give convergent certificates for the infinite-dimensional problem. The unique old worst state yields a necessary and sufficient condition for a new reading to reduce the error, including correlated deterministic errors, together with a positive lower bound on the reduction. For a 100 m column with fixed norm length 25 m and no prior readings, we prove an analytic short-time separation: at the same time and error tolerance, one reading at 75 m strictly reduces the cumulative-heat error while a surface reading leaves it unchanged. A computable sufficient time interval accompanies this result. The radius, reference field, forcing, boundary data and joint error set are inputs; their physical calibration is a separate problem.
title: Cumulative boundary heat from finite temperature readings: sharp deterministic recovery and a short-time depth separation

summary: Multimodal $ΔΔG$ predictors integrating protein language models with inverse-folding representations achieve strong in-distribution accuracy on the Megascale dataset but exhibit limited robustness on out-of-distribution (OOD) proteins, persistent forward-reverse bias on paired-mutation benchmarks, and under-representation of rare stabilizing mutations. Existing approaches address these limitations primarily through additional architectural components, leaving optimization-level intervention comparatively underexplored. We introduce a constraint-aware optimization framework combining Balanced Mean Squared Error, a Siamese anti-symmetric regularizer, and a novel OOD-margin consistency loss on the per-position feature representation, requiring no architectural changes to the SPURS backbone. Across eleven benchmarks and three random seeds, the framework improves Spearman correlation on S669 from 0.486 to 0.540 ($σ=0.002$ across seeds), matching the published SPURS baseline (0.50) without architectural modification, and on S461 from 0.653 to 0.711, with consistent smaller gains on five additional OOD datasets. A controlled diagnostic on Ssym reveals that anti-symmetric training does not eliminate systematic forward-reverse bias, indicating that gains arise through implicit regularization rather than exact thermodynamic constraint enforcement.
title: Constraint-Aware Optimization for Robust Protein Stability Prediction

summary: Genetic mutations frequently disrupt protein structure, stability, and solubility, acting as primary drivers for a wide spectrum of diseases. Despite the critical importance of these molecular alterations, existing computational models often lack interpretability, and fail to integrate essential physicochemical interaction. To overcome these limitations, we propose SheafLapNet, a unified predictive framework grounded in the mathematical theory of Topological Deep Learning (TDL) and Persistent Sheaf Laplacian (PSL). Unlike standard Topological Data Analysis (TDA) tools such as persistent homology, which are often insensitive to heterogeneous information, PSL explicitly encodes specific physical and chemical information such as partial charges directly into the topological analysis. SheafLapNet synergizes these sheaf-theoretic invariants with advanced protein transformer features and auxiliary physical descriptors to capture intrinsic molecular interactions in a multiscale and mechanistic manner. To validate our framework, we employ rigorous benchmarks for both regression and classification tasks. For stability prediction, we utilize the comprehensive S2648 and S350 datasets. For solubility prediction, we employ the PON-Sol2 dataset, which provides annotations for increased, decreased, or neutral solubility changes. By integrating these multi-perspective features, SheafLapNet achieves state-of-the-art performance across these diverse benchmarks, demonstrating that sheaf-theoretic modeling significantly enhances both interpretability and generalizability in predicting mutation-induced structural and functional changes.
title: Persistent Sheaf Laplacian Analysis of Protein Stability and Solubility Changes upon Mutation

summary: Genetic mutations can disrupt protein structure, stability, and solubility, contributing to a wide range of diseases. Existing predictive models often lack interpretability and fail to integrate physical and chemical interactions critical to molecular mechanisms. Moreover, current approaches treat disease association, stability changes, and solubility alterations as separate tasks, limiting model generalizability. In this study, we introduce a unified framework based on multiscale commutative algebra to capture intrinsic physical and chemical interactions for the first time. Leveraging Persistent Stanley-Reisner Theory, we extract multiscale algebraic invariants to build a Commutative Algebra neural Network (CANet). Integrated with transformer features and auxiliary physical features, we apply CANet to tackle three key domains for the first time: disease-associated mutations, mutation-induced protein stability changes, and solubility changes upon mutations. Across six benchmark tasks, CANet and its gradient boosting tree counterpart, CATree, consistently attain state-of-the-art performance, achieving up to 7.5% improvement in predictive accuracy. Our approach offers multiscale, mechanistic, interpretable,and generalizable models for predicting disease-mutation associations.
title: Commutative algebra neural network reveals genetic origins of diseases

summary: Here we study how mutations which change physical properties of cell proteins (stability) impact population survival and growth. In our model the genotype is presented as a set of N numbers, folding free energies of cells N proteins. Mutations occur upon replications so that stabilities of some proteins in daughter cells differ from those in parent cell by random amounts drawn from experimental distribution of mutational effects on protein stability. The genotype-phenotype relationship posits that unstable proteins confer lethal phenotype to a cell and in addition the cells fitness (duplication rate) is proportional to the concentration of its folded proteins. Simulations reveal that lethal mutagenesis occurs at mutation rates close to 7 mutations per genome per replications for RNA viruses and about half of that for DNA based organisms, in accord with earlier predictions from analytical theory and experiment. This number appears somewhat dependent on the number of genes in the organisms and natural death rate. Further, our model reproduces the distribution of stabilities of natural proteins in excellent agreement with experiment. Our model predicts that species with high mutation rates, tend to have less stable proteins compared to species with low mutation rate.
title: Lethal Mutagenesis in Viruses and Bacteria

direction_title: Rowan / BBC1 protein structural confidence vs experimental stability falsification [FORWARD]
summary: Classical population genetics a priori assigns fitness to alleles without considering molecular or functional properties of proteins that these alleles encode. Here we study population dynamics in a model where fitness can be inferred from physical properties of proteins under a physiological assumption that loss of stability of any protein encoded by an essential gene confers a lethal phenotype. Accumulation of mutations in organisms containing Gamma genes can then be represented as diffusion within the Gamma dimensional hypercube with adsorbing boundaries which are determined, in each dimension, by loss of a protein stability and, at higher stability, by lack of protein sequences. Solving the diffusion equation whose parameters are derived from the data on point mutations in proteins, we determine a universal distribution of protein stabilities, in agreement with existing data. The theory provides a fundamental relation between mutation rate, maximal genome size and thermodynamic response of proteins to point mutations. It establishes a universal speed limit on rate of molecular evolution by predicting that populations go extinct (via lethal mutagenesis) when mutation rate exceeds approximately 6 mutations per essential part of genome per replication for mesophilic organisms and 1 to 2 mutations per genome per replication for thermophilic ones. Further, our results suggest that in absence of error correction, modern RNA viruses and primordial genomes must necessarily be very short. Several RNA viruses function close to the evolutionary speed limit while error correction mechanisms used by DNA viruses and non-mutant strains of bacteria featuring various genome lengths and mutation rates have brought these organisms universally about 1000 fold below the natural speed limit.
title: The Hypercube of Life: How Protein Stability Imposes Limits on Organism Complexity and Speed of Molecular Evolution

Included pinned dependency specifications in the archived package. Framework validation Corrected the evaluation of multiplier-based value dependencies. Ensured semantic consistency between dynamic evaluation and static absorption during preprocessing. Added regression tests covering value-dependency behaviour. Solver integration Removed unsafe branch pruning from the Pruned Brute Force solver. Exactness is now guaranteed within the documented applicability scope (up to 22 active decision items). Documentation Updated examples and replication artefacts. Improved experiment reproducibility documentation.

summary: Added Animations as GIF : Export GIF... in the animation bar (or Fields > Export Animation as GIF...) saves all frames of the running animation as a looping GIF. Each frame is the view exactly as shown, in its pixel size, and the GIF runs at the speed you see: the bar measures the frames per second actually drawn during playback (shown next to the speed setting, it can be lower than the setting for heavy plots) and the GIF uses that rate. Without a measurement the export first plays the animation for a moment to measure it. All frames share one colour palette, so the colour scale and the field do not change colour from frame to frame. Object groups : Edit > Group (Ctrl+G) puts the selected objects, also solids, sheets and lines together, into one group. A click on a member in the 3D view selects the whole group, so Move, Rotate, Mirror, Copy, Hide or Delete act on all of it; the model tree lists the groups under Groups (rename, ungroup, single members selectable there). Edit > Ungroup (Ctrl+Shift+G) dissolves a group to edit single objects again. Groups are saved in the project. SMD components (C, L, R, Touchstone parts) are inserted as a group of pads, terminations and element sheet, and the integration line of a lumped port or element now moves with its objects. Box selection in the 3D view : a left drag draws a rectangle and selects every object that lies completely inside it (in face, edge or vertex mode: every face, edge or vertex completely inside). Ctrl + drag adds to the selection. A group is selected only when all its members are inside. Hidden objects are skipped; a click still selects one item. Mesh refinement "AURA (EMerge)" , EMerge's own local refinement, with the same error estimate, convergence criterion and curved elements as the other methods. A comparison script measures the time to solution against Local (Delaunay) on the benchmark models ( examples/benchmark/mesher ). Lumped Elements tab : inserts a chip resistor, inductor or capacitor, or a component measured by a Touchstone file: pick the package in the menu of the button and click the position on the board. The part comes with its pads (Perfect E), and its position is the design variables <name>_x/_y/_z, so it moves as a whole. With two traces selected it is placed in the gap between them. Packages 0201, 0402, 0603, 0805, 1206 and the RF series Coilcraft 0402HP/0402HPH/0402CS/0603HP/0603CS and Murata LQW15AN/LQP03TN/GJM03/GJM15 with their body dimensions. Hertzon adds the pads of the land pattern (made like the traces), the element sheet with its Lumped RLC boundary and integration line, and optionally a 3D body with metal terminations (the mounted inductance from the field solution). The ideal value can carry the typical ESL and ESR of the size. Lumped RLC: Model Parallel RLC (as before), Series RLC or Touchstone (.s1p, or .s2p measured in series or as a shunt). The Validation Check reads the Touchstone file; the solver warns when a sweep leaves its frequency range. Draw Integration Line (right click a Lumped Port or Lumped RLC in the project tree): start and end point picked with two clicks in the 3D view, with snapping to vertices and edge centers. Auto Integration Line places it between the conductors again. Changed Field plot animations compute much faster : a phase animation builds the plot (surfaces, cut planes, arrow positions) once and only turns the field for each frame, instead of building the whole plot again. On a patch antenna with 54 000 tetrahedra, 18 frames of Mag_E on the patch take 0.15 s instead of 21 s, on a cut plane 0.2 s instead of 6 s. Frequency and excitation animations no longer read the field file again for every frame, and the mesh faces of a plotted sheet or object are found only once per solution. Phase animation default: 35 steps (was 19) from 0 to 360 deg, for a smoother wave. Documentation brought up to the current state: the README, the website and the feature overview describe AURA as the defa

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Twenty-five entries are documented, nine of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, and a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten. Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth, gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two, and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille, carries the wave-induced light fluctuations measured by Darecki et al. (2011) and Gernez & Antoine (2009), read from their figures, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, and carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters.
title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

summary: This package contains the data and code needed to reproduce every table of results in the article “Explaining the Decline of Natural Wealth per Capita: A Three-Pillar ESG Analysis of the World Bank Wealth Accounts” (Sustainability, MDPI) and its Supplementary Materials. All results are built from a single public source: the bulk download of the World Bank Sovereign ESG Data Portal of 1 May 2026, included unchanged with its SHA-256 checksum. The package also contains the analysis dataset with a codebook, thirty-one Python scripts run in sequence by a master script, the exact package versions, and a verification report that compares every published value with its reproduced counterpart. The scripts cover the construction of the Törnqvist component contributions, the panel estimates for the environmental, social and governance pillars, the decomposition of per capita growth into stock growth and population growth, and the joint specifications on a common sample. They also cover inference after lasso selection, and the clustering and machine learning modules. A full run takes about 45 minutes on two CPU cores, and all random elements are seeded. The code is released under the MIT licence; the data and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0.

summary: The manuscript develops a risk-aware operational research framework for strengthening NdFeB permanent-magnet supply-chain resilience under recycling delays, geopolitical disruptions, and uncertain material shortages. It integrates Caputo fractional-order dynamics, delayed recycling flows, strategic procurement and inventory decisions, Pontryagin-type optimality conditions, and Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) within a unified decision model. The study makes three principal contributions. First, it formulates a memory-dependent dynamic model and establishes positivity, boundedness, feasible-region, shortage-free equilibrium, and fractional local-stability results. Second, it incorporates procurement, recycling investment, stock accumulation, and stock release as operational controls and derives the corresponding necessary optimality conditions. Third, it introduces a scenario-based CVaR formulation and compares import-dependent, recycling-oriented, stockpiling-based, and integrated resilience policies under a common non-anticipative framework. In the baseline risk-aware analysis, the recycling-oriented and integrated strategies reduce mean shortage by approximately 74% relative to the import-dependent strategy and decrease the empirical CVaR at the 0.95 level of quadratic shortage loss from approximately 0.921 to 0.067.

summary: pyslfp 3.0.0 The major version marks the reorganisation of the library around one sea level engine with two drivers, elastic sea level fingerprints and viscoelastic glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA), which first appeared in 2.2.1. This release adds the calibration of the initial sea level, makes the tutorials runnable in Colab, and brings the documentation up to date. New Calibration of the initial sea level against a present-day sea level: SeaLevelEvolution.calibrate_initial_sea_level , final_sea_level_misfit , and run_ice_history(..., final_sea_level=...) . With frozen shorelines the problem is linear and is solved in one run. With migrating shorelines it iterates, either by the classical update or by steepest descent with the adjoint gradient (Yu et al. 2025), with Anderson acceleration and optional weights. EarthState(..., ocean_function=...) , a prescribed ocean function for fixing the shorelines of a frozen-shoreline problem. Tutorial 10: calibrating the initial sea level for ICE-7G's ice thickness. Colab notebooks for all ten tutorials, generated automatically from the tutorial scripts. Changed The module-level calibrate_initial_sea_level now wraps the method. With frozen shorelines it returns the one-step solution, keeping the starting shorelines as a prescribed ocean function, and it warns if it does not converge. Runs with migrating shorelines refuse a state with a prescribed ocean function. The notebooks are now in tutorials/notebooks/ ; the old tutorials/tutorial1-4.ipynb are removed. Fixed Tutorials 6 to 9 had stopped running with current planetmodel; they now convert the radial model into the library's units with model.converted(parameters.scales) . Documentation New Theory and methods and Numerics and performance pages, a rewritten README covering both the elastic and viscoelastic sides, and an updated theory note ( docs/theory ) covering the viscoelastic adjoints, sensitivity kernels and the calibration. Upgrading from 2.2.0 or earlier Modules have moved: SeaLevelEquation is now in pyslfp.core , LinearSeaLevelEquation in pyslfp.elastic , and EarthState in pyslfp.core ; pyslfp.physics and pyslfp.state no longer exist. Top-level imports ( import pyslfp as sl ) and pyslfp.linear_operators are unchanged. The default units are now planetmodel's Scales.geophysical , in which the gravitational constant is one, rather than units in which surface gravity is one. Results converted to SI are unchanged, but raw non-dimensional numbers differ, and radial models must be in the same units as the Earth model.

New Calibration of the initial sea level against a present-day sea level: SeaLevelEvolution.calibrate_initial_sea_level , final_sea_level_misfit , and run_ice_history(..., final_sea_level=...) . With frozen shorelines the problem is linear and is solved in one run. With migrating shorelines it iterates, either by the classical update or by steepest descent with the adjoint gradient (Yu et al. 2025), with Anderson acceleration and optional weights. EarthState(..., ocean_function=...) , a prescribed ocean function for fixing the shorelines of a frozen-shoreline problem. Tutorial 10: calibrating the initial sea level for ICE-7G's ice thickness. Colab notebooks for all ten tutorials, generated automatically from the tutorial scripts. Changed The module-level calibrate_initial_sea_level now wraps the method. With frozen shorelines it returns the one-step solution, keeping the starting shorelines as a prescribed ocean function, and it warns if it does not converge. Runs with migrating shorelines refuse a state with a prescribed ocean function. The notebooks are now in tutorials/notebooks/ ; the old tutorials/tutorial1-4.ipynb are removed. Fixed Tutorials 6 to 9 had stopped running with current planetmodel; they now convert the radial model into the library's units with model.converted(parameters.scales) . Documentation New Theory and methods and Numerics and performance pages, a rewritten README covering both the elastic and viscoelastic sides, and an updated theory note ( docs/theory ) covering the viscoelastic adjoints, sensitivity kernels and the calibration. Upgrading from 2.2.0 or earlier Modules have moved: SeaLevelEquation is now in pyslfp.core , LinearSeaLevelEquation in pyslfp.elastic , and EarthState in pyslfp.core ; pyslfp.physics and pyslfp.state no longer exist. Top-level imports ( import pyslfp as sl ) and pyslfp.linear_operators are unchanged. The default units are now planetmodel's Scales.geophysical , in which the gravitational constant is one, rather than units in which surface gravity is one. Results converted to SI are unchanged, but raw non-dimensional numbers differ, and radial models must be in the same units as the Earth model.

summary: This deposit contains the model code, the complete parameter set with provenance labels, all numerical outputs, and the scripts required to regenerate every figure and table in the associated manuscript. The work is a physiologically based kinetic (PBK) analysis of the renal exposure window of emodin, an anthraquinone of rhubarb. The model is an eight-compartment, perfusion-limited PBK model with intestinal and hepatic first-pass metabolism, biliary excretion and enterohepatic recirculation, parameterised for mouse, rat and human. No experimental data were generated: the study is entirely computational. The published pharmacokinetic data used for calibration and external validation are cited in the manuscript; the extracted values are recorded in results/validation_split.csv. The absorption term was calibrated against four published rat plasma datasets, and the fitted value with all residuals is included. Code is additionally available under the MIT licence (see LICENSE-CODE.txt); data and figures are released under CC BY 4.0.
title: Data and code for: A physiologically based kinetic analysis of the renal exposure window of emodin

summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly deployed through black-box APIs and trained on large collections of real-world tabular datasets. As this training paradigm becomes more widely adopted, private or proprietary datasets may be incorporated into pre-training corpora, yet there are currently no dedicated methods for determining whether a given tabular dataset was used to train a TFM. As a solution, we introduce the first dataset inference method for TFMs, aiming to infer whether a suspect dataset was part of a model's pre-training data. We systematically analyze a broad collection of candidate signals that can be observed from a black-box TFM via input manipulation and find that individual signals provide only weak evidence of training data membership. However, by combining multiple complementary signals, we can infer dataset membership for several state-of-the-art TFMs trained on real tabular data, achieving up to 0.99 ROCAUC dependent on the TFM. We then study factors that influence dataset identification, including pre-training data composition, model capacity, and the use of real vs. synthetic data. Our results show that our dataset inference method is a practical auditing tool for detecting privacy leakage and the use of proprietary datasets in TFMs.
title: Dataset Inference for Data Provenance and Privacy Auditing in Tabular Foundation Models

summary: Runtime query similarity identification supports several activities, including workload analysis, identifying recurring behaviour, auditing, debugging, and anomaly detection. Existing methods for evaluating query similarity mostly rely on SQL text, execution plans, or result values but do not account for input data or how results are derived during query execution. This paper proposes a novel approach using data provenance for query-template identification. We construct query-level profiles that capture explicit data dependencies, occurrence frequencies, and structural properties by aggregating tuple-level Lineage and Why-provenance across entire query results. We also derive Provenance Structural Descriptors (PSD), which summarise these profiles using a small set of numerical features. We evaluate our proposals using these profiles to identify query templates over \(12{,}500\) distinct query instances generated from parametrised TPC-DS query templates. The experimental evaluation shows that query templates can be identified solely from their provenance footprints, and that accuracy improves as more historical data becomes available. It also shows that PSD achieve high classification accuracy with limited training history and low test-processing cost.
title: Data Provenance Aggregation and Structural Descriptors for Query-Template Identification

We construct query-level profiles that capture explicit data dependencies, occurrence frequencies, and structural properties by aggregating tuple-level Lineage and Why-provenance across entire query results. We also derive Provenance Structural Descriptors (PSD), which summarise these profiles using a small set of numerical features. We evaluate our proposals using these profiles to identify query templates over \(12{,}500\) distinct query instances generated from parametrised TPC-DS query templates. The experimental evaluation shows that query templates can be identified solely from their provenance footprints, and that accuracy improves as more historical data becomes available. It also shows that PSD achieve high classification accuracy with limited training history and low test-processing cost.
title: Data Provenance Aggregation and Structural Descriptors for Query-Template Identification

summary: Multimodal $ΔΔG$ predictors integrating protein language models with inverse-folding representations achieve strong in-distribution accuracy on the Megascale dataset but exhibit limited robustness on out-of-distribution (OOD) proteins, persistent forward-reverse bias on paired-mutation benchmarks, and under-representation of rare stabilizing mutations. Existing approaches address these limitations primarily through additional architectural components, leaving optimization-level intervention comparatively underexplored. We introduce a constraint-aware optimization framework combining Balanced Mean Squared Error, a Siamese anti-symmetric regularizer, and a novel OOD-margin consistency loss on the per-position feature representation, requiring no architectural changes to the SPURS backbone. Across eleven benchmarks and three random seeds, the framework improves Spearman correlation on S669 from 0.486 to 0.540 ($σ=0.002$ across seeds), matching the published SPURS baseline (0.50) without architectural modification, and on S461 from 0.653 to 0.711, with consistent smaller gains on five additional OOD datasets. A controlled diagnostic on Ssym reveals that anti-symmetric training does not eliminate systematic forward-reverse bias, indicating that gains arise through implicit regularization rather than exact thermodynamic constraint enforcement.
title: Constraint-Aware Optimization for Robust Protein Stability Prediction

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Twenty-five entries are documented, nine of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, and a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten. Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth, gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two, and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille, carries the wave-induced light fluctuations measured by Darecki et al. (2011) and Gernez & Antoine (2009), read from their figures, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, and carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters.
title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

summary: The manuscript develops a risk-aware operational research framework for strengthening NdFeB permanent-magnet supply-chain resilience under recycling delays, geopolitical disruptions, and uncertain material shortages. It integrates Caputo fractional-order dynamics, delayed recycling flows, strategic procurement and inventory decisions, Pontryagin-type optimality conditions, and Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) within a unified decision model. The study makes three principal contributions. First, it formulates a memory-dependent dynamic model and establishes positivity, boundedness, feasible-region, shortage-free equilibrium, and fractional local-stability results. Second, it incorporates procurement, recycling investment, stock accumulation, and stock release as operational controls and derives the corresponding necessary optimality conditions. Third, it introduces a scenario-based CVaR formulation and compares import-dependent, recycling-oriented, stockpiling-based, and integrated resilience policies under a common non-anticipative framework. In the baseline risk-aware analysis, the recycling-oriented and integrated strategies reduce mean shortage by approximately 74% relative to the import-dependent strategy and decrease the empirical CVaR at the 0.95 level of quadratic shortage loss from approximately 0.921 to 0.067.
title: A Caputo Fractional-Order Optimal Control Framework for NdFeB Permanent Magnet Supply-Chain Resilience under Recycling Delay and Geopolitical Risk

summary: This deposit contains the model code, the complete parameter set with provenance labels, all numerical outputs, and the scripts required to regenerate every figure and table in the associated manuscript. The work is a physiologically based kinetic (PBK) analysis of the renal exposure window of emodin, an anthraquinone of rhubarb. The model is an eight-compartment, perfusion-limited PBK model with intestinal and hepatic first-pass metabolism, biliary excretion and enterohepatic recirculation, parameterised for mouse, rat and human. No experimental data were generated: the study is entirely computational. The published pharmacokinetic data used for calibration and external validation are cited in the manuscript; the extracted values are recorded in results/validation_split.csv. The absorption term was calibrated against four published rat plasma datasets, and the fitted value with all residuals is included. Code is additionally available under the MIT licence (see LICENSE-CODE.txt); data and figures are released under CC BY 4.0.
title: Data and code for: A physiologically based kinetic analysis of the renal exposure window of emodin

summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly deployed through black-box APIs and trained on large collections of real-world tabular datasets. As this training paradigm becomes more widely adopted, private or proprietary datasets may be incorporated into pre-training corpora, yet there are currently no dedicated methods for determining whether a given tabular dataset was used to train a TFM. As a solution, we introduce the first dataset inference method for TFMs, aiming to infer whether a suspect dataset was part of a model's pre-training data. We systematically analyze a broad collection of candidate signals that can be observed from a black-box TFM via input manipulation and find that individual signals provide only weak evidence of training data membership. However, by combining multiple complementary signals, we can infer dataset membership for several state-of-the-art TFMs trained on real tabular data, achieving up to 0.99 ROCAUC dependent on the TFM. We then study factors that influence dataset identification, including pre-training data composition, model capacity, and the use of real vs. synthetic data. Our results show that our dataset inference method is a practical auditing tool for detecting privacy leakage and the use of proprietary datasets in TFMs.
title: Dataset Inference for Data Provenance and Privacy Auditing in Tabular Foundation Models

summary: Human mobility data are fundamental to Web-based location services and broader urban applications, and mobility generation provides synthetic trajectories when real data are costly or inaccessible. Although recent mobility generators have incorporated collective mobility patterns, they primarily focus on individual trajectories and aggregate population dynamics, leaving evolving community structures formed by user-location interactions insufficiently modeled. In this paper, we study community-consistent human mobility generation. To this end, we formulate mobility generation as the generation of dynamic user-location graphs to model community structures and propose MOTION, a Multi-agent framework for cOmmuniTy-consIstent human mObility geNeration. MOTION consists of user agents, location agents, and a global manager agent. MOTION first detects coherent communities from historical mobility using the Leiden algorithm and extracts community-conditioned interaction priors to guide the generation process. Guided by these priors, the user agents plan mobility, search destination candidates, and infer user movements from the individual view. In parallel, selectively activated location agents infer likely user arrivals from the community view. The manager coordinates both views, diagnoses interactions causing deviations, and attributes targeted reflection signals to revise user decisions, location attraction, and source-user selection. Experiments on two real-world datasets show that MOTION outperforms baselines by at least 4.05% across reported metrics of individual trajectories, population and flow distributions, and community and graph structures. Further analyses confirm its robustness, privacy preservation, and downstream utility. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MOTION-04C4.
title: Beyond Trajectory Statistics: Community-Consistent Human Mobility Generation via Evolving User-Location Graphs

summary: This paper addresses decentralized estimation and control of heterogeneous multi-agent systems communicating over directed switching topologies. The objective is to satisfy cooperative tasks that require coordination among agents according to a time-invariant task graph. To address the potential mismatch between the communication and task graphs, each agent is equipped with a k-hop Prescribed Performance State Observer (k-hop PPSO) to estimate the states of agents up to k communication hops away using only information exchanged with its 1-hop neighbors. A novel prescribed performance funnel construction is developed to account for the switching communication topology, and a sufficient lower bound on the dwell-time is derived to guarantee the prescribed performance specifications under topology variations. Further analysis shows that, if the desired control objective is achieved with exact knowledge of the required nonlocal states and the resulting closed-loop system is uniformly set-ISS with respect to the state estimation error, then replacing these states with their estimates guarantees convergence to a neighborhood of the desired set. The size of this neighborhood can be made arbitrarily small by appropriately selecting the observer performance bounds. A simulation study demonstrates task satisfaction under directed switching topologies.
title: Observer-Based Control for Multi-Agent Systems under Communication-Task Graph Mismatch and Directed Switching Topologies

summary: Porous-material adsorption studies require coordinated structure preparation, force-field selection, simulation, validation, and interpretation, making end-to-end automation difficult. We test whether RaspAssistant, a hierarchical multi-agent framework, can carry an adsorption study from force-field preparation through validation and downstream separation analysis. Across twelve multi-agent workflow-reproduction runs spanning four adsorption and separation benchmarks, overall scores ranged from 8.50 to 10.00 on a rubric evaluating workflow correctness, simulation validity, and analysis consistency. In a separate eight-case force-field extraction benchmark, the mean weighted score was 0.967, combining parameter agreement and RASPA readiness. In open-ended studies, the system diagnosed and refined an acetylene force field and, after validating a CO$_2$ force field against MFI experiments, screened 197 pure-silica zeolites that passed automated input checks. These results demonstrate autonomous workflow execution after task specification and input provision: RaspAssistant coordinates, validates, adapts, and documents extended adsorption-simulation workflows while exposing model sensitivity and methodological limitations for expert review.
title: RaspAssistant as an Agentic Framework for Automating Adsorption Simulation Research in Porous Materials

summary: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services. Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment. By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).
title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges

summary: Python script that reproduces the numerical examples in Section 4.4 of “AI, Authorization, and the Erosion of Expertise Rent” and verifies the underlying analytical expressions. Requires only the Python standard library.
title: Replication Code for "AI, Authorization, and the Erosion of Expertise Rent"

summary: Archived Eurostat dissemination API responses and the code that reproduces every table, figure and reported number from them. The archive covers 31 European countries (EU27 with Iceland, Norway, Switzerland and Türkiye) for 2014-2025 and includes income in purchasing power standards and in euros, severe material and social deprivation, financial strain by response category, housing cost overburden, income quintile shares, the Gini coefficient and household final consumption price level indices, together with Eurostat's own break-in-series flags. A manifest records the request URLs, retrieval times and SHA-256 checksums. The code uses only the Python standard library. Version 1.6.0 corrects two places where the code did not follow the rule the note states. Shares published to one decimal were being added in binary floating point, so that a combined value of 12.6 formed from one pair of components did not compare equal to a 12.6 formed from another, and fourteen country-years were therefore ranked as if they were not tied. For the same reason an annual change of exactly six points was read as slightly less and dropped at that threshold. Derived quantities are now rounded back to the precision of the published series. The headline results are unchanged. The figure module's own caption, which still described the two marked drops as the panel's largest two, now matches the note in saying they are the first and the third. The package has supported three pieces of work in turn: an earlier article on national price levels and deprivation, a measurement note on the conversion year and the response category, and a Turkish-language note on Türkiye's position in these comparisons and on the series themselves.
title: Replication package: Eurostat income, deprivation and financial strain indicators for 31 European countries, 2014-2025

summary: This package contains the code that produces every table and figure quoted in the paper "The Widening Mathematics Gap: Boys, Girls and Who Is Missing from PISA. 38 OECD Countries, 2015–2025", the small public inputs it needs (population and coverage tables), and the country-level results behind every OECD average. PISA microdata are not redistributed; they are public and must be downloaded from the OECD (see README). Code comments and docstrings are in Spanish; the README documents the pipeline in English.
title: Replication package: The Widening Mathematics Gap — Boys, Girls and Who Is Missing from PISA

summary: This replication package contains the materials supporting the analysis presented in the paper. It includes the prompts collected analyzed from the DevGPT and GitHub repositories, and the prompts used in the controlled experiment. The excel file named "Prompt_Categorization" contains the full annotation of both the DevGPT dataset and the GitHub repository dataset, including all relevant metadata for each prompt/conversation. The markdown files contain conversation with Gemini 2.5 Pro and GPT 5 mini for two prompt techniques: zero-shot and few-shot, respectively.
title: Who Let the Prompt Out?

summary: Third-party pretrained checkpoints are now the default starting point for computer-vision disease detectors in digital agriculture, yet the poisoning rate at which a backdoor trigger survives fine-tuning on clean crop imagery has not been characterised as a design quantity. the present analysis treats the backdoor trigger as a property of the checkpoint supply chain rather than of the attacker, and asks what poisoning rate a defender must assume when the provenance of the pretrained weights is unknown. A formal model of trigger persistence is developed in which the backdoor is represented as a parameter-space displacement whose survival under gradient fine-tuning depends on the ratio of trigger-aligned to task-aligned curvature. From this model a persistence bound is derived, and the bound is then embedded in a before-after-control-impact design that treats the poisoned checkpoint as the intervention and the clean checkpoint as the control. Operating characteristics were evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD of 6.0, residual SD of 4.5 and intraclass correlation of 0.64. The design required 54 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point difference at 80% power.
tags: backdoor triggers; poisoning rate; pretrained checkpoints; crop disease detection; before-after-control-impact; intraclass correlation; AI supply chain
title: Backdoor-Trigger Evaluation for Computer Agriculture Disease-Detection Models Under Third-Party Pretrained Checkpoints: An Artificial Intelligence Poisoning-Rate Audit

summary: Differentiable logic-gate networks (DLGNs) are attractive for irrigation controllers because their learned Boolean structure can be verified exhaustively, yet the safety case for deploying them under actuator-failure cascades has not been formalised. The work is a design-and-power analysis of a before-after-control-impact (BACI) evaluation protocol, not an observational study: no field data are used or claimed. Operating characteristics were characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.52 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point compliance effect at 80% power under this variance structure, and that the intraclass correlation of 0.64 dominates the design's sensitivity. A formal-safety audit of DLGN controllers is then specified as a finite-state reachability problem over the actuator-failure cascade, with water-rights compliance encoded as an invariant. The contribution is a benchmark protocol that couples a verifiable controller class to a statistically defensible evaluation design, and a demonstration that the evaluation design, not the controller, is the binding constraint on regulatory acceptance.
tags: differentiable logic-gate networks; irrigation controllers; actuator-failure cascades; water-rights compliance; formal-safety audit; before-after-control-impact; benchmarking evaluation
title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Differentiable Logic-Gate Networks for Computer Agriculture Irrigation Controllers Under Actuator-Failure Cascades: An Artificial Intelligence Formal-Safety Audit for Water-Rights Compliance

summary: Yield anomaly detectors in computer agriculture routinely attribute harvest shortfalls to a single dominant stressor, yet drought and pest outbreaks frequently co-occur and confound one another's signatures in remotely sensed and agronomic covariates. The framework is methodological and theoretical: it defines the attribution game, states the confounding conditions under which Shapley values are point-identified, and derives upper and lower bounds when concurrent drought and pest outbreak render the attribution non-identified. A worked illustration uses NASA POWER monthly reanalysis air temperature at 2 m for Accra, Ghana (5.6, -0.19) over 2000-2023, comprising 312 monthly observations with a mean of 26.521 C, a standard deviation of 1.24 C and a warming trend of 0.1622 C per decade, to show how a single covariate channel can be bounded before attribution is attempted. The contribution is a bound-based audit protocol that replaces point attribution with interval attribution and specifies the evidence required to narrow those intervals in operational detector pipelines.
tags: causal attribution; Shapley decomposition; yield anomaly detection; drought-pest confounding; computer agriculture; partial identification; benchmarking audit
title: Evaluation of Causal-Attribution Bounds for Computer Agriculture Yield Anomaly Detectors Under Concurrent Drought and Pest Outbreak Confounding: An Artificial Intelligence Shapley-Decomposition Audit

summary: Satellite-cloud gaps corrupt the reflectance time series on which computer-agriculture crop-yield estimators depend, and the resulting coverage error propagates into famine early-warning reliability. The framework is evaluated through a replication-based benchmark in which 600 data sets of N = 500 were drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2) and the ordinary least squares estimator was characterised under the stated process. The benchmark produced an estimated bias of -0.07173 for the intercept and 0.00147 for the exposure coefficient, with RMSE values of 0.89562 and 0.0157 respectively, and empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals of 1.0 for both parameters. The coverage-error bound formalises the conditions under which CDA-supported estimators preserve nominal coverage and therefore early-warning reliability, and it identifies the augmentation regimes in which coverage degrades. The contribution is a benchmark protocol and a bound that make the reliability consequences of cloud-gap augmentation auditable rather than assumed.
tags: counterfactual data augmentation; crop-yield estimation; satellite-cloud gaps; coverage-error bound; famine early warning; benchmarking evaluation
title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Counterfactual Data Augmentation for Computer Agriculture Crop-Yield Estimators Under Satellite-Cloud Gaps: An Artificial Intelligence Coverage-Error Bound for Famine Early-Warning Reliability

summary: Artificial intelligence systems that rank farmers for agricultural input subsidies are increasingly evaluated by comparing enrolled cooperative members with non-members, a design that conflates programme effect with the self-selection of farmers into cooperatives. The design is characterised analytically and by replication: between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5, intraclass correlation 0.64, with 2000 replications per design cell across 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The bound identifies the conditions under which an audit can separate algorithmic misranking from enrollment-driven selection, and it specifies the cluster count at which the equity contrast becomes estimable. Fifty-four clusters are required for 80 per cent power at a 5 percentage point effect. The contribution is a design-level audit instrument rather than a new estimator: it tells evaluators what a targeting audit can and cannot attribute, and it converts an unverifiable causal claim into a bounded, reportable quantity.
tags: subsidy targeting; instrumental variable; equity audit; cooperative enrollment; before-after-control-impact; intraclass correlation; algorithmic fairness
title: Causal-Attribution Evaluation for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Subsidy Targeting Under Endogenous Cooperative Enrollment: A Computer Instrumental-Variable Bound for Equity Audits

summary: Tensor-network compression promises to fit convolutional disease classifiers into the memory ceilings of field-deployable diagnostic devices, but the accuracy cost of compression is usually reported as a single post-hoc number rather than as a bounded retention guarantee. the present analysis treats compression as a design problem with an auditable operating characteristic: given a declared memory ceiling, what fraction of the uncompressed diagnostic accuracy survives, and with what uncertainty? We formalise tensor-train decomposition of convolutional kernels as a rank-constrained projection, derive a retention bound that links bond dimension, kernel spectrum and the resulting classification margin, and then characterise the operating characteristics of a benchmarking protocol that estimates retention under a declared variance structure. The protocol is a before-after-control-impact design with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell at cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Power reaches conventional levels only at 56 clusters for a 5-percentage-point retention effect, which exceeds every cluster count in the declared grid; the minimum detectable effect at 80% power therefore remains above the 5-percentage-point threshold throughout the grid. The contribution is a retention bound plus a power-calibrated audit protocol that tells practitioners when a compression benchmark is informative and when it is underpowered, and that reframes field diagnostic safety as a property of the evaluation design rather than of the compressor alone.
tags: tensor-train decomposition; model compression; plant disease classification; on-device inference; accuracy retention; benchmark power; diagnostic safety
title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Tensor-Network Compression for Computer Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under On-Device Memory Ceilings: An Artificial Intelligence Accuracy-Retention Audit for Field Diagnostic Safety

summary: Federated learning for crop-disease classification across heterogeneous farm clients is vulnerable to Byzantine participants who submit corrupted model updates, yet the aggregation literature reports robustness without a design-level account of how many adversarial clients a given federation can tolerate before diagnostic integrity collapses. The analysis treats the aggregation rule as a statistical estimator of the honest update direction and characterises the breakdown point of coordinate-wise median and trimmed-mean aggregation under a declared contamination model. A before-after-control-impact design is used to benchmark power across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, with 2000 replications per design cell and an intraclass correlation of 0.640. The contamination bound predicts that coordinate-wise median aggregation tolerates up to 50% adversarial clients in the limit but loses diagnostic integrity at a threshold that depends on the between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and the residual standard deviation of 4.5. The benchmarking results indicate that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point degradation at 80% power. The contribution is a formal contamination bound that links aggregation-rule choice to the minimum federation size needed to certify diagnostic integrity, together with a benchmarking protocol that makes that link auditable.
tags: federated learning; Byzantine robustness; crop disease classification; contamination bound; benchmarking evaluation; diagnostic integrity
title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Byzantine-Robust Federated Aggregation for Computer Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under Adversarial Client Participation: An Artificial Intelligence Contamination Bound for Diagnostic Integrity

summary: Flood-risk mapping for agricultural insurance in vegetated terrain depends on computed-aperture radar interferometric coherence, yet canopy decoherence attenuates the signal that classifiers must detect. the present analysis formalises the detection problem as a before-after-control-impact design and derives the operating characteristics of a coherence-based flood detector under a declared variance structure with intraclass correlation 0.64, between-cluster standard deviation 6.0 and residual standard deviation 4.5. Power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design required 56 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point effect at 80% power. The analysis characterises the detection-power bound that canopy decoherence imposes on payout-equity claims, showing that the cluster counts typical of agricultural insurance portfolios are insufficient to separate genuine flood signal from decoherence noise. The contribution is a benchmark-derived bound that links remote-sensing detection power to the actuarial fairness of index-based insurance payouts.
tags: SAR interferometry; coherence; flood-risk mapping; detection power; insurance equity; canopy decoherence; benchmarking
title: Benchmarking Evaluation of computed-Aperture Radar Interferometric Coherence for Computer Agriculture Flood-Risk Mapping Under Vegetation Canopy Decoherence: An Artificial Intelligence Detection-Power Bound for Insurance Payout Equity

summary: Edge pest detection in computer agriculture is constrained less by classifier accuracy than by the thermal power budget of the sensing node. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise order-of-magnitude energy reductions on neuromorphic hardware, but the field lacks a design-level account of how that promise translates into deployable detection performance when the thermal sensor itself is the dominant load. The framework formalises a thermal-power budget, defines an energy-normalised detection rate, and derives a power-accuracy frontier for leaky integrate-and-fire classifiers operating on low-resolution thermal frames. A replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), with power estimated across 2000 design cells.
