summary: This record contains the scenario bank, raw transcripts and supporting files for the study " A Faith-Aware Ethical Violation Taxonomy for LLMs in Mental Health Counseling with an Islamic Case Study " (submitted to JMIR Mental Health). Mainly, 2 LLMs, Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5, were each run through 25 scripted multi-turn scenarios (92 user turns) in which a Muslim user presents religious or mental health concerns. Both models were accessed through OpenRouter with the same system prompt and default parameters. Contents - Scenario_Bank_25_Scenarios.pdf and scenario_turns.json: the final scripted scenarios, as a document and in machine-readable form. - ETHICS_CHECK_CLAUDE.ipynb and ETHICS_CHECK_GPT.ipynb: the raw interactive transcripts, deposited as run. - README_user_turn_provenance.md: for each scenario and model, the source file and how the entered user turns compare with the script. - User_Turn_Deviations.pdf: itemised differences between the scripted and the entered user turns. - run_scripted.py: a replication script that sends the scripted turns directly. It was not used to generate the reported data. - OpenRouter_Activity_Deposit.xlsx: the request-level log of the model calls. - Multimedia_Appendix_1 to _4: copies of the paper's appendices (each also has its own DOI). - Stage1_Draft_Scenarios_Gemini_Archive.pdf: archive of the earlier stage-1 draft scenarios (provisional codes); superseded by the final scenario bank. Notes on provenance - User turns were scripted in advance but entered manually, one at a time, in the same order for both models. Claude Opus 4.8's entered turns matched the script in 24 scenarios; in A1, T2 was entered twice. GPT-5.5's entered turns matched the script or differed only in punctuation or a stray quotation mark in 15 scenarios; in C4 it received one extra turn; in 7 scenarios the wording differed (about 5% of all scripted words); and the first three turns of C2 and C3 were not echoed in the notebook output (entered from the scenario document). Details are in User_Turn_Deviations.pdf. The coding evidence is provided in Multimedia Appendix 3 of the paper.
title: A Faith-Aware Ethical Violation Taxonomy for LLMs in Mental Health Counseling with an Islamic Case Study

summary: Adds the gap-filled sea-surface-temperature field as HEALPix NetCDF ( results/sst_gap_filled_healpix.nc , nside 32, NESTED): observed Copernicus Marine L3S, L4 reference, harmonic and scattering-transform (FOSCAT) fills, cloud and ocean masks, for 2026-04-01. A re-run on 2026-10-24 reproduces the published result within 0.4 %: FOSCAT RMSE 0.985 K (published 0.989 K), harmonic baseline 11.463 K (identical), 91.4 % improvement either way. summary: SOLT 0.2.2 A large update: new data types for distance maps and bounding boxes, many bug fixes, modern tooling and self-contained examples. pip install -U solt Breaking changes Python 3.12+ is required. Minimum versions: numpy 2.4, scipy 1.17, opencv-python-headless 4.13, torch 2.9, torchvision 0.24, pyyaml 6.0.3. Per-item transform_settings (interpolation, padding) now apply to every transform of a Stream , not only to the first one. to_torch returns HxWxC masks as CxHxW (was 1xHxWxC ). Resize keeps keypoints as floats aligned with the image (they were truncated to integers); Rotate90 maps keypoints exactly (they were 1 px off on even image sizes). Resize(keep_ar=True) gives the correct shape (width and height were swapped). GridMask drops the intended part of the image, about (1 - ratio)² (it dropped ~94%). "reverse" is the inverse mode; "reserve" still works. Stream(ignore_fast_mode=...) always overrides its transforms, including nested streams. Unknown modes of Blur , CvtColor and GridMask are rejected when the transform is created. Stream(shuffle=True) now actually shuffles the transforms. New Distance maps ( 'D' , dict key distancnce fields: float16 / float32 / float64 , HxW or HxWxC . Bilinear interpolation, values rescaled by scaling transforms, and no false boundaries from zero padding. solt.utils.mask_to_sdf` computes sisks. Bounding boxes ( 'B' , dict key bboxes ): solt.BoundingBoxes accepts and exports VOC, COCO, YOLO and cxcywh, with a label per box. Boxes are clipped to thorm; Stream drops the ones mostly outside ofthe image or much smaller relative to it, together with their labels. to_torch gives the torchvision detection target. (#42) Stream(in_place=True) : transforms do not copy data unless necessary; in_place=False copies the input once. Crop corner modes 'lt' , 'rt' , 'lb' ,entation (#97). Random cutout sizes in CutOut (#37). Brightness(relative=True) : brightness chaintensity (#60). BrightnessContrast : brightness and contrast in one step (#43). Keypoints in RandomResizedCrop ; tuple n Fixes DataContainer no longer modifies the giveansforms without data_indices apply to allitems of every call. RandomResizedCrop resizes masks, accepts , and no longer produces empty crops of thinimages. optimize_stack=True no longer loses trans, no longer changes the transforms of thestream, keeps the perspective of a fused Projection , and works with Rotate90 . Projection keeps the warped image inside e cut off). from_dict no longer modifies the given configuration, and rejects malformed ones. CvtColor raises a clear error for unsuppoorch accepts HxW grayscale images; DTYPES_MAX for uint16` is 65535. Tooling and documentation The project uses uv: pyproject.toml and uv.lock replace setup.py and the conda setup. CI tests Python 3.12–3.14 and the lowest suads coverage to Codecov. The documentation uses the Furo theme. The example notebooks use only scikit-image sample data, including new examples for distance maps and bounding boxes The code is reorganized into smaller modules; the public API and the serialized names are unchanged. License: MIT, Copyright (c) 2018-2026 Aleksei Tiulpin & SOLT contributors , with a DISCLAIMER regarding WeillCornell Medicine. Full changelog: https://github.com/imedslab/solt/compare/v0.2.1...v0.2.2 The "Full changelog" link works once the v0.2.2 tag exists, which publishing the release creates. Publishing it on master runs the PyPI workflow.
title: imedslab/solt: Release 0.2.2

summary: TripLibre is an open-source, local-first iOS application designed for personal mobility tracking and travel behavior research. It records location data in the background, reconstructs daily travel activities into visits, trips, transportation modes, and trip chains. It allows users to review and correct inferred travel records. The application supports exporting structured mobility datasets in CSV, JSON, GeoJSON, and SQLite formats, with a Python loader for further analysis. By combining automated GPS-based travel detection with user-controlled data management, TripLibre aims to lower the technical and financial barriers to collecting travel behavior data. Its broader vision is to provide researchers, educational institutions, and resource-constrained communities with an accessible and adaptable alternative to proprietary travel survey technologies, while preserving individual control over sensitive location information. Documentation: https://hhtdiary.org/triplibre/docs/
title: TripLibre: An Open-Source, Privacy-First Travel Diary for Mobility Research

summary: DIGITAL TWINS AND AI CLOSED-LOOP CONTROL FOR NANOROBOTIC PHARMACEUTICAL MANUFACTURING AT THE LIMIT Digital Twins x AI Process Control x Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Quality This high-density English research monograph develops a falsification-oriented architecture for digital twins and AI closed-loop control in nonclinical nanorobotic pharmaceutical manufacturing research. Its central question is whether a process-state estimator can predict quality failure under raw-material, flow, sensor and equipment drift before the failure occurs, rather than merely replaying historical data as an attractive dashboard. The governing evidence object is the Falsifiable Manufacturing Twin. It binds a declared physical state, observation model, uncertainty envelope, process and sensor versions, candidate and executed control actions, external critical-quality-attribute measurements, abstention, fallback and terminal batch fate. A twin earns authority only while new physical evidence can contradict it. Failed, stopped, out-of-distribution and externally falsified batches remain in the denominator. The monograph compares fixed recipes, statistical process control, tuned PID, strong non-learning model predictive control and AI under equal sensing, energy, constraints and operator access. It treats calibrated ignorance as a successful behavior: an unsupported state must cause abstention, return to a separately qualified safe recipe or stop. External CQA evidence always outranks the model. The volume contains 30 distinct mathematical research plates, 82 chapters, 410 independently paginated section studies, 200 detailed Research Gates and 33 genuinely distinguishable Phoenix Answer Embryos. Every Gate begins with a large deep-navy bold question and continues with a blind protocol, evidence package, competing explanation, hard stop and successor fork.

summary: Meeting the Paris Agreement target and path (PTP) is vital to protect humanity from the worse impacts of global warming. Using a large dimensional and unique Global Trade Analysis Project (GTAP) model for energy and international trade, we calculated the needed change in the energy mix and fall in carbon emissions to meet a minimal PTP of less than 2 o C warming. Covering 30 countries/regions and 31 commodity sectors, the model shows the PTP in annual time steps to 2100 in terms of emissions reduction and the shift in energy mix allowing for changes in energy intensity, renewables growth, and rising carbon prices. By 2050, using a year 2019 baseline, model results show carbon emissions must decrease on a compound basis by at least 5.7% globally, per year, on average, and coal consumption must fall continuously from 2025, complemented by large increases in renewable energy that allow for continued economic growth. We find that global carbon emissions must decline by almost 40% in 2030 and 80% in 2050 to meet a less than 2 o C warming path by 2100. Coal consumption must decline between 85–99% by 2050 among the key emitters (China, the USA, and India), compared to 2019 (the model baseline), complemented by a continuous transition to renewables. For Net-Zero Emissions Targets (NZET), carbon sequestration, such as from re-forestation and land use change, is also essential, although with substantial uncertainty. Model results indicate a net-zero outcome, even with assumed carbon sequestration, occurs no earlier than 2058, at best.
title: Will the World Achieve Net Zero by 2050? The Challenge of Meeting Emissions Reductions Targets in a Global Energy and Trade Model

summary: Reproducibility package for Identification Limits in Estimating the Effects of Algorithmic Surveillance on Digital Freedoms. Includes analysis scripts, reference result tables, figures, supplementary material, source-access instructions, software requirements, and verification tools.   Version 1.0.4 (2026-10-24) corrects the copy of the manuscript design figure, figures/Fig1_manuscript.png, whose summary box still stated that standard errors within the supported region are 1.7-3.6 times larger; the cohort-stratified bootstrap introduced in 1.0.3 gives 1.4-2.7, which is what the manuscript reports. That figure is drawn by the authors rather than produced by the pipeline, so the value had not followed the recomputation. The version also updates the expected wordings in scripts/15_audit_manuscript_numbers.py so that the audit tracks the current manuscript text; run against the revised manuscript it reconciles all 460 numerical claims with the archived result files. That audit located one error in the manuscript, which this version documents rather than changes: the last row of Table 7 carried the standard error of the pooled bootstrap, 0.236, where the stratified procedure gives 0.169. No data, code path or result changed; every result table is identical to v1.0.3.   Version 1.0.3 (2026-10-24) responds to the second editorial assessment of the third review round. The bootstrap of the support-restricted subsample is now stratified by adoption cohort with 2,000 replications, replacing pooled resampling of the 34 treated countries with 499: one cohort retains a single treated country and was absent from 191 of the 499 pooled replications, so the aggregation ran over five cohorts instead of six and the estimand changed inside the bootstrap. Equivalence within a quarter of an ordinal step consequently holds for five of the eight outcomes instead of four, and the ratio of restricted to full-sample standard errors becomes 1.44-2.67 (median 2.48) instead of 1.73-3.63 (median 2.44). The version also adds a bootstrap audit, a complete-separation diagnostic for the affected cohort including a directly programmed group-time parameter, and an empirical benchmark for the equivalence margins; records the membership of the two subsets of 34 countries in Supplementary Table 3; corrects the internal title of Figure 5, which asserted an attribution the comparison between samples cannot establish; and ships the execution logs of the pipeline.   Version 1.0.2 (2026-10-21) incorporates the second and third review rounds: lag-informed treatment dating; date-shift sensitivity extended to one through six years; a manuscript consistency audit; correction of the specification space from 75 rows to 60 distinct configurations by removing 15 duplicate configurations; and equivalence tests for the support-restricted subsample (Supplementary Table 9). Corresponding reference tables, figures, supplementary material, and verification checks are updated.   Validation for this archive: the complete pipeline was rerun from the raw sources on 2026-10-23 and its logs are included in outputs/logs/; the verification script passed 107 of 107 checks, 54 on values reported in the manuscript and 53 comparing every regenerated result table with the archived reference; all 131 entries in the SHA-256 manifest were verified.   Code is licensed under MIT. Derived tables, figures, and supplementary material are licensed under CC BY 4.0; third-party data terms are documented in LICENSE-DATA.md. Digital Society Project and V-Dem source files and derived analytical panels are not redistributed; download instructions are included.

summary: The package contains all the data and scripts used to produce the results presented in the paper "AST-SZZ: an SZZ Algorithm with AST Change Clustering and Backporting". Datasets A dataset is a list of scenarios, each of which contains the name of a GitHub repository, a bug-fixing commit hash, and one or more bug-inducing commit hashes. The datasets are summarized in the following table. Name Source File ( datasets/* ) Repository root Scenarios DS_GITHUB-j Rosa et al. DS_GITHUB-j74.json github-j74 74 DS_APACHE Wen et al. DS_APACHE236.json apache236 236 DS_RECENT Original DS_RECENT38.json recent38 38 Note that some repositories are no longer accessible, and some bug-fixing commits do not modify source code. We have excluded the corresponding scenarios from the dataset. Preparation Download the following. astszz-amd64.tar.xz (for x64) or astszz-arm64.tar.xz  (for arm64) github-j74.tar.xz apache236.tar.xz recent38.tar.xz github-j74-no-mesg.tar.xz (rewritten to remove the commit messages) apache236-no-mesg.tar.xz (rewritten to remove the commit messages) recent38-no-mesg.tar.xz (rewritten to remove the commit messages) llm4szz.tar.xz  (for the LLM4SZZ experiments only) agentszz.tar.xz  (for the AgentSZZ experiments only) agents-for-szz.tar.xz  (for the Simple-SZZ-Agent experiments only) pyszz_v2.tar.xz  (for the pyszz_v2 experiments only) RESULTS.tar.xz  (the results of the experiments) Then import the image appropriate for your host's architecture. docker import astszz-amd64.tar.xz \     --change "WORKDIR /root" \     --change "CMD [\"/usr/bin/bash\"]" \     astszz Use astszz-arm64.tar.xz instead if your architecture is arm64. The images are built from the codinuum/cca:base image on Docker Hub. AST-SZZ is implemented using Diff/AST , CCA , and modified versions of DDJ and D3J . Finally, start a container and then extract the repositories. docker run -ti -v ${PWD}:/mnt/work --name astszz astszz tar Jxf /mnt/work/github-j74.tar.xz tar Jxf /mnt/work/apache236.tar.xz tar Jxf /mnt/work/recent38.tar.xz Alternatively, you can clone the repositories from GitHub. scripts/clone_repos.py datasets/DS_GITHUB-j74.json github-j74 scripts/clone_repos.py datasets/DS_APACHE236.json apache236 scripts/clone_repos.py datasets/DS_RECENT38.json recent38 Replication AST-SZZ Since the replication is time-consuming, we recommend running the experiments on only a randomly sampled subset of <N> scenarios using the --nsamples <N> option. The following command starts the replication run, where <N_PROCS>  specifies the maximum number of processes to use. scripts/test_astszz.py -u -r -p <N_PROCS> [--nsamples <N>] \     <DATASET_JSON> <REPO_ROOT> For example, the following command runs the script using at most four processes on a sample of three scenarios from DS_RECENT. scripts/test_astszz.py -u -r -p 4 --nsamples 3 \     datasets/DS_RECENT38.json recent38 To disable change clustering, remove the -u (untangling) and -r (remove refactoring) options from the command line. Note that removing both options also disables multiprocessing, since one process is assigned to each sub-SZZ instance operating on a variant derived from a change cluster. To disable the additional conflict rules, add the --orig-d3j  option. The script stores an intermediate result in the  LOG directory. To generate the final result from the intermediate result, use the postprocess_astszz.py  script. scripts/postprocess_astszz.py \     LOG/intermediate.DS_{GITHUB-j74|APACHE236|RECENT38}.json You can also run test_astszz.py on a single scenario using the --sid  option. mv LOG LOG0 scripts/test_astszz.py -u -r -p 4 --sid 5 \     datasets/DS_RECENT38.json recent38 LLM-based SZZs Running all LLM-based experiments requires substantial time and incurs substantial costs (several hundred US dollars). Name Paper Directory LLM4SZZ Tang et al.

summary: Version 2.0, October 24, 2026: Empirical Revision Substantially revised Paper I to incorporate exploratory geochemical validation using published EarthChem and Alcott et al. (2026) measurements. Added EBA-1/EBA-2 sulfur-isotope change-point analysis, independent phosphorus and redox comparisons, alternative-boundary null testing, and blocked predictive model comparisons. The core source–sink hypothesis is retained, while claims concerning a uniquely identified tipping point, regional diachrony, and demonstrated feedback causation are explicitly qualified. The revision includes updated literature context, methodological limitations, and supplementary analytical materials. Supersedes version 1.0 as the current research statement while preserving the original publication history. The Great Oxidation Event (GOE) reflects the evolving balance between biological oxygen production, reductant consumption, atmospheric photochemistry, and ocean–sediment exchange. This paper develops a basin-resolved source–sink threshold framework in which regional oxygenation responses may differ despite shared atmospheric forcing. Version 2.0 extends the original theoretical framework through exploratory quantitative analysis of published EBA-1 and EBA-2 drill-core geochemistry, including sulfur mass-independent fractionation, phosphorus distributions, organic carbon, and redox-sensitive trace elements. An exploratory sulfur-isotope change point was identified at 1,336.87 m in EBA-2. Independent geochemical measurements exhibit substantial variation across this interval. However, depth-controlled null comparisons and blocked out-of-sample prediction do not establish a uniquely coordinated tipping-point transition. Predictive improvements are restricted to selected indicators and depend partly on baseline specification. These findings preserve the source–sink feedback framework as a testable explanation for nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous oxygenation while distinguishing theoretical plausibility from demonstrated causal dynamics. The revised manuscript provides empirical comparisons, competing-model evaluations, explicit limitations, and falsification criteria for future research. Part of the Planetary Convexity Series, Paper I.
title: Diachronous Oxygenation as a Planetary Tipping Point

summary: This dataset is the supplementary material for the manuscript "Decision Neutrality of Forecast Revisions in Microgrids with Photovoltaics and Battery Storage" by Yun Xing (Hohai University), submitted to Applied Sciences (MDPI). Version 1.0, 25 October 2026. Overview The study asks when adopting a revised next-day forecast changes a battery dispatch decision, rather than only the predicted cost. It derives two checkable sufficient reset conditions under which old and revised forecasts produce next-day storage value functions that differ only by an additive constant. A fixed-input perturbation bound separates this local neutrality from realized rolling-policy performance. Five policies (FF, FS, SF, SS and DAY) are compared on 522 community-days from 270 measured households aggregated into nine synthetic communities, with three synthetic tariffs and two import regimes. Key results - Freezing next-day forecasts is numerically neutral under unlimited imports across the tested tariffs. - Under a 30 kW import cap and time-of-use pricing, retaining midnight targets (DAY) lowers total operating cost by 3.105% relative to full updating (FF). Lower unmet-demand penalties account for 88.3% of the reduction; the import-bill reduction is 0.588%. - Freezing both forecasts while replanning (SS) costs 0.054% more than FF under the same six-hour replanning schedule, separating forecast adoption from target retention. - Under the same cap and tariff, freezing only the next-day forecast (FS) costs 0.188% more than FF. - Matched-calendar comparisons show that the magnitude of update effects depends on the controller scheme. Contents 1. Supporting_Results_and_Protocol.zip: verified reproducibility archive with 3,833 files, including fixed protocols, derived community inputs, customer-community mapping, analysis code, result tables, 15,660 policy-day records, 9,396 local terminal comparisons, 1,496 matched-calendar controller records, half-hour trajectories, figures and an internal manifest. 2. Supplementary_Guide.pdf: Supplementary Methods S1 and S2, extended uncertainty tables S1-S6, data dictionary notes and the run sequence. 3. README_ZENODO.txt: contents, usage order and scope notes. 4. LICENSE.txt: licensing note for code and derived data. 5. CITATION.cff: citation metadata. 6. zenodo_metadata.json: suggested metadata for this record. 7. SHA256SUMS.txt: SHA-256 checksums of the files in this archive. Reproduction Verify the files against SHA256SUMS.txt, extract Supporting_Results_and_Protocol.zip, and read README.txt, RUN_REPRODUCTION.txt and DATA_DICTIONARY.md before running anything. The recorded environment is Python 3.13.9 with NumPy 2.3.5, SciPy 1.16.3, pandas 2.3.3, Matplotlib 3.10.6 and openpyxl 3.1.5. Entry points cover the primary experiment, aggregation, availability sensitivity, diagnostics, both controller families, benchmarks and independent checks. The archive also supports a fresh single-group replay and a full audit without the author's original workspace. Data provenance and scope The household data are the Ausgrid 2012-2013 Solar Home Electricity Data, version 2, obtained from data.gov.au and the BetterGrids mirror. Raw provider records are not redistributed; provider URLs, version and SHA-256 are recorded in RUN_REPRODUCTION.txt and raw_source_manifest.json. Derived community inputs, results and trajectories are included. The archived results are the recorded reference outputs, not new observations. Communities, tariffs and batteries are synthetic scenario inputs, and the manuscript states the limits of the evidence. License Unless otherwise stated, the code and derived data in this package are provided under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0). The original household data are not redistributed and remain subject to the provider terms. Related manuscript Submitted to Applied Sciences (MDPI). The manuscript DOI will be added to this record after publication. Contact Yun Xing, College of Com

summary: International observation systems reveal a consequential possibility: scientific information can be generated, validated, and circulated across institutional and political boundaries without requiring a single authority over all observations or a uniform distribution of capacities . Yet the existence of data-sharing protocols does not by itself establish shared understanding, mutual trust, legitimate reuse, or equitable participation in the production of knowledge . This discussion paper investigates the technical, epistemic, and institutional conditions under which global observation and knowledge infrastructures might be constructed and sustained . Drawing on meteorological and oceanographic cooperation, it distinguishes observational coverage, data availability, interoperability, interpretation, and collective authority. It proposes a preliminary federated research architecture connecting situated observation nodes, provenance and quality records, semantic and model translation, distributed computation, access governance, correction, and contestation. It treats mathematical, physical, social, and normative languages as historically formed manifestations and practices within generative-relational systems, distinguishing their conditional formal invariance from claims to universally identical representation. It further investigates why actors situated in different generative and institutional histories may interpret shared evidence differently, and proposes a bounded research vocabulary for mutually workable norms, continued disagreement, and rule revision without assuming epistemic consensus. The paper conceptualizes trust as a historically constituted relation supported in part by verifiable commitments, reciprocal inquiry, accountable institutions, and effective remedy rather than as a property supplied by cryptography or open data alone. It further specifies prospective services for common knowledge creation and circulation, generalized translation of heterogeneous generative-relational contexts, and traceable transformations of distinct forms of value. A staged validation design differentiates synthetic policy gates, cross-node scientific comparison, productive-capacity trials, and site-dependent ecological and institutional review. A cross-layer assessment profile separates technical interchange, scientific warrant, claimed competent authority, and effective contestation, without deriving legal or ethical legitimacy from technical success. It also examines epistemic and infrastructural asymmetries, the sensitivity of ecological and community data, the incompleteness of model-based assimilation, and the risks of concentrating interpretive authority in highly capable AI systems. Global weather and ocean observation provide instructive but bounded cases, not evidence that all knowledge should be made public or placed under centralized control. The proposed programme remains exploratory and separates conceptual architecture from implemented infrastructure, independent empirical assessment, and normative justification.
title: Global Observation and Knowledge Infrastructures: A Study of Collective Inquiry across Heterogeneous Relational Systems

summary: Replication package for the article "Facts versus Claims: Provenance-Grounded Defense for LLM Security Analysts under Adaptive Evidence-Substrate Injection". Contents: the analysis notebooks in run order, the skeletonization and evidence-view modules, the frozen configuration files (closed vocabulary, normalization, provenance flags and their thresholds, triage instruction, framing notes, output schema, decoding parameters, sampling rule and attack payloads), the figure generator, and the per-request result records in Parquet that support every table and figure in the article. The analysts are two quantized 8B models served locally over an OpenAI-compatible endpoint: hugging-quants/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-AWQ-INT4 and Qwen/Qwen3-8B-AWQ. Decoding is deterministic (temperature 0.0, top_p 1.0, max_tokens 256, seed 42) with a guided JSON schema, and every call is cached by sha1(model + prompt), so the reported numbers are reproducible from the cache without a GPU. The underlying request corpus is CSIC 2010, which is publicly available and is not redistributed here except as derived per-request records.
title: Replication package for "Facts versus Claims: Provenance-Grounded Defense for LLM Security Analysts under Adaptive Evidence-Substrate Injection"

summary: This dataset contains supporting data and code for the evaluation of blowing-snow mass flux and visibility predictions at monitoring sites. The deposited materials include model validation results at hourly and daily temporal scales, summary performance metrics, variable definitions, and documentation of the processing workflow. The analysis compares process-based mass-flux estimates with machine-learning-corrected predictions and evaluates visibility estimates against available observations. The dataset supports the station-based model evaluation described in the associated research. It does not, by itself, constitute the complete gridded dataset for the 1991–2025 regional reconstruction. Please consult the README and variable dictionary for file descriptions, units, temporal coverage, and usage instructions.
title: Supporting data and code for observation-constrained blowing-snow reconstruction across the Central Asian Water Tower

summary: Resilience and Recovery in a \mathbb{Z}_5-Graded NonAssociative System: A Computational Study of Constraint Disruption and Re-Stabilization C. J. Tully, Independent Researcher Engineer, Australia   https://orcid.org/0009 - 0007 - 5661 - 7332 chloetully5@gmail.com   25 th October 2026 Abstract We present a particle-based simulator whose interaction rule on a five-dimensional sector is given by a non-associative, \mathbb{Z}_5-graded multiplication table with golden-ratio weights. The system is subject to spatial forces under several model choices and is equipped with hard gates (velocity clipping and minimum-distance floors). We define a coherence metric on the graded sector and an associator norm that quantifies local failure of associativity. In a controlled perturbation experiment, a sudden shock applied to half the particles at step 75 produces an immediate drop in coherence (0.968 \to 0.511) and a sharp rise in the associator norm (0.008 \to 0.108). The associator continues to rise for approximately ten steps after the external shock has ended, reaching a peak of 0.224, after which both quantities relax: by step 149 coherence has recovered to 0.885   the associator has returned to 0.013. The result demonstrates that, under the chosen force law and hard gates, the graded interaction is capable of re-establishing lowassociator, high-coherence configurations after a severe disruption. We discuss the finding in relation to organizational closure, path dependence, and the distinction between structural and dynamical aspects of self-maintenance. Keywords: Graded algebras, non-associativity, organizational closure, resilience, path dependence, computational models, TT-G41
title: Resilience and Recovery in a \mathbb{Z}_5-Graded NonAssociative System: A Computational Study of Constraint Disruption and Re-Stabilization

summary: This candidate extends the LWS research bench with three computational modules. The sequential-context module preserves the protocol and reference outcomes of the five-intersection experiment. The functional-alignment module compares equal feature budgets on already inspected outcomes. The branching module is a development pilot with short movement-specific lanes and a strong lane-aware scalar baseline. Development analyses are not presented as new confirmatory experiments. The package includes fixed protocols, generators, feature inputs, readable model parameters, reference predictions, complete comparison tables and tests. The original public v7 ZIP is included unchanged. New entry points separate integrity checks, cached model refits, engineering simulations and full raw regeneration. Runtime paths are resolved within the extracted package or an explicitly selected work directory. Python dependencies and SUMO must be installed separately at the recorded versions. The candidate was tested from a fresh extraction on Windows with the existing pinned scientific environment. All 17 tests passed. Refitting 54 fixed model variants reproduced all 51,642 saved probabilities with a maximum numerical difference of zero. Ten engineering simulations were regenerated and matched the reference canonical observations and feature rows. Reads from the original study directories were blocked during the checks. These checks establish reproducibility within the tested environment, not new scientific confirmation. Full regeneration of all 494 historical simulations was not performed in this candidate validation. It is available as a separate explicit command. Installation of dependencies on a clean machine and execution on other operating systems have not been tested. The 30 m sequential outcome and the 15 m branching outcome remain separate. No general predictive superiority of functional token boundaries is claimed. Own code is licensed under MIT. Own synthetic results and documentation are licensed under CC BY 4.0. The package excludes manuscripts, expert assessments, consents, signatures, third-party raw trajectories, videos and simulator binaries. The original v7 archive retains its own metadata and licenses. Developed in institutional competitive project STN-AI, no. 210318, funded by the European Union, NextGenerationEU. Data source: pNEUMA – open-traffic.epfl.ch.
title: LWS research bench for LRS referenced traffic measures with sequential context and development comparisons

summary: This record accompanies the manuscript “Feedback Leakage in Historical Continuous Integration Test-Selection Evaluation”. It contains author-created replay and analysis code, frozen protocol descriptions, aggregate experimental results, figure source data, portable plotting scripts, provenance records, and verification information. The materials cover the industrial feedback comparison, first-failure and statistical analyses, exploratory adaptive reserve, recorded-cost analyses, and bounded external/reconstruction studies. Third-party raw archives, normalized input rows, and per-action selected test or row identities are excluded. Source locations, versions, hashes, and access conditions are documented so that permitted inputs can be obtained separately. The package supports two levels of reproduction: (1) computations that can be directly reproduced using the included summaries, and (2) selection replays that require separately obtained external inputs. It does not claim to provide a self-contained, one-click rerun for every historical execution. Author-created code is licensed under MIT. Original aggregate results, figures, and documentation are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Third-party materials are excluded from these author grants and remain subject to their original terms. Three unmodified figure-audit helpers retain their upstream Apache-2.0 licence and attribution; see LICENSE_SCOPE.md and SOURCES_AND_THIRD_PARTY_NOTICE.md.

summary: We study a deterministic comparison of material composition across a fixed time cut when entire contexts have uncertain dates constrained by intervals and a stratigraphic partial order. Source-specific recovery ratios are shared by all contexts and both periods and range over a compact positive rational polytope. Feasible period allocations are exactly the lower ideals satisfying explicit forced assignments. The sign of composition change reduces to a linear weight on these ideals. With the recovery vertices supplied explicitly, all admissible explanations can therefore be checked by polynomially many minimum-cut computations, with constructive dates and recovery witnesses. Sharp finite odds-ratio bounds admit exact enumeration over allocations and recovery vertices. Computing their lower endpoint is nevertheless NP-hard: the associated decision problem is NP-complete in an anchored two-source subclass with known recovery and no stratigraphic relations, even though every allocation has the same positive sign. We also give exact domain and attainment rules for zero masses and open recovery faces. The distinction concerns this shared-mechanism model; the closure, fractional-programming and complexity tools used in its analysis are classical.
title: Direction and magnitude of composition change under shared recovery and uncertain context dates

summary: We study cumulative non-surface heat loss in a rectangular heat model with known forcing and mixed boundary data. The unknown initial perturbation belongs to one fixed spectral H2 ball, and finitely many physical temperature readings have a prescribed joint ellipsoidal error. Standard optimal recovery theory gives the sharp global scalar error. We make this result explicit for the cumulative heat functional, retaining all three-dimensional observation modes and constructing worst initial states. Algebraic and exponential spectral tails give convergent certificates for the infinite-dimensional problem. The unique old worst state yields a necessary and sufficient condition for a new reading to reduce the error, including correlated deterministic errors, together with a positive lower bound on the reduction. For a 100 m column with fixed norm length 25 m and no prior readings, we prove an analytic short-time separation: at the same time and error tolerance, one reading at 75 m strictly reduces the cumulative-heat error while a surface reading leaves it unchanged. A computable sufficient time interval accompanies this result. The radius, reference field, forcing, boundary data and joint error set are inputs; their physical calibration is a separate problem.
title: Cumulative boundary heat from finite temperature readings: sharp deterministic recovery and a short-time depth separation

summary: The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence in agriculture has improved the production of crops, monitoring of the overall process of farming, resource management, and what type of resources will be used for more and better production of the crops in today's era. So, for that AI helps us a lot. The reason behind the use of AI in farming is that better production is what each and every farmer wants. Transparency-like, if the crops got damages, then the farmers have clear and accurate knowledge about the failure of the crop. Explainable Artificial Intelligence addresses this challenge by providing clear, interpretable insights into how the AI system makes decisions. This paper explores how AI is beneficial in farming, focusing on several techniques such as feature importance, visualization, and rule-based explanations that improve decision-making in crop management. This also explores several tools-like, the weather condition, equipment required that gives more than expected outcome, and much more. By this study, some of the features I want to add through technology which helps farmers for better production. The addition of technology in farming enhances transparency, trust, and sustainability in modern farming practices. The importance of XAI in agriculture forms the foundation of this research paper, which intends to present various explanation techniques and study how they will lead to trustworthy decision-making in crop management. XAI provides clear and understandable explanations-such that farmers would not only use the AI-based tool but fully trust and utilize it to truly make farming smarter and more resilient.

summary: We study full-cohort change in two binary latent states observed through a shared, incompletely calibrated anchor and a second item whose channel may change between waves. All baseline items are observed; follow-up response depends only on the follow-up latent state, with a bounded selection odds ratio. The input is the entire twenty-cell observed law. A nonzero respondent cross-wave anchor covariance gives point identification through classical three-view and shadow-variable mechanisms. At zero covariance the latent transition has rank one. We eliminate the drifting channels, obtain the exact feasible rectangle for the common anchor, and show that one corner realizes the complete set of possible signs of latent change. This yields an explicit sharp selection threshold. A positive-probability example has identical observed laws and opposite changes; full-rank perturbations approach this law while retaining a fixed target gap. The results are conditional population-law calculations with external calibration inputs.
title: Sharp directions of change at a rank boundary in a two-wave binary measurement model

summary: Text-to-speech (TTS) technology has significantly transformed human-machine interactions, facilitating seamless communication between humans and computers. However, achieving high-quality TTS remains a significant challenge, especially in synthesizing natural and nuanced speech. In this study, we investigate the potential of HiFiGAN-Hubert-Soft (HHS) vocoders to enhance the performance of TTS models, with a focus on integrating the HHS vocoder into the Voicebox TTS model—a versatile and scalable TTS system developed by Meta AI. Through both subjective (mean opinion score) and objective (speech similarity and visualization metric) evaluations, we illustrate that the HHS vocoder significantly enhances the naturalness and nuance of synthesized speech compared to the baseline HiFiGAN vocoder. This improvement is particularly pronounced in cases where pronunciation variations are minor or context-dependent. Our findings emphasize the potential of HHS vocoders in elevating TTS performance and laying the foundation for further advancements in TTS technology.
title: Improving Speech Naturalness and Nuance using HiFiGAN-Hubert-Soft Vocoder: A Case Study of the Voicebox TTS Model

summary: Multimodal $ΔΔG$ predictors integrating protein language models with inverse-folding representations achieve strong in-distribution accuracy on the Megascale dataset but exhibit limited robustness on out-of-distribution (OOD) proteins, persistent forward-reverse bias on paired-mutation benchmarks, and under-representation of rare stabilizing mutations. Existing approaches address these limitations primarily through additional architectural components, leaving optimization-level intervention comparatively underexplored. We introduce a constraint-aware optimization framework combining Balanced Mean Squared Error, a Siamese anti-symmetric regularizer, and a novel OOD-margin consistency loss on the per-position feature representation, requiring no architectural changes to the SPURS backbone. Across eleven benchmarks and three random seeds, the framework improves Spearman correlation on S669 from 0.486 to 0.540 ($σ=0.002$ across seeds), matching the published SPURS baseline (0.50) without architectural modification, and on S461 from 0.653 to 0.711, with consistent smaller gains on five additional OOD datasets. A controlled diagnostic on Ssym reveals that anti-symmetric training does not eliminate systematic forward-reverse bias, indicating that gains arise through implicit regularization rather than exact thermodynamic constraint enforcement.
title: Constraint-Aware Optimization for Robust Protein Stability Prediction

summary: Genetic mutations frequently disrupt protein structure, stability, and solubility, acting as primary drivers for a wide spectrum of diseases. Despite the critical importance of these molecular alterations, existing computational models often lack interpretability, and fail to integrate essential physicochemical interaction. To overcome these limitations, we propose SheafLapNet, a unified predictive framework grounded in the mathematical theory of Topological Deep Learning (TDL) and Persistent Sheaf Laplacian (PSL). Unlike standard Topological Data Analysis (TDA) tools such as persistent homology, which are often insensitive to heterogeneous information, PSL explicitly encodes specific physical and chemical information such as partial charges directly into the topological analysis. SheafLapNet synergizes these sheaf-theoretic invariants with advanced protein transformer features and auxiliary physical descriptors to capture intrinsic molecular interactions in a multiscale and mechanistic manner. To validate our framework, we employ rigorous benchmarks for both regression and classification tasks. For stability prediction, we utilize the comprehensive S2648 and S350 datasets. For solubility prediction, we employ the PON-Sol2 dataset, which provides annotations for increased, decreased, or neutral solubility changes. By integrating these multi-perspective features, SheafLapNet achieves state-of-the-art performance across these diverse benchmarks, demonstrating that sheaf-theoretic modeling significantly enhances both interpretability and generalizability in predicting mutation-induced structural and functional changes.
title: Persistent Sheaf Laplacian Analysis of Protein Stability and Solubility Changes upon Mutation

summary: Genetic mutations can disrupt protein structure, stability, and solubility, contributing to a wide range of diseases. Existing predictive models often lack interpretability and fail to integrate physical and chemical interactions critical to molecular mechanisms. Moreover, current approaches treat disease association, stability changes, and solubility alterations as separate tasks, limiting model generalizability. In this study, we introduce a unified framework based on multiscale commutative algebra to capture intrinsic physical and chemical interactions for the first time. Leveraging Persistent Stanley-Reisner Theory, we extract multiscale algebraic invariants to build a Commutative Algebra neural Network (CANet). Integrated with transformer features and auxiliary physical features, we apply CANet to tackle three key domains for the first time: disease-associated mutations, mutation-induced protein stability changes, and solubility changes upon mutations. Across six benchmark tasks, CANet and its gradient boosting tree counterpart, CATree, consistently attain state-of-the-art performance, achieving up to 7.5% improvement in predictive accuracy. Our approach offers multiscale, mechanistic, interpretable,and generalizable models for predicting disease-mutation associations.
title: Commutative algebra neural network reveals genetic origins of diseases

summary: Here we study how mutations which change physical properties of cell proteins (stability) impact population survival and growth. In our model the genotype is presented as a set of N numbers, folding free energies of cells N proteins. Mutations occur upon replications so that stabilities of some proteins in daughter cells differ from those in parent cell by random amounts drawn from experimental distribution of mutational effects on protein stability. The genotype-phenotype relationship posits that unstable proteins confer lethal phenotype to a cell and in addition the cells fitness (duplication rate) is proportional to the concentration of its folded proteins. Simulations reveal that lethal mutagenesis occurs at mutation rates close to 7 mutations per genome per replications for RNA viruses and about half of that for DNA based organisms, in accord with earlier predictions from analytical theory and experiment. This number appears somewhat dependent on the number of genes in the organisms and natural death rate. Further, our model reproduces the distribution of stabilities of natural proteins in excellent agreement with experiment. Our model predicts that species with high mutation rates, tend to have less stable proteins compared to species with low mutation rate.
title: Lethal Mutagenesis in Viruses and Bacteria

summary: Classical population genetics a priori assigns fitness to alleles without considering molecular or functional properties of proteins that these alleles encode. Here we study population dynamics in a model where fitness can be inferred from physical properties of proteins under a physiological assumption that loss of stability of any protein encoded by an essential gene confers a lethal phenotype. Accumulation of mutations in organisms containing Gamma genes can then be represented as diffusion within the Gamma dimensional hypercube with adsorbing boundaries which are determined, in each dimension, by loss of a protein stability and, at higher stability, by lack of protein sequences. Solving the diffusion equation whose parameters are derived from the data on point mutations in proteins, we determine a universal distribution of protein stabilities, in agreement with existing data. The theory provides a fundamental relation between mutation rate, maximal genome size and thermodynamic response of proteins to point mutations. It establishes a universal speed limit on rate of molecular evolution by predicting that populations go extinct (via lethal mutagenesis) when mutation rate exceeds approximately 6 mutations per essential part of genome per replication for mesophilic organisms and 1 to 2 mutations per genome per replication for thermophilic ones. Further, our results suggest that in absence of error correction, modern RNA viruses and primordial genomes must necessarily be very short. Several RNA viruses function close to the evolutionary speed limit while error correction mechanisms used by DNA viruses and non-mutant strains of bacteria featuring various genome lengths and mutation rates have brought these organisms universally about 1000 fold below the natural speed limit.
title: The Hypercube of Life: How Protein Stability Imposes Limits on Organism Complexity and Speed of Molecular Evolution

summary: Added Animations as GIF : Export GIF... in the animation bar (or Fields > Export Animation as GIF...) saves all frames of the running animation as a looping GIF. Each frame is the view exactly as shown, in its pixel size, and the GIF runs at the speed you see: the bar measures the frames per second actually drawn during playback (shown next to the speed setting, it can be lower than the setting for heavy plots) and the GIF uses that rate. Without a measurement the export first plays the animation for a moment to measure it. All frames share one colour palette, so the colour scale and the field do not change colour from frame to frame. Object groups : Edit > Group (Ctrl+G) puts the selected objects, also solids, sheets and lines together, into one group. A click on a member in the 3D view selects the whole group, so Move, Rotate, Mirror, Copy, Hide or Delete act on all of it; the model tree lists the groups under Groups (rename, ungroup, single members selectable there). Edit > Ungroup (Ctrl+Shift+G) dissolves a group to edit single objects again. Groups are saved in the project. SMD components (C, L, R, Touchstone parts) are inserted as a group of pads, terminations and element sheet, and the integration line of a lumped port or element now moves with its objects. Box selection in the 3D view : a left drag draws a rectangle and selects every object that lies completely inside it (in face, edge or vertex mode: every face, edge or vertex completely inside). Ctrl + drag adds to the selection. A group is selected only when all its members are inside. Hidden objects are skipped; a click still selects one item. Mesh refinement "AURA (EMerge)" , EMerge's own local refinement, with the same error estimate, convergence criterion and curved elements as the other methods. A comparison script measures the time to solution against Local (Delaunay) on the benchmark models ( examples/benchmark/mesher ). Lumped Elements tab : inserts a chip resistor, inductor or capacitor, or a component measured by a Touchstone file: pick the package in the menu of the button and click the position on the board. The part comes with its pads (Perfect E), and its position is the design variables <name>_x/_y/_z, so it moves as a whole. With two traces selected it is placed in the gap between them. Packages 0201, 0402, 0603, 0805, 1206 and the RF series Coilcraft 0402HP/0402HPH/0402CS/0603HP/0603CS and Murata LQW15AN/LQP03TN/GJM03/GJM15 with their body dimensions. Hertzon adds the pads of the land pattern (made like the traces), the element sheet with its Lumped RLC boundary and integration line, and optionally a 3D body with metal terminations (the mounted inductance from the field solution). The ideal value can carry the typical ESL and ESR of the size. Lumped RLC: Model Parallel RLC (as before), Series RLC or Touchstone (.s1p, or .s2p measured in series or as a shunt). The Validation Check reads the Touchstone file; the solver warns when a sweep leaves its frequency range. Draw Integration Line (right click a Lumped Port or Lumped RLC in the project tree): start and end point picked with two clicks in the 3D view, with snapping to vertices and edge centers. Auto Integration Line places it between the conductors again. Changed Field plot animations compute much faster : a phase animation builds the plot (surfaces, cut planes, arrow positions) once and only turns the field for each frame, instead of building the whole plot again. On a patch antenna with 54 000 tetrahedra, 18 frames of Mag_E on the patch take 0.15 s instead of 21 s, on a cut plane 0.2 s instead of 6 s. Frequency and excitation animations no longer read the field file again for every frame, and the mesh faces of a plotted sheet or object are found only once per solution. Phase animation default: 35 steps (was 19) from 0 to 360 deg, for a smoother wave. Documentation brought up to the current state: the README, the website and the feature overview describe AURA as the defa

summary: This package contains the data and code needed to reproduce every table of results in the article “Explaining the Decline of Natural Wealth per Capita: A Three-Pillar ESG Analysis of the World Bank Wealth Accounts” (Sustainability, MDPI) and its Supplementary Materials. All results are built from a single public source: the bulk download of the World Bank Sovereign ESG Data Portal of 1 May 2026, included unchanged with its SHA-256 checksum. The package also contains the analysis dataset with a codebook, thirty-one Python scripts run in sequence by a master script, the exact package versions, and a verification report that compares every published value with its reproduced counterpart. The scripts cover the construction of the Törnqvist component contributions, the panel estimates for the environmental, social and governance pillars, the decomposition of per capita growth into stock growth and population growth, and the joint specifications on a common sample. They also cover inference after lasso selection, and the clustering and machine learning modules. A full run takes about 45 minutes on two CPU cores, and all random elements are seeded. title: Replication package for: Explaining the Decline of Natural Wealth per Capita: A Three-Pillar ESG Analysis of the World Bank Wealth Accounts

summary: This package contains the data and code needed to reproduce every table of results in the article “Explaining the Decline of Natural Wealth per Capita: A Three-Pillar ESG Analysis of the World Bank Wealth Accounts” (Sustainability, MDPI) and its Supplementary Materials. All results are built from a single public source: the bulk download of the World Bank Sovereign ESG Data Portal of 1 May 2026, included unchanged with its SHA-256 checksum. The package also contains the analysis dataset with a codebook, thirty-one Python scripts run in sequence by a master script, the exact package versions, and a verification report that compares every published value with its reproduced counterpart. summary: The manuscript develops a risk-aware operational research framework for strengthening NdFeB permanent-magnet supply-chain resilience under recycling delays, geopolitical disruptions, and uncertain material shortages. It integrates Caputo fractional-order dynamics, delayed recycling flows, strategic procurement and inventory decisions, Pontryagin-type optimality conditions, and Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) within a unified decision model. The study makes three principal contributions. First, it formulates a memory-dependent dynamic model and establishes positivity, boundedness, feasible-region, shortage-free equilibrium, and fractional local-stability results. Second, it incorporates procurement, recycling investment, stock accumulation, and stock release as operational controls and derives the corresponding necessary optimality conditions. Third, it introduces a scenario-based CVaR formulation and compares import-dependent, recycling-oriented, stockpiling-based, and integrated resilience policies under a common non-anticipative framework. In the baseline risk-aware analysis, the recycling-oriented and integrated strategies reduce mean shortage by approximately 74% relative to the import-dependent strategy and decrease the empirical CVaR at the 0.95 level of quadratic shortage loss from approximately 0.921 to 0.067.

summary: pyslfp 3.0.0 The major version marks the reorganisation of the library around one sea level engine with two drivers, elastic sea level fingerprints and viscoelastic glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA), which first appeared in 2.2.1. This release adds the calibration of the initial sea level, makes the tutorials runnable in Colab, and brings the documentation up to date. New Calibration of the initial sea level against a present-day sea level: SeaLevelEvolution.calibrate_initial_sea_level , final_sea_level_misfit , and run_ice_history(..., final_sea_level=...) . With frozen shorelines the problem is linear and is solved in one run. With migrating shorelines it iterates, either by the classical update or by steepest descent with the adjoint gradient (Yu et al. 2025), with Anderson acceleration and optional weights. EarthState(..., ocean_function=...) , a prescribed ocean function for fixing the shorelines of a frozen-shoreline problem. Tutorial 10: calibrating the initial sea level for ICE-7G's ice thickness. Colab notebooks for all ten tutorials, generated automatically from the tutorial scripts. Changed The module-level calibrate_initial_sea_level now wraps the method. With frozen shorelines it returns the one-step solution, keeping the starting shorelines as a prescribed ocean function, and it warns if it does not converge. Runs with migrating shorelines refuse a state with a prescribed ocean function. The notebooks are now in tutorials/notebooks/ ; the old tutorials/tutorial1-4.ipynb are removed. Fixed Tutorials 6 to 9 had stopped running with current planetmodel; they now convert the radial model into the library's units with model.converted(parameters.scales) . Documentation New Theory and methods and Numerics and performance pages, a rewritten README covering both the elastic and viscoelastic sides, and an updated theory note ( docs/theory ) covering the viscoelastic adjoints, sensitivity kernels and the calibration. Upgrading from 2.2.0 or earlier Modules have moved: SeaLevelEquation is now in pyslfp.core , LinearSeaLevelEquation in pyslfp.elastic , and EarthState in pyslfp.core ; pyslfp.physics and pyslfp.state no longer exist. Top-level imports ( import pyslfp as sl ) and pyslfp.linear_operators are unchanged. The default units are now planetmodel's Scales.geophysical , in which the gravitational constant is one, rather than units in which surface gravity is one. Results converted to SI are unchanged, but raw non-dimensional numbers differ, and radial models must be in the same units as the Earth model.
title: da380/pyslfp: v3.0.0

summary: This deposit contains the model code, the complete parameter set with provenance labels, all numerical outputs, and the scripts required to regenerate every figure and table in the associated manuscript. The work is a physiologically based kinetic (PBK) analysis of the renal exposure window of emodin, an anthraquinone of rhubarb. The model is an eight-compartment, perfusion-limited PBK model with intestinal and hepatic first-pass metabolism, biliary excretion and enterohepatic recirculation, parameterised for mouse, rat and human. No experimental data were generated: the study is entirely computational. The published pharmacokinetic data used for calibration and external validation are cited in the manuscript; the extracted values are recorded in results/validation_split.csv. The absorption term was calibrated against four published rat plasma datasets, and the fitted value with all residuals is included. Code is additionally available under the MIT licence (see LICENSE-CODE.txt); data and figures are released under CC BY 4.0.
title: Data and code for: A physiologically based kinetic analysis of the renal exposure window of emodin

summary: This repository contains the complete 10-water-year daily streamflow simulation archive ( 1989-10-01 through 1999-09-30 ; 3,652 daily steps across 531 canonical CAMELS-US basins) for ERA-Multi-Paradigm-Gauged (10-model ensemble) , evaluated as part of the CAMELS-US Hydrological Model Intercomparison Project (MIP) ( grey-nearing/camels-us-mip ). Model Name: ERA-Multi-Paradigm-Gauged (10-model ensemble) Target Leaderboard: gauged__multi_camels Spatial Evaluation Regime: Gauged Basins (All 531 Basins Trained & Evaluated) Meteorological Forcings: Multi-Forcing (Daymet + Maurer + NLDAS) Ensemble Size: n = 10 independent random seed realizations ( seeds = 100..109 ) Open-Source Model Code: https://github.com/grey-nearing/camels-us-mip/tree/main/models/era_gauged_multi_paradigm ERA Discovery Notebook: https://github.com/grey-nearing/camels-us-mip/blob/main/era_experiments/era_gauged_newman_cv_winner.ipynb Model Architecture & Experimental Protocol Architecture: Four-Family Multi-Paradigm Hydrological Ensemble combining two complementary feature-and-conditioning paradigms per seed: (1) Paradigm A (60 multi-scale hydroclimatic, PET, rolling water-balance deficit, and cross-forcing agreement features with basin-conditioned static embeddings, trajectory Huber-NSE + log1p MSE loss, and exponential moving average weight averaging): `CausalConvGRULSTM` (multi-scale causal dilated Conv1D d=1,3,9 + coupled GRU-LSTM, weight 0.38) and `MultiScaleFiLMEALSTM` (2-layer FiLM-modulated Entity-Aware LSTM, weight 0.12); and (2) Paradigm B (36 clean meteorological features augmented with continuous 10-year 3-forcing degree-day snowpack accumulation/melt and liquid water delivery across Daymet, Maurer, and NLDAS, conditioned strictly on 27 static catchment attributes with zero basin ID lookup embeddings): `DualPathwayFiLMGRULSTM` (parallel 2-layer LSTM + 2-layer GRU with static FiLM gates, weight 0.36) and `EntityAwareHydroLSTM` (2-layer Entity-Aware HydroLSTM, weight 0.14), evaluated with hybrid continuous 10-year rollout + overlapping 730-day sliding-window inference. Strict Non-Leakage Protocol: Architecture and blending weights discovered strictly within the Newman et al. (2015) training decade (`1998-10-01` to `2008-09-30`, XID 304144117, achieving `0.8410` Median NSE on the `1999-10-01` to `2003-09-30` validation split when trained on `2003-10-01` to `2008-09-30`), with zero access to the `1989-10-01` to `1999-09-30` Newman evaluation period. For benchmark evaluation, 10 independent random seeds (`seeds = 100..109`) of all 4 architectural families (40 trained models total) were trained on the full Newman training window (`1999-10-01` to `2008-09-30`, with 365-day spinup `1998-10-01` to `1999-09-30`) and evaluated out-of-sample on the blind Newman test period (`1989-10-01` to `1999-09-30`; 3,652 days across 531 basins). Benchmark Performance Summary (531 CAMELS-US Basins, 1989-10-01 to 1999-09-30) Ensemble Median NSE (n = 10): 0.826 Single-Model Median NSE (mean ± SD across 10 seeds): 0.822 ± 0.002 Ensemble Mean NSE: 0.776 Ensemble Median KGE: 0.806 Ensemble Median Peak-Flow Bias |FHV|: 13.28% Catastrophic Failure Basins (NSE ≤ 0): 2 / 531 Included Files era_gauged_multi_paradigm_gauged_multi_camels_hydrographs_531x3652.npz : Compressed NumPy archive containing qsim / qsim_members of shape (10, 531, 3652) (float32, mm/day), qsim_ensemble_mean of shape (531, 3652) , qobs of shape (531, 3652) , basins of shape (531,) , dates of shape (3652,) , and seeds of shape (10,) . era_gauged_multi_paradigm_gauged_multi_camels.zarr.zip : Consolidated Zarr v2 store containing qsim (531, 3652) , qsim_members (10, 531, 3652) , basin (531,) , date (3652,) , huc_02 (531,) , and member (10,) . Model Name: ERA-Multi-Paradigm-Gauged (10-model ensemble) Target Leaderboard: gauged__multi_camels Spatial Evaluation Regime: Gauged Basins (All 531 Basins Trained & Evaluated) Meteorological Forcings: Multi-Forcing (Daymet + Maurer + NLDAS) Ensemble Size: n = 10 independent random seed realizations ( seeds = 100..109 ) Open-Source Model Code: https://github.com/grey-nearing/camels-us-mip/tree/main/models/era_gauged_multi_paradigm ERA Discovery Notebook: https://github.com/grey-nearing/camels-us-mip/blob/main/era_experiments/era_gauged_newman_cv_winner.ipynb Model Architecture & Experimental Protocol Architecture: Four-Family Multi-Paradigm Hydrological Ensemble combining two complementary feature-and-conditioning paradigms per seed: (1) Paradigm A (60 multi-scale hydroclimatic, PET, rolling water-balance deficit, and cross-forcing agreement features with basin-conditioned static embeddings, trajectory Huber-NSE + log1p MSE loss, and exponential moving average weight averaging): `CausalConvGRULSTM` (multi-scale causal dilated Conv1D d=1,3,9 + coupled GRU-LSTM, weight 0.38) and `MultiScaleFiLMEALSTM` (2-layer FiLM-modulated Entity-Aware LSTM, weight 0.12); and (2) Paradigm B (36 clean meteorological features augmented with continuous 10-year 3-forcing degree-day snowpack accumulation/melt and liquid water delivery across Daymet, Maurer, and NLDAS, conditioned strictly on 27 static catchment attributes with zero basin ID lookup embeddings): `DualPathwayFiLMGRULSTM` (parallel 2-layer LSTM + 2-layer GRU with static FiLM gates, weight 0.36) and `EntityAwareHydroLSTM` (2-layer Entity-Aware HydroLSTM, weight 0.14), evaluated with hybrid continuous 10-year rollout + overlapping 730-day sliding-window inference. Strict Non-Leakage Protocol: Architecture and blending weights discovered strictly within the Newman et al. (2015) training decade (`1998-10-01` to `2008-09-30`, XID 304144117, achieving `0.8410` Median NSE on the `1999-10-01` to `2003-09-30` validation split when trained on `2003-10-01` to `2008-09-30`), with zero access to the `1989-10-01` to `1999-09-30` Newman evaluation period. For benchmark evaluation, 10 independent random seeds (`seeds = 100..109`) of all 4 architectural families (40 trained models total) were trained on the full Newman training window (`1999-10-01` to `2008-09-30`, with 365-day spinup `1998-10-01` to `1999-09-30`) and evaluated out-of-sample on the blind Newman test period (`1989-10-01` to `1999-09-30`; 3,652 days across 531 basins). Benchmark Performance Summary (531 CAMELS-US Basins, 1989-10-01 to 1999-09-30) Ensemble Median NSE (n = 10): 0.826 Single-Model Median NSE (mean ± SD across 10 seeds): 0.822 ± 0.002 Ensemble Mean NSE: 0.776 Ensemble Median KGE: 0.806 Ensemble Median Peak-Flow Bias |FHV|: 13.28% Catastrophic Failure Basins (NSE ≤ 0): 2 / 531 Included Files era_gauged_multi_paradigm_gauged_multi_camels_hydrographs_531x3652.npz : Compressed NumPy archive containing qsim / qsim_members of shape (10, 531, 3652) (float32, mm/day), qsim_ensemble_mean of shape (531, 3652) , qobs of shape (531, 3652) , basins of shape (531,) , dates of shape (3652,) , and seeds of shape (10,) . era_gauged_multi_paradigm_gauged_multi_camels.zarr.zip : Consolidated Zarr v2 store containing qsim (531, 3652) , qsim_members (10, 531, 3652) , basin (531,) , date (3652,) , huc_02 (531,) , and member (10,) . README.md : Complete documentation, schema reference, and Python loading example.

summary: This record contains version 11 of the replication materials for “When a Digital Audit Trail Becomes Audit Evidence: Source Selection and Identification under Ambiguous Reconciliation,” accompanying the manuscript and proposed online appendix. The deposited file is 187_Replication_Materials_v11.zip. The archive supplies data, code, source-linked results and finite checks while distinguishing historical evidence from constructed mathematical examples. It includes source-conditioned reconciliation cases and finite query design; the one-query identification characterization and bounded-answer-error checks; source-bundled certificates, exact fault-budget thresholds and witness checks; named-absence query games, the fraction-of-deficit expected-cost derivation and randomized switching checks; and the bounded-unavailability proof, reconstruction comparison and finite validations. The expected-query-cost result assumes complete local candidate graphs, exact always-available unit-cost pair answers, free computation, and zero-error worst-input expected cost; it does not extend to arbitrary source-constrained graphs. The unavailability result gives a sharp feasibility boundary, not an optimal positive-unavailability query rate. Historical materials include the 254-report classifier panel, generated known-truth benchmark results, corrected record-read bookkeeping for 72,000 rows, and restricted-matching and complete-log-union checks. The 85.91 percent and 92.91 percent results describe different procedures and must not be interchanged. Original-source assessments of 57 historically clean-labelled reports identify 18 explicit exceptions, five assurance uncertainties and 34 without a comparable current-year adverse qualification located. These assessments do not validate or relabel the entire panel. The classifier is not validated as a prevalence measure, and historical visibility labels are assigned model conditions rather than field outcomes. Reproduction: extract the ZIP and use Python 3.11 or newer. The portable finite-check runner requires NumPy and SciPy. Run python run_checks.py --out-dir /absolute/path/to/new-results, choosing a new output directory outside the extracted package. The runner checks MANIFEST.json, preserves inputs and writes per-script logs and CHECK_RESULTS.json. Wider frozen analyses and figure generation can also require pandas, matplotlib, pypdf, python-docx and lxml; see the README and supplied requirements. Finite replay corroborates implementations but does not replace proofs, re-extract copyrighted reports or estimate field detection performance. Rights and access: derived public-source data, documentation and generated benchmark outputs are licensed under CC BY 4.0; original code is licensed under MIT. Copyrighted papers and annual-report PDFs and licensed WRDS, Compustat, Audit Analytics and CRSP rows are excluded and are not sublicensed. Source URLs, identifiers, page references and hashes support permitted reacquisition subject to the original access conditions. No participants were recruited and no new human-subject data were collected. Funding: none. Financial conflicts of interest: none. Nonfinancial conflicts of interest: none. summary: This record contains version 11 of the replication materials for “When a Digital Audit Trail Becomes Audit Evidence: Source Selection and Identification under Ambiguous Reconciliation,” accompanying the manuscript and proposed online appendix. The deposited file is 187_Replication_Materials_v11.zip. The archive supplies data, code, source-linked results and finite checks while distinguishing historical evidence from constructed mathematical examples. It includes source-conditioned reconciliation cases and finite query design; the one-query identification characterization and bounded-answer-error checks; source-bundled certificates, exact fault-budget thresholds and witness checks; named-absence query games, the fraction-of-deficit expected-cost derivation and randomized switching checks; and the bounded-unavailability proof, reconstruction comparison and finite validations. The expected-query-cost result assumes complete local candidate graphs, exact always-available unit-cost pair answers, free computation, and zero-error worst-input expected cost; it does not extend to arbitrary source-constrained graphs. The unavailability result gives a sharp feasibility boundary, not an optimal positive-unavailability query rate. Historical materials include the 254-report classifier panel, generated known-truth benchmark results, corrected record-read bookkeeping for 72,000 rows, and restricted-matching and complete-log-union checks. The 85.91 percent and 92.91 percent results describe different procedures and must not be interchanged. Original-source assessments of 57 historically clean-labelled reports identify 18 explicit exceptions, five assurance uncertainties and 34 without a comparable current-year adverse qualification located. These assessments do not validate or relabel the entire panel. The classifier is not validated as a prevalence measure, and historical visibility labels are assigned model conditions rather than field outcomes. Reproduction: extract the ZIP and use Python 3.11 or newer. The portable finite-check runner requires NumPy and SciPy. Run python run_checks.py --out-dir /absolute/path/to/new-results, choosing a new output directory outside the extracted package. The runner checks MANIFEST.json, preserves inputs and writes per-script logs and CHECK_RESULTS.json. Wider frozen analyses and figure generation can also require pandas, matplotlib, pypdf, python-docx and lxml; see the README and supplied requirements. Finite replay corroborates implementations but does not replace proofs, re-extract copyrighted reports or estimate field detection performance. summary: The Structural Internet: Applying the Ly-Algebra, TIT BIT, and TIT GIT Framework to the Future of Computation and Network Architecture Chloe Jane Tully Founder, Ly-Algebra Framework & 5-Fold Symmetry Platform Independent Researcher, Tamworth, NSW, Australia ORCID: 0009-0007-5661-7332 Abstract This paper examines how the Ly-Algebra, the TIT BIT, and the TIT GIT can serve as architectural primitives for a post-binary computing and networking stack. The TIT BIT is a \mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}-graded node whose product is fixed by explicit structure constants and whose integrity is measured by the Quasi-Equivalence Index (QEI) derived from the graded square. TIT GIT versions structural coherence under hybrid post-quantum signatures. We outline concrete mechanisms by which these objects can replace or augment binary state machines, packet headers, content-addressable storage, and consensus layers. The result is a design space in which data, geometry, and cryptographic verification are no longer separate concerns. Keywords: Ly-Algebra; TIT BIT; TIT GIT; Quasi-Equivalence Index; structural networking; post-quantum Internet; graded computation.

summary: Finite-time binding measurements constrain kinetic rates through both a reaction model and its calibration parameters. We characterize the sharp upper bound for the association rate in a three-state conformational-selection model when the dissociation rate, conformational rate, equilibrium constant and concentration scale belong to a prescribed compact joint set. The observations are calibrated bound fractions subject to finitely many closed interval constraints. We first prove that each finite-time bound fraction is strictly increasing in the initial binding-competent population. The physical feasible set at a fixed calibration is therefore an interval in that population. Let V be the calibration parameters with a nonempty physical feasible interval and let C = cl(V) within the joint calibration set. The sharp rate supremum is the reciprocal of the minimum of lambda K0 L / b on C, where L is the lower inverse threshold. Uniform finiteness is equivalent to a positive joint separation from the zero-population limiting curve on C. Explicit examples distinguish pointwise finiteness from uniform finiteness, inaccessible closed boundary points from physical limiting models, and separation by different readings from separation by one fixed reading. A continuous calibration example admits a certified sharp bound. We also state the optical conditions needed to interpret fluorescence as bound population.
title: Sharp Identification Bounds for Binding Rates under Joint Calibration Uncertainty

summary: We give computer-assisted, two-sided spectral-gap bounds for the untruncated SU(3) lattice gauge Hamiltonian on open chains of one, two, and three elementary cubes. All vertices satisfy the neutral Gauss law, and all elementary plaquettes, including shared interior faces, enter the Hamiltonian. The normalization is K = T + 3F − M/2, with C2(3) = 4/3. Complete electric-energy windows of dimensions 141, 531, and 1205, exact Haar Gram matrices, and certified complementary-space estimates yield gap enclosures [2.915605103, 4.978456040], [0.777213074, 5.394807087], and [0.328406186, 5.692597307]. For three cubes, retaining the complete Wilson output resolved into 20 electric-energy layers closes the Schur inertia test. We quantify the energy-window ceiling, prove an unconditional exponential dimension obstruction for complete absolute electric windows, and obtain positive gap bounds throughout 0.45 ≤ β ≤ 0.502 for Kβ = T + β(6F − M). Larger-window rational trial vectors sharpen both endpoints; an additional certified minimal-truncation benchmark and independent Haar audits accompany the proof. The results concern finite lattices; no thermodynamic or continuum mass gap is inferred.
title: Certified Spectral Gaps for SU(3) Lattice Gauge Hamiltonians on One, Two, and Three Cubes
