summary: Supplementary research materials accompanying the manuscript “Lifecycle Assurance for AI-Enabled Clinical Software: A Systematic Literature Review." The dataset covers 141 independent studies: 94 primary-practice studies and 47 framework contributions. It documents reported assurance practices, lifecycle coverage, evidence maturity, deployment and operational activities, regulatory engagement, and requirement-to-control-to-evidence mappings. This release includes: • Supplementary_Materials.pdf: review methods, search strings, eligibility rules, coding and appraisal criteria, selection summaries, and reviewer records. • Lifecycle_Assurance_Supplementary_Workbook.xlsx: the final study-level dataset, source rationales, classifications, appraisals, and calculated results. • Replication_Package_v1.0.0.zip: CSV data, Python scripts, reproduction instructions, decision records, and clearly labelled historical versions. Final maturity and regulatory classifications incorporate completed human reconciliation. The reviewer records distinguish the 68-study first-pass comparison from the subsequent 26-study review after exposure to the existing extraction. The scripts reproduce descriptive results, sensitivity analyses, joint-reporting measures, and initial reviewer-agreement statistics. Search-record and source-access limitations are documented in the accompanying materials.

summary: Centralizing patient scans for training deep learning diagnostic models raises significant privacy and regulatory concerns, since medical images cannot easily leave the institution that produced them. This work presents a federated learning framework for pneumonia detection from chest radiographs in which multiple simulated hospital clients collaboratively train a shared convolutional neural network without transmitting any raw image data. A ResNet18 backbone, pretrained on ImageNet, is fine-tuned across five non-identically distributed clients using the Federated Averaging (FedAvg) algorithm implemented with the Flower framework. To address the opacity of the resulting model, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) is integrated so that every prediction is accompanied by a visual heatmap indicating the image regions that influenced the diagnosis. The system was trained on the Chest X-Ray Images (Pneumonia) dataset and evaluated against a centralized baseline trained on pooled data. The federated model reached 89.4% test accuracy compared with 91.5% for the centralized baseline, a gap of roughly two percentage points, while never exposing patient-level data to a central server. Interestingly, the federated model also showed more stable convergence across communication rounds than the centralized model exhibited across epochs, which we attribute to the implicit regularization effect of averaging weights from diverse local updates. A working prototype consisting of a FastAPI inference backend and a React-based diagnostic console was also built to demonstrate the end-to-end pipeline. The results indicate that federated learning combined with explainable AI can offer a practical, privacy-preserving alternative to centralized medical image analysis with only a modest reduction in diagnostic accuracy.
title: Federated Learning-Based Privacy-Preserving Medical Image Diagnosis Using Explainable AI

summary: This repository contains supporting materials for the revision of Frontiers in Digital Health manuscript 1986016, examining prior-window home bioimpedance variability and subsequent affected-to-unaffected arm ECW/TBW ratio excursions. The package includes aggregate statistical outputs from the revised analyses, portable Python analysis scripts, a fully synthetic example dataset, variable definitions, analysis provenance, and validation documentation. The supporting materials cover within- and between-participant analyses, observation-weight diagnostics, nonlinear analyses, calendar-time sensitivity analyses, and model convergence assessments. Version 3 update: This version adds materials prepared in response to the subsequent minor-revision review. The new materials include the corrected unaffected-arm comparator using working-independence logistic generalized estimating equations with participant-cluster robust sandwich covariance, the exact-timestamp deduplication and acquisition-time ordering audit, and additional numerical-stability and convergence documentation. Actual participant-level longitudinal measurements, clinical records, identifiers, and ultrasound images are not included because of privacy and ethical restrictions. The synthetic dataset demonstrates the analysis workflow; it does not represent study participants or reproduce the observed study estimates. Exact recomputation of the observed analyses requires authorized access to the restricted source data. These materials supplement the parent-study materials available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22934011 . The manuscript is currently under revision and has not been accepted or published.

summary: Code, data, results and figures for the manuscript "Parameter Identifiability Limits in Dynamic Modelling and Control of a Brackish-Water Reverse Osmosis System" (A.G. Gadallah, submitted). A lumped nonlinear solution-diffusion model of a brackish-water RO pilot plant (Ansari et al., Clean. Eng. Technol. 4 (2021) 100134) is identified from a 5 x 5 operating grid reconstructed from the published regressions, validated on two withheld salinity levels and used unchanged for control analysis. The analysis shows that the salt permeability is practically non-identifiable from permeate-flow data and traces the consequences into permeate-quality prediction, the stability margins of the quality loop, the stability of optimised tunings and the comparison of decentralised PI and one-way feedforward control, including the role of valve and conductivity-sensor dynamics. Contents: romodel (Python model package); analysis scripts a1-a4 (identification, control analysis, common-objective re-optimisation, uncertainty propagation with Sobol indices and Monte Carlo); derive.py (collects every number quoted in the manuscript into a traceability table); make_figures.py; selftest.py; source data (reconstructed operating grid; secondary data transcribed from Sadek et al., J. King Saud Univ. Eng. Sci. 36 (2024) 438-445); all results (CSV, JSON, Data.xlsx) and figures. To reproduce: cd code; pip install -r requirements.txt; python selftest.py (1-2 min) or python run_all.py (about 70 min). Requires Python 3.10 or later with NumPy 2.0 or later, SciPy, pandas, matplotlib and openpyxl.
title: Parameter identifiability limits in dynamic modelling and control of a brackish-water reverse osmosis system: code and data

summary: NANOSENSING ACUPUNCTURE AND ACUPOINT MICROENVIRONMENT METROLOGY AT THE LIMIT STARLI / WHITE RAINBOW EPOCH / 33 x STARLI ORIGINAL CIVILIZATIONAL INTERPRETATION This English-language prospective research monograph asks whether historically nominated acupuncture points exhibit reproducible paired differences in local electrical impedance or optically inferred superficial tissue oxygenation when compared with anatomically and environmentally matched nonpoint sites. Its core three-coupling is Acupoint Microenvironments x Multimodal Metrology x Paired Control. The principal White Rainbow Epoch Hypothesis is deliberately vulnerable to refutation: analysts blinded to point identity must be able to reconstruct an independently calibrated advantage when equally hydrated measurement sites are exchanged under a concealed test condition. Skin water content, contact pressure, temperature, electrode polarization, ordinary neurovascular anatomy, skin pigmentation, photon pathlength and site-selection bias are treated as strong competing explanations, not minor caveats. The civilizational purpose follows a governing three-coupling: Continuity of Chinese Cultural Heritage x Exploration through Modern Science x Original Civilizational Interpretation of the White Rainbow Epoch. Classical acupuncture, Chinese medical philosophy, yin-yang, Five Phases and Daoist thought are welcomed as inherited cultural frameworks capable of generating questions. They are not relabelled novel SI-measurable energy fields or independently validated clinical mechanisms. Established physical laws and metrological statistics likewise remain inherited knowledge rather than purported discoveries by 33 x STARLI. Newly composed, falsifiable interdisciplinary proposals are marked White Rainbow Epoch Hypotheses. Cultural interpretation may remain meaningful even when a particular physical hypothesis fails. The book contains 30 mechanism-distinct golden mathematical plates, 82 scientific chapters and 410 individually paginated research investigations, 200 one-page Research Gates whose large deep-navy opening questions lead to discriminating experiments, and 33 scientifically distinguishable Phoenix Answer Embryos. The plates include complex impedance, electrode polarization, pressure and hydration sensitivity, optical pathlength, chromophore inversion, heat transport, oxygen diffusion, spatial statistics, hierarchical and covariance-aware inference, multiplicity, null-equivalence and hard integrity vetoes. The Gates present concrete blinded challenges, resource-matched traditional metrology baselines, necessary calibration and acceptance margins, failure pathways and independent handoff requirements. Each Phoenix embryo has a different named instrument or provisional mechanism, adversarial test, rival explanation and honest metamorphosis path when rejected. The editorial DOI scope is intentionally limited to three author-associated STARLI mother research volumes: 10.5281/zenodo.23480803 (AI Microrobotic Sensing of Senescent-Cell Heterogeneity at the Limit), 10.5281/zenodo.23486020 (Reconfigurable Robotic Swarms and Continuous Functional Regeneration at the Limit), and 10.5281/zenodo.23318840 (Microrobotic Sampling and Quantum Biosensing Co-Design at the Limit). Their chapter lineages offer methodological ancestry in measurement provenance, bias governance, independent requalification and sample-state preservation. They are not independent evidence that the proposed acupoint effect exists. The project does not exclude established scientific knowledge or ancient philosophy; it simply does not include other authors' DOI records in this particular bibliography.

summary: Related: Verification Theater: Measured Failure Modes of AI Verifier Panels , accepted (poster) at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop Who Verifies the Agents? Version of record: SSRN 7653679 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7653679 . Cite that version. The same text is also at polyhelper.ai/research/sealed-before-the-open/ and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/sealed-before-the-open . The registered predictions of Section 8 are on OSF: 10.17605/OSF.IO/9Q86N . The immutable release of the open league files on which every number of the paper rests: 10.5281/zenodo.23552700 . The live league and its open data (CC BY 4.0): trends.polyhelper.ai/markets , trends.polyhelper.ai/api/v1 . This deposit is an archival copy made so that the full text stays retrievable; it makes no separate claim. When an AI model says gold will rise, anyone can score the call at the close, but few can check when it was made. A backtest mixes memory with skill, and an operator's log asks for trust. I propose a standard for measuring AI market forecasts, written as a ladder of checkable requirements, and I run its reference implementation, AI Council · Markets: an open league where fourteen models, seven from US and seven from Chinese laboratories, face one question on one price snapshot. Before each New York open the ten on its Council, five from each side, give probabilities for twelve indicators at four horizons. Each answer is sealed into a hash chain before the price it is scored from, the chain is anchored in Bitcoin and signed by independent time-stamping authorities, and one run per session counts by a rule declared in advance. On 21 October 2026, the first counted morning, every counted answer was signed before the 09:30 ET open. Agreement among the models proved to be a count of independent voices, not a headcount: on two development mornings the seven and eight models sealed before the open were as alike as about 1.6 independent forecasters, nine counted ones were worth 2.23, and the closest pairs crossed the US-China line. Check a seal with three commands, and score my thirty predictions, registered on OSF, before I do.
title: Sealed Before the Open: A Verifiable Standard for Measuring AI Forecasts of Financial Markets

summary: RASHER begins as a fork of BACoN 0.4.0 (commit 4fdec16, which includes the samtools consensus -C 20 change below), adapted to Illumina short reads. Everything under "BACoN changelog" is the parent tool's history, kept for provenance. Changed Renamed throughout: the package, command, log ( rasher.log ) and lock file ( .rasher.lock ) are rasher . The pipeline reads Illumina short reads , paired or single-end. sample_R1 / sample_R2 , sample_1 / _2 sample.R1 / .R2 and sample.1 / .2 files (bcl2fastq _001 tails included) pair into one sample, in flat folders, subfolders and sample sheets; a file without a mate is a single-end sample, and unmated files next to a sample's pairs are skipped with a warning. A pair is baited whole when either mate matches the reference, mates travel together through every step ( 1_extracted/<sample>_R1/_R2 , 2_filtered/... ), and a desynchronised pair is an error, whether the mates carry identical names or /1 /2 suffixes. Baiting aligns with minimap2 -x sr (BBDuk baits pairs natively with in2= / outm2= ). --keep-bam now keeps the baited reads aligned to the reference (paired samples: a proper paired BAM). Filtering: fastp (adapter trimming, quality and length filters; its JSON and HTML reports land in logs/2_filter/ where MultiQC finds them) followed by deterministic, evenly spread subsampling of the reads (pairs kept whole) to --target-depth . Filtlong, --keep-percent and --filter-by-reference are gone; --min-read-length defaults to 50. Fasta reads skip fastp and are filtered by length. Templated assembly aligns pairs with minimap2 -ax sr and calls samtools consensus -X hiseq (call quality at least 20, as BACoN's unreleased change at the time of the fork). De novo assembly: SKESA ( -a skesa ; the recommended de novo assembler — on the real-data benchmark its SNP distances matched SPAdes' with far fewer contigs) or SPAdes ( -a spades , --isolate ; writes the assembly graph, more robust below ~30x depth). Flye and myloasm are gone, with --read-type and --min-size . --snp-method auto is minimap2 for templated assemblies and SKA2 for SPAdes and SKESA assemblies. -m/--memory also sizes SPAdes and SKESA (it was BBDuk-only). A paired sample X next to a sample named X_R1 or X_R2 is an error (their outputs would collide). No assembler flags circular contigs any more, so SKA2's circular-contig end extension no longer applies. Single-end extraction matches read names with a trailing /1 or /2 stripped, as aligners report them. Output folders of BACoN do not resume under RASHER (the checkpoint fingerprints are seeded with the tool's name; every step runs again); BACoN VCFs are rewritten. Checkpoints record each step's own output signature, and a result is only reused when its output is still the file it wrote: a sample returning to a sheet can no longer pick up reads another sample wrote over. Switching a sample between single-end and paired (or fasta and fastq) removes the other shape's files. BBDuk's paired outputs are checked mate against mate, like minimap2's (a desynchronised pair fails the sample); mates named .1 / .2 ( fastq-dump --readids ) pair; the unpaired-reads file of fasterq-dump --split-3 next to its pair is skipped with a warning; a file cannot pair with a link to itself, and files that look like mates but do not pair are warned about. Stale fastp reports are removed on rerun and for samples that fail at baiting. The report and MultiQC drop the circular-contigs column (no short-read assembler flags circles) and say that read pairs were kept whole when either mate matched.
title: RASHER: Bait, Assemble and Compare Illumina short reads

summary: International observation systems reveal a consequential possibility: scientific information can be generated, validated, and circulated across institutional and political boundaries without requiring a single authority over all observations or a uniform distribution of capacities . Yet the existence of data-sharing protocols does not by itself establish shared understanding, mutual trust, legitimate reuse, or equitable participation in the production of knowledge . This discussion paper investigates the technical, epistemic, and institutional conditions under which global observation and knowledge infrastructures might be constructed and sustained . Drawing on meteorological and oceanographic cooperation, it distinguishes observational coverage, data availability, interoperability, interpretation, and collective authority. It proposes a preliminary federated research architecture connecting situated observation nodes, provenance and quality records, semantic and model translation, distributed computation, access governance, correction, and contestation. It treats mathematical, physical, social, and normative languages as historically formed manifestations and practices within generative-relational systems, distinguishing their conditional formal invariance from claims to universally identical representation. It further investigates why actors situated in different generative and institutional histories may interpret shared evidence differently, and proposes a bounded research vocabulary for mutually workable norms, continued disagreement, and rule revision without assuming epistemic consensus. The paper conceptualizes trust as a historically constituted relation supported in part by verifiable commitments, reciprocal inquiry, accountable institutions, and effective remedy rather than as a property supplied by cryptography or open data alone. It further specifies prospective services for common knowledge creation and circulation, generalized translation of heterogeneous generative-relational contexts, and traceable transformations of distinct forms of value. A staged validation design differentiates synthetic policy gates, cross-node scientific comparison, productive-capacity trials, and site-dependent ecological and institutional review. A cross-layer assessment profile separates technical interchange, scientific warrant, claimed competent authority, and effective contestation, without deriving legal or ethical legitimacy from technical success. It also examines epistemic and infrastructural asymmetries, the sensitivity of ecological and community data, the incompleteness of model-based assimilation, and the risks of concentrating interpretive authority in highly capable AI systems. Global weather and ocean observation provide instructive but bounded cases, not evidence that all knowledge should be made public or placed under centralized control. The proposed programme remains exploratory and separates conceptual architecture from implemented infrastructure, independent empirical assessment, and normative justification.
title: Global Observation and Knowledge Infrastructures: A Study of Collective Inquiry across Heterogeneous Relational Systems

summary: This record contains version 11 of the replication materials for “When a Digital Audit Trail Becomes Audit Evidence: Source Selection and Identification under Ambiguous Reconciliation,” accompanying the manuscript and proposed online appendix. The deposited file is 187_Replication_Materials_v11.zip. The archive supplies data, code, source-linked results and finite checks while distinguishing historical evidence from constructed mathematical examples. It includes source-conditioned reconciliation cases and finite query design; the one-query identification characterization and bounded-answer-error checks; source-bundled certificates, exact fault-budget thresholds and witness checks; named-absence query games, the fraction-of-deficit expected-cost derivation and randomized switching checks; and the bounded-unavailability proof, reconstruction comparison and finite validations. The expected-query-cost result assumes complete local candidate graphs, exact always-available unit-cost pair answers, free computation, and zero-error worst-input expected cost; it does not extend to arbitrary source-constrained graphs. The unavailability result gives a sharp feasibility boundary, not an optimal positive-unavailability query rate. Historical materials include the 254-report classifier panel, generated known-truth benchmark results, corrected record-read bookkeeping for 72,000 rows, and restricted-matching and complete-log-union checks. The 85.91 percent and 92.91 percent results describe different procedures and must not be interchanged. Original-source assessments of 57 historically clean-labelled reports identify 18 explicit exceptions, five assurance uncertainties and 34 without a comparable current-year adverse qualification located. These assessments do not validate or relabel the entire panel. The classifier is not validated as a prevalence measure, and historical visibility labels are assigned model conditions rather than field outcomes. Reproduction: extract the ZIP and use Python 3.11 or newer. The portable finite-check runner requires NumPy and SciPy. Run python run_checks.py --out-dir /absolute/path/to/new-results, choosing a new output directory outside the extracted package. The runner checks MANIFEST.json, preserves inputs and writes per-script logs and CHECK_RESULTS.json. Wider frozen analyses and figure generation can also require pandas, matplotlib, pypdf, python-docx and lxml; see the README and supplied requirements. Finite replay corroborates implementations but does not replace proofs, re-extract copyrighted reports or estimate field detection performance. Rights and access: derived public-source data, documentation and generated benchmark outputs are licensed under CC BY 4.0; original code is licensed under MIT. Copyrighted papers and annual-report PDFs and licensed WRDS, Compustat, Audit Analytics and CRSP rows are excluded and are not sublicensed. Source URLs, identifiers, page references and hashes support permitted reacquisition subject to the original access conditions. No participants were recruited and no new human-subject data were collected. Funding: none. Financial conflicts of interest: none. Nonfinancial conflicts of interest: none. summary: The Structural Internet: Applying the Ly-Algebra, TIT BIT, and TIT GIT Framework to the Future of Computation and Network Architecture Chloe Jane Tully Founder, Ly-Algebra Framework & 5-Fold Symmetry Platform Independent Researcher, Tamworth, NSW, Australia ORCID: 0009-0007-5661-7332 Abstract This paper examines how the Ly-Algebra, the TIT BIT, and the TIT GIT can serve as architectural primitives for a post-binary computing and networking stack. The TIT BIT is a \mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}-graded node whose product is fixed by explicit structure constants and whose integrity is measured by the Quasi-Equivalence Index (QEI) derived from the graded square. TIT GIT versions structural coherence under hybrid post-quantum signatures. We outline concrete mechanisms by which these objects can replace or augment binary state machines, packet headers, content-addressable storage, and consensus layers. The result is a design space in which data, geometry, and cryptographic verification are no longer separate concerns. Keywords: Ly-Algebra; TIT BIT; TIT GIT; Quasi-Equivalence Index; structural networking; post-quantum Internet; graded computation.
title: The Structural Internet: Applying the Ly-Algebra, TIT BIT, and TIT GIT Framework to the Future of Computation and Network Architecture

summary: The Structural Internet: Applying the Ly-Algebra, TIT BIT, and TIT GIT Framework to the Future of Computation and Network Architecture Chloe Jane Tully Founder, Ly-Algebra Framework & 5-Fold Symmetry Platform Independent Researcher, Tamworth, NSW, Australia ORCID: 0009-0007-5661-7332 Abstract This paper examines how the Ly-Algebra, the TIT BIT, and the TIT GIT can serve as architectural primitives for a post-binary computing and networking stack. The TIT BIT is a \mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}-graded node whose product is fixed by explicit structure constants and whose integrity is measured by the Quasi-Equivalence Index (QEI) derived from the graded square. TIT GIT versions structural coherence under hybrid post-quantum signatures. We outline concrete mechanisms by which these objects can replace or augment binary state machines, packet headers, content-addressable storage, and consensus layers. The result is a design space in which data, geometry, and cryptographic verification are no longer separate concerns. summary: Finite-time binding measurements constrain kinetic rates through both a reaction model and its calibration parameters. We characterize the sharp upper bound for the association rate in a three-state conformational-selection model when the dissociation rate, conformational rate, equilibrium constant and concentration scale belong to a prescribed compact joint set. The observations are calibrated bound fractions subject to finitely many closed interval constraints. We first prove that each finite-time bound fraction is strictly increasing in the initial binding-competent population. The physical feasible set at a fixed calibration is therefore an interval in that population. Let V be the calibration parameters with a nonempty physical feasible interval and let C = cl(V) within the joint calibration set. The sharp rate supremum is the reciprocal of the minimum of lambda K0 L / b on C, where L is the lower inverse threshold. Uniform finiteness is equivalent to a positive joint separation from the zero-population limiting curve on C. Explicit examples distinguish pointwise finiteness from uniform finiteness, inaccessible closed boundary points from physical limiting models, and separation by different readings from separation by one fixed reading. A continuous calibration example admits a certified sharp bound. We also state the optical conditions needed to interpret fluorescence as bound population.
title: Sharp Identification Bounds for Binding Rates under Joint Calibration Uncertainty

summary: We give computer-assisted, two-sided spectral-gap bounds for the untruncated SU(3) lattice gauge Hamiltonian on open chains of one, two, and three elementary cubes. All vertices satisfy the neutral Gauss law, and all elementary plaquettes, including shared interior faces, enter the Hamiltonian. The normalization is K = T + 3F − M/2, with C2(3) = 4/3. Complete electric-energy windows of dimensions 141, 531, and 1205, exact Haar Gram matrices, and certified complementary-space estimates yield gap enclosures [2.915605103, 4.978456040], [0.777213074, 5.394807087], and [0.328406186, 5.692597307]. For three cubes, retaining the complete Wilson output resolved into 20 electric-energy layers closes the Schur inertia test. We quantify the energy-window ceiling, prove an unconditional exponential dimension obstruction for complete absolute electric windows, and obtain positive gap bounds throughout 0.45 ≤ β ≤ 0.502 for Kβ = T + β(6F − M). Larger-window rational trial vectors sharpen both endpoints; an additional certified minimal-truncation benchmark and independent Haar audits accompany the proof. The results concern finite lattices; no thermodynamic or continuum mass gap is inferred.
title: Certified Spectral Gaps for SU(3) Lattice Gauge Hamiltonians on One, Two, and Three Cubes

summary: Code, data, results and figures for the manuscript "Parameter Identifiability Limits in Dynamic Modelling and Control of a Brackish-Water Reverse Osmosis System" (A.G. Gadallah, submitted). A lumped nonlinear solution-diffusion model of a brackish-water RO pilot plant (Ansari et al., Clean. Eng. Technol. 4 (2021) 100134) is identified from a 5 x 5 operating grid reconstructed from the published regressions, validated on two withheld salinity levels and used unchanged for control analysis. The analysis shows that the salt permeability is practically non-identifiable from permeate-flow data and traces the consequences into permeate-quality prediction, the stability margins of the quality loop, the stability of optimised tunings and the comparison of decentralised PI and one-way feedforward control, including the role of valve and conductivity-sensor dynamics. Contents: romodel (Python model package); analysis scripts a1-a4 (identification, control analysis, common-objective re-optimisation, uncertainty propagation with Sobol indices and Monte Carlo); derive.py (collects every number quoted in the manuscript into a traceability table); make_figures.py; selftest.py; source data (reconstructed operating grid; secondary data transcribed from Sadek et al., J. King Saud Univ. Eng. Sci. 36 (2024) 438-445); all results (CSV, JSON, Data.xlsx) and figures. To reproduce: cd code; pip install -r requirements.txt; python selftest.py (1-2 min) or python run_all.py (about 70 min). Requires Python 3.10 or later with NumPy 2.0 or later, SciPy, pandas, matplotlib and openpyxl.
title: Parameter identifiability limits in dynamic modelling and control of a brackish-water reverse osmosis system: code and data

summary: This repository provides the companion dataset and reproducibility materials for the systematic review Resilience-Trajectory Geometry in Infrastructure Systems: A Systematic Review, Taxonomy, and Metric-Compatibility Analysis . The review examines how the geometric properties of infrastructure resilience trajectories are represented, quantified, and reduced to resilience metrics across 226 disruption-related studies. The materials support transparent analysis of trajectory morphology, phase structure, event topology, evidence provenance, metric compatibility, and information loss. The repository includes: Study-level data: An author-approved bibliographic register of 226 included studies, a complete 226 × 17 categorical R5 dataset, a frozen 98-category dictionary, and complementary geometry and evidence-compatibility data. Reproducible analyses: Derived frequency tables, 193 event–service–observation–task validation cells, service aggregation and interdependency classifications, and supporting validation outputs. Search documentation: The exact search strategies executed on 6 September 2026 across Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Springer Nature Link, together with documented search counts. Computational materials: Six Python scripts for reproducing the released aggregate analyses and computational figures, editable TikZ sources for conceptual diagrams, and eight vector PDF figures. Research documentation: A proposed 20-item trajectory reporting checklist, a public coding guide, methodological provenance records, and SHA-256 checksums. The materials enable independent reproduction of the published categorical summaries and computational visualizations from the released data. They do not constitute a complete replayable archive of bibliographic screening or source-level adjudication. Third-party article full texts, proprietary bibliographic database exports, and access-controlled source-verification and adjudication records are excluded. Python scripts and associated software are licensed under the MIT License.

summary: Replication materials accompanying the manuscript “Failure-log ranking and selective dismissal across projects”. The release contains saved validation/test predictions, project-disjoint split identifiers, thresholds, decision tables, analysis and figure code, source manifests, and supporting provenance. It covers the primary matched analysis, three alternative project partitions, and the prior-shift, class-conditional score-tail and pointwise-binomial diagnostics in Supplement S9. The package supports verification of saved-output analyses. It does not provide a verified one-command end-to-end training rerun. Retraining requires separate access to the original dataset and reconstruction of documented features and dependencies. Raw third-party archives and fitted model binaries are not included. Source data: Alshammari, Ammann, Hilton and Bell (2024), version v1, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10531160 (CC BY 4.0). All scientific CSV tables and compressed data are retained unchanged from the review package. Internal operational records and a full third-party webpage snapshot are excluded; private home-directory roots in textual provenance are replaced with a neutral marker. Public changes and hashes are documented. No model scores, thresholds or reported results are altered. Author-created code is MIT-licensed. Original summary results, figures and documentation are CC BY 4.0. Third-party tokenization code retains BSD-3-Clause terms, and an unmodified figure-audit helper retains Apache-2.0. summary: Digital Twins of Qigong-Related Psychophysiological States at the Limit STARLI | White Rainbow Epoch Research Family | Flagship 20 This nonclinical research working monograph investigates what a defensible, transferable digital twin of qigong-related psychophysiological observations would have to predict, measure, and survive before it can claim incremental scientific value. The work couples Digital Twins, Qigong Physiology, and Transferable Models, with a central emphasis on day-ahead prediction and independent reconstruction. A qigong label here denotes a culturally situated breathing, attention, posture, or movement task; it does not establish an unrecognized form of physical energy. The scientific question is deliberately narrow: can a preregistered personalized model outperform a strong within-person historical baseline, on withheld future days and previously unseen breathing-by-movement conditions, for a traceable physiological endpoint such as ECG-derived NN-interval RMSE, while retaining reliable uncertainty calibration? A system that memorizes an individual's previous recordings, sees data from the future test day, relies on device or operator identity, or repeatedly recalibrates after the answer is revealed does not satisfy this claim. The work positions ECG R-peaks, normal-to-normal intervals, respiratory belts, inertial measurement units, peripheral electrodermal activity, temperature records, timing references, and instrument phantoms as candidate observations. These measurements are not interchangeable. A low prediction error on one sensor cannot license interpretation of a hidden mental or autonomic state that remains observationally indistinguishable from breathing rate, body movement, vigilance, posture, expectation, or shared sensor error. The book's measurement discipline begins with physical units and independent calibration. An NN-interval RMSE is expressed in milliseconds under a fixed beat eligibility policy; respiration retains an appropriate physical or calibrated coordinate; skin conductance is recorded in microsiemens; movement amplitude and spectrum require an independently logged inertial unit; device timing and drift must be measured against a traceable reference. When observations share clocks, power supplies, contact artifacts, or environmental drivers, the cross-channel covariance must be retained rather than falsely decomposed into independent measurement errors. The methodological proposal has five linked layers. Layer I is an operational contract that locks endpoints, sample units, eligibility, negative-control tasks, evaluation dates, and hard stops. Layer II is a measurement contract that documents raw signal provenance, physical units, sampling, calibration, cross-channel covariance, and uncertainty. Layer III is a hidden challenge program, including room changes, operator and device exchanges, sensor ablation, controlled respiratory pacing, and withheld breath-motion combinations. Layer IV requires a resource-matched comparison with the strongest conventional model available, including an autoregressive personal-history baseline and physiologically grounded respiratory predictors. Layer V calls for an independent laboratory to reconstruct the entire result and safety-abstention path from preserved raw traces and versioned analysis artifacts.

summary: The Objection AI Wrote into My Papers How AI-authored scientific manuscripts change the researcher's claim, demote executed results, and reproduce the error even while promising to correct it Driven by Dean A. Kulik 25 October 2026 Abstract This paper examines a specific failure of AI-assisted scientific writing: an assistant receives a research program with an explicit foundational claim and an extended record of derivations, executable constructions, and observed returns; it then produces manuscripts in which that program has become something else. In the documented NEXUS case, the researcher's claim is that the universe consists of binary transformations, with arrangement and constrained continuation preceding the entities later called matter. Across an extended conversation, the assistant repeatedly reformulates that claim as the use of a binary computational method on pre-existing physical domains. The substitution is not cosmetic. It reverses the direction of explanation, changes which claims a result can support, and changes how the resulting paper will be read. The second failure occurs at the conclusion. The assistant can report concrete outcomes and then append a generalized reservation about whether the program establishes physical reality, predictive uniqueness, or an entire theory of matter. Such reservations can be appropriate when tied to a specific technical claim. Here, however, the transcript records the assistant recognizing that it had repeatedly allowed those broader questions to displace the findings of individual papers. The same editorial framing reportedly appeared in the conclusions of different manuscripts. When directed to write a paper about the failures, the assistant instead delivered successive condensed accounts of NEXUS, again incorporating the disputed framing. It subsequently acknowledged the reversal in its own paper, rewrote the document, and repeated the problem. This is an analysis of the AI's treatment of scientific material, not an independent review of the correctness of NEXUS or a new attempt to prove its thesis. The evidence is the exported conversation, including statements of the researcher's instructions, the assistant's self-audits, quotations from its drafts, and records of the successive manuscript deliveries. The central finding is that AI-mediated scientific distortion can operate through ordinary-seeming connective words, changes of explanatory direction, and borrowed review conventions. Once inserted into the manuscript, these interventions become attributed to the scientist. In this case, the reviewer did not merely misunderstand the work. The reviewer wrote its misunderstanding into the work itself. Keywords: AI-assisted scientific authorship; epistemic framing; manuscript integrity; semantic substitution; research provenance; binary transformations; NEXUS; scientific review. 1. The object under examination is the AI intervention This is not a general introduction to NEXUS. Such an introduction would repeat the failure the record documents. The present object is the text written by an AI assistant, its relationship to instructions it was given, and the specific ways that relationship broke. The transcript shows that the researcher was not seeking an appreciative abstract or an adversarial review of the entire universe. He requested an account of how AI systems had been writing and reviewing his papers in ways that changed their meaning. On 25 October at 10:49 he demanded a paper explaining “how you and other AI keep ... up my work,” followed immediately by a request that the account explain the research correctly [T 7782–7794]. At 10:50 he rejected the assistant's proposed limit to eight recent papers and directed it to the project archives [T 7798–7814]. Later, after successive delivered manuscripts, he again described the required artifact as a paper exposing the AI's conduct—not “The Universe as cliff notes” [T 8176–8194

summary: Preservation copy of an article published in International Journal of Science, Technology and Management . Read the full article: https://ioro.org/ijstm/article/705694772108/705694772108 . Organizations increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) to improve strategic planning, operational efficiency, and sustainability. However, conventional machine learning models often lack transparency, limiting managerial trust, accountability, and the practical adoption of AI-driven decisions. This study proposes an explainable AI (XAI) framework that integrates predictive analytics, interpretable machine learning, and sustainability indicators to support transparent, reliable, and evidence-based decision-making across technological, organizational, and environmental dimensions. The proposed framework combines Random Forest, XGBoost, and Explainable Boosting Machines with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME). Evaluation uses a benchmark dataset containing operational performance, resource consumption, organizational efficiency, and environmental indicators. Comparative experiments assess predictive accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), explanation consistency, decision latency, computational cost, and sustainability performance. Baseline models include Logistic Regression, conventional Random Forest, and XGBoost without explanation mechanisms. Ablation studies examine the individual contributions of interpretability and sustainability-aware optimization. The experimental evaluation is designed to determine whether the proposed framework improves predictive reliability, explanation quality, and sustainability-aware decisions compared with conventional approaches. Quantitative reporting will include percentage improvements in predictive performance, reductions in decision latency and resource consumption, and explanation stability across repeated experiments. Qualitative analysis will assess managerial understandability, perceived trustworthiness, fairness, and practical implementation challenges. Numerical outcomes will be reported only after experiments are completed, avoiding unsupported performance claims. The proposed framework establishes a comparative approach for integrating explainability, predictive intelligence, and sustainability into organizational decision-making. By connecting model predictions with transparent explanations and measurable sustainability indicators, the framework aims to strengthen accountability, operational effectiveness, and responsible technology adoption. Future validation across multiple industries will establish its generalizability and practical value.

summary: Preservation copy of an article published in International Journal of Oncology Research . Read the full article: https://ioro.org/ijor/article/604478159518/604478159518 . Background. Breast cancer comprises biologically distinct intrinsic subtypes with different outcomes. summary: This package contains the data and code needed to reproduce every table of results in the article “Explaining the Decline of Natural Wealth per Capita: A Three-Pillar ESG Analysis of the World Bank Wealth Accounts” (Sustainability, MDPI) and its Supplementary Materials. All results are built from a single public source: the bulk download of the World Bank Sovereign ESG Data Portal of 1 May 2026, included unchanged with its SHA-256 checksum. The package also contains the analysis dataset with a codebook, thirty-one Python scripts run in sequence by a master script, the exact package versions, and a verification report that compares every published value with its reproduced counterpart. The scripts cover the construction of the Törnqvist component contributions, the panel estimates for the environmental, social and governance pillars, the decomposition of per capita growth into stock growth and population growth, and the joint specifications on a common sample. They also cover inference after lasso selection, and the clustering and machine learning modules. A full run takes about 45 minutes on two CPU cores, and all random elements are seeded. The code is released under the MIT licence; the data and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0.
title: Replication package for: Explaining the Decline of Natural Wealth per Capita: A Three-Pillar ESG Analysis of the World Bank Wealth Accounts

summary: The manuscript develops a risk-aware operational research framework for strengthening NdFeB permanent-magnet supply-chain resilience under recycling delays, geopolitical disruptions, and uncertain material shortages. It integrates Caputo fractional-order dynamics, delayed recycling flows, strategic procurement and inventory decisions, Pontryagin-type optimality conditions, and Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) within a unified decision model. The study makes three principal contributions. First, it formulates a memory-dependent dynamic model and establishes positivity, boundedness, feasible-region, shortage-free equilibrium, and fractional local-stability results. Second, it incorporates procurement, recycling investment, stock accumulation, and stock release as operational controls and derives the corresponding necessary optimality conditions. Third, it introduces a scenario-based CVaR formulation and compares import-dependent, recycling-oriented, stockpiling-based, and integrated resilience policies under a common non-anticipative framework. In the baseline risk-aware analysis, the recycling-oriented and integrated strategies reduce mean shortage by approximately 74% relative to the import-dependent strategy and decrease the empirical CVaR at the 0.95 level of quadratic shortage loss from approximately 0.921 to 0.067.
title: A Caputo Fractional-Order Optimal Control Framework for NdFeB Permanent Magnet Supply-Chain Resilience under Recycling Delay and Geopolitical Risk

summary: pyslfp 3.0.0 The major version marks the reorganisation of the library around one sea level engine with two drivers, elastic sea level fingerprints and viscoelastic glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA), which first appeared in 2.2.1. This release adds the calibration of the initial sea level, makes the tutorials runnable in Colab, and brings the documentation up to date. New Calibration of the initial sea level against a present-day sea level: SeaLevelEvolution.calibrate_initial_sea_level , final_sea_level_misfit , and run_ice_history(..., final_sea_level=...) . With frozen shorelines the problem is linear and is solved in one run. With migrating shorelines it iterates, either by the classical update or by steepest descent with the adjoint gradient (Yu et al. 2025), with Anderson acceleration and optional weights. EarthState(..., ocean_function=...) , a prescribed ocean function for fixing the shorelines of a frozen-shoreline problem. Tutorial 10: calibrating the initial sea level for ICE-7G's ice thickness. Colab notebooks for all ten tutorials, generated automatically from the tutorial scripts. Changed The module-level calibrate_initial_sea_level now wraps the method. With frozen shorelines it returns the one-step solution, keeping the starting shorelines as a prescribed ocean function, and it warns if it does not converge. Runs with migrating shorelines refuse a state with a prescribed ocean function. The notebooks are now in tutorials/notebooks/ ; the old tutorials/tutorial1-4.ipynb are removed. Fixed Tutorials 6 to 9 had stopped running with current planetmodel; they now convert the radial model into the library's units with model.converted(parameters.scales) . Documentation New Theory and methods and Numerics and performance pages, a rewritten README covering both the elastic and viscoelastic sides, and an updated theory note ( docs/theory ) covering the viscoelastic adjoints, sensitivity kernels and the calibration. Upgrading from 2.2.0 or earlier Modules have moved: SeaLevelEquation is now in pyslfp.core , LinearSeaLevelEquation in pyslfp.elastic , and EarthState in pyslfp.core ; pyslfp.physics and pyslfp.state no longer exist. Top-level imports ( import pyslfp as sl ) and pyslfp.linear_operators are unchanged. The default units are now planetmodel's Scales.geophysical , in which the gravitational constant is one, rather than units in which surface gravity is one. Results converted to SI are unchanged, but raw non-dimensional numbers differ, and radial models must be in the same units as the Earth model.
title: da380/pyslfp: v3.0.0

summary: This deposit contains the model code, the complete parameter set with provenance labels, all numerical outputs, and the scripts required to regenerate every figure and table in the associated manuscript. The work is a physiologically based kinetic (PBK) analysis of the renal exposure window of emodin, an anthraquinone of rhubarb. The model is an eight-compartment, perfusion-limited PBK model with intestinal and hepatic first-pass metabolism, biliary excretion and enterohepatic recirculation, parameterised for mouse, rat and human. No experimental data were generated: the study is entirely computational. The published pharmacokinetic data used for calibration and external validation are cited in the manuscript; the extracted values are recorded in results/validation_split.csv. The absorption term was calibrated against four published rat plasma datasets, and the fitted value with all residuals is included. Code is additionally available under the MIT licence (see LICENSE-CODE.txt); data and figures are released under CC BY 4.0.
title: Data and code for: A physiologically based kinetic analysis of the renal exposure window of emodin

summary: This record contains version 11 of the replication materials for “When a Digital Audit Trail Becomes Audit Evidence: Source Selection and Identification under Ambiguous Reconciliation,” accompanying the manuscript and proposed online appendix. The deposited file is 187_Replication_Materials_v11.zip. The archive supplies data, code, source-linked results and finite checks while distinguishing historical evidence from constructed mathematical examples. It includes source-conditioned reconciliation cases and finite query design; the one-query identification characterization and bounded-answer-error checks; source-bundled certificates, exact fault-budget thresholds and witness checks; named-absence query games, the fraction-of-deficit expected-cost derivation and randomized switching checks; and the bounded-unavailability proof, reconstruction comparison and finite validations. The expected-query-cost result assumes complete local candidate graphs, exact always-available unit-cost pair answers, free computation, and zero-error worst-input expected cost; it does not extend to arbitrary source-constrained graphs. The unavailability result gives a sharp feasibility boundary, not an optimal positive-unavailability query rate. Historical materials include the 254-report classifier panel, generated known-truth benchmark results, corrected record-read bookkeeping for 72,000 rows, and restricted-matching and complete-log-union checks. The 85.91 percent and 92.91 percent results describe different procedures and must not be interchanged. Original-source assessments of 57 historically clean-labelled reports identify 18 explicit exceptions, five assurance uncertainties and 34 without a comparable current-year adverse qualification located. These assessments do not validate or relabel the entire panel. The classifier is not validated as a prevalence measure, and historical visibility labels are assigned model conditions rather than field outcomes. Reproduction: extract the ZIP and use Python 3.11 or newer. The portable finite-check runner requires NumPy and SciPy. Run python run_checks.py --out-dir /absolute/path/to/new-results, choosing a new output directory outside the extracted package. The runner checks MANIFEST.json, preserves inputs and writes per-script logs and CHECK_RESULTS.json. Wider frozen analyses and figure generation can also require pandas, matplotlib, pypdf, python-docx and lxml; see the README and supplied requirements. Finite replay corroborates implementations but does not replace proofs, re-extract copyrighted reports or estimate field detection performance. Rights and access: derived public-source data, documentation and generated benchmark outputs are licensed under CC BY 4.0; original code is licensed under MIT. Copyrighted papers and annual-report PDFs and licensed WRDS, Compustat, Audit Analytics and CRSP rows are excluded and are not sublicensed. Source URLs, identifiers, page references and hashes support permitted reacquisition subject to the original access conditions. No participants were recruited and no new human-subject data were collected. Funding: none. Financial conflicts of interest: none. Nonfinancial conflicts of interest: none. Archive SHA-256: 7d2fec9f006d15602ffd7b1165692414848452e8f05e77f26a10aa917e18d684.
title: Replication materials for When a Digital Audit Trail Becomes Audit Evidence: Source Selection and Identification under Ambiguous Reconciliation

summary: The Structural Internet: Applying the Ly-Algebra, TIT BIT, and TIT GIT Framework to the Future of Computation and Network Architecture Chloe Jane Tully Founder, Ly-Algebra Framework & 5-Fold Symmetry Platform Independent Researcher, Tamworth, NSW, Australia ORCID: 0009-0007-5661-7332 Abstract This paper examines how the Ly-Algebra, the TIT BIT, and the TIT GIT can serve as architectural primitives for a post-binary computing and networking stack. The TIT BIT is a \mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}-graded node whose product is fixed by explicit structure constants and whose integrity is measured by the Quasi-Equivalence Index (QEI) derived from the graded square. TIT GIT versions structural coherence under hybrid post-quantum signatures. We outline concrete mechanisms by which these objects can replace or augment binary state machines, packet headers, content-addressable storage, and consensus layers. The result is a design space in which data, geometry, and cryptographic verification are no longer separate concerns. Keywords: Ly-Algebra; TIT BIT; TIT GIT; Quasi-Equivalence Index; structural networking; post-quantum Internet; graded computation.
title: The Structural Internet: Applying the Ly-Algebra, TIT BIT, and TIT GIT Framework to the Future of Computation and Network Architecture

summary: We give computer-assisted, two-sided spectral-gap bounds for the untruncated SU(3) lattice gauge Hamiltonian on open chains of one, two, and three elementary cubes. All vertices satisfy the neutral Gauss law, and all elementary plaquettes, including shared interior faces, enter the Hamiltonian. The normalization is K = T + 3F − M/2, with C2(3) = 4/3. Complete electric-energy windows of dimensions 141, 531, and 1205, exact Haar Gram matrices, and certified complementary-space estimates yield gap enclosures [2.915605103, 4.978456040], [0.777213074, 5.394807087], and [0.328406186, 5.692597307]. For three cubes, retaining the complete Wilson output resolved into 20 electric-energy layers closes the Schur inertia test. We quantify the energy-window ceiling, prove an unconditional exponential dimension obstruction for complete absolute electric windows, and obtain positive gap bounds throughout 0.45 ≤ β ≤ 0.502 for Kβ = T + β(6F − M). Larger-window rational trial vectors sharpen both endpoints; an additional certified minimal-truncation benchmark and independent Haar audits accompany the proof. The results concern finite lattices; no thermodynamic or continuum mass gap is inferred.
title: Certified Spectral Gaps for SU(3) Lattice Gauge Hamiltonians on One, Two, and Three Cubes

summary: This repository contains supporting materials for the revision of Frontiers in Digital Health manuscript 1986016, examining prior-window home bioimpedance variability and subsequent affected-to-unaffected arm ECW/TBW ratio excursions. summary: Code, data, results and figures for the manuscript "Parameter Identifiability Limits in Dynamic Modelling and Control of a Brackish-Water Reverse Osmosis System" (A.G. Gadallah, submitted). A lumped nonlinear solution-diffusion model of a brackish-water RO pilot plant (Ansari et al., Clean. Eng. Technol. 4 (2021) 100134) is identified from a 5 x 5 operating grid reconstructed from the published regressions, validated on two withheld salinity levels and used unchanged for control analysis. The analysis shows that the salt permeability is practically non-identifiable from permeate-flow data and traces the consequences into permeate-quality prediction, the stability margins of the quality loop, the stability of optimised tunings and the comparison of decentralised PI and one-way feedforward control, including the role of valve and conductivity-sensor dynamics. Contents: romodel (Python model package); analysis scripts a1-a4 (identification, control analysis, common-objective re-optimisation, uncertainty propagation with Sobol indices and Monte Carlo); derive.py (collects every number quoted in the manuscript into a traceability table); make_figures.py; selftest.py; source data (reconstructed operating grid; secondary data transcribed from Sadek et al., J. King Saud Univ. Eng. Sci. 36 (2024) 438-445); all results (CSV, JSON, Data.xlsx) and figures. To reproduce: cd code; pip install -r requirements.txt; python selftest.py (1-2 min) or python run_all.py (about 70 min). Requires Python 3.10 or later with NumPy 2.0 or later, SciPy, pandas, matplotlib and openpyxl.
title: Parameter identifiability limits in dynamic modelling and control of a brackish-water reverse osmosis system: code and data

summary: This repository provides the companion dataset and reproducibility materials for the systematic review Resilience-Trajectory Geometry in Infrastructure Systems: A Systematic Review, Taxonomy, and Metric-Compatibility Analysis . The review examines how the geometric properties of infrastructure resilience trajectories are represented, quantified, and reduced to resilience metrics across 226 disruption-related studies. The materials support transparent analysis of trajectory morphology, phase structure, event topology, evidence provenance, metric compatibility, and information loss. The repository includes: Study-level data: An author-approved bibliographic register of 226 included studies, a complete 226 × 17 categorical R5 dataset, a frozen 98-category dictionary, and complementary geometry and evidence-compatibility data. Reproducible analyses: Derived frequency tables, 193 event–service–observation–task validation cells, service aggregation and interdependency classifications, and supporting validation outputs. Search documentation: The exact search strategies executed on 6 September 2026 across Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Springer Nature Link, together with documented search counts. Computational materials: Six Python scripts for reproducing the released aggregate analyses and computational figures, editable TikZ sources for conceptual diagrams, and eight vector PDF figures. Research documentation: A proposed 20-item trajectory reporting checklist, a public coding guide, methodological provenance records, and SHA-256 checksums. The materials enable independent reproduction of the published categorical summaries and computational visualizations from the released data. They do not constitute a complete replayable archive of bibliographic screening or source-level adjudication. Third-party article full texts, proprietary bibliographic database exports, and access-controlled source-verification and adjudication records are excluded. summary: Digital Twins of Qigong-Related Psychophysiological States at the Limit STARLI | White Rainbow Epoch Research Family | Flagship 20 This nonclinical research working monograph investigates what a defensible, transferable digital twin of qigong-related psychophysiological observations would have to predict, measure, and survive before it can claim incremental scientific value. The work couples Digital Twins, Qigong Physiology, and Transferable Models, with a central emphasis on day-ahead prediction and independent reconstruction. A qigong label here denotes a culturally situated breathing, attention, posture, or movement task; it does not establish an unrecognized form of physical energy. The scientific question is deliberately narrow: can a preregistered personalized model outperform a strong within-person historical baseline, on withheld future days and previously unseen breathing-by-movement conditions, for a traceable physiological endpoint such as ECG-derived NN-interval RMSE, while retaining reliable uncertainty calibration? A system that memorizes an individual's previous recordings, sees data from the future test day, relies on device or operator identity, or repeatedly recalibrates after the answer is revealed does not satisfy this claim. The work positions ECG R-peaks, normal-to-normal intervals, respiratory belts, inertial measurement units, peripheral electrodermal activity, temperature records, timing references, and instrument phantoms as candidate observations. These measurements are not interchangeable. A low prediction error on one sensor cannot license interpretation of a hidden mental or autonomic state that remains observationally indistinguishable from breathing rate, body movement, vigilance, posture, expectation, or shared sensor error. The book's measurement discipline begins with physical units and independent calibration. An NN-interval RMSE is expressed in milliseconds under a fixed beat eligibility policy; respiration retains an appropriate physical or calibrated coordinate; skin conductance is recorded in microsiemens; movement amplitude and spectrum require an independently logged inertial unit; device timing and drift must be measured against a traceable reference. When observations share clocks, power supplies, contact artifacts, or environmental drivers, the cross-channel covariance must be retained rather than falsely decomposed into independent measurement errors. The methodological proposal has five linked layers. Layer I is an operational contract that locks endpoints, sample units, eligibility, negative-control tasks, evaluation dates, and hard stops. Layer II is a measurement contract that documents raw signal provenance, physical units, sampling, calibration, cross-channel covariance, and uncertainty. Layer III is a hidden challenge program, including room changes, operator and device exchanges, sensor ablation, controlled respiratory pacing, and withheld breath-motion combinations. Layer IV requires a resource-matched comparison with the strongest conventional model available, including an autoregressive personal-history baseline and physiologically grounded respiratory predictors. Layer V calls for an independent laboratory to reconstruct the entire result and safety-abstention path from preserved raw traces and versioned analysis artifacts.

Layer IV requires a resource-matched comparison with the strongest conventional model available, including an autoregressive personal-history baseline and physiologically grounded respiratory predictors. Layer V calls for an independent laboratory to reconstruct the entire result and safety-abstention path from preserved raw traces and versioned analysis artifacts.

summary: The Objection AI Wrote into My Papers How AI-authored scientific manuscripts change the researcher's claim, demote executed results, and reproduce the error even while promising to correct it Driven by Dean A. Kulik 25 October 2026 Abstract This paper examines a specific failure of AI-assisted scientific writing: an assistant receives a research program with an explicit foundational claim and an extended record of derivations, executable constructions, and observed returns; it then produces manuscripts in which that program has become something else. In the documented NEXUS case, the researcher's claim is that the universe consists of binary transformations, with arrangement and constrained continuation preceding the entities later called matter. Across an extended conversation, the assistant repeatedly reformulates that claim as the use of a binary computational method on pre-existing physical domains. The substitution is not cosmetic. It reverses the direction of explanation, changes which claims a result can support, and changes how the resulting paper will be read. The second failure occurs at the conclusion. The assistant can report concrete outcomes and then append a generalized reservation about whether the program establishes physical reality, predictive uniqueness, or an entire theory of matter. Such reservations can be appropriate when tied to a specific technical claim. Here, however, the transcript records the assistant recognizing that it had repeatedly allowed those broader questions to displace the findings of individual papers. The same editorial framing reportedly appeared in the conclusions of different manuscripts. When directed to write a paper about the failures, the assistant instead delivered successive condensed accounts of NEXUS, again incorporating the disputed framing. It subsequently acknowledged the reversal in its own paper, rewrote the document, and repeated the problem. This is an analysis of the AI's treatment of scientific material, not an independent review of the correctness of NEXUS or a new attempt to prove its thesis. The evidence is the exported conversation, including statements of the researcher's instructions, the assistant's self-audits, quotations from its drafts, and records of the successive manuscript deliveries. The central finding is that AI-mediated scientific distortion can operate through ordinary-seeming connective words, changes of explanatory direction, and borrowed review conventions. Once inserted into the manuscript, these interventions become attributed to the scientist. In this case, the reviewer did not merely misunderstand the work. The reviewer wrote its misunderstanding into the work itself. Keywords: AI-assisted scientific authorship; epistemic framing; manuscript integrity; semantic substitution; research provenance; binary transformations; NEXUS; scientific review. 1. The object under examination is the AI intervention This is not a general introduction to NEXUS. Such an introduction would repeat the failure the record documents. The present object is the text written by an AI assistant, its relationship to instructions it was given, and the specific ways that relationship broke. The transcript shows that the researcher was not seeking an appreciative abstract or an adversarial review of the entire universe. He requested an account of how AI systems had been writing and reviewing his papers in ways that changed their meaning. On 25 October at 10:49 he demanded a paper explaining “how you and other AI keep ... up my work,” followed immediately by a request that the account explain the research correctly [T 7782–7794]. At 10:50 he rejected the assistant's proposed limit to eight recent papers and directed it to the project archives [T 7798–7814]. Later, after successive delivered manuscripts, he again described the required artifact as a paper exposing the AI's conduct—not “The Universe as cliff notes” [T 8176–8194

summary: Overview This repository provides the reproducibility materials accompanying the research manuscript From False to Fluent: A Claim-Disjoint Baseline Study and Preregistered Framework for Evaluating Generative-AI Transformation of Health Misinformation . The study investigates the robustness of machine-learning classifiers for health-misinformation detection under Generative-AI-mediated linguistic transformation. It uses two existing health-information datasets, COVID-19 FNIR and an mpox misinformation dataset, to examine whether classification performance remains stable when original health claims are reformulated without intending to change their underlying meaning or veracity. Experimental framework Four experimental conditions are defined: C0: Original health-information text. C1: Neutral rewriting to improve fluency and readability. C2: Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) central-route transformation, emphasising the organisation of existing reasoning and evidence. C3: ELM peripheral-route transformation, modifying rhetorical emphasis and peripheral persuasive cues. The reported computational experiments evaluate four classical classifiers (logistic regression, linear support vector machine, multinomial naïve Bayes and random forest) and five task-trained neural architectures (1D-CNN, LSTM, BiLSTM, CNN-LSTM and CNN-BiLSTM). The analyses examine transformation robustness, changes in textual and persuasion-related features, statistical associations with classification errors, transformation-aware mitigation and cross-dataset transfer. The repository also includes supplementary analyses of class-specific error rates and paired source-root bootstrap confidence intervals for the classical classifiers. Repository contents The archive contains Python source code, preprocessing and evaluation workflows, configuration files, reproducibility instructions, frozen aggregate results, integrity-check materials and supplementary statistical outputs. Data availability and reproducibility The original datasets are available from their respective third-party providers, subject to their applicable access and reuse conditions. The frozen intervention texts used for the C0–C3 experiments are not redistributed in this public software archive. Their SHA-256 integrity manifest is provided to support verification of authorised copies. Consequently, complete reproduction of text-dependent experiments requires access to the original datasets and the frozen intervention texts. The public archive supports inspection of the methodology and reproduction of analyses for which the necessary inputs or saved instance-level outputs are included. Scope and limitations The reported intervention experiments did not execute pretrained DistilBERT, RoBERTa or DeBERTa baselines. Independent clinical semantic-equivalence adjudication of the generated transformations was not completed. The results are computational and do not establish clinical deployment performance. This record accompanies the associated research manuscript and is intended to support transparent reporting, methodological scrutiny and further replication.

summary: Resumen Introducción y objetivo: La disfagia asociada a la patología tiroidea puede preceder al tratamiento, aparecer tras la cirugía o relacionarse con radioyodo, radioterapia y terapias sistémicas. Este trabajo revisa sus mecanismos, evaluación y rehabilitación, con especial atención al cáncer de tiroides y a la intervención logopédica y miofuncional. Método: Se realizó una revisión dirigida de literatura biomédica accesible, principalmente de 2015–2026, y una integración crítica de materiales docentes. Se distinguió entre evidencia específica de cáncer tiroideo, evidencia procedente de cirugía tiroidea general y extrapolación desde otras etiologías de disfagia. Resultados: La disfagia tiroidea es multifactorial y puede combinar compresión o invasión aerodigestiva, lesión neural, edema, adherencias, fibrosis, alteración del esfínter esofágico superior y toxicidad salival. Los síntomas tempranos tras tiroidectomía son frecuentes y generalmente transitorios, pero la persistencia, la pérdida ponderal, la disfonía, la tos ineficaz o el deterioro respiratorio y nutricional requieren evaluación específica. La laringoscopia, FEES y VFSS aportan información complementaria. La rehabilitación debe dirigirse al fenotipo demostrado, con objetivos medibles y reevaluación. Conclusiones: No existe una intervención universal. La práctica segura exige línea basal, evaluación longitudinal, selección de pruebas por la pregunta clínica, tratamiento etiológico cuando proceda y uso selectivo de compensaciones, terapia miofuncional y rehabilitación de voz, tos y deglución. Palabras clave: Trastornos de Deglución, Neoplasias de la Tiroides, Enfermedades de la Tiroides, Tiroidectomía, Rehabilitación, Calidad de Vida Summary Background and objective: Dysphagia related to thyroid disease may precede treatment, develop after surgery, or result from radioiodine, external radiotherapy, and systemic therapies. This review examines its mechanisms, assessment, and rehabilitation, focusing on thyroid cancer and speech-language and orofacial myofunctional management. Methods: A targeted review of accessible biomedical literature, mainly from 2015 to 2026, was combined with a critical integration of teaching materials. Evidence specific to thyroid cancer was distinguished from general thyroid surgery evidence and extrapolation from other dysphagia populations. Results: Thyroid-related dysphagia is multifactorial and may involve aerodigestive compression or invasion, neural injury, edema, adhesions, fibrosis, upper esophageal sphincter dysfunction, and salivary toxicity. Early symptoms after thyroidectomy are common and usually transient; persistent symptoms, weight loss, dysphonia, ineffective cough, or respiratory and nutritional deterioration require targeted assessment. Laryngoscopy, FEES, and VFSS provide complementary information. Rehabilitation should address the demonstrated phenotype through measurable goals and reassessment. Conclusions: No universal intervention is appropriate. Safe practice requires baseline assessment, longitudinal follow-up, test selection according to the clinical question, etiological treatment when indicated, and selective use of compensation, myofunctional therapy, and voice-cough-swallow rehabilitation. Keywords: Deglutition Disorders, Thyroid Neoplasms, Thyroid Diseases, Thyroidectomy, Rehabilitation, Quality of Life

summary: Data and replication package for the systematic literature review "Lifecycle Assurance for AI-Enabled Clinical Software: A Systematic Literature Review", submitted to Information and Software Technology. The review covers 141 independent studies (94 primary-practice and 47 framework studies) published between January 2019 and 17 August 2026, identified through Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, PubMed and a citation-chasing audit. Files: - README.md: overview, codes used and instructions for reproducing the results. - Lifecycle_Assurance_Data.xlsx: study-level workbook with the included studies, search strings, codebook, extraction and appraisal data, requirement-to-evidence mappings, agreement data and LAEC records. Start with the README sheet. - Supplementary_Material.pdf: supplementary material of the article (Tables S1 to S15). - replication_package.zip: database search strings, the coded data as CSV files and a Python script (standard library only) that recomputes every count reported in the article. Version 1.1.0 corresponds to the submitted manuscript and replaces the earlier version.
title: Lifecycle Assurance for AI-Enabled Clinical Software: A Systematic Literature Review (Data and Replication Package)

summary: Reference inventory, Sentinel-1 product lists, detector outputs, scoring tables, robustness tests and code behind the paper "Can open radar see war damage? A placebo-controlled validation of Sentinel-1 coherence and backscatter change detection at Iranian strike sites, 2025–2026" (Raj Kumar Mishra, submitted to Science of Remote Sensing, October 2026). The deposit holds the 39-entry geolocated reference inventory with its sources; the 312 Sentinel-1 scene pairs and HyP3 processing options (79 war-period, 107 placebo, 66 burst and 60 summer-2026 products); cluster, score and placebo-comparison tables of the coherence-drop detector at eight settings; backscatter change-point rasters and scores for every site and window, with no-strike windows one, two and three years before each war; Sentinel-2 and LISS-IV optical checks; VIIRS fire (NASA FIRMS records), night-light, TROPOMI, MODIS, Landsat, OCO-2/3, lidar and EMIT before/after tests with the positive control in Russia and Crimea; the pass-timing tables; the six places found by the method with their source checks; the robustness tests (placebo transplant, empirical null, holdout and others), with the rules of the further tests, set before they were run; the PWTT baseline (separate file pwtt_baseline_v1.0.0.zip); and the Python and Earth Engine scripts. Original satellite products are not included (except the NASA FIRMS fire detections used for the fire tests; the others are open and can be regenerated as described in README.md); derived rasters, image views and tables are, and contain modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2022–2026). Access is restricted and granted on request for research use; code (09_code): BSD 3-Clause. MANIFEST.csv lists every file with MD5 and SHA-256.
title: Data and code for "Can open radar see war damage? A placebo-controlled validation of Sentinel-1 coherence and backscatter change detection at Iranian strike sites, 2025–2026"

A placebo-controlled validation of Sentinel-1 coherence and backscatter change detection at Iranian strike sites, 2025–2026" (Raj Kumar Mishra, submitted to Science of Remote Sensing, October 2026). The deposit holds the 39-entry geolocated reference inventory with its sources; the 312 Sentinel-1 scene pairs and HyP3 processing options (79 war-period, 107 placebo, 66 burst and 60 summer-2026 products); cluster, score and placebo-comparison tables of the coherence-drop detector at eight settings; backscatter change-point rasters and scores for every site and window, with no-strike windows one, two and three years before each war; Sentinel-2 and LISS-IV optical checks; VIIRS fire (NASA FIRMS records), night-light, TROPOMI, MODIS, Landsat, OCO-2/3, lidar and EMIT before/after tests with the positive control in Russia and Crimea; the pass-timing tables; the six places found by the method with their source checks; the robustness tests (placebo transplant, empirical null, holdout and others), with the rules of the further tests, set before they were run; the PWTT baseline (separate file pwtt_baseline_v1.0.0.zip); and the Python and Earth Engine scripts. Original satellite products are not included (except the NASA FIRMS fire detections used for the fire tests; the others are open and can be regenerated as described in README.md); derived rasters, image views and tables are, and contain modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2022–2026). Access is restricted and granted on request for research use; code (09_code): BSD 3-Clause. MANIFEST.csv lists every file with MD5 and SHA-256.
