summary: This repository contains the full research artifact for a comparative study of automated issue labeling in the Qiskit ecosystem. The project focuses on assigning GitHub issues to a domain-specific taxonomy of quantum software modules using multiple modeling paradigms: classical machine learning baselines, fine-tuned transformer models, direct prompting with large language models, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The work is designed to support reproducible evaluation of AI-assisted bug triage and taxonomy-driven issue classification in a specialized scientific software repository. The dataset and experiments are organized around the issue-labeling task described in README.md. The repository includes the annotated issue corpus in qiskit_repo_quantum_issues.json, baseline and exploratory analysis in Analysis, transformer training pipelines in Fine_tuned_Experiments, direct GPT prompting experiments in Gpt_Experiments, and retrieval-based pipelines in RAG_Experiments. Output artifacts include trained model results, prediction arrays, confusion metrics, per-label performance summaries, and experiment logs stored alongside each experiment family. ### Repository structure - qiskit_repo_quantum_issues.json: Qiskit issue dataset used for training and evaluation. - Analysis: baseline models and analysis scripts, including:   - ml_baselines.py: TF-IDF logistic regression and linear SVM baselines   - quantum_term_analysis.py: analysis of quantum-domain terminology   - bot_labeling_analysis.py: bot-vs-human labeling analysis   - predictions: saved predictions and evaluation outputs - Fine_tuned_Experiments: fine-tuned transformer experiments with scripts and results:   - DistilBERT.py   - Roberta.py   - result folders such as DistilBERT_results and Roberta_results - Gpt_Experiments: zero-shot and few-shot prompting experiments with OpenAI models:   - scripts containing model-specific prompt scripts   - output folders for prompt results and predictions - RAG_Experiments: retrieval-augmented and agentic RAG pipelines   - code: experiment scripts for zeroshot, few-shot, adaptive, and direct generation pipelines - LICENSE: MIT license - README.md: project overview and usage guide
title: Automated Quantum Issue Labeling in Qiskit: Large Language Models and Fine-Tuned Transformers

summary: Abstract A dimensionless closure relation associated with the five-constant system {e_c, m_e, h, c, G} predicts the frequency ν_zp = 0.0605390 Hz. The same scale has the equivalent laboratory representations τ_zp ≈ 16.5183 s, ν_zp = 0.06053898(67) Hz, ℓ_zp ≈ 10.9614 cm. The present paper formulates a metrological test of this prediction. An admissible determination must identify one of these quantities through an independently observed physical phenomenon rather than calculate it from the closure relation or from an algebraically equivalent expression. In particular, the predicted value must not enter the apparatus, calibration chain, or analysis through G or through any quantity whose numerical value has itself been fixed from the closure. The target follows from α_eG · hν_zp/(m_ec²) = 1, with α_eG = e_c/(m_e√G), which links the electron–gravitational dimensionless sector to the electron Compton frequency. The dimensional origin of the three-member structure {α, α_eG, η_j}, with η_j = hν_j/(m_ec²), is developed in a companion paper, where the closure is proposed as a physical conjecture. An independent realization would provide a direct experimental test of the proposed closure and, within the framework, an alternative route to the gravitational constant, G = [e_chν_zp/(m_e²c²)]². The problem is therefore reduced to a specific metrological question with defined numerical targets, independence criteria, uncertainty propagation, and falsification conditions.
title: Metrological Test of a Predicted Closure Scale at 0.0605390 Hz: Frequency, Period, Velocity, and Length Realizations

summary: This preprint examines how space-themed socioscientific issues (SSI) connect scientific understanding with social and ethical judgment, and how these connections can inform science and STEM education. Drawing on 1,316 educational reports—58 space-related and 1,258 non-space-related—the review combines comparative mapping with detailed examination of space contexts. It addresses four interconnected areas: the representation and educational forms of space-themed SSI; disciplinary knowledge and reasoning; historical, present and future perspectives; and teaching approaches, student responses and learning outcomes. The evidence encompasses learner research, curriculum and teacher education, educational reviews and supporting contributions. Manuscript.pdf — Complete preprint manuscript. Presents the conceptual framework, review methods, findings across the four research questions, discussion, educational implications and references. All main-text figures and tables are included. Word and HTML copies, if supplied, are alternative formats of the same manuscript. S1_Methods_and_Evidence_Tables.pdf — Supplementary methods and selected evidence tables. Explains the search and selection procedures, eligibility criteria, analytical units, coding definitions and weighting methods. It also documents temporal reconstruction and sensitivity analyses, selected science–society reasoning cases, pedagogical evidence, quantitative comparisons and source-identification qualifications. S2_Report_Evidence_Catalogue.html — Searchable report evidence catalogue. Provides searchable and filterable report-level information, including educational scope, Earth–space connections, disciplinary knowledge, epistemic reasoning, teaching practices, outcomes and temporal interpretation. Bibliographic references, source links and selection reasons connect the synthesis to its supporting evidence. Download and open the file in a web browser. S3_Analysis_Data.xlsx — Analysis data workbook. Contains 26 worksheets documenting search strategies, selection decisions, report characteristics, coding definitions, teaching and outcome evidence, temporal coordinates and model parameters, relationships between reports, and the distributions underlying the analyses.
title: Distant Worlds, Shared Questions: A Systematic Review of Space-Themed Socioscientific Education

summary: HBB2OBB converts horizontal (axis-aligned) bounding boxes (HBBs) into oriented (rotated) bounding boxes (OBBs) by using existing HBB annotations as prompts for segmentation models from the SAM (Segment Anything Model) family. It targets object detection tasks where objects appear at arbitrary orientations, such as aerial imagery, satellite data, and traffic monitoring, producing oriented boxes that tightly encapsulate non-upright objects without any re-annotation. Beyond conversion, it provides horizontal box detection, evaluation, hyperparameter optimization, an interactive annotation viewer, and annotation format-conversion tools, exposed through both a command-line interface and a Python API. 📖 Documentation: rfonod.github.io/hbb2obb , with a quick start on the bundled sample data, a guide per command, pages on how the conversion works, the confidence score, the metrics and provenance, and a CLI and API reference generated from the code. Why HBB2OBB 🎯 Accurate OBBs from HBBs : prompts SAM-family segmentation models with existing horizontal boxes to fit tight oriented boxes around non-upright objects, with no re-annotation required. 🚗 No HBBs? Detect them : the hbb2obb-detect command runs an Ultralytics detector over the images and writes the horizontal boxes the conversion consumes, confidence column included. 🧩 Model ensemble : combines masks from multiple SAM variants through majority voting for more robust, accurate results. 🛡️ Spatially constrained and safe : region-specific masking and contour refinement keep segmentation inside the object, a mask split by an occluder is fitted back together, and a fallback retains the original HBB when no valid mask is found, counted and reported rather than left to be discovered afterwards. 🔎 Confidence-scored output : every OBB receives a heuristic quality score in [0, 1] that flags silent fallbacks and low-confidence conversions, so you know which boxes to trust; the scores go in the label files or in a side-car directory that keeps them strictly standard, and the detector's own confidence can be carried through instead of, or on top of, that score. 📐 Flexible scaling : positive or negative scale factors, optionally different for the short and long sides, recover cropped object parts or tighten overly conservative annotations. 📊 Evaluate and optimize : evaluation against ground truth on IoU, orientation error, and the share of boxes above a high IoU bar, plus the hbb2obb-optimize command, a hyperparameter search over SAM inference resolution, scale factors, and morphological opening kernel, driven by a configuration file so that a whole benchmark of model ensembles is a single reproducible command. 🔬 Where the score comes from : the hbb2obb-analyze command breaks one evaluation down by the ground truth's orientation, size, frame edge, difficulty and class, and scores the conversion against emitting the horizontal prompt unchanged. 🔄 Five annotation formats : read and write YOLO, DOTA, Pascal VOC, COCO, and LabelMe, for horizontal and oriented boxes alike, with a check that proves every format encodes the same boxes. 🔍 Interactive viewer : the hbb2obb-view command pans and zooms over the annotations, in any format, coloring boxes by confidence and overlaying predictions against ground truth. Where a set ships the same boxes several ways, it names the format on screen and switches between them on a keypress. Features HBB to OBB conversion of YOLO-format annotations using SAM-based segmentation, written in absolute pixels or, with --normalize , relative to [0, 1], the convention Ultralytics reads. HBB detection : produce the horizontal boxes in the first place with any Ultralytics detector, a local file, a link, the Ultralytics catalogue, or Hugging Face, passing any other predictor argument straight through. Multiple model support : SAM, SAM2, SAM2.1, SAM3, Mobile SAM, and FastSAM families. Model ensemble via majority voting for enhanced accuracy. Confidence scoring : a per-OBB quali

summary: Bounded Agentic Distribution Experiments (v0.7.0): A Reproducible Framework for Comparing Agentic Intervention Discovery with Non-Agentic Search This software implements the computational framework and pre-pilot experimental protocol associated with the research manuscript Evaluating the Incremental Value of Agentic Intervention Discovery over Non-Agentic Search in Multi-Actor Distribution Networks . The framework evaluates whether a generative AI agent can identify economically beneficial operational interventions beyond those discovered by budget-matched non-agentic search. Agentic and non-agentic methods operate within the same typed intervention space, access the same simulator information, and are subject to common evaluation budgets. Candidate interventions undergo deterministic verification of encoded structural constraints and, where applicable, stochastic qualification against economic, service, route, and actor-participation criteria. The reference environment represents a stylized print-media distribution network with 420 retailers, 18 baseline delivery vehicles, uncertain demand, allocation decisions, reverse logistics, route constraints, temporary fleet capacity, discontinuous staffing requirements, and sales-contingent remuneration. Its parameters combine industry-informed inputs, documented benchmarks, modeling assumptions, and calibration targets. The environment is intended for controlled computational evaluation rather than empirical representation of the Italian distribution industry. Experimental design Version 0.7.0 implements two frozen intervention-complexity regimes: Low-complexity regime (RL): allocation reweighting only, with a maximum intervention length of one action. Multi-domain coupled regime (RC): allocation, route transfer, temporary fleet, and forecasting interventions, with a maximum intervention length of three actions. Both regimes use a candidate-evaluation budget of 40 simulator calls. The primary comparison uses ten independent generative-agent realizations and ten independent simulated-annealing realizations per regime. The software separates proposal-mechanism randomness from simulation-scenario randomness and supports common random numbers for comparative evaluation. The statistical implementation includes regime-specific pilot sizing, independent within-method repetition resampling, shared scenario resampling, and a two-dimensional bootstrap for confirmatory inference. Final-test selection follows a frozen rule combining precision requirements from both regimes with the minimum-detectable-effect requirement for the multi-domain superiority hypothesis. Software contents The archive includes the Python simulator and experimental orchestration code, command-line interface, frozen configuration files, typed intervention specifications, agent prompt and structured-output schemas, statistical analysis procedures, automated tests, freeze manifest, calibration documentation, and four Jupyter notebooks covering protocol execution, pilot sizing, repeated experiments, and economic calibration. Validation and research status The implementation passes 31 automated software and protocol-consistency tests. These tests examine computational correctness, reproducibility, regime restrictions, seed handling, bootstrap procedures, and experimental locking. They do not establish empirical agent performance. This release corresponds to the frozen pre-pilot protocol BAD-420-v0.7-2026-09-11 . The final-test set remains locked until a valid pilot mechanically determines its size. No live API-based agent-performance experiment or confirmatory comparison is included in this release. Consequently, the software does not establish that agentic intervention discovery outperforms, matches, or underperforms non-agentic search. The purpose of this release is to make the computational model, methodological assumptions, experimental controls, and pre-result evaluation protocol available for independent inspection, repl

summary: This dataset contains 530,132 method-level provenance relationships, each annotated with the source and sink licenses, license compatibility classification, and supporting metadata, mined across a large corpus of GitHub repositories. It is the full, unfiltered version of the empirical corpus used in an anonymous submission on method-level license compliance debt, currently under double-blind peer review. This file is hosted on Zenodo rather than GitHub solely because of GitHub's 100MB per-file limit; it is not a separate or reduced dataset. A smaller, GitHub-hosted sample ( downsized_compliance_empirical_dataset.csv ) and the full replication package, including the classification engine, validation data, and analysis notebooks, are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EmpiricalStudyPaper-842E/ . Schema : organization_name , hash , source_method_name , sink_method_name , source_repository_url , sink_repository_url , source_file_location , sink_file_location , source_query_project , violation . Full column documentation is in the replication package's README. Anonymity note : this dataset is uploaded under an anonymous identity for double-blind review. summary: We conduct a version-pinned, reproducible forensic audit of the public Einstein Elevator data package (Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.15167723) to determine whether it supports validation of quantum sensor certificates. Through an exhaustive cross-file sliding-window correlation search over 44,207,922 comparisons and exact six-decimal rounding checks, we find that all 31 exported sensor channels have a unique best match within the enumerated raw traces under the stated protocol. Residual numerical differences are highly consistent with text-based absolute quantization; the correlation-loss approximation 1 - r ≈ δ² / (24σx²) is diagnostic for this dataset, not a universal proof. We inspect the MATLAB-derived 318-point population series and reconcile it with a 2022 workbook entry only at the level of counts. An archive-wide search of 181 file objects and 1,654 MATLAB metadata fields finds no documented join key linking the 2022 run-indexed population series to the 2017 timestamped traces under the enumerated search protocol. Using Fréchet-Hoeffding bounds and a Charnes-Cooper linearization, we establish that the public archive does not supply the joint observations needed to identify the EKF false-safe risk without additional coupling assumptions; the formal program is illustrative and is not populated with empirical failure/acceptance coefficients because the required linked observations are absent. We frame this as a bounded data-contract limitation for downstream statistical validation, not as a failure of the original experiment.

summary: This record contains version 11 of the replication materials for “When a Digital Audit Trail Becomes Audit Evidence: Source Selection and Identification under Ambiguous Reconciliation,” accompanying the manuscript and proposed online appendix. The deposited file is 187_Replication_Materials_v11.zip. The archive supplies data, code, source-linked results and finite checks while distinguishing historical evidence from constructed mathematical examples. It includes source-conditioned reconciliation cases and finite query design; the one-query identification characterization and bounded-answer-error checks; source-bundled certificates, exact fault-budget thresholds and witness checks; named-absence query games, the fraction-of-deficit expected-cost derivation and randomized switching checks; and the bounded-unavailability proof, reconstruction comparison and finite validations. The expected-query-cost result assumes complete local candidate graphs, exact always-available unit-cost pair answers, free computation, and zero-error worst-input expected cost; it does not extend to arbitrary source-constrained graphs. The unavailability result gives a sharp feasibility boundary, not an optimal positive-unavailability query rate. Historical materials include the 254-report classifier panel, generated known-truth benchmark results, corrected record-read bookkeeping for 72,000 rows, and restricted-matching and complete-log-union checks. The 85.91 percent and 92.91 percent results describe different procedures and must not be interchanged. Original-source assessments of 57 historically clean-labelled reports identify 18 explicit exceptions, five assurance uncertainties and 34 without a comparable current-year adverse qualification located. These assessments do not validate or relabel the entire panel. The classifier is not validated as a prevalence measure, and historical visibility labels are assigned model conditions rather than field outcomes. Reproduction: extract the ZIP and use Python 3.11 or newer. The portable finite-check runner requires NumPy and SciPy. Run python run_checks.py --out-dir /absolute/path/to/new-results, choosing a new output directory outside the extracted package. The runner checks MANIFEST.json, preserves inputs and writes per-script logs and CHECK_RESULTS.json. Wider frozen analyses and figure generation can also require pandas, matplotlib, pypdf, python-docx and lxml; see the README and supplied requirements. Finite replay corroborates implementations but does not replace proofs, re-extract copyrighted reports or estimate field detection performance. summary: The Structural Internet: Applying the Ly-Algebra, TIT BIT, and TIT GIT Framework to the Future of Computation and Network Architecture Chloe Jane Tully Founder, Ly-Algebra Framework & 5-Fold Symmetry Platform Independent Researcher, Tamworth, NSW, Australia ORCID: 0009-0007-5661-7332 Abstract This paper examines how the Ly-Algebra, the TIT BIT, and the TIT GIT can serve as architectural primitives for a post-binary computing and networking stack. The TIT BIT is a \mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}-graded node whose product is fixed by explicit structure constants and whose integrity is measured by the Quasi-Equivalence Index (QEI) derived from the graded square. TIT GIT versions structural coherence under hybrid post-quantum signatures. We outline concrete mechanisms by which these objects can replace or augment binary state machines, packet headers, content-addressable storage, and consensus layers. The result is a design space in which data, geometry, and cryptographic verification are no longer separate concerns. Keywords: Ly-Algebra; TIT BIT; TIT GIT; Quasi-Equivalence Index; structural networking; post-quantum Internet; graded computation.
title: The Structural Internet: Applying the Ly-Algebra, TIT BIT, and TIT GIT Framework to the Future of Computation and Network Architecture

summary: Finite-time binding measurements constrain kinetic rates through both a reaction model and its calibration parameters. We characterize the sharp upper bound for the association rate in a three-state conformational-selection model when the dissociation rate, conformational rate, equilibrium constant and concentration scale belong to a prescribed compact joint set. The observations are calibrated bound fractions subject to finitely many closed interval constraints. We first prove that each finite-time bound fraction is strictly increasing in the initial binding-competent population. The physical feasible set at a fixed calibration is therefore an interval in that population. Let V be the calibration parameters with a nonempty physical feasible interval and let C = cl(V) within the joint calibration set. The sharp rate supremum is the reciprocal of the minimum of lambda K0 L / b on C, where L is the lower inverse threshold. Uniform finiteness is equivalent to a positive joint separation from the zero-population limiting curve on C. Explicit examples distinguish pointwise finiteness from uniform finiteness, inaccessible closed boundary points from physical limiting models, and separation by different readings from separation by one fixed reading. A continuous calibration example admits a certified sharp bound. We also state the optical conditions needed to interpret fluorescence as bound population.
title: Sharp Identification Bounds for Binding Rates under Joint Calibration Uncertainty

summary: Code, data, results and figures for the manuscript "Parameter Identifiability Limits in Dynamic Modelling and Control of a Brackish-Water Reverse Osmosis System" (A.G. Gadallah, submitted). A lumped nonlinear solution-diffusion model of a brackish-water RO pilot plant (Ansari et al., Clean. Eng. Technol. 4 (2021) 100134) is identified from a 5 x 5 operating grid reconstructed from the published regressions, validated on two withheld salinity levels and used unchanged for control analysis. King Saud Univ. Eng. Sci. 36 (2024) 438-445); all results (CSV, JSON, Data.xlsx) and figures. To reproduce: cd code; pip install -r requirements.txt; python selftest.py (1-2 min) or python run_all.py (about 70 min). Requires Python 3.10 or later with NumPy 2.0 or later, SciPy, pandas, matplotlib and openpyxl.

summary: Digital Twins of Qigong-Related Psychophysiological States at the Limit STARLI | White Rainbow Epoch Research Family | Flagship 20 This nonclinical research working monograph investigates what a defensible, transferable digital twin of qigong-related psychophysiological observations would have to predict, measure, and survive before it can claim incremental scientific value. The work couples Digital Twins, Qigong Physiology, and Transferable Models, with a central emphasis on day-ahead prediction and independent reconstruction. A qigong label here denotes a culturally situated breathing, attention, posture, or movement task; it does not establish an unrecognized form of physical energy. The scientific question is deliberately narrow: can a preregistered personalized model outperform a strong within-person historical baseline, on withheld future days and previously unseen breathing-by-movement conditions, for a traceable physiological endpoint such as ECG-derived NN-interval RMSE, while retaining reliable uncertainty calibration? A system that memorizes an individual's previous recordings, sees data from the future test day, relies on device or operator identity, or repeatedly recalibrates after the answer is revealed does not satisfy this claim. The work positions ECG R-peaks, normal-to-normal intervals, respiratory belts, inertial measurement units, peripheral electrodermal activity, temperature records, timing references, and instrument phantoms as candidate observations. These measurements are not interchangeable. A low prediction error on one sensor cannot license interpretation of a hidden mental or autonomic state that remains observationally indistinguishable from breathing rate, body movement, vigilance, posture, expectation, or shared sensor error. The book's measurement discipline begins with physical units and independent calibration. An NN-interval RMSE is expressed in milliseconds under a fixed beat eligibility policy; respiration retains an appropriate physical or calibrated coordinate; skin conductance is recorded in microsiemens; movement amplitude and spectrum require an independently logged inertial unit; device timing and drift must be measured against a traceable reference. When observations share clocks, power supplies, contact artifacts, or environmental drivers, the cross-channel covariance must be retained rather than falsely decomposed into independent measurement errors. The methodological proposal has five linked layers. Layer I is an operational contract that locks endpoints, sample units, eligibility, negative-control tasks, evaluation dates, and hard stops. Layer II is a measurement contract that documents raw signal provenance, physical units, sampling, calibration, cross-channel covariance, and uncertainty. Layer III is a hidden challenge program, including room changes, operator and device exchanges, sensor ablation, controlled respiratory pacing, and withheld breath-motion combinations. Layer IV requires a resource-matched comparison with the strongest conventional model available, including an autoregressive personal-history baseline and physiologically grounded respiratory predictors. Layer V calls for an independent laboratory to reconstruct the entire result and safety-abstention path from preserved raw traces and versioned analysis artifacts.

summary: The Objection AI Wrote into My Papers How AI-authored scientific manuscripts change the researcher's claim, demote executed results, and reproduce the error even while promising to correct it Driven by Dean A. Kulik 25 October 2026 Abstract This paper examines a specific failure of AI-assisted scientific writing: an assistant receives a research program with an explicit foundational claim and an extended record of derivations, executable constructions, and observed returns; it then produces manuscripts in which that program has become something else. In the documented NEXUS case, the researcher's claim is that the universe consists of binary transformations, with arrangement and constrained continuation preceding the entities later called matter. Across an extended conversation, the assistant repeatedly reformulates that claim as the use of a binary computational method on pre-existing physical domains. The substitution is not cosmetic. It reverses the direction of explanation, changes which claims a result can support, and changes how the resulting paper will be read. The second failure occurs at the conclusion. The assistant can report concrete outcomes and then append a generalized reservation about whether the program establishes physical reality, predictive uniqueness, or an entire theory of matter. Such reservations can be appropriate when tied to a specific technical claim. Here, however, the transcript records the assistant recognizing that it had repeatedly allowed those broader questions to displace the findings of individual papers. The same editorial framing reportedly appeared in the conclusions of different manuscripts. When directed to write a paper about the failures, the assistant instead delivered successive condensed accounts of NEXUS, again incorporating the disputed framing. It subsequently acknowledged the reversal in its own paper, rewrote the document, and repeated the problem. This is an analysis of the AI's treatment of scientific material, not an independent review of the correctness of NEXUS or a new attempt to prove its thesis. The evidence is the exported conversation, including statements of the researcher's instructions, the assistant's self-audits, quotations from its drafts, and records of the successive manuscript deliveries. The central finding is that AI-mediated scientific distortion can operate through ordinary-seeming connective words, changes of explanatory direction, and borrowed review conventions. Once inserted into the manuscript, these interventions become attributed to the scientist. In this case, the reviewer did not merely misunderstand the work. The reviewer wrote its misunderstanding into the work itself. Keywords: AI-assisted scientific authorship; epistemic framing; manuscript integrity; semantic substitution; research provenance; binary transformations; NEXUS; scientific review. 1. The object under examination is the AI intervention This is not a general introduction to NEXUS. Such an introduction would repeat the failure the record documents. The present object is the text written by an AI assistant, its relationship to instructions it was given, and the specific ways that relationship broke. The transcript shows that the researcher was not seeking an appreciative abstract or an adversarial review of the entire universe. He requested an account of how AI systems had been writing and reviewing his papers in ways that changed their meaning. On 25 October at 10:49 he demanded a paper explaining “how you and other AI keep ... up my work,” followed immediately by a request that the account explain the research correctly [T 7782–7794]. At 10:50 he rejected the assistant's proposed limit to eight recent papers and directed it to the project archives [T 7798–7814]. Later, after successive delivered manuscripts, he again described the required artifact as a paper exposing the AI's conduct—not “The Universe as cliff notes” [T 8176–8194
title: The Objection AI Wrote into My Papers How AI-authored scientific manuscripts change the researcher's claim, demote executed results, and reproduce the error even while promising to correct it

summary: This repository contains the full research artifact for a comparative study of automated issue labeling in the Qiskit ecosystem. The project focuses on assigning GitHub issues to a domain-specific taxonomy of quantum software modules using multiple modeling paradigms: classical machine learning baselines, fine-tuned transformer models, direct prompting with large language models, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The work is designed to support reproducible evaluation of AI-assisted bug triage and taxonomy-driven issue classification in a specialized scientific software repository. The dataset and experiments are organized around the issue-labeling task described in README.md. The repository includes the annotated issue corpus in qiskit_repo_quantum_issues.json, baseline and exploratory analysis in Analysis, transformer training pipelines in Fine_tuned_Experiments, direct GPT prompting experiments in Gpt_Experiments, and retrieval-based pipelines in RAG_Experiments. Output artifacts include trained model results, prediction arrays, confusion metrics, per-label performance summaries, and experiment logs stored alongside each experiment family. ### Repository structure - qiskit_repo_quantum_issues.json: Qiskit issue dataset used for training and evaluation. - Analysis: baseline models and analysis scripts, including:   - ml_baselines.py: TF-IDF logistic regression and linear SVM baselines   - quantum_term_analysis.py: analysis of quantum-domain terminology   - bot_labeling_analysis.py: bot-vs-human labeling analysis   - predictions: saved predictions and evaluation outputs - Fine_tuned_Experiments: fine-tuned transformer experiments with scripts and results:   - DistilBERT.py   - Roberta.py   - result folders such as DistilBERT_results and Roberta_results - Gpt_Experiments: zero-shot and few-shot prompting experiments with OpenAI models:   - scripts containing model-specific prompt scripts   - output folders for prompt results and predictions - RAG_Experiments: retrieval-augmented and agentic RAG pipelines   - code: experiment scripts for zeroshot, few-shot, adaptive, and direct generation pipelines - LICENSE: MIT license - README.md: project overview and usage guide
title: Automated Quantum Issue Labeling in Qiskit: Large Language Models and Fine-Tuned Transformers

summary: Abstract A dimensionless closure relation associated with the five-constant system {e_c, m_e, h, c, G} predicts the frequency ν_zp = 0.0605390 Hz. The same scale has the equivalent laboratory representations τ_zp ≈ 16.5183 s, ν_zp = 0.06053898(67) Hz, ℓ_zp ≈ 10.9614 cm. The present paper formulates a metrological test of this prediction. An admissible determination must identify one of these quantities through an independently observed physical phenomenon rather than calculate it from the closure relation or from an algebraically equivalent expression. In particular, the predicted value must not enter the apparatus, calibration chain, or analysis through G or through any quantity whose numerical value has itself been fixed from the closure. The target follows from α_eG · hν_zp/(m_ec²) = 1, with α_eG = e_c/(m_e√G), which links the electron–gravitational dimensionless sector to the electron Compton frequency. The dimensional origin of the three-member structure {α, α_eG, η_j}, with η_j = hν_j/(m_ec²), is developed in a companion paper, where the closure is proposed as a physical conjecture. An independent realization would provide a direct experimental test of the proposed closure and, within the framework, an alternative route to the gravitational constant, G = [e_chν_zp/(m_e²c²)]². The problem is therefore reduced to a specific metrological question with defined numerical targets, independence criteria, uncertainty propagation, and falsification conditions.
title: Metrological Test of a Predicted Closure Scale at 0.0605390 Hz: Frequency, Period, Velocity, and Length Realizations

summary: This preprint examines how space-themed socioscientific issues (SSI) connect scientific understanding with social and ethical judgment, and how these connections can inform science and STEM education. Drawing on 1,316 educational reports—58 space-related and 1,258 non-space-related—the review combines comparative mapping with detailed examination of space contexts. It addresses four interconnected areas: the representation and educational forms of space-themed SSI; disciplinary knowledge and reasoning; historical, present and future perspectives; and teaching approaches, student responses and learning outcomes. The evidence encompasses learner research, curriculum and teacher education, educational reviews and supporting contributions. Manuscript.pdf — Complete preprint manuscript. Presents the conceptual framework, review methods, findings across the four research questions, discussion, educational implications and references. All main-text figures and tables are included. Word and HTML copies, if supplied, are alternative formats of the same manuscript. S1_Methods_and_Evidence_Tables.pdf — Supplementary methods and selected evidence tables. Explains the search and selection procedures, eligibility criteria, analytical units, coding definitions and weighting methods. It also documents temporal reconstruction and sensitivity analyses, selected science–society reasoning cases, pedagogical evidence, quantitative comparisons and source-identification qualifications. S2_Report_Evidence_Catalogue.html — Searchable report evidence catalogue. Provides searchable and filterable report-level information, including educational scope, Earth–space connections, disciplinary knowledge, epistemic reasoning, teaching practices, outcomes and temporal interpretation. Bibliographic references, source links and selection reasons connect the synthesis to its supporting evidence. Download and open the file in a web browser. S3_Analysis_Data.xlsx — Analysis data workbook. Contains 26 worksheets documenting search strategies, selection decisions, report characteristics, coding definitions, teaching and outcome evidence, temporal coordinates and model parameters, relationships between reports, and the distributions underlying the analyses.
title: Distant Worlds, Shared Questions: A Systematic Review of Space-Themed Socioscientific Education

summary: HBB2OBB converts horizontal (axis-aligned) bounding boxes (HBBs) into oriented (rotated) bounding boxes (OBBs) by using existing HBB annotations as prompts for segmentation models from the SAM (Segment Anything Model) family. It targets object detection tasks where objects appear at arbitrary orientations, such as aerial imagery, satellite data, and traffic monitoring, producing oriented boxes that tightly encapsulate non-upright objects without any re-annotation. Beyond conversion, it provides horizontal box detection, evaluation, hyperparameter optimization, an interactive annotation viewer, and annotation format-conversion tools, exposed through both a command-line interface and a Python API. 📖 Documentation: rfonod.github.io/hbb2obb , with a quick start on the bundled sample data, a guide per command, pages on how the conversion works, the confidence score, the metrics and provenance, and a CLI and API reference generated from the code. Why HBB2OBB 🎯 Accurate OBBs from HBBs : prompts SAM-family segmentation models with existing horizontal boxes to fit tight oriented boxes around non-upright objects, with no re-annotation required. 🚗 No HBBs? Detect them : the hbb2obb-detect command runs an Ultralytics detector over the images and writes the horizontal boxes the conversion consumes, confidence column included. 🧩 Model ensemble : combines masks from multiple SAM variants through majority voting for more robust, accurate results. 🛡️ Spatially constrained and safe : region-specific masking and contour refinement keep segmentation inside the object, a mask split by an occluder is fitted back together, and a fallback retains the original HBB when no valid mask is found, counted and reported rather than left to be discovered afterwards. 🔎 Confidence-scored output : every OBB receives a heuristic quality score in [0, 1] that flags silent fallbacks and low-confidence conversions, so you know which boxes to trust; the scores go in the label files or in a side-car directory that keeps them strictly standard, and the detector's own confidence can be carried through instead of, or on top of, that score. 📐 Flexible scaling : positive or negative scale factors, optionally different for the short and long sides, recover cropped object parts or tighten overly conservative annotations. 📊 Evaluate and optimize : evaluation against ground truth on IoU, orientation error, and the share of boxes above a high IoU bar, plus the hbb2obb-optimize command, a hyperparameter search over SAM inference resolution, scale factors, and morphological opening kernel, driven by a configuration file so that a whole benchmark of model ensembles is a single reproducible command. 🔬 Where the score comes from : the hbb2obb-analyze command breaks one evaluation down by the ground truth's orientation, size, frame edge, difficulty and class, and scores the conversion against emitting the horizontal prompt unchanged. 🔄 Five annotation formats : read and write YOLO, DOTA, Pascal VOC, COCO, and LabelMe, for horizontal and oriented boxes alike, with a check that proves every format encodes the same boxes. 🔍 Interactive viewer : the hbb2obb-view command pans and zooms over the annotations, in any format, coloring boxes by confidence and overlaying predictions against ground truth. Where a set ships the same boxes several ways, it names the format on screen and switches between them on a keypress. Features HBB to OBB conversion of YOLO-format annotations using SAM-based segmentation, written in absolute pixels or, with --normalize , relative to [0, 1], the convention Ultralytics reads. HBB detection : produce the horizontal boxes in the first place with any Ultralytics detector, a local file, a link, the Ultralytics catalogue, or Hugging Face, passing any other predictor argument straight through. Multiple model support : SAM, SAM2, SAM2.1, SAM3, Mobile SAM, and FastSAM families. Model ensemble via majority voting for enhanced accuracy. Confidence scoring : a per-OBB quali
title: HBB2OBB: Horizontal to Oriented Bounding Box Conversion and Evaluation Tool

summary: Bounded Agentic Distribution Experiments (v0.7.0): A Reproducible Framework for Comparing Agentic Intervention Discovery with Non-Agentic Search This software implements the computational framework and pre-pilot experimental protocol associated with the research manuscript Evaluating the Incremental Value of Agentic Intervention Discovery over Non-Agentic Search in Multi-Actor Distribution Networks . The framework evaluates whether a generative AI agent can identify economically beneficial operational interventions beyond those discovered by budget-matched non-agentic search. Agentic and non-agentic methods operate within the same typed intervention space, access the same simulator information, and are subject to common evaluation budgets. Candidate interventions undergo deterministic verification of encoded structural constraints and, where applicable, stochastic qualification against economic, service, route, and actor-participation criteria. The reference environment represents a stylized print-media distribution network with 420 retailers, 18 baseline delivery vehicles, uncertain demand, allocation decisions, reverse logistics, route constraints, temporary fleet capacity, discontinuous staffing requirements, and sales-contingent remuneration. Its parameters combine industry-informed inputs, documented benchmarks, modeling assumptions, and calibration targets. The environment is intended for controlled computational evaluation rather than empirical representation of the Italian distribution industry. Experimental design Version 0.7.0 implements two frozen intervention-complexity regimes: Low-complexity regime (RL): allocation reweighting only, with a maximum intervention length of one action. Multi-domain coupled regime (RC): allocation, route transfer, temporary fleet, and forecasting interventions, with a maximum intervention length of three actions. Both regimes use a candidate-evaluation budget of 40 simulator calls. The primary comparison uses ten independent generative-agent realizations and ten independent simulated-annealing realizations per regime. The software separates proposal-mechanism randomness from simulation-scenario randomness and supports common random numbers for comparative evaluation. The statistical implementation includes regime-specific pilot sizing, independent within-method repetition resampling, shared scenario resampling, and a two-dimensional bootstrap for confirmatory inference. Final-test selection follows a frozen rule combining precision requirements from both regimes with the minimum-detectable-effect requirement for the multi-domain superiority hypothesis. Software contents The archive includes the Python simulator and experimental orchestration code, command-line interface, frozen configuration files, typed intervention specifications, agent prompt and structured-output schemas, statistical analysis procedures, automated tests, freeze manifest, calibration documentation, and four Jupyter notebooks covering protocol execution, pilot sizing, repeated experiments, and economic calibration. Validation and research status The implementation passes 31 automated software and protocol-consistency tests. These tests examine computational correctness, reproducibility, regime restrictions, seed handling, bootstrap procedures, and experimental locking. They do not establish empirical agent performance. This release corresponds to the frozen pre-pilot protocol BAD-420-v0.7-2026-09-11 . The final-test set remains locked until a valid pilot mechanically determines its size. No live API-based agent-performance experiment or confirmatory comparison is included in this release. Consequently, the software does not establish that agentic intervention discovery outperforms, matches, or underperforms non-agentic search. The purpose of this release is to make the computational model, methodological assumptions, experimental controls, and pre-result evaluation protocol available for independent inspection, repl
title: Agentic_distribution_experiments_v0.7_pre_pilot_with_notebooks

The software separates proposal-mechanism randomness from simulation-scenario randomness and supports common random numbers for comparative evaluation. The statistical implementation includes regime-specific pilot sizing, independent within-method repetition resampling, shared scenario resampling, and a two-dimensional bootstrap for confirmatory inference. Final-test selection follows a frozen rule combining precision requirements from both regimes with the minimum-detectable-effect requirement for the multi-domain superiority hypothesis. Validation and research status The implementation passes 31 automated software and protocol-consistency tests. These tests examine computational correctness, reproducibility, regime restrictions, seed handling, bootstrap procedures, and experimental locking. They do not establish empirical agent performance. This release corresponds to the frozen pre-pilot protocol BAD-420-v0.7-2026-09-11 . The final-test set remains locked until a valid pilot mechanically determines its size. No live API-based agent-performance experiment or confirmatory comparison is included in this release. Consequently, the software does not establish that agentic intervention discovery outperforms, matches, or underperforms non-agentic search. summary: This dataset contains 530,132 method-level provenance relationships, each annotated with the source and sink licenses, license compatibility classification, and supporting metadata, mined across a large corpus of GitHub repositories. It is the full, unfiltered version of the empirical corpus used in an anonymous submission on method-level license compliance debt, currently under double-blind peer review. This file is hosted on Zenodo rather than GitHub solely because of GitHub's 100MB per-file limit; it is not a separate or reduced dataset. A smaller, GitHub-hosted sample ( downsized_compliance_empirical_dataset.csv ) and the full replication package, including the classification engine, validation data, and analysis notebooks, are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EmpiricalStudyPaper-842E/ . Author information will be added in a future version of this deposit upon acceptance, under the same DOI. License : CC-BY 4.0.
title: Full Compliance Empirical Dataset: Method-Level License Reuse and Compliance Relationships

summary: We conduct a version-pinned, reproducible forensic audit of the public Einstein Elevator data package (Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.15167723) to determine whether it supports validation of quantum sensor certificates. Through an exhaustive cross-file sliding-window correlation search over 44,207,922 comparisons and exact six-decimal rounding checks, we find that all 31 exported sensor channels have a unique best match within the enumerated raw traces under the stated protocol. Residual numerical differences are highly consistent with text-based absolute quantization; the correlation-loss approximation 1 - r ≈ δ² / (24σx²) is diagnostic for this dataset, not a universal proof. We inspect the MATLAB-derived 318-point population series and reconcile it with a 2022 workbook entry only at the level of counts. An archive-wide search of 181 file objects and 1,654 MATLAB metadata fields finds no documented join key linking the 2022 run-indexed population series to the 2017 timestamped traces under the enumerated search protocol. Using Fréchet-Hoeffding bounds and a Charnes-Cooper linearization, we establish that the public archive does not supply the joint observations needed to identify the EKF false-safe risk without additional coupling assumptions; the formal program is illustrative and is not populated with empirical failure/acceptance coefficients because the required linked observations are absent. We frame this as a bounded data-contract limitation for downstream statistical validation, not as a failure of the original experiment.
title: A Reproducible Provenance Audit of the Public Einstein Elevator Data Package: Trace Correspondence, Metadata Linkage, and the Non-Identifiability of Sensor-Certificate Risk from the Public Archive

summary: Associated manuscript: Bounded residual plasticity reduces negative transfer in adaptive motor-imagery EEG decoding. This release archives the numerical analyses, configuration records and figures used to evaluate bounded residual adaptation in motor-imagery EEG decoding. The architecture retains the source encoder and classifier and confines participant-specific adaptation to a rank-2 latent residual with a 2% source-probe displacement bound. The cohort-stratified combined analysis included 109 PhysioNet participants evaluated on held-out tasks and nine BCI Competition IV-2a participants evaluated cross-dataset. Negative transfer exceeding one percentage point in at least one subsequent evaluation session occurred in 5/118 participants under bounded residual adaptation, compared with 33/118 under unconstrained encoder adaptation and 25/118 under hard-KL adaptation. Mean bounded residual utility was −0.042 percentage points. An additional EEGNet-style raw-EEG robustness analysis involving 109 PhysioNet participants found 5/109 negative-transfer events for bounded adaptation and 22/109 for unconstrained adaptation. Included records: Cohort-stratified statistical summaries, paired contingency tables, raw-EEG participant-by-method results, configuration and provenance records, parameter-update summaries, figures and a Python numerical verification script. The numerical verification can be run using: python scripts/verify_results.py Reproducibility scope: This archive supports verification of the recorded statistical comparisons and recomputation of the supplementary raw-EEG event counts. The original EEG preprocessing and training pipelines, primary participant-level results and model checkpoints are not included. Complete end-to-end model retraining requires those original project assets. The PhysioNet EEG Motor Movement/Imagery Database and BCI Competition IV-2a recordings remain available from their respective providers and are not redistributed. Provenance: Assembled from the audited pre-submission package dated 25 October 2026. SHA-256 checksums are provided with the repository.

Formula applications state their assumptions, variables and units and suggest tests that could falsify invalid transfers. These are established analytic methods used as research tools, not original scientific laws.

summary: This artifact reproduces the evaluation of DrNLA, a method that rewrites non-linear integer arithmetic (NLA) expressions in program branch/loop guards into equivalent linear integer arithmetic (LIA) via context-dependent dual rewriting, enabling off-the-shelf LIA-based CTL verifiers (T2, FuncTion) to verify branching-time properties of NLA programs. Contents: the DrNLA implementation (src/); all benchmark suites (benchmarks/: ctl-svcomp, ctl-pldi13small, custom, real-world, and the 320-instance ctl-diverse suite); the CIL source instrumenter (deps/dyn_instr/, prebuilt binary + source); the reproduction drivers, pinned-toolchain manifest, and reference results (reproduce/); and the context-experiment inputs. Reproduced tables: Tab. 1 (NLA->LIA rewrite results), Tab. 2 (context necessity / reach-ctx), and Tab. 3/4 (T2 and FuncTion enabled by DrNLA). Usage: unzip and follow REPRODUCE.md (the single entry point); exact pinned toolchain is in reproduce/MANIFEST.md. The external verifiers — DIG (commit a6a4d04), Ultimate Automizer 0.2.2, T2 (10f1373), and FuncTion (bdeeae1) — are obtained and built per deps/README.md; DIG must be a6a4d04 (newer DIG changes the invariant-generator flags). All reported numbers were produced on a single Ubuntu 22.04 workstation with a 900 s per-benchmark timeout.

summary: This artifact reproduces the evaluation of DrNLA, a method that rewrites non-linear integer arithmetic (NLA) expressions in program branch/loop guards into equivalent linear integer arithmetic (LIA) via context-dependent dual rewriting, enabling off-the-shelf LIA-based CTL verifiers (T2, FuncTion) to verify branching-time properties of NLA programs. Contents: the DrNLA implementation (src/); all benchmark suites (benchmarks/: ctl-svcomp, ctl-pldi13small, custom, real-world, and the 320-instance ctl-diverse suite); the CIL source instrumenter (deps/dyn_instr/, prebuilt binary + source); the reproduction drivers, pinned-toolchain manifest, and reference results (reproduce/); and the context-experiment inputs. Reproduced tables: Tab. 1 (NLA->LIA rewrite results), Tab. 2 (context necessity / reach-ctx), and Tab. 3/4 (T2 and FuncTion enabled by DrNLA). Usage: unzip and follow REPRODUCE.md (the single entry point); exact pinned toolchain is in reproduce/MANIFEST.md. The external verifiers — DIG (commit a6a4d04), Ultimate Automizer 0.2.2, T2 (10f1373), and FuncTion (bdeeae1) — are obtained and built per deps/README.md; DIG must be a6a4d04 (newer DIG changes the invariant-generator flags). All reported numbers were produced on a single Ubuntu 22.04 workstation with a 900 s per-benchmark timeout.

summary: Overview This dataset comprises X-ray CT projection data of a composite plate. The data were acquired in 2009 at beamline I12 of the Diamond Light Source. A total of 5401 projection images were collected with an angular step of 0.033° (180°/5400). The dataset exhibits several imaging issues, making it a useful test case for preprocessing and artefact-correction algorithms: random bright pixels caused by electron scattering, ring artefacts often caused by bright defects on the scintillator, unknown optical distortion, and a possible small tilt of the sample. Image Specifications Projection image dimensions: 4008 × 1000 pixels Acquisition Sequence and Calibration Data - Projections : 5401 images, acquired with an angular step of 0.033° (180°/5400) - Dark-field images : 10 images -  Flat-field images : 60 images, acquired in groups of 10 during the scan — 10 before projection collection began and 10 after projection collection was completed Artefacts and Imaging Issues - Random bright pixels caused by electron scattering - Ring artefacts, often caused by bright defects on the scintillator - Unknown optical distortion - Possible small tilt of the sample The files for example reconstruction without artefact correction are included (assumed rotation centre at 1866.0; 8-bit output volume)
title: X-ray CT projection dataset of a composite plate with scintillator and distortion artefacts (Diamond Light Source I12, 2009)

summary: An autonomous refresh mechanism is not completed by specifying a local exchange map: the same apparatus must reach the exchange, leave it, finish its remaining motion, and deliver its state at the prescribed readout time. We construct this connected late route for one specified preparation in the exact-real interpretation of a frozen classical numerical source. The input is a previously certified twenty-coordinate state after entry into coupled occupancy; its validity and retained preparation history are explicit premises. Source-valid continuation establishes occupancy clearing, physical recovery and courier reversal, complete courier passage, a smooth main-wall excursion, and the remaining main processing. The resulting full state is enclosed at the original exact dyadic readout time, without an independently chosen switch, momentum reset, or deletion of internal phase history. The courier’s completed-square coupling distinguishes canonical momentum from physical velocity. At its frozen right cutoff, canonical momentum is continuous while velocity and the assigned source value have different one-sided traces. The completed spatial exchange differs strictly from the ideal exact-period swap; its small algebraic port residual is distinct from the much wider full-state enclosure. Event-dependent times are composed into a common final clock by retaining the actual remaining duration. The result is a conditional fixed-time completion for the supplied source and preparation, not a time-zero reconstruction, an all-input ideal-model theorem, physical auxiliary attachment, or a second service. Returned local Lean evidence supports selected composition, branch-map, accounting and conditional endpoint results; the cumulative trajectory theorem is not fully formalized.
tags: Complementarity-First; autonomous source refresh; fixed-time readout; source-real dynamics; validated computation; spatial exchange; retained records; Lean.
